blocks: Amplitude Modulation: Sidebands and Transmitted Power is a core model in Communication Systems: AM carries information by letting the message scale a carrier's amplitude, and the power bookkeeping shows why the scheme is wasteful: most energy ships in the information-free carrier. The model is used within these stated limits: Single-tone modulation at index m; m above 1 overmodulates, distorting envelope detection and splattering adjacent channels.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: combined sideband power - the information-carrying part
Single-tone modulation at index m; m above 1 overmodulates, distorting envelope detection and splattering adjacent channels.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Multiplying a carrier by (1 + m cos omega_m t) and expanding with the product-to-sum identity produces exactly three sinusoids: the carrier plus two sidebands at the carrier frequency shifted by +/- the message frequency. Squaring each term for power gives P_c for the carrier and m^2 P_c / 4 per sideband - so at full modulation m = 1 the two information-bearing sidebands together carry only one third of the total power. That arithmetic is the whole story of AM's inefficiency, and the reason suppressed-carrier schemes (DSB-SC, SSB) exist wherever power matters more than receiver simplicity.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A 10 kW carrier is amplitude-modulated at m = 0.8. Find total transmitted power and the share carrying information.
13.2 kW transmitted; only about a quarter of it carries the message - even at m = 1 the share would be just 33%.

blocks: Heating into the austenite region dissolves carbon and resets the microstructural clock; what happens next is entirely cooling rate, as the TTT/CCT maps dictate. Furnace cooling gives the equilibrium-soft coarse pearlite of full annealing - the state for machining and cold forming. Air cooling (normalizing) refines the pearlite, homogenizes cast or forged structures and raises strength modestly. Quenching traps martensite - hard but too brittle and stressed to use - so tempering follows: reheating to moderate temperature lets carbon precipitate as fine carbides, deliberately trading some hardness for toughness and relieving stress. The trio (quench, temper, and the anneal/normalize pretreatments) is the full vocabulary of steel's mechanical tailoring.

Normalize -> machine -> quench & temper -> surface harden: each step exists because cooling rate, not chemistry, is the control variable.

blocks: Arrhenius Kinetics: Activation Energy and Temperature Sensitivity is a core model in Chemical Reaction Engineering: Reaction rates climb exponentially with temperature, and the activation energy sets the steepness - high-Ea reactions are temperature levers, low-Ea ones are not. The model is used within these stated limits: Elementary or lumped reactions over moderate temperature ranges; A and E_a are fitted constants, and the exponential form is why a 10 K rise can double or triple a rate.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Elementary or lumped reactions over moderate temperature ranges; A and E_a are fitted constants, and the exponential form is why a 10 K rise can double or triple a rate.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Only molecular encounters with energy above the barrier E_a react, and the Boltzmann factor e^(-E_a/RT) is precisely that fraction - so the rate constant is the encounter frequency A times the fraction energetic enough. Taking ratios cancels A and exposes the sensitivity: the same 10 K step multiplies the rate far more for a high-Ea reaction than a low-Ea one. This single fact organizes reactor operation: temperature is the fastest handle on rate and selectivity (parallel reactions with different Ea split products differently with temperature), and runaway safety analysis is this exponential read against cooling capacity that grows only linearly.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A reaction has E_a = 80 kJ/mol. How much does its rate constant rise from 300 K to 310 K?
A 10 K rise nearly triples the rate - and the same step on a 40 kJ/mol reaction would give only about 1.7x, the Ea leverage made visible.

Assumes the metric is a fair load proxy and roughly balanced across replicas; scale-down needs a stabilization window or the loop oscillates.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: If the fleet should hold each replica at U_target, then total measured load divided by U_target is the replica count that would achieve it - the ceiling covers indivisible machines. The autoscaler runs this as a feedback loop each period: add replicas on sustained overshoot, remove on sustained undershoot. Control-loop discipline matters: instant scale-down on a momentary dip causes flapping, so production loops average the metric over a window and cool down between actions - the same stability reasoning that gives thermostats hysteresis.

blocks: B-Tree Indexes: Fan-Out and Logarithmic Search is a core model in Database Management Systems: An index is a search structure shaped for disks: each node holds many keys so the tree stays shallow, and height - not key count - decides how many block reads a lookup costs. The model is used within these stated limits: Worst case assumes every node only half full (the B-tree guarantee after splits); real trees sit well under the bound because nodes average ~69% full.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Worst case assumes every node only half full (the B-tree guarantee after splits); real trees sit well under the bound because nodes average ~69% full.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Disk reads cost milliseconds, so the design goal is few levels: pack m-1 keys and m child pointers per block-sized node. A B-tree keeps every leaf at the same depth and forces nodes to stay at least half full on split, which caps the height logarithmically in n with base m/2. Searching descends by binary-searching inside each node and following one child pointer - one block read per level. With m = 100 the base is 50, so millions of keys cost three or four reads: this is why indexed lookups 'feel constant' while full scans grow linearly.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: An index of order 100 covers n = 1,000,000 keys. Bound the worst-case block reads.
Apply the height bound with half-full nodes.
Minimum fan-out is ceil(100/2) = 50. Levels below the root hold at least 50, 50^2 = 2,500, 50^3 = 125,000, 50^4 = 6,250,000 keys - so root plus 4 levels suffice, and typical trees are shallower.
At most about 5 block reads worst case, typically 3-4, versus 1,000,000 row reads for a scan.

blocks: Bandwidth-Delay Product and Window Sizing is a core model in Computer Networks: A transport window that is smaller than the path's bandwidth-delay product wastes the link: throughput becomes window divided by round-trip time, whatever the capacity says. The model is used within these stated limits: One bottleneck link, no packet loss, no queueing beyond the bottleneck, and acknowledgements that return promptly. Loss or a small receive buffer reduces the achievable rate further.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Bandwidth-delay product and the resulting throughput ceiling
bandwidth-delay product: bytes in flight to keep a pipe full
send and receive window actually available
One bottleneck link, no packet loss, no queueing beyond the bottleneck, and acknowledgements that return promptly. Loss or a small receive buffer reduces the achievable rate further.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: With a window of W unacknowledged bytes, the sender can keep at most W bytes on the wire. After one round trip the earliest data is acknowledged and the window slides, so the pipeline repeats every RTT: the sustained rate is W/RTT. If W/RTT is below the link capacity C, the link spends part of every round trip idle and the sender, not the network, is the bottleneck. Setting W equal to C times RTT puts exactly one round trip's worth of data in flight, which is the smallest window that keeps the pipe full. This is why a long path with a small window behaves like a slow link even when the provider's capacity is high.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A 1 Gbit/s path has a 40 ms round trip and a 1 MB window. What throughput results, and what window would saturate the path?
Convert bytes to bits, divide the window by the RTT, then compare with the capacity.
A 1 MB window is 8 x 10^6 bits, so throughput = 8 x 10^6 / 0.04 = 2 x 10^8 bit/s. BDP = 10^9 x 0.04 = 4 x 10^7 bits = 5 MB.
200 Mbit/s, one fifth of the path. A window of at least 5 MB is needed to reach 1 Gbit/s, which requires window scaling since the base TCP header field caps the window at 65,535 bytes.
What throughput does the unassisted 16-bit TCP window allow on a path with a 40 ms round trip?
Take the largest window the header can express and divide by the RTT.
About 13.1 Mbit/s. Window scaling with a factor of 128 lifts the ceiling above the RTT-limited requirement, and a 5 MB window then reaches the 1 Gbit/s capacity.

blocks: Banker's Algorithm and Safe Sequences is a core model in Operating Systems: Deadlock avoidance grants a request only if the system can still prove a completion order exists for every process with the resources left over. The model is used within these stated limits: Requires processes to declare maximum claims up front and resources to be non-preemptible and countable - the assumptions real systems usually refuse, which is why kernels prefer detection over avoidance.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Need=Max-Alloc; safe if ∃ order with Need_i≤Work ∀ i
available plus recoverable resources in the trial order

Requires processes to declare maximum claims up front and resources to be non-preemptible and countable - the assumptions real systems usually refuse, which is why kernels prefer detection over avoidance.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Model the worst case: every process will one day demand its full Max. A state is safe if some sequence exists in which each process, when its turn comes, can be satisfied from Work plus everything earlier processes return on completion. The algorithm simulates: find a process whose Need fits Work, pretend to run it, add its Alloc back to Work, repeat. If all processes finish in the simulation, grant the request; if no process can proceed, the state is unsafe and the request must wait - unsafe is not yet deadlocked, but deadlock-avoidance refuses to gamble.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: One resource type, 12 units. Processes A, B, C hold 4, 3, 2 with Max 8, 5, 4. Available = 3. Is the state safe?
Compute Need, then search for a completion order.
Need = Max - Alloc: A needs 4, B needs 2, C needs 2. B fits (2 <= 3): run B, Work = 3 + 3 = 6. C fits (2 <= 6): Work = 6 + 2 = 8. A fits (4 <= 8): Work = 12.
Safe, with sequence <B, C, A>. If A's request for one more unit made Need-order unsatisfiable, the Banker would delay it.

blocks: The unit weight is geometry: a round bar's cross-section pi d^2/4 times steel's density simplifies, with d in millimetres, to the memorable d^2/162 kilograms per metre. blocks: Bayes' Theorem and the Base-Rate Trap is a core model in Engineering Mathematics II: A test result is not a diagnosis: the probability that a positive result means what you think it means depends on how common the condition is, and the arithmetic is unforgiving when it is rare. The model is used within these stated limits: A clearly defined condition and test, a prevalence that applies to the population being tested, and independence between repeat tests. Screening a low-prevalence population changes the answer dramatically.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Posterior probability of a condition given a positive test
sensitivity: probability of a positive result when the condition is present
false positive rate: one minus specificity

A clearly defined condition and test, a prevalence that applies to the population being tested, and independence between repeat tests. Screening a low-prevalence population changes the answer dramatically.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Bayes' theorem is bookkeeping on a two-by-two table: the probability of a true positive is the sensitivity multiplied by the prevalence, the probability of a false positive is the false positive rate multiplied by the complement of the prevalence, and the posterior is the first divided by their sum. The reason the result surprises people is that the base rate enters as a multiplier, so when the condition is rare the false positives from the large healthy population can easily outnumber the true positives from the small affected one. The practical lesson generalises well beyond medicine, to spam filters, fault detection and fraud alerts: a highly accurate test applied to a rare event still produces mostly false alarms, which is why two-stage testing and confirmation are built into any real detection system.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A condition affects 1 % of a population. A test is 95 % sensitive and 90 % specific. What is the probability that a positive result is a true positive?
Compute the true positive and false positive contributions, then form the ratio.
True positive contribution = 0.95 x 0.01 = 0.0095. False positive contribution = 0.10 x 0.99 = 0.099. Posterior = 0.0095/(0.0095 + 0.099) = 0.0095/0.1085 = 0.0876.
Only about 8.8 %: eleven of every twelve positives are false alarms, because the healthy population is a hundred times larger.
The test's specificity improves to 99 %. What is the posterior now?
Recompute with a false positive rate of 0.01.
About 49 %, still a coin flip: at a 1 % prevalence, specificity has to be extremely high before a positive result is more likely true than false.

blocks: Bending Stress and Section Modulus is a core model in Strength of Materials: A beam's fibres stretch and compress linearly through its depth, so bending stress peaks at the extreme fibre and the section modulus packages the geometry that resists it. The model is used within these stated limits: Linear-elastic material, pure bending of a prismatic symmetric section; plane sections remain plane, and shear deformation is neglected.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Linear-elastic material, pure bending of a prismatic symmetric section; plane sections remain plane, and shear deformation is neglected.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: With plane sections staying plane, longitudinal strain varies linearly with distance from the neutral axis, and Hooke's law carries that linearity into stress. Equilibrium then fixes the two unknowns: the axial-force balance places the neutral axis at the centroid, and the moment balance gives sigma = My/I, where I is the second moment of area - the geometric stiffness. Collecting I/y_max into the section modulus Z makes design a one-step check: sigma_max = M/Z versus allowable stress, and I-shapes win because they park most material at large y where the stress lives.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A rectangular beam 100 mm wide, 200 mm deep carries a moment of 10 kN m. Find the maximum bending stress.
Compute I for the rectangle, then apply the flexure formula.
15 MPa at the extreme fibres - and doubling the depth to 400 mm would quarter the stress, since I grows as h^3.

blocks: Start with Euler's equation for inviscid flow along a streamline:
For an incompressible fluid the density is constant, so every term is an exact differential and can be integrated directly between two points on the same streamline:
p_1 + \frac{1}{2}\rho v_1^2 + \rho g h_1 = p_2 + \frac{1}{2}\rho v_2^2 + \rho g h_2
Dividing throughout by rho*g expresses the same statement in metres of head, which is how it is used in hydraulic engineering.

blocks: Water flows through a horizontal pipe that narrows from 100 mm to 50 mm diameter. The pressure in the wide section is 200 kPa and the velocity is 2 m/s. Find the pressure in the narrow section.
Use continuity to find the velocity in the narrow section, then apply Bernoulli between the two sections (horizontal, so the elevation terms cancel).
A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2 \Rightarrow v_2 = v_1 \left(\frac{d_1}{d_2}\right)^2 = 2 \times \left(\frac{100}{50}\right)^2 = 8\ \text{m/s}

blocks: Bias-Variance Decomposition and Model Selection is a core model in Machine Learning: Prediction error splits into squared bias, variance and irreducible noise, and the split explains why bigger models can test worse: they trade bias for variance. The model is used within these stated limits: Decomposition holds for squared loss; the noise term is beyond any model's reach, so the only controllable trade is bias against variance.

blocks: Write the error against the model's average over training sets, adding and subtracting that average. Expanding the square produces three surviving terms: how far the average model sits from the truth (bias squared), how much individual fits scatter around their own average (variance), and the data noise. Flexible models have small bias - they can reach the truth - but fit each sample's noise differently, so variance grows; rigid models do the opposite. The test-error minimum sits at the balance point, which is what regularization and cross-validation search for.

blocks: Big-O Reasoning for Loops and Nested Loops is a core model in Programming Fundamentals: Counting how often the inner statement executes as input grows is all that is needed to classify most everyday code - nesting multiplies, sequence adds. The model is used within these stated limits: Counts growth, not seconds; constants and lower-order terms are dropped, which is accurate for large n and misleading for tiny n.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Counts growth, not seconds; constants and lower-order terms are dropped, which is accurate for large n and misleading for tiny n.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Trace the innermost statement's execution count as a function of n. One loop over n items executes it n times; a second loop nested inside multiplies by another n; loops in sequence add. Big-O keeps only the fastest-growing term because as n doubles, that term eventually dominates every constant factor - which is exactly why an O(n^2) report script that feels instant at n = 100 crawls at n = 100,000.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A report scans all pairs of 500 orders to find duplicates. How many pair comparisons run, and what does doubling to 1,000 orders do?
Apply T(n) = n^2 (or n(n-1)/2 for distinct pairs).
Distinct pairs = 500 x 499 / 2 = 124,750. At n = 1,000: 1,000 x 999 / 2 = 499,500 - four times the work, not two.
About 125 thousand comparisons, quadrupling to about 500 thousand - the O(n^2) signature.

blocks: For an n-bit pattern, the unsigned value is the sum of b_i 2^i. The two's complement value of the same pattern is -b_{n-1} 2^{n-1} plus the remaining unsigned bits. The range is -2^{n-1} to 2^{n-1}-1.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: signed value of the bit pattern
Fixed width. A carry out of bit n-1 is discarded, not stored.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Start from the unsigned sum and move the weight of the top bit from +2^{n-1} to -2^{n-1}. That single sign change is the definition. To negate a value x, compute (2^n - x) mod 2^n. Inverting the bits gives (2^n - 1 - x); adding one gives 2^n - x. The 2^n term falls off the end of an n-bit adder, which is why invert-and-add-one works.

Databases use B-trees and B+ trees rather than binary ones. A B+ tree node holds hundreds of keys, so the tree is three or four levels deep for a billion rows — and since each level is typically one disk page, that is three or four I/O operations. A binary tree of the same size would be about thirty levels deep, which is thirty page reads. Node fan-out, not comparison count, is what matters when storage is involved.

blocks: Trees are how hierarchical data is stored, and the traversal order usually encodes meaning rather than being an implementation detail.

A compiler walks its abstract syntax tree in post-order to evaluate: children first, then the operator. The same order is used by expression evaluators and by build systems resolving dependencies. Pre-order is the natural choice for serialising a tree, because the root appears before its children, so a reader can rebuild the structure in one pass. Level-order is what a DOM renderer uses to paint parent containers before children.
File systems are trees with hard links making them general graphs, which is why
need cycle detection. The DOM, JSON documents and XML are all trees, which is why XPath and CSS selectors are tree queries.

The traversal choice is also a performance decision: a recursive traversal needs stack depth proportional to tree height, so on a degenerate tree of a million nodes it will overflow. Production parsers iterate with an explicit stack for exactly that reason.

blocks: Bioreactor Scale-Up: Constant Power per Volume is a core model in Bioprocess Engineering: Geometric scale-up multiplies volume by the cube of the size ratio, so no operating variable survives unchanged - the scale-up criterion chooses which physics to hold constant, and mixing power per volume is the usual vote. The model is used within these stated limits: Geometrically similar vessels in the turbulent regime; constant P/V preserves mixing and kLa tendency but lowers tip speed and shear - other criteria (constant tip speed, constant kLa) favor different products.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: impeller power, proportional to N^3 D^5

Geometrically similar vessels in the turbulent regime; constant P/V preserves mixing and kLa tendency but lowers tip speed and shear - other criteria (constant tip speed, constant kLa) favor different products.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Rushton-turbine power scales as N^3 D^5 while volume scales as D^3, so power per volume scales as N^3 D^2. Demanding P/V stay constant while D grows forces N down as D^(-2/3) - the big tank turns slower. That single choice cascades: kLa roughly holds (good for aerobic cultures), but tip speed pi N D rises only mildly while shear per passage falls, and mixing time lengthens. Shear-sensitive cells want constant tip speed (even slower N); filamentous fungi sometimes want constant mixing time. There is no neutral scale-up - the criterion embeds a theory of what limits the process, which is why pilot plants exist between the formulas and the production vessel.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A 0.5 m pilot vessel runs at 200 rpm. Its production counterpart is geometrically similar at 2 m diameter. Find the production speed under constant P/V.
About 79 rpm - 64 times the volume at 40% of the speed, with power per volume (and roughly kLa) preserved by design.

blocks: Blanking Force and Die Clearance is a core model in Manufacturing Processes: Punching a shape out of sheet needs a press whose force covers the whole cut perimeter at once, and a clearance between punch and die set as a fraction of sheet thickness. The model is used within these stated limits: The whole perimeter is sheared simultaneously, the shear strength is taken from the material data sheet, and the press rating must also cover stripping and friction. Clearance values depend on material ductility, with harder sheet needing slightly more.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: ultimate shear strength of the sheet

The whole perimeter is sheared simultaneously, the shear strength is taken from the material data sheet, and the press rating must also cover stripping and friction. Clearance values depend on material ductility, with harder sheet needing slightly more.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: The punch pushes through the sheet only after every point on the perimeter has exceeded the material's shear strength, so the force is the perimeter multiplied by thickness - the sheared area - times that strength. Because the multiplication is linear in both geometry and strength, the arithmetic is quick, and the result usually surprises: a small increase in perimeter from a more elaborate profile raises the required press tonnage proportionally. The clearance between punch and die decides whether the cut is clean: enough clearance lets the fracture zones from both sides meet, too little causes secondary shearing and a torn edge, too much causes a ragged burr. The clearance rule sets it as a few percent of thickness, which is why tooling for thin sheet is made to tolerances an order of magnitude finer than the sheet itself.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A 400 mm perimeter is blanked from 2 mm sheet with a shear strength of 300 MPa. Find the force and the clearance per side at 5 %.
Multiply perimeter by thickness by strength; take the clearance as a fraction of thickness.
F = 400 x 2 x 300 = 240,000 N = 240 kN. Clearance = 0.05 x 2 = 0.1 mm per side, 0.2 mm total.
240 kN of shearing force, so a press rated above 250 kN with allowance for stripping, and a punch-die gap of 0.1 mm per side.
The same part is made from 3 mm sheet of the same strength. What happens to the force?
360 kN, a 50 % increase for a 50 % thicker sheet, which may push the job onto a larger press and change the clearance to 0.15 mm per side.

blocks: Blasting Design: Powder Factor, Burden and Fragmentation is a core model in Mine Planning & Operations: A production blast is engineered rock-breaking: burden and spacing set the broken volume per hole, and the powder factor prices the energy that fragments it. The model is used within these stated limits: Hard-rock bench blasting with a single free face; subdrilling, stemming and decking refine the basic pattern, and PF is compared across sites at equal energy, not equal mass.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: burden (to free face) and spacing (between holes)
powder factor - explosive mass (or energy) per volume broken
Hard-rock bench blasting with a single free face; subdrilling, stemming and decking refine the basic pattern, and PF is compared across sites at equal energy, not equal mass.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Each hole breaks the rock burden in front of it across its spacing and down the bench - the B x S x H block. The explosive charge must deliver enough energy per cubic metre of that block to fracture it to the target size: too little leaves boulders and toes, too much wastes money, generates oversize flyrock and over-crushes into fines the mill did not ask for. The powder factor - typically 0.3-0.6 kg/m^3 in hard rock - is the single number comparing patterns, and the burden is the first variable tuned when rock hardness or the fragmentation target changes, because it directly sets both volume per hole and the confinement the shock wave works against.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A 10 m bench is drilled on a 3 m burden and 3.5 m spacing. Find the volume per hole and the charge for a 0.5 kg/m^3 powder factor.
Compute the broken block, then scale by the powder factor.
V_hole = 3 x 3.5 x 10 = 105 m^3. Charge = 0.5 x 105 = 52.5 kg of explosive per hole.
105 m^3 per hole at 52.5 kg of explosive - tightening the burden to 2.75 m would drop the block to 96 m^3 and refine fragmentation at slightly more drilling per tonne.

standard.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Each hole breaks the rock burden in front of it across its spacing and down the bench - the B x S x H block. The explosive charge must deliver enough energy per cubic metre of that block to fracture it to the target size: too little leaves boulders and toes, too much wastes money, generates oversize flyrock and over-crushes into fines the mill did not ask for. The powder factor - typically 0.3-0.6 kg/m^3 in hard rock - is the single number comparing patterns, and the burden is the first variable tuned when rock hardness or the fragmentation target changes, because it directly sets both volume per hole and the confinement the shock wave works against.

blocks: A 10 m bench is drilled on a 3 m burden and 3.5 m spacing. Find the volume per hole and the charge for a 0.5 kg/m^3 powder factor.
Compute the broken block, then scale by the powder factor.
V_hole = 3 x 3.5 x 10 = 105 m^3. Charge = 0.5 x 105 = 52.5 kg of explosive per hole.
105 m^3 per hole at 52.5 kg of explosive - tightening the burden to 2.75 m would drop the block to 96 m^3 and refine fragmentation at slightly more drilling per tonne.

blocks: Bolted Joints: Preload and Load Sharing is a core model in Machine Design: A properly preloaded bolted joint makes the clamped members absorb most of the external load - the bolt only feels the stiffness fraction, and the joint never separates. The model is used within these stated limits: Joint remains in compression (F_ext below the separation load F_i/(1-C)); bolt and members act as springs in series-parallel around the load path.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Joint stiffness factor and bolt load
fraction of external load the bolt additionally carries
Joint remains in compression (F_ext below the separation load F_i/(1-C)); bolt and members act as springs in series-parallel around the load path.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Tightening stores the bolt in tension and the clamped parts in compression - two springs preloaded against each other. When an external tensile load arrives it partly relaxes the member compression and partly stretches the bolt further, in proportion to their stiffnesses: soft bolt, stiff members means C is small (typically 0.2-0.3) and the bolt barely notices the external load. That is the whole secret of preloading: high F_i keeps the interface clamped (no slip, no fretting, no fatigue-prone load swing in the bolt), while the members - not the bolt - carry the working load. Overload separation, not bolt breakage, is the failure the preload prevents.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A joint has k_b = 1 MN/mm and k_m = 4 MN/mm, preloaded to 20 kN, under 10 kN external tension. Find the bolt load and check separation.
Compute C, then the bolt load and separation margin.
C = 1/(1+4) = 0.2. F_b = 20 + 0.2 x 10 = 22 kN. Separation needs F_ext > F_i/(1-C) = 20/0.8 = 25 kN - the 10 kN load is well inside.
The bolt carries 22 kN while the members absorb 8 kN of the external load; the interface stays clamped with 2.5x separation margin.

industry.title: Real-world applications

blocks: Karnaugh maps are how a human minimises a small logic function, and automated tools took over everything larger.

The map is practical up to about four or five variables. Beyond that it stops being something a person can see, and synthesis tools — Espresso, and the logic minimisation inside every FPGA toolchain — handle functions with thousands of terms. So the skill matters for understanding what the tool does and for small glue logic, not for designing a processor.

What still matters in real design is hazard avoidance, which the map makes visible. Two adjacent product terms that differ in one variable can produce a brief glitch as the signal propagates, because the paths have different delays. Adding a redundant term that covers the overlap removes the hazard. In combinational logic feeding a clock, such a glitch can be latched and become a real fault — which is why the extra term is sometimes worth the gate.

In FPGAs the picture changes again. Logic is mapped onto lookup tables of four or six inputs, so minimisation in the classical sense matters less than how the function packs into those tables. The synthesis tool optimises for table count and routing, which is not the same objective as gate count.

The practical warnings: don't hand-minimise a function you are going to describe in HDL — write the behaviour and let the tool work; do use the map when debugging why a combinational output glitches; and remember that Gray-code ordering and edge wraparound are what make the map work, since binary ordering would break the adjacency the whole method depends on.

blocks: Karnaugh maps are how a human minimises a small logic function, and automated tools took over everything larger.

The map is practical up to about four or five variables. Beyond that it stops being something a person can see, and synthesis tools — Espresso, and the logic minimisation inside every FPGA toolchain — handle functions with thousands of terms. So the skill matters for understanding what the tool does and for small glue logic, not for designing a processor.

What still matters in real design is hazard avoidance, which the map makes visible. Two adjacent product terms that differ in one variable can produce a brief glitch as the signal propagates, because the paths have different delays. Adding a redundant term that covers the overlap removes the hazard. In combinational logic feeding a clock, such a glitch can be latched and become a real fault — which is why the extra term is sometimes worth the gate.

In FPGAs the picture changes again. Logic is mapped onto lookup tables of four or six inputs, so minimisation in the classical sense matters less than how the function packs into those tables. The synthesis tool optimises for table count and routing, which is not the same objective as gate count.

The practical warnings: don't hand-minimise a function you are going to describe in HDL — write the behaviour and let the tool work; do use the map when debugging why a combinational output glitches; and remember that Gray-code ordering and edge wraparound are what make the map work, since binary ordering would break the adjacency the whole method depends on.

blocks: Boost Converter Design: Duty, Inductor Ripple and Output Ripple is a core model in Power Electronics: A boost converter's duty ratio sets its voltage ratio, its inductor sets the current ripple and its capacitor sets the output ripple - three numbers that can be chosen independently. The model is used within these stated limits: Continuous conduction mode with an ideal switch and diode, negligible equivalent series resistance, and a steady-state duty ratio. Parasitic elements and the diode drop reduce the achievable ratio.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: inductor current and output voltage ripple
Continuous conduction mode with an ideal switch and diode, negligible equivalent series resistance, and a steady-state duty ratio. Parasitic elements and the diode drop reduce the achievable ratio.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: During the switch-on interval the inductor is connected across the input and stores energy; when the switch opens, the inductor's voltage adds to the input and forces current into the output through the diode. Setting the average inductor voltage to zero over a cycle - the volt-second balance that steady state demands - gives the duty ratio as a function of the voltage ratio, and the same balance gives the ripple in terms of the applied voltage, the inductance and the frequency. The output capacitor supplies the load while the diode is off, so its ripple follows from the load current, the duty ratio and the capacitance. The three relations separate cleanly, which is what makes the topology easy to design: choose L for acceptable ripple current, choose C for acceptable ripple voltage, and choose the switching frequency to trade component size against switching loss.

With a 2 A load and a 100 microfarad output capacitor, what is the output voltage ripple?
Apply the capacitor ripple relation with the duty ratio already found.
0.1 V peak to peak, which for a 24 V output is about 0.4 %; doubling the capacitor would halve it, at the cost of size and inrush current.

blocks: Buffers and the Henderson-Hasselbalch Equation is a core model in Engineering Chemistry: A buffer resists pH change because it contains both members of an acid-base pair, and the ratio of their concentrations sets where it holds. The model is used within these stated limits: A weak acid and its conjugate base in dilute aqueous solution at a temperature near 25 degrees C, with concentrations well above the dissociation constant so the equilibrium approximations hold. Ionic strength shifts pKa slightly.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: negative logarithm of the acid dissociation constant

A weak acid and its conjugate base in dilute aqueous solution at a temperature near 25 degrees C, with concentrations well above the dissociation constant so the equilibrium approximations hold. Ionic strength shifts pKa slightly.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: The dissociation equilibrium of a weak acid fixes the ratio of the two species to the hydrogen ion concentration, and taking logarithms turns that relation into a linear one in pH: the pH is the acid's pKa when the two species are equal, and it moves by one unit for each tenfold change in their ratio. That is why a buffer holds pH best when the ratio is close to one and why its useful range is about one pH unit either side of the pKa. Buffer capacity - the amount of acid or base the solution can absorb before the pH moves appreciably - grows with the total concentration of the pair, so a buffered system is designed by choosing a pair with the right pKa and then choosing how much of it to use.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: An acetate buffer has a pKa of 4.76 and equal concentrations of acetic acid and sodium acetate. What is its pH, and what happens to the pH when the ratio becomes ten to one?
The logarithm is zero at equal concentrations and one at a tenfold ratio.
At equal concentrations the pH is 4.76. At a ten-to-one ratio the pH is 4.76 + log(10) = 5.76.
pH 4.76 at the midpoint, rising by a full unit at a tenfold ratio, which is why the practical buffering range is narrow.
A litre of the equimolar acetate buffer contains 0.1 mol of each species. What is the pH after adding 0.01 mol of strong acid, compared with adding it to pure water?
The acid converts base into acid form, so recompute the ratio; in pure water the strong acid sets the pH directly.
The buffer now has 0.11 mol of acid form and 0.09 mol of base form, so pH = 4.76 + log(0.09/0.11) = 4.76 - 0.087 = 4.67. In pure water, 0.01 mol in a litre gives pH 2.
4.67 against 2.00: the buffer absorbed the addition with a 0.09 unit change, which is the entire purpose of a buffer.

standard.title: Formula and variables

blocks: The dissociation equilibrium of a weak acid fixes the ratio of the two species to the hydrogen ion concentration, and taking logarithms turns that relation into a linear one in pH: the pH is the acid's pKa when the two species are equal, and it moves by one unit for each tenfold change in their ratio. That is why a buffer holds pH best when the ratio is close to one and why its useful range is about one pH unit either side of the pKa. Buffer capacity - the amount of acid or base the solution can absorb before the pH moves appreciably - grows with the total concentration of the pair, so a buffered system is designed by choosing a pair with the right pKa and then choosing how much of it to use.
standard.title: Derivation

blocks: An acetate buffer has a pKa of 4.76 and equal concentrations of acetic acid and sodium acetate. What is its pH, and what happens to the pH when the ratio becomes ten to one?
The logarithm is zero at equal concentrations and one at a tenfold ratio.
At equal concentrations the pH is 4.76. At a ten-to-one ratio the pH is 4.76 + log(10) = 5.76.
pH 4.76 at the midpoint, rising by a full unit at a tenfold ratio, which is why the practical buffering range is narrow.
A litre of the equimolar acetate buffer contains 0.1 mol of each species. What is the pH after adding 0.01 mol of strong acid, compared with adding it to pure water?
The acid converts base into acid form, so recompute the ratio; in pure water the strong acid sets the pH directly.
The buffer now has 0.11 mol of acid form and 0.09 mol of base form, so pH = 4.76 + log(0.09/0.11) = 4.76 - 0.087 = 4.67. In pure water, 0.01 mol in a litre gives pH 2.
4.67 against 2.00: the buffer absorbed the addition with a 0.09 unit change, which is the entire purpose of a buffer.

blocks: A response's Cache-Control tells every cache along the path how long the body may be served without asking. After that window, the copy is stale but not useless: the client revalidates by sending the stored ETag in If-None-Match. If the resource is unchanged the origin answers 304 with headers and no body - a few hundred bytes confirming that a cached megabyte is still current. Correct header design therefore cuts both latency and egress cost, and getting it wrong either serves stale data too long or revalidates every click.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A 45 KB JSON asset carries max-age 300 and an ETag. A client fetches it again after 420 s. Describe the exchange and its cost.
Compare age with freshness, then revalidate.

Age 420 > 300, so the copy is stale: the client sends If-None-Match. The server's current ETag matches, so it replies 304 with no body. Transfer: a few hundred bytes instead of 45 KB, and the cache's freshness timer restarts.
One conditional round-trip, ~2% of the original payload - correctness of the ETag, not guesswork about change frequency, does the saving.

industry.title: Real-world applications

blocks: The concepts generalize past the CPU cache, and that is where they are usually applied in application work.

Application-level caching is the same trade-off with different numbers. A Redis lookup is microseconds versus milliseconds for a database round trip, so the hit rate decides the cost. The invalidation problem is the hard part: a cache that can serve stale data must either expire entries or be told when the underlying data changes, and the second is where most cache bugs live.

Database buffer pools are caches over pages, and their hit rate is the single best predictor of query latency. A working set that fits in the pool runs entirely in memory; one that does not turns every query into disk I/O. This is why memory sizing for a database is about working-set size rather than total data size.

CDNs are caches at the network layer, with the same invalidation problem at a much larger scale — which is why cache-busting filenames and short TTLs on HTML with long TTLs on hashed assets is the standard pattern.

The unifying lesson is that every cache introduces a second copy of the truth and a window in which they disagree. The design question is never whether to cache but how long the disagreement is acceptable, and what happens when it is detected.

blocks: Capacity Requirements from Demand, Work Content and OEE is a core model in Production Planning & Control: Capacity planning is arithmetic on three numbers: how much work a part needs, how many parts are wanted, and what fraction of the available time the equipment is actually productive. The model is used within these stated limits: One product or a stable mix, planned time excluding breaks and planned maintenance, and an OEE measured rather than assumed. Mixed models need the work content weighted by mix, and shared equipment needs a load profile by period.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: planned production time per machine per period
overall equipment effectiveness: availability x performance x quality

One product or a stable mix, planned time excluding breaks and planned maintenance, and an OEE measured rather than assumed. Mixed models need the work content weighted by mix, and shared equipment needs a load profile by period.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Demand multiplied by work content gives the hours of work the period requires, and each machine contributes only the fraction of its planned hours it is actually productive, so dividing required hours by effective hours per machine gives the machine count. The reason to multiply rather than add the three OEE components is that they compound: a machine available 90 % of the time, running 85 % of its rated speed and passing 99 % quality gives 0.757, so nearly a quarter of the available hours are lost before any scheduling happens. This is also why improving the weakest OEE component pays: the product is what any improvement multiplies.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A cell must make 480 parts in an 8 hour shift with 4.5 minutes of work content each and an OEE of 0.75. How many machines are needed?
Convert the work content to hours, multiply by demand, then divide by effective hours per machine.
Work required = 480 x 0.075 h = 36 machine-hours. Effective hours per machine = 8 x 0.75 = 6 h. n = 36/6 = 6.
Six machines, with no spare capacity for a demand increase or an unplanned breakdown.
OEE improves to 0.85. What happens to the required machine count, and what if demand then rises 20 percent?
Recompute effective hours at the new OEE, then reapply the same formula to the higher demand.
Effective hours = 8 x 0.85 = 6.8 h, so n = 36/6.8 = 5.3, rounding to 6 machines. At 20 % more demand: work required = 43.2 h, so n = 43.2/6.8 = 6.35.
The same six machines now run with headroom, and a twenty percent demand increase needs a seventh machine or a further OEE improvement.

blocks: Carnot Efficiency and the Reversible Limit is a core model in Engineering Thermodynamics: No engine between two temperatures can beat the Carnot fraction, so the second law hands every heat engine a ceiling computed from temperatures alone. The model is used within these stated limits: Temperatures must be absolute; the bound applies to engines exchanging heat with two reservoirs, and real engines fall below it through irreversibilities.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Temperatures must be absolute; the bound applies to engines exchanging heat with two reservoirs, and real engines fall below it through irreversibilities.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: A reversible engine's entropy intake at T_H must be rejected at T_C with no net entropy creation, forcing Q_C/Q_H = T_C/T_H. Efficiency is work over heat input, 1 - Q_C/Q_H, which becomes 1 - T_C/T_H. Any irreversibility creates entropy, which demands extra heat rejection at the cold end, so every real engine sits below the bound. The engineering reading: efficiency improves by raising T_H (materials permitting) or lowering T_C (ambient permitting) - and the gap between actual and Carnot efficiency is the second-law efficiency, the honest measure of how well a machine uses its temperature window.

blocks: Carrier Transport: Drift and Diffusion Currents is a core model in Electronic Devices & Circuits: Current in a semiconductor flows two ways - carriers pushed by an electric field and carriers spreading down their own concentration gradient - and junctions run on both at once. The model is used within these stated limits: Low-field regime where mobility is constant; D and mu are tied by the Einstein relation D = (kT/q) mu, about 0.026 V x mu at room temperature.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: J_drift=q n μ E, J_diff=q D (dn)/(dx)
Low-field regime where mobility is constant; D and mu are tied by the Einstein relation D = (kT/q) mu, about 0.026 V x mu at room temperature.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Drift is Ohm's law at the particle level: each carrier averages a velocity mu E, and n carriers per volume each carrying q give the current density. Diffusion needs no field at all - random thermal motion moves more carriers out of crowded regions than into them, producing a net flow down the gradient. Inside a PN junction both act simultaneously: the built-in field drives carriers one way while concentration gradients diffuse them the other, and equilibrium is exactly the balance of these two currents - the same balance, with the Einstein relation substituted, that yields the diode equation.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: n-type silicon has n = 1e16 cm^-3, electron mobility 1000 cm^2/(V s), and a field of 100 V/cm. Find the drift current density.
Multiply charge, concentration, mobility and field.

blocks: Casting: Chvorinov's Rule and Riser Design is a core model in Manufacturing Processes: Solidification time scales with the square of a casting's volume-to-surface ratio - the rule that decides riser size, placement and whether a casting shrinks sound or porous. The model is used within these stated limits: Same mould conditions for casting and riser; the riser must solidify later than the casting it feeds, and exothermic sleeves effectively raise the riser's B.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: mould constant (mould material, metal, pouring temperature)
Same mould conditions for casting and riser; the riser must solidify later than the casting it feeds, and exothermic sleeves effectively raise the riser's B.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Heat leaving the casting must pass through the mould wall; more volume stores more latent and sensible heat, while more surface area drains it faster. Dimensionally the time combines as (V/A)^2 times a mould constant B that experiments determine. Feed metal for solidification shrinkage flows from the riser only while the riser is still liquid, so the design rule is direct: the riser's (V/A)^2 must exceed the casting's - typically 1.2x or more in time. A sphere is the slowest-cooling shape for its volume, which is why risers are squat cylinders approaching it, and why thin sections freeze first and stop feeding paths.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A plate casting has V = 1000 cm^3 and A = 600 cm^2 with B = 2 min/cm^2. What solidification time must the riser beat, and does a riser with V/A = 2.5 cm qualify?
Compute both times with Chvorinov's rule.
Casting: V/A = 1.667 cm, t_s = 2 x 1.667^2 = 5.6 min. Riser: t_s = 2 x 2.5^2 = 12.5 min.
Riser solidifies in 12.5 min versus the casting's 5.6 - it stays liquid long enough to feed shrinkage throughout.

Same mould conditions for casting and riser; the riser must solidify later than the casting it feeds, and exothermic sleeves effectively raise the riser's B.
standard.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Heat leaving the casting must pass through the mould wall; more volume stores more latent and sensible heat, while more surface area drains it faster. Dimensionally the time combines as (V/A)^2 times a mould constant B that experiments determine. Feed metal for solidification shrinkage flows from the riser only while the riser is still liquid, so the design rule is direct: the riser's (V/A)^2 must exceed the casting's - typically 1.2x or more in time. A sphere is the slowest-cooling shape for its volume, which is why risers are squat cylinders approaching it, and why thin sections freeze first and stop feeding paths.

blocks: A plate casting has V = 1000 cm^3 and A = 600 cm^2 with B = 2 min/cm^2. What solidification time must the riser beat, and does a riser with V/A = 2.5 cm qualify?
Compute both times with Chvorinov's rule.
Casting: V/A = 1.667 cm, t_s = 2 x 1.667^2 = 5.6 min. Riser: t_s = 2 x 2.5^2 = 12.5 min.
Riser solidifies in 12.5 min versus the casting's 5.6 - it stays liquid long enough to feed shrinkage throughout.

blocks: Clausius-Clapeyron Equation and Vapour Pressure is a core model in Chemical Engineering Thermodynamics: Vapour pressure rises exponentially with temperature, and the Clausius-Clapeyron relation quantifies the climb from one known point plus the heat of vaporization. The model is used within these stated limits: Constant Delta H_vap over the range and ideal vapour - fair over tens of kelvin, poor across phase-diagram extremes; it is the same equation behind the Arrhenius plot's shape.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: vapour pressures at the two temperatures
enthalpy of vaporization, ~40.7 kJ/mol for water
Constant Delta H_vap over the range and ideal vapour - fair over tens of kelvin, poor across phase-diagram extremes; it is the same equation behind the Arrhenius plot's shape.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Clapeyron's exact slope dP/dT = Delta H / (T Delta V) simplifies for a liquid-vapour line: the vapour volume dwarfs the liquid's, and ideal-gas substitution turns the slope into d(ln P)/d(1/T) = -Delta H/R. Integrating between two states gives the working form - a straight line of ln P against 1/T whose slope carries the heat of vaporization. The exponential in temperature is why boilers gain so much from pressure, why high-altitude cooking slows (water boils at 90 C on a 3000 m ridge), and why Antoine-table data can be extrapolated a short distance with confidence.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: Water boils at 373 K under 101.325 kPa with Delta H_vap = 40.7 kJ/mol. Estimate its boiling pressure at 363 K.
About 70.5 kPa (steam tables: 70.1) - the estimate is within half a percent over a 10 K span.

blocks: CMOS Inverter Switching Threshold and Noise Margins is a core model in VLSI Design: The inverter's switching point is where both transistors saturate and their currents match; sizing the pair sets that point, and the transfer curve's shape sets the noise margins. The model is used within these stated limits: Long-channel matching argument; hole mobility being ~2-3x lower than electrons means equal W/L does NOT give equal k - PMOS is widened to reach V_M = V_DD/2.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: input voltage where output crosses input
unity-gain points of the transfer curve
Long-channel matching argument; hole mobility being ~2-3x lower than electrons means equal W/L does NOT give equal k - PMOS is widened to reach V_M = V_DD/2.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: At the switching threshold both devices conduct in saturation with V_in = V_out, so their currents must be equal: setting the two square-law currents equal solves for V_M, which lands mid-supply exactly when the drive factors match. Because electron mobility dominates, a minimum-size PMOS is weaker and V_M droops low - digital designers widen the PMOS (typically 2-3x) to restore the midpoint and balanced rise/fall. Noise margins then read off the transfer curve at its unity-gain points: the flatter the transition, the wider the margins, and ratioed logic (skewed sizing) deliberately trades one margin for the other.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A 3.3 V inverter uses equal drive strengths. Estimate V_M and typical symmetric margins if V_IH = 2.1 V and V_IL = 1.2 V.
Apply the threshold rule and margin definitions.
Matched drives give V_M = 3.3/2 = 1.65 V. NM_H = 3.3 - 2.1 = 1.2 V; NM_L = 1.2 - 0 = 1.2 V.
V_M = 1.65 V with 1.2 V margins both sides - and a process corner that shifts V_M by 0.3 V still leaves 0.9 V of usable margin.

blocks: CNC Interpolation: Linear and Circular Toolpaths is a core model in CAD / CAM: An interpolator turns a programmed path and feed rate into synchronized axis commands, so the tool tip traces the geometry at exactly the surface speed the process needs. The model is used within these stated limits: Continuous-path (G01/G02/G03) interpolation; rapid moves (G00) do not guarantee a straight line, and axis acceleration limits bend corners unless the look-ahead slows them.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Feed decomposition along a linear move
programmed feed rate along the path
individual axis velocities the interpolator commands
Continuous-path (G01/G02/G03) interpolation; rapid moves (G00) do not guarantee a straight line, and axis acceleration limits bend corners unless the look-ahead slows them.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: The path geometry (a line between points, an arc by centre and direction) and the feed rate are the program; the machine only knows axis positions. The interpolator subdivides the path into tiny time slices - computing each axis's share of the path vector so the resultant tip speed equals F - and streams position commands at the servo rate. Circular interpolation does the same along an arc parameterized by angle. The engineering consequences are visible in the G-code: a 3-4-5 triangle move at F = 100 splits into 60 and 80 mm/min axis feeds, corner dwell appears when one axis saturates, and lookahead smoothing exists because axes cannot instantly redirect at full feed.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A G01 move goes X+30, Y+40 at F = 100 mm/min. Find the path length, time, and each axis's velocity.
Decompose the feed along the path vector.
50 mm in 30 seconds with axes synchronized at 60 and 80 mm/min - the tip speed stays exactly 100 mm/min throughout.

blocks: Collision Resistance and the Birthday Bound is a core model in Cryptography & Network Security: The security level of a hash is not its output size: collisions are found in about the square root of the output space, so a 256-bit digest is a 128-bit commitment. The model is used within these stated limits: The hash behaves as a random function, outputs are independent and uniformly distributed, and the attacker can store or recompute candidate values. Chosen-prefix attacks and structural weaknesses are excluded.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Birthday-bound work factor for finding a collision
expected number of evaluations to find a collision
the constant sqrt(pi/2) for a 50 % success probability

The hash behaves as a random function, outputs are independent and uniformly distributed, and the attacker can store or recompute candidate values. Chosen-prefix attacks and structural weaknesses are excluded.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: If k values are drawn uniformly from a space of size N, the probability that all are distinct falls as 1 minus the exponential of minus k squared over two N. Setting that probability to one half and solving for k gives k approximately 1.177 times the square root of N; counting the work for a 50 % chance with the standard constant gives about 1.253 times root N, which is the familiar two to the n over two. The consequence is a factor-two loss of security level compared with preimage resistance: finding a specific preimage still costs two to the n, while finding any pair that collides costs about two to the n over two. Truncation is therefore not a free optimisation, and short digests must never be treated as identities.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: An attacker can evaluate 10^12 hashes per second. How long does a collision attack on SHA-256 take?
Use 2^128 as the expected work, then divide by the rate and by the seconds in a year.
2^128 = 3.4 x 10^38 evaluations. At 10^12 per second that is 3.4 x 10^26 seconds; a year is about 3.15 x 10^7 seconds, so the time is 1.1 x 10^19 years.
About 10^19 years. A preimage attack would cost 2^256, which is astronomically more; the practical statement is that SHA-256 is safe against both for the foreseeable future.
A system stores 64-bit truncated hashes as file identities. How much work is needed to forge a collision?
Apply the birthday bound with n = 64.
Work is about 2^32 = 4.3 x 10^9 evaluations, which is minutes to hours on commodity hardware.
A 64-bit digest provides roughly 32 bits of collision resistance and is unusable as an identity, however strong the underlying function is.

blocks: Combined Loading: Principal Stresses and the von Mises Criterion is a core model in Strength of Materials: A component under simultaneous bending, torsion and axial load fails according to a criterion applied to a single equivalent stress, and both the principal stresses and that equivalent are computed from the same three numbers. The model is used within these stated limits: Plane stress, isotropic linear-elastic material, and stresses at a point after stress concentration factors are applied. Ductile materials are assessed with the von Mises criterion, brittle ones with a maximum normal stress criterion.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Principal stresses and the von Mises equivalent for plane stress

Plane stress, isotropic linear-elastic material, and stresses at a point after stress concentration factors are applied. Ductile materials are assessed with the von Mises criterion, brittle ones with a maximum normal stress criterion.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Any state of plane stress can be rotated to an orientation where the shear vanishes, and the two normal stresses in that orientation are the principal stresses; the Mohr circle shows them as the centre plus or minus the radius, which is what the first relation expresses. A failure criterion needs to condense that pair back into one number comparable with a tensile test, and the von Mises equivalent does so by combining the principal stresses with the energy of distortion - the part of the strain energy that changes shape rather than volume. For a shaft under bending and torsion the result is that an equivalent stress slightly above the larger principal stress governs, and the safety factor is the yield strength divided by that equivalent.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A point carries 100 MPa tension in x, 20 MPa tension in y and 30 MPa shear. Find the principal stresses and the von Mises equivalent.
Apply the principal-stress relation, then combine the pair with the von Mises expression.

Centre = (100 + 20)/2 = 60 MPa; radius = sqrt(40^2 + 30^2) = 50 MPa, so sigma 1 = 110 MPa and sigma 2 = 10 MPa. Von Mises = sqrt(110^2 - 110 x 10 + 10^2) = sqrt(12,100 - 1,100 + 100) = sqrt(11,100) = 105.4 MPa.
Principal stresses 110 and 10 MPa, equivalent stress 105.4 MPa. Against a 250 MPa yield the safety factor is 2.37.
The same point is assessed with the maximum shear stress criterion. What is the safety factor against a 250 MPa yield?
Maximum shear stress is the circle radius, and the allowable shear for a ductile material is taken as half the tensile yield.
Radius = 50 MPa, allowable shear = 250/2 = 125 MPa, so the safety factor is 125/50 = 2.5.
2.5 by maximum shear stress against 2.37 by von Mises, which is the expected ordering: Tresca is the more conservative criterion.

Centre = (100 + 20)/2 = 60 MPa; radius = sqrt(40^2 + 30^2) = 50 MPa, so sigma 1 = 110 MPa and sigma 2 = 10 MPa. Von Mises = sqrt(110^2 - 110 x 10 + 10^2) = sqrt(12,100 - 1,100 + 100) = sqrt(11,100) = 105.4 MPa.
Principal stresses 110 and 10 MPa, equivalent stress 105.4 MPa. Against a 250 MPa yield the safety factor is 2.37.
The same point is assessed with the maximum shear stress criterion. What is the safety factor against a 250 MPa yield?
Maximum shear stress is the circle radius, and the allowable shear for a ductile material is taken as half the tensile yield.

blocks: Principal stresses and the von Mises equivalent for plane stress

Plane stress, isotropic linear-elastic material, and stresses at a point after stress concentration factors are applied. Ductile materials are assessed with the von Mises criterion, brittle ones with a maximum normal stress criterion.
standard.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Any state of plane stress can be rotated to an orientation where the shear vanishes, and the two normal stresses in that orientation are the principal stresses; the Mohr circle shows them as the centre plus or minus the radius, which is what the first relation expresses. A failure criterion needs to condense that pair back into one number comparable with a tensile test, and the von Mises equivalent does so by combining the principal stresses with the energy of distortion - the part of the strain energy that changes shape rather than volume. For a shaft under bending and torsion the result is that an equivalent stress slightly above the larger principal stress governs, and the safety factor is the yield strength divided by that equivalent.

The model is used within these stated limits: Complete combustion; each fuel's theoretical air comes from its elemental balance (C to CO2, H to H2O, S to SO2), and air carries 21% O2 by mole.

mol or kg per fuel unit
the measurement excess air shows up as
Complete combustion; each fuel's theoretical air comes from its elemental balance (C to CO2, H to H2O, S to SO2), and air carries 21% O2 by mole.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Balance the fuel's elements against oxygen: methane needs two O2 per molecule, which is 2/0.21 = 9.52 moles of air. Actual furnaces run more - excess air guarantees the oxygen finds every fuel molecule despite imperfect mixing. The percentage excess is the controlled variable because it trades two losses: too little leaves unburnt fuel (chemical loss, smoke, CO); too much heats surplus nitrogen and oxygen straight up the stack (dry flue-gas loss). Flue-gas oxygen readings convert directly to excess air, which is why the O2 analyzer is the combustion-controller's primary instrument.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A furnace burns methane with 20% excess air. Find the air supplied per mole of fuel and the flue-gas composition's oxygen content basis.
Balance the stoichiometric reaction, then add the excess.

CH4 + 2 O2 -> CO2 + 2 H2O. Theoretical air = 2/0.21 = 9.52 mol/mol fuel. With 20% excess: 11.43 mol air, delivering 2.4 mol O2 of which 2.0 reacts - 0.4 mol O2 exits in the flue gas alongside CO2, H2O and 9.06 mol N2.
11.43 mol air per mol methane; the unreacted 0.4 mol O2 in the stack is the signature a flue analyzer reads back as 20% excess.

blocks: Composite Sections: Centroid and Second Moment of Area is a core model in Engineering Mechanics: A section's bending stiffness is not its area: the same material placed further from the neutral axis resists bending far better, and the parallel-axis theorem quantifies exactly how much. The model is used within these stated limits: A symmetric composite of rectangles with the material homogeneous and the components rigidly connected. Stiffness still depends on the material's modulus, which enters when the section is used.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Centroid and second moment of a composite section
\bar y=\frac{\sum A_i y_i}{\sum A_i},\qquad I=\sum\left(I_{c,i}+A_i d_i^{2}\right)
centroid position of the component measured from a datum
second moment of the component about its own centroidal axis
distance between the component centroid and the section centroid
second moment of the composite section
A symmetric composite of rectangles with the material homogeneous and the components rigidly connected. Stiffness still depends on the material's modulus, which enters when the section is used.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: The centroid is the area-weighted average position, so it is found by summing each component's area times its own centroid's distance and dividing by the total area. The second moment about that axis is then the sum of each component's own second moment plus its area times the square of its distance from the composite centroid - the parallel-axis theorem. The squared distance term is why the arrangement matters so much: moving material away from the axis adds stiffness with the square of the distance, while area alone adds linearly. This is the geometer's version of the structural engineer's rule that depth is cheap and material is expensive, and it is why an I-beam, a T-section and a hollow tube beat a solid rectangle of the same area.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A T-section has a 100 mm by 20 mm flange on top of a 20 mm by 80 mm web. Find the centroid height from the bottom and the second moment about it.
Take areas and centroid positions, then apply the parallel-axis theorem for each component.
Centroid at 67.8 mm from the bottom, second moment about 3.14 million mm^4, dominated by the parallel-axis contributions rather than by the components' own second moments.
The same 3600 mm^2 of material is arranged as a 60 mm by 60 mm square. How do the second moments compare?
Compute the square's second moment and compare with the T-section's.
I = 60 x 60^3/12 = 1.08 x 10^6 mm^4 against 3.14 x 10^6 mm^4 for the T-section.
The T-section is about three times stiffer in bending for the same area, entirely because more of its material sits far from the neutral axis.

blocks: Centroid and second moment of a composite section
\bar y=\frac{\sum A_i y_i}{\sum A_i},\qquad I=\sum\left(I_{c,i}+A_i d_i^{2}\right)
centroid position of the component measured from a datum
second moment of the component about its own centroidal axis
distance between the component centroid and the section centroid
second moment of the composite section
A symmetric composite of rectangles with the material homogeneous and the components rigidly connected. Stiffness still depends on the material's modulus, which enters when the section is used.
standard.title: Formula and variables

blocks: The centroid is the area-weighted average position, so it is found by summing each component's area times its own centroid's distance and dividing by the total area. The second moment about that axis is then the sum of each component's own second moment plus its area times the square of its distance from the composite centroid - the parallel-axis theorem. The squared distance term is why the arrangement matters so much: moving material away from the axis adds stiffness with the square of the distance, while area alone adds linearly. This is the geometer's version of the structural engineer's rule that depth is cheap and material is expensive, and it is why an I-beam, a T-section and a hollow tube beat a solid rectangle of the same area.
standard.title: Derivation

blocks: A T-section has a 100 mm by 20 mm flange on top of a 20 mm by 80 mm web. Find the centroid height from the bottom and the second moment about it.
Take areas and centroid positions, then apply the parallel-axis theorem for each component.
Centroid at 67.8 mm from the bottom, second moment about 3.14 million mm^4, dominated by the parallel-axis contributions rather than by the components' own second moments.
The same 3600 mm^2 of material is arranged as a 60 mm by 60 mm square. How do the second moments compare?
Compute the square's second moment and compare with the T-section's.
I = 60 x 60^3/12 = 1.08 x 10^6 mm^4 against 3.14 x 10^6 mm^4 for the T-section.
The T-section is about three times stiffer in bending for the same area, entirely because more of its material sits far from the neutral axis.

blocks: An inherited method sees the subclass's overridden state mid-construction and across every future edit - the fragile base class problem: a parent change silently breaks children it has never met. blocks: Compound Gear Trains: Ratio, Torque and the Cost of Each Stage is a core model in Theory of Machines: A compound train multiplies ratios and loses a little power in every mesh, so the output speed and torque follow from the product of the stages and their efficiencies. The model is used within these stated limits: External spur gears with no slip, negligible idler effects, and efficiency per mesh treated as constant. Helical and bevel stages have different efficiency values and add axial loads that the bearing arrangement must carry.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Compound train ratio and output torque
tooth counts of the meshing pair

External spur gears with no slip, negligible idler effects, and efficiency per mesh treated as constant. Helical and bevel stages have different efficiency values and add axial loads that the bearing arrangement must carry.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Each meshing pair changes speed by the inverse ratio of its tooth counts, and stages arranged in series multiply, so the overall ratio is the product. Because power is conserved apart from friction, torque rises by the same overall ratio multiplied by the efficiency of every mesh in the path, which is why a two-stage reducer delivers slightly less torque than the ideal ratio suggests. The same arithmetic makes the design decision visible: one large reduction in a single stage needs a very small pinion with few teeth and a very large wheel, so accuracy, wear and envelope all suffer, while splitting the reduction into two stages keeps each mesh reasonable at the cost of an extra pair of bearings and an extra bite out of the efficiency. That is the trade every gearbox designer works.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A two-stage reducer has 20-tooth drivers and 60-tooth wheels in each stage, driven at 1500 rpm. Find the output speed, and the output torque if the input power is 2 kW with 95 % efficiency per mesh.
Multiply the stage ratios, divide the input speed, then apply the efficiency to the power and divide by the output angular speed.
Stage ratio 60/20 = 3, so overall r = 9 and output speed = 1500/9 = 166.7 rpm = 17.45 rad/s. Output power = 2000 x 0.95^2 = 1805 W, so torque = 1805/17.45 = 103.4 N m.
166.7 rpm and 103 N m, against an input torque of 12.7 N m: a torque multiplication of about 8.1 rather than the ideal 9, the difference being the two meshes' losses.
What input power is needed at the same output torque if a single-stage reducer with one mesh were used instead?
With one mesh, efficiency loss is paid once, and the ratio would have to come from a single pair.
Output power required = 1805 W in the two-stage case. A single mesh at the same total torque would need 1805/0.95 = 1900 W, but would need a 9:1 pair with a 9-tooth pinion against an 81-tooth wheel.
Slightly less input power for one mesh, but a much less practical pair: the two-stage arrangement spends about 5 % of the power to keep the geometry workable.

blocks: Mix design in practice is dominated by admixtures and by variability, which is where the textbook treatment stops.

Superplasticisers are the key tool. They disperse the cement particles so the mix flows at a much lower water content, which is what makes high-strength concrete possible at all — strength is governed by the water-cement ratio, and without an admixture workability would force too much water. Self-compacting concrete, which flows through congested reinforcement without vibration, is essentially a superplasticiser plus a viscosity modifier.

Supplementary cementitious materials replace part of the cement. Fly ash and slag reduce cost and the carbon footprint and usually improve long-term strength and durability, but they slow early strength gain. That trade matters on a programme: a slab reaching stripping strength a day later changes the schedule, so the decision is commercial as much as technical.

The site realities cause most failures. Adding water to improve workability is the most common, and it silently reduces strength. Aggregate moisture varies with weather, so the batch water must be adjusted or the actual ratio drifts. Curing is routinely cut short, and concrete that dries early never reaches its design strength however good the mix was.

Quality control is statistical, not deterministic. Cubes or cylinders are tested at 7 and 28 days, and the characteristic strength is the value below which only 5% of results fall. A plant with high variability must therefore target a much higher mean strength to meet the same specification — which is why consistency of production is worth as much as the mix itself.

blocks: Confirmations, Reorganisation Risk and the Safety Bound is a core model in Distributed Ledger & Smart Contract Engineering: Confirmation depth is a risk decision: the chance that a chain is replaced falls exponentially with depth for an attacker holding a minority of the mining or staking power. The model is used within these stated limits: The attacker's share is below one half, blocks arrive from independent races, and the attacker can mine in private but cannot rewrite history without producing a longer chain. Larger q or a different consensus rule changes the model.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: probability the attacker's chain overtakes the honest one

The attacker's share is below one half, blocks arrive from independent races, and the attacker can mine in private but cannot rewrite history without producing a longer chain. Larger q or a different consensus rule changes the model.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: An attacker who wants to reverse a transaction must produce a chain longer than the honest chain from the point before that transaction. With a minority share q, each block the attacker produces is matched by more than one honest block on average, so the deficit grows; the probability that a random walk starting k blocks behind ever reaches zero is approximately the ratio q over p raised to k. Because that ratio is below one, each additional confirmation multiplies the remaining risk by the same factor, so risk falls geometrically rather than linearly. The formula also shows why settlement policy is a business decision: six confirmations is not a law of nature but a point on this curve chosen to make reversal cost more than the transaction is worth.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: An attacker holds 10 % of block production. Compute the reversal probability after six confirmations.
Form the ratio q/p and raise it to the number of confirmations.
About 1.9 in a million. Six confirmations is standard for this reason; a 10 % attacker would need on the order of hundreds of thousands of attempts to succeed once.
Same 10 % attacker, but the service accepts three confirmations. How much riskier is that than six?
Compare the two values of the same geometric series.
Three confirmations: 0.1111^3 = 1.37 x 10^-3. Six confirmations: 1.88 x 10^-6, so the ratio is about 730.
Roughly seven hundred times riskier. Halving the confirmation depth multiplied the risk by the reciprocal of the ratio q/p.

blocks: Congestion Control: Slow Start and AIMD is a core model in Computer Networks: TCP discovers the network's capacity by probing multiplicatively and backing off multiplicatively, converging to fairness without any router telling it the answer. The model is used within these stated limits: Describes classic Reno behaviour; slow start doubles w per RTT until the slow-start threshold, then AIMD takes over, and modern CUBIC/BBR reshape the probe curve.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: w\leftarrow w+1\ \text{per RTT (additive)};\qquad w\leftarrow w/2\ \text{on loss (multiplicative)}
warrow w+1 per RTT (additive); warrow w/2 on loss (multiplicative)
packet drop or triple duplicate ACK treated as congestion
Describes classic Reno behaviour; slow start doubles w per RTT until the slow-start threshold, then AIMD takes over, and modern CUBIC/BBR reshape the probe curve.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: No router reserves a lane for you, so capacity must be inferred from loss. Slow start begins tiny and doubles per RTT - exponential because each acknowledged window funds the next - until loss or a threshold says 'too far'. AIMD then oscillates: add one segment per RTT to creep upward, halve instantly on loss to retreat. Halving (not resetting) keeps throughput; adding (not multiplying) keeps stability. Two flows doing this sawtooth toward an equal split, which is where TCP's celebrated fairness comes from.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A flow's window is 40 segments when loss occurs. What are the windows over the next few RTTs under Reno?
Apply the multiplicative decrease, then additive increase.
On loss: w = 40/2 = 20. Then +1 per RTT: 21, 22, 23, ... reaching 30 after 10 RTTs, until the next loss halves it again.
Sawtooth between 20 and the next loss point - average window about 3/4 of the peak for this cycle.

blocks: No router reserves a lane for you, so capacity must be inferred from loss. Slow start begins tiny and doubles per RTT - exponential because each acknowledged window funds the next - until loss or a threshold says 'too far'. AIMD then oscillates: add one segment per RTT to creep upward, halve instantly on loss to retreat. Halving (not resetting) keeps throughput; adding (not multiplying) keeps stability. Two flows doing this sawtooth toward an equal split, which is where TCP's celebrated fairness comes from.
