Sawtooth between 20 and the next loss point - average window about 3/4 of the peak for this cycle.

blocks: Consensus Trade-Offs: Fault Tolerance Bounds and Finality is a core model in Distributed Ledger & Smart Contract Engineering: Byzantine consensus needs more than two-thirds honest participation to certify anything, and 'final' means different things - probabilistic in Nakamoto chains, absolute in BFT voting. The model is used within these stated limits: Asynchronous or partially synchronous networks with Byzantine faults; crash-only fault tolerance needs just n >= 2f+1, and no protocol beats 3f+1 with unknown membership.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: n≥ 3f+1 nodes to tolerate f Byzantine faults
votes needed to certify a block
Asynchronous or partially synchronous networks with Byzantine faults; crash-only fault tolerance needs just n >= 2f+1, and no protocol beats 3f+1 with unknown membership.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: To decide a value, honest nodes must be sure no conflicting value was certified elsewhere. With f Byzantine nodes able to vote both ways and messages delayed arbitrarily, a quorum must overlap every other quorum in at least one honest member - set arithmetic forces quorums above 2n/3, hence n >= 3f+1. Nakamoto consensus trades this crisp voting for hash-power lotteries: blocks become 'final' only probabilistically, each confirmation making reversal exponentially costlier, with six confirmations the Bitcoin convention. BFT chains instead gather 2f+1 signatures for absolute finality in seconds, at the cost of a known, bounded validator set - the permissionless-versus-fast-finality divide is this theorem expressed as product design.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A BFT chain has 100 validators. How many Byzantine failures can it certify through, and how many votes seal a block?
Apply the 3f+1 bound and quorum rule.

n = 100 >= 3f + 1 gives f <= 33: it tolerates 33 arbitrarily misbehaving validators. A block certifies with 2f + 1 = 67 votes - any two certifying quorums share at least 34 honest nodes, making conflicting certification impossible.
33 faults tolerated, 67 votes to finalize - and the same arithmetic says 4 validators tolerate exactly 1 traitor.

blocks: Consolidation: Time Factor and Settlement Rate is a core model in Soil Mechanics / Geotechnical Engineering: Clay settles as water squeezes out, and Terzaghi's time factor says how long that takes - proportional to the square of the drainage path, which is why drains accelerate it. The model is used within these stated limits: Terzaghi one-dimensional theory: saturated clay, small strains, constant c_v; the square-root-of-time early behaviour is what field graphs exploit to measure c_v.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Time factor and degree of consolidation
longest drainage path (half the layer for double drainage)
Terzaghi one-dimensional theory: saturated clay, small strains, constant c_v; the square-root-of-time early behaviour is what field graphs exploit to measure c_v.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Settlement magnitude comes from compression of the clay skeleton, but the rate is set by how fast pore water can escape - flow through a very low-permeability medium driven by shrinking pressure gradients. Solving the diffusion equation for the layer gives the time factor: consolidation progress depends on c_v t over the drainage path squared. The squaring is the design lever: halving H_dr with a drain or a fill surcharge quarters the time. Early consolidation grows as sqrt(time), so 50% takes a quarter of the time 100% would by extrapolation - and structures on clay are routinely designed to tolerate the decades-long tail.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A 10 m clay layer drains both ways (H_dr = 5 m) with c_v = 3 m^2/year. How long to 90% consolidation? What if a drain system halves H_dr to 2.5 m?
7.1 years collapses to 1.8 - the square law pays for drainage systems many times over on schedule-critical projects.

blocks: Context-Free Grammars, Parse Trees and Ambiguity is a core model in Theory of Computation: A grammar generates a language by rewriting variables, and a string's parse tree is the derivation made visible - ambiguous grammars hand the same string two different trees. The model is used within these stated limits: Context-free means each production rewrites a single variable regardless of surrounding context - exactly the freedom that lets one variable nest inside itself.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: derivation drawn as a tree; leaves spell the string
Context-free means each production rewrites a single variable regardless of surrounding context - exactly the freedom that lets one variable nest inside itself.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Derivation is repeated replacement: expand the leftmost (or any) variable until only terminals remain; recording each expansion as a node yields the parse tree, whose depth is the number of nested rewrites. The same string can have two genuinely different trees under one grammar - the classic dangling-else, where an unmatched else binds to either of two ifs. Ambiguity is a property of the grammar, not the language: precedence and associativity rules, or grammar restructuring, restore a unique intended tree, which is why expression grammars are layered by precedence.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: Derive aaabbb from S -> aSb | epsilon, and state the parse-tree depth.
Expand S three times, then terminate with epsilon.
S => aSb => aaSbb => aaaSbbb => aaabbb. Three recursive expansions plus the epsilon step; the tree has four levels of S nodes above the terminals.
Derivation length 4; the nesting depth equals n = 3, which is exactly what a finite automaton could not track.

blocks: Contours: Interval, Gradient and Interpolation is a core model in Surveying: Contour lines are the terrain's level curves, and their spacing on a map is an inverse reading of slope - dense means steep, with the interval setting the scale of legibility. The model is used within these stated limits: Uniform slope between the two contours; spacing is read perpendicular to the lines and scaled by the map's representative fraction.

advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: A contour connects points of equal elevation, so walking from one contour to the next climbs exactly CI metres; the horizontal distance covered sets the slope as CI over spacing. Contours never cross (except cliffs and overhangs), close on themselves, and cross ridges and valleys in V or U patterns pointing uphill - reading those patterns is terrain literacy. The interval is chosen by purpose: 0.5-1 m for detailed site design, 5-20 m for regional mapping; too small an interval crowds the sheet, too large erases the relief the map exists to show. Interpolation places intermediate contours proportionally between surveyed spot heights.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A 1:1000 map with 2 m contour interval shows adjacent contours 25 mm apart. Find the ground gradient.
Scale the map spacing to the ground, then form the ratio.
Ground spacing = 25 mm x 1000 = 25 m. Gradient = 2 m / 25 m = 1 in 12.5 = 8%.
An 8% slope - steep for roads (design limits run 4-6% on highways), fine for drainage swales.

blocks: Control flow is where correctness and testability are decided, and the tooling around it is mature.

Cyclomatic complexity is not academic: it is a standard gate in static analysis. Teams commonly fail a build above ten or fifteen per function, because past that the number of paths makes review and testing ineffective. It is also used to prioritise refactoring — the highest-complexity functions in a codebase are reliably the ones with the most defects.

Branch coverage is the practical target rather than path coverage, since path coverage is exponential. A suite with 100% branch coverage can still miss bugs in how branches interact, which is why mutation testing exists: it injects faults and checks whether the suite catches them, giving a much more honest measure of test quality than coverage percentage.

The most common real defect here is an off-by-one in a loop bound or a condition that can never change. Compilers warn about the obvious ones; fuzzing finds the rest, which is why it is standard practice on parsers and protocol handlers.

blocks: Controlled Rectifiers: Firing Angle and Average Output is a core model in Power Electronics: Delaying each thyristor's turn-on by the firing angle chops the waveform's front and lowers the average output predictably - the cosine law of phase control. The model is used within these stated limits: Continuous load current (a large inductor or motor armature keeps it flowing); with discontinuous current the average sits higher and needs waveform-specific integration.

blocks: Average output of a full-wave controlled rectifier
firing (delay) angle from the natural commutation point

blocks: An uncontrolled bridge conducts each half-cycle from its zero crossing, averaging to 2V_m/pi. A thyristor bridge waits alpha degrees into each half-cycle before firing, so the waveform loses its leading slice: integrating cos over the conduction window [alpha, pi] yields the same 2V_m/pi scaled by cos alpha. The control is smooth and lossless in principle - the delay steers energy rather than burning it - and at alpha beyond 90 degrees the average goes negative, turning the rectifier into an inverter feeding power back toward the AC source, which is how DC drives regenerate.

blocks: An uncontrolled bridge conducts each half-cycle from its zero crossing, averaging to 2V_m/pi. A thyristor bridge waits alpha degrees into each half-cycle before firing, so the waveform loses its leading slice: integrating cos over the conduction window [alpha, pi] yields the same 2V_m/pi scaled by cos alpha. The control is smooth and lossless in principle - the delay steers energy rather than burning it - and at alpha beyond 90 degrees the average goes negative, turning the rectifier into an inverter feeding power back toward the AC source, which is how DC drives regenerate.

blocks: All convective heat ultimately crosses the near-stationary fluid layer at the wall by conduction, but that layer's thickness and the temperature difference across it depend on the flow - too complex to solve per case. Newton's law packages the complexity into h. Dividing the convective flux by the conductive flux scale k(T_s - T_inf)/L yields the dimensionless Nusselt number: Nu = 1 means pure conduction across length L, and real flows run Nu of tens (free convection) to thousands (boiling, high-speed flow). Engineering correlations therefore report Nu(Re, Pr), and h follows by multiplying through k/L.

In communications, the received signal is the transmitted one convolved with the channel, so recovering the data means estimating the channel's impulse response and inverting it — equalisation. A known training sequence is sent, the response is measured, and the equaliser is built from it. This is why a modem takes a moment to sync.

blocks: Sensible cooling changes dry-bulb temperature; latent cooling condenses vapour at nearly constant temperature, paying the enthalpy of vaporization per kilogram of water removed. The space load has its own SHR from occupancy, ventilation and infiltration moisture; the coil delivers an SHR set by its surface temperature relative to the dew point. If the coil's SHR is higher (drier) than the load's, humidity accumulates; lower, and the space overcools while the coil over-dehumidifies - which is why coil selection starts on the psychrometric chart by drawing the room SHR line to the apparatus dew point.

If the coil's SHR is higher (drier) than the load's, humidity accumulates; lower, and the space overcools while the coil over-dehumidifies - which is why coil selection starts on the psychrometric chart by drawing the room SHR line to the apparatus dew point.

The model is used within these stated limits: One-dimensional heat conduction through a plate with constant mould wall temperature and temperature-independent properties; a real part also loses heat through ribs, bosses and the runner, and the ejection criterion is a mechanical rather than a thermal choice.

blocks: Cooling time for a plate of thickness 2s
thermal diffusivity of the melt, about 10^-7
temperature at which the part is stiff enough to eject

One-dimensional heat conduction through a plate with constant mould wall temperature and temperature-independent properties; a real part also loses heat through ribs, bosses and the runner, and the ejection criterion is a mechanical rather than a thermal choice.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Heat must diffuse out of the melt to the mould walls, and the time for a diffusion-limited process scales with the square of the distance the heat travels, which is why the half-thickness appears squared. The logarithmic term compares the driving temperature difference at the start with the one that remains when the part is stiff enough to eject: raising the mould temperature or ejecting hotter changes it only logarithmically, while thickness changes the answer quadratically. Cooling typically accounts for two thirds of the cycle, so the effect on output rate is direct. This is the arithmetic behind the design rule that wall thickness should be uniform and as thin as the part's stiffness allows.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A part has 2 mm half-thickness, melt at 230 degrees C, a mould at 60 degrees C and an ejection temperature of 90 degrees C. Estimate the cooling time with a diffusivity of 10^-7 m^2/s.
Substitute into the cooling-time relation, taking care with the logarithmic term.
s^2/alpha = 4 x 10^-6/10^-7 = 40 s. The logarithm is ln(4 x 170/(pi x 30)) = ln(7.215) = 1.976. So the cooling time is 40 x 1.976/pi^2 = 40 x 1.976/9.870 = 8.0 s.
About 8 seconds of cooling for a 4 mm section, which with filling and ejection sets a cycle near 12 seconds.
Wall thickness is doubled to 8 mm. What happens to cooling time and to output?
The quadratic term dominates; recompute with the doubled half-thickness.
s^2 becomes 16 x 10^-6, so the cooling time becomes 4 x 8.0 = 32 s.
Cooling rises from 8 to 32 seconds, so a cycle that was 12 seconds becomes about 36 - output falls to a third for a part of twice the wall thickness.

blocks: Corrosion Cells and Cathodic Protection is a core model in Engineering Chemistry: Corrosion is a short-circuited electrochemical cell: the more active metal becomes the anode and dissolves, and protection works by forcing that role onto a cheaper metal. The model is used within these stated limits: Standard potentials compare tendencies at standard conditions; real rates also need an electrolyte path, and potentials shift with environment per Nernst.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: reduction potential of the cathodic site
reduction potential of the anodic metal
net driving potential for the corrosion current
Standard potentials compare tendencies at standard conditions; real rates also need an electrolyte path, and potentials shift with environment per Nernst.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Two metals in electrical contact within an electrolyte form half-cells. The metal with the lower (more negative) reduction potential oxidizes - it is the anode - and electrons flow to the cathode where oxygen or hydrogen is reduced. Cathodic protection attaches a still more active metal (or an impressed current) so the structure becomes the cathode of the cell and stops dissolving.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: Iron has E° = -0.44 V and zinc E° = -0.76 V. Which corrodes when they touch in wet soil, and what is the driving potential?
Compare reduction potentials; the more negative one is the anode.
Zinc is more negative, so zinc oxidizes and iron is protected. E_cell = E_cathode - E_anode = (-0.44) - (-0.76) = 0.32 V.
Zinc corrodes sacrificially with a 0.32 V driving potential; the iron stays intact.

blocks: Counters: Ripple versus Synchronous and Modulus Design is a core model in Digital Electronics: A counter is flip-flops plus steering logic; ripple counters pay delay per stage while synchronous counters pay it once - and the modulus decides how many stages are needed. The model is used within these stated limits: Worst-case ripple delay assumes the count transition toggles every stage (e.g. 0111 -> 1000); synchronous counters confine that to one clock-to-output plus the decoding logic.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: number of states before recycle (e.g. 10 for a decade counter)
delay of the next-state combinational logic
Worst-case ripple delay assumes the count transition toggles every stage (e.g. 0111 -> 1000); synchronous counters confine that to one clock-to-output plus the decoding logic.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: In a ripple counter each flip-flop clocks from the previous one's output, so a change propagates stage by stage - the total count is briefly wrong while the ripple travels, and the worst case multiplies the per-stage delay by N. A synchronous counter clocks all stages together and computes each stage's toggle condition (T inputs) from the current count with combinational logic, so all bits settle within one flip-flop delay plus the logic. Modulus design is state selection: N stages give 2^N states, and the counter recycles from the chosen terminal count by decoding it and clearing or presetting the stages.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: Design a decade (MOD-10) counter with flip-flops of t_ff = 10 ns. Compare worst-case ripple delay against a synchronous implementation with 8 ns decode logic.
Compute stages, then both delays and their speed limits.
N = ceil(log2 10) = 4 stages. Ripple worst case (7 -> 8 toggles several stages): 4 x 10 = 40 ns, limiting counting to 25 MHz. Synchronous: 10 + 8 = 18 ns, allowing about 55 MHz.
Same 4 flip-flops; the synchronous version more than doubles the maximum count rate and never shows intermediate ripple states.

blocks: In a ripple counter each flip-flop clocks from the previous one's output, so a change propagates stage by stage - the total count is briefly wrong while the ripple travels, and the worst case multiplies the per-stage delay by N. blocks: Counting: Permutations, Combinations and Pigeonhole is a core model in Discrete Mathematics: Order matters in permutations and not in combinations, and the pigeonhole principle turns any surplus of items over boxes into a guaranteed collision. The model is used within these stated limits: Without repetition; pigeonhole: n+1 items in n boxes force one box to hold at least two, with the generalized form giving ceil(n/k) for k boxes.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Without repetition; pigeonhole: n+1 items in n boxes force one box to hold at least two, with the generalized form giving ceil(n/k) for k boxes.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Choose r of n in order: n options, then n-1, and so on for r factors - that is n!/(n-r)!. If order does not matter, every unordered set was counted r! times (once per arrangement), so divide it out. The pigeonhole principle needs no formula, only counting: if items exceed boxes, some box repeats - and its power is that the guarantee holds for every possible arrangement, which turns 'could collide' into 'must collide'.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: From 10 engineers, choose a 3-person committee. Then: among any 13 people, what is guaranteed about birth months?
Apply C(n,r), then pigeonhole with 12 boxes.
C(10,3) = 10!/(3! 7!) = (10 x 9 x 8)/6 = 120 committees (order irrelevant; P(10,3) = 720 would overcount by 3! = 6). Thirteen people into twelve months: ceil(13/12) = 2.
120 committees; at least two people share a birth month - guaranteed, not merely likely.

blocks: Coupling Metrics and the Dependency-Pointing Rule is a core model in Object Oriented Programming: Package level coupling can be measured and then governed: a package's instability is the share of its dependencies that point outward, and stable packages are the ones that must be abstract. The model is used within these stated limits: Counts are taken on compiled or imported units of one package; the metric treats all dependencies as equally strong and ignores runtime-only links such as reflection and configuration.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Instability and distance from the main sequence
abstractness: abstract types divided by total types
Counts are taken on compiled or imported units of one package; the metric treats all dependencies as equally strong and ignores runtime-only links such as reflection and configuration.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: A package with no outgoing dependencies cannot be broken by changing what it depends on, so it is maximally stable: I = 0. A package with many outgoing dependencies and few dependents is flexible: I approaches 1. Because I is a fraction of outgoing links, it rises monotonically with the share of dependencies pointing outward, which is exactly the quantity that decides how safe it is to change. The stable-dependencies principle follows: a dependency arrow should point toward stability, so that volatile code depends on stable code and not the reverse. Adding abstractness to the picture gives D: stable-and-concrete (A = 0, I = 0) is the zone of pain, unstable-and-abstract (A = 1, I = 1) is the zone of uselessness, and D = 0 means the package sits where its stability justifies its level of abstraction.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: Package api has 12 incoming dependencies and none outgoing, with 3 abstract types among its 12 types. Package client depends on 6 packages and is depended on by 2. Compute I and D for both.
Instability is a ratio of counts, abstractness is a ratio of type counts, and D measures the distance of their sum from 1.

api is stable but concrete and 0.75 off the main sequence; client is unstable and close to it. The actionable finding is that api, the package everything depends on, is the one that needs an interface seam.
A package has A = 0.8 and I = 0.8. What does D say, and what is the likely problem?
Compute D = |A + I - 1| and interpret the sign of the error.
D = |0.8 + 0.8 - 1| = 0.6. Both abstractness and instability are high, which is the zone of uselessness.
D = 0.6: the package is mostly interfaces and still depends on six other packages. Either it should own its dependencies or the abstractions do not belong there.

industry.title: Real-world applications

blocks: Real schedulers do not run a textbook algorithm; they run multi-level feedback queues, because no single policy serves interactive and batch work at once.

Linux's CFS uses a virtual runtime and a red-black tree rather than a fixed quantum, so a process that has run less gets to run next — proportional sharing without explicit priorities per class. Interactive work stays responsive because it accumulates virtual runtime slowly.

The engineering problems are rarely the algorithm. They are priority inversion (a low-priority thread holds a lock a high-priority thread needs, solved by priority inheritance), CPU affinity (keeping a thread on one core so its cache stays warm, which can matter more than the scheduling decision), and the tickless kernel (avoiding timer interrupts so an idle machine actually idles).

For latency-critical work the answer is usually to leave the general scheduler entirely: real-time classes, CPU isolation, or a dedicated core. General-purpose schedulers optimise throughput and fairness, which is the opposite of a hard latency guarantee.

blocks: Creep, Shrinkage and Durability Cover is a core model in Concrete Technology: Concrete keeps deforming long after it hardens - creep under load, shrinkage as it dries - and the cover depth decides how long the reinforcement survives the environment. The model is used within these stated limits: Long-term loading at moderate stress; creep grows with load age youth, humidity deficit and member slenderness, and shrinkage strain (~300-500 microstrain) adds independently of load.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: creep coefficient (typically 2-3 for loading at 28 days)
instantaneous elastic strain at the applied stress
concrete depth over reinforcement protecting it
Long-term loading at moderate stress; creep grows with load age youth, humidity deficit and member slenderness, and shrinkage strain (~300-500 microstrain) adds independently of load.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: The cement gel flows viscously under sustained stress, so deformation continues for years: the creep coefficient phi expresses that extra strain as a multiple of the initial elastic strain - typically doubling or tripling long-term deflection, which is why beam camber and deflection checks use effective moduli. Drying shrinkage strains the surface and, restrained by reinforcement or adjacent concrete, opens cracks long before any load arrives. Cover is the durability budget: carbonation and chloride fronts advance roughly with sqrt(time), and the cover depth buys the decades before they reach the steel and start corrosion - exposure classes in the codes are cover tables in disguise.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A member loaded at 28 days shows elastic strain 333 microstrain (10 MPa on E = 30 GPa) with creep coefficient 2.5. Find the long-term strain, and the shrinkage share if drying shrinkage adds 400 microstrain.
Apply the creep multiplier, then add shrinkage.
Creep strain = 2.5 x 333 = 833 microstrain; total load-related = 333 + 833 = 1166 microstrain. Drying shrinkage adds 400 more, load-independent: 1566 microstrain overall.
Long-term deformation is about 4.7 times the instantaneous elastic value - the multiplier deflection design cannot ignore.

blocks: Critical Path Method and Project Float is a core model in Operations Research & Optimization: A project's duration is its longest dependency chain, and every activity off that chain carries float - slack that scheduling software hides and schedulers must manage. The model is used within these stated limits: Deterministic durations and finish-to-start logic; PERT generalizes with three-point estimates, and resource levelling can turn float into fiction when crews are shared.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: earliest start/finish from the forward pass
latest start/finish from the backward pass
delay an activity absorbs without delaying the project
Deterministic durations and finish-to-start logic; PERT generalizes with three-point estimates, and resource levelling can turn float into fiction when crews are shared.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: A forward pass propagates earliest times from the start: each activity starts when all predecessors finish, and the project duration is the largest finish. A backward pass propagates latest times from that duration: each activity must finish early enough for its successors' latest starts. The gap between latest and earliest is float - free scheduling room. Activities with zero float cannot move at all: they are the critical path, and only shortening them shortens the project. Crashing decisions then become arithmetic: cost-per-day-saved against the next-longest path that becomes critical once the first is compressed.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: Activity A (3 d) precedes C (6 d); B (5 d) precedes D (2 d); A and B start together, C and D finish the project. Find duration, critical path and float on B-D.
Run both passes on the two parallel chains.
Chain A-C: 3 + 6 = 9 d. Chain B-D: 5 + 2 = 7 d. T_proj = 9 d, critical path A-C. B-D float = 9 - 7 = 2 d: B can start as late as day 2, D as late as day 7, without delaying the project.
Duration 9 days via A-C; the B-D chain carries 2 days of float - and crashing A by 2 days would make both chains critical, so further crashing must hit both.

blocks: The design equation for a continuous stirred tank sets the volume equal to the molar feed rate times the conversion divided by the reaction rate evaluated at the outlet conditions. For second-order kinetics that rate contains the square of the outlet concentration, which itself falls as one minus the conversion. Combining the two effects makes the volume grow far faster than linearly: at ninety percent conversion the reactor sees a tenth of the feed concentration and a rate a hundredth of the inlet value. This is the strongest argument for plug-flow or batch operation when high conversion is required, and it is also why a train of two or three stirred tanks in series outperforms a single one - the intermediate conversions between the tanks reduce the average penalty of working at the lowest concentration.

blocks: A second-order reaction runs at 0.5 L/(mol min) with a feed of 2 mol/L and 10 L/min, targeting 80 % conversion. Find the reactor volume.
Compute the molar feed rate, the outlet rate of reaction, then apply the design equation.
F_A0 = 2 x 10 = 20 mol/min. At X = 0.8 the concentration is 0.4 mol/L, so the rate is 0.5 x 0.16 = 0.08 mol/(L min). Volume = 20 x 0.8/0.08 = 200 L.
200 litres for 80 % conversion in a single stirred tank.
Conversion is raised to 90 %. What volume is required, and how does it compare?
Recompute the outlet concentration and rate at the higher conversion.
Concentration at X = 0.9 is 0.2 mol/L, so the rate is 0.5 x 0.04 = 0.02 mol/(L min). Volume = 20 x 0.9/0.02 = 900 L.
900 litres against 200: a 4.5-fold volume increase for ten percentage points more conversion, which is why the last increment is the most expensive.

blocks: Cut-Off Grade and Break-Even Economics is a core model in Mine Planning & Operations: The grade at which a tonne of ore pays for its own mining and processing is a single equation, and it moves with the metal price - which is why reserves are re-reported whenever prices change. The model is used within these stated limits: Costs and prices held constant and an orebody whose tonnes and grade can be estimated. Real scheduling adds capacity constraints, blending requirements and the difference between mill feed and waste mining cost.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: mining, processing and administration cost per tonne of ore
metal price per unit of contained metal
payable fraction after smelting or refining terms

Costs and prices held constant and an orebody whose tonnes and grade can be estimated. Real scheduling adds capacity constraints, blending requirements and the difference between mill feed and waste mining cost.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Each tonne mined and milled costs a fixed amount. The revenue it generates is its grade multiplied by the metal price, the recovery achieved in the plant and the payable fraction after refining deductions. Setting revenue equal to cost and solving for grade gives the cut-off, and the result is immediately useful because it converts an economic assumption into a grade boundary that a geologist or an engineer can apply in the field. The sensitivity is direct: a lower metal price raises the cut-off, which turns marginal ore into waste and shrinks the reported reserve, exactly the mechanism behind reserve writedowns when prices fall.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: Milling costs 30 per tonne, recovery is 85 %, the payable fraction is 95 % and the metal price is 8000 per tonne. Find the break-even grade.
Divide the cost by the product of price, recovery and payable fraction.
A break-even grade of 0.46 %; ore below that grade loses money at the stated costs and price.
The metal price falls to 6000 per tonne. What happens to the cut-off?
The cut-off rises from 0.46 % to 0.62 %, a third higher, so material that was ore becomes waste and the reserve shrinks without any change in the ground.

blocks: Cyclomatic Complexity and Basis Path Testing is a core model in Software Engineering: The number of independent paths through a routine is a small integer you can compute from its flow graph - and it is the minimum count of tests that can claim to have exercised its logic. The model is used within these stated limits: Per connected routine with a single entry and exit; the two forms (edges-nodes+2, predicates+1) agree, and V(G) above about 10 flags a routine for refactoring rather than testing.

advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Each binary decision doubles the conceptual execution scenarios but adds only one independent path: the new path that first takes the branch not yet taken. Graph theory counts exactly these - the cycle rank of the control-flow graph - which is why edges minus nodes plus two equals predicates plus one. A basis set of V(G) independent paths guarantees every statement and every branch direction is executed at least once; fewer tests provably leave some decision combination untouched, which converts 'we tested it' from an opinion into a count.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A routine's flow graph has 10 nodes and 12 edges, with 3 if-statements. Compute V(G) both ways.
V(G) = E - N + 2 = 12 - 10 + 2 = 4. Predicate form: 3 binary ifs + 1 = 4. Consistent.
V(G) = 4: at least four independent-path tests are needed for full branch coverage of this routine.

blocks: Darcy friction factor from the Moody chart/Colebrook
Fully developed incompressible flow in a straight constant-diameter pipe; f depends on Reynolds number and relative roughness, and fittings add their own K-factors.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Dimensional analysis of wall shear in a pipe leaves one dimensionless loss coefficient times the dynamic head v^2/2g, with the geometry entering as L/D. The friction factor absorbs the physics: laminar flow gives the exact f = 64/Re, turbulent flow follows the Colebrook equation blending Reynolds number and relative roughness - read off the Moody chart. The velocity-squared dependence is the design message: doubling flow quadruples friction loss, which is why pipe sizing dominates pumping cost.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: Water flows at 2 m/s through 100 m of 100 mm pipe with friction factor 0.02. Find the head loss.
About 4.1 m of head (0.4 bar) lost - and doubling the velocity to 4 m/s would cost 16.3 m, four times as much.

blocks: A position tolerance at MMC must guarantee assembly with the mating part at its worst-case size. blocks: A hole is specified 10.00/+0.10 mm with a position tolerance of 0.20 mm at MMC. The produced hole measures 10.08 mm. What position tolerance is allowed?

blocks: DC Machine Speed, Back EMF and Field Weakening is a core model in Electrical Machines I: A DC machine's speed follows its back-EMF law: at fixed field, speed falls with armature drop, and weakening the field raises speed at the cost of torque. The model is used within these stated limits: Constant field, negligible armature reaction and saturation, steady state with no mechanical losses in the ideal form. The constants absorb winding and pole geometry and differ between machines.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Constant field, negligible armature reaction and saturation, steady state with no mechanical losses in the ideal form. The constants absorb winding and pole geometry and differ between machines.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: The armature of a rotating machine generates a voltage proportional to speed and field flux, and in steady state the supply has to overcome that voltage plus the resistive drop, which gives the speed relation directly: for a fixed terminal voltage, speed is set by the difference between supply and back EMF. Because the same flux and armature current also set torque, the two relations describe the machine's whole operating envelope. Loading the machine increases armature current, which increases the resistive drop, which lowers back EMF and therefore speed: a DC motor's natural droop under load. Reducing the flux with a fixed back EMF must increase speed to restore the balance, and the same reduction costs torque for the same current, which is the field-weakening trade.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A machine runs at 1000 rpm with 220 V applied and an armature drop of 10 V. What speed results if the drop rises to 25 V?
Speed is proportional to back EMF at constant flux, so use the ratio of the two back EMFs.
About 929 rpm, a 7 % droop from the 15 V increase in armature drop.
The field flux is reduced to 80 % of its nominal value at the same back EMF. What speed and torque result?
Speed is inversely proportional to flux at fixed back EMF; torque is proportional to flux at fixed armature current.
N = 1000/0.8 = 1250 rpm. Torque falls to 0.8 of its former value for the same armature current.
1250 rpm with 20 % less torque per ampere, which is exactly the constant-power region of a DC drive.

blocks: A deadlock is a state in which a set of processes is permanently blocked because each holds at least one resource while waiting for a resource held by another member of the set. The four necessary conditions are mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption and circular wait.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: The four necessary conditions and Banker's safety test
mutual exclusion - a resource is held by one thread
hold and wait - a thread holds one and waits for another
no preemption - a resource cannot be taken away
circular wait - a cycle in the wait-for graph

All four must hold simultaneously, so breaking any one prevents deadlock entirely. Banker's algorithm grants a request only if the resulting state is safe, meaning some order exists in which every thread can finish.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Deadlock is a graph property, and that is what makes it detectable.
Vertices are threads, and an edge
holds. A thread blocked on a held resource cannot proceed until the holder releases it, so a cycle means every thread in it is waiting on another that is itself waiting:
Conversely, if the graph is acyclic there is always a thread with no outgoing edge; it can finish and release, so progress continues. Deadlock is therefore
the presence of a cycle, which a DFS detects in
Rather than detecting, it avoids: a request is granted only if the resulting state is
, meaning some ordering of the remaining threads lets each finish. Checking safety is the same as repeatedly finding a thread whose needs are met by currently available resources:
resource types, which is why it is applied at request time rather than continuously.

Impose a total order on resources and require every thread to acquire in that order. Then all edges point in one direction, so no cycle can exist — the proof is one line, and the rule costs nothing at runtime.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: Two threads each lock A then B, but in opposite orders. Show the deadlock and fix it.
Draw the wait-for graph; a cycle proves deadlock. Break it by enforcing one global lock order.

# Deadlock-prone
# T1: lock(A); lock(B)
# T2: lock(B); lock(A)

# Safe: always acquire in a canonical order
order = sorted([A, B], key=id)
for lock in order:
    lock.acquire()
A total ordering on lock acquisition makes circular wait impossible.

blocks: Deadlock is handled differently depending on whether it can be tolerated, and most systems choose detection and recovery over prevention.

Databases are the clear example. PostgreSQL and MySQL both run a wait-for graph check periodically, find a cycle, and abort one transaction — the victim. They accept that deadlocks happen because preventing them would require every transaction to declare its locks up front, which is impractical. The guidance to developers is to lock tables in a consistent order, which removes the cycles without any runtime cost.

Operating systems mostly ignore the problem. The classic dining philosophers setup is a teaching device; real kernels rarely deadlock because they acquire few resources at once and use lock ordering conventions. Where they do, the result is a hang and a crash dump.

The practical engineering rule is lock ordering. Give every lock a rank, always acquire in ascending rank, and cycles become impossible by construction. It is enforced by convention and review, sometimes by static analysis, and violations show up as rare hangs that are extremely hard to reproduce — which is why the convention is worth being strict about.

blocks: A deadlock is a state in which a set of processes is permanently blocked because each holds at least one resource while waiting for a resource held by another member of the set. The four necessary conditions are mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption and circular wait.

Hold and wait: a process holds resources while requesting more.

mutual exclusion - a resource is held by one thread
hold and wait - a thread holds one and waits for another

All four must hold simultaneously, so breaking any one prevents deadlock entirely. Banker's algorithm grants a request only if the resulting state is safe, meaning some order exists in which every thread can finish.

blocks: Defect Removal Efficiency and Release Readiness is a core model in Software Engineering: Release readiness is a ratio, not a feeling: the share of defects found before release, and the sample size needed to reach a target. The model is used within these stated limits: Defects must be counted with the same severity threshold and the same observation window before and after release; a short window understates post-release defects for long-latency fields.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: defects reported after release in the observation window
fraction of defects removed before escape
Defects must be counted with the same severity threshold and the same observation window before and after release; a short window understates post-release defects for long-latency fields.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: DRE answers a single question: of all the defects that existed at the moment of release, what fraction had already been found. It is written as a ratio rather than a count because both terms are estimates of the same population - defects that exist - measured through two different instruments. A high DRE means verification is doing its job; a low DRE with a high pre-release count means the product is large and inspected lightly. Because the denominator is the true defect population, the ratio also implies a sample size: to reach a target DRE with an assumed escape rate, the number of pre-release finds must be large enough that the escapes are a small fraction.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A release finds 92 defects in test and the first 30 days of production report 8. What is the DRE?
Divide defects found before release by the total found.
0.92, or 92 %. For safety-related software that would be well short of a 0.99 target; for an internal dashboard it may be more than sufficient.
History says about 8 defects escape a release of this size. How many must be found before release to reach a DRE of 0.98?
Set DRE = 0.98 with 8 expected escapes and solve for the pre-release count.
D_pre/(D_pre + 8) = 0.98, so D_pre = 0.98 D_pre + 7.84, giving 0.02 D_pre = 7.84.
D_pre at least 392 pre-release finds. The target is only realistic if verification has the capacity to find that many, which is the planning decision the number exposes.

blocks: Defibrillator Energy Delivery and Transthoracic Impedance is a core model in Biomedical Instrumentation & Devices: A defibrillator dumps a controlled joule-count through the chest, and the current that actually reaches the heart depends on energy, waveform and the patient's transthoracic impedance. The model is used within these stated limits: Monophasic damped-sine figures quoted; biphasic truncated waveforms achieve equal or better success at lower energies and currents, and impedance varies with pad placement, size and contact.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Monophasic damped-sine figures quoted; biphasic truncated waveforms achieve equal or better success at lower energies and currents, and impedance varies with pad placement, size and contact.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: The capacitor stores the dose - half C V squared - and discharge across the chest converts it to current through the myocardium, which must exceed a defibrillation threshold to reset chaotic electrical activity. Ohm's law through the torso says current falls as impedance rises, so a high-impedance chest (poor pad contact, hairy or dry skin, small paddles) receives less current from the same joules - the clinical reason for firm pad contact, conductive gel and anterior-lateral placement. Modern biphasic devices measure impedance during the shock and adjust voltage to deliver the selected energy anyway, turning the variability this formula exposes into a controlled parameter.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A defibrillator's 100 uF capacitor charges to 2000 V. Verify the 200 J dose and estimate peak current through a 75 ohm chest.
Apply the energy and Ohm's-law relations.
E = 0.5 x 100e-6 x (2000)^2 = 0.5 x 100e-6 x 4e6 = 200 J. I_peak = 2000/75 = 26.7 A (monophasic order of magnitude; biphasic waveforms deliver comparable energy at lower peak current).
200 J stored, tens of amperes peak through the torso - small currents relative to the myocardial threshold are why impedance management and waveform shape decide success.

blocks: Each edge touches two endpoints, so summing degrees counts every edge exactly twice - the handshaking lemma, which immediately forces the number of odd-degree vertices to be even. blocks: Patterns are vocabulary for design review, and their value in a team is mostly communicative.

Saying "use an Observer here" conveys a whole structure in one word, which makes design discussion faster and code review more precise. That is the strongest practical argument for knowing them, stronger than any claim about code quality.

The ones that appear constantly in real systems: Strategy and Command behind plugin and job systems; Observer behind event buses and reactive frameworks; Factory and Builder behind object construction in frameworks where the concrete type is decided by configuration; Adapter behind every integration layer that reconciles two APIs; Facade behind SDKs that hide a complicated backend.

The equally important lesson is over-application. The original book's examples were in C++ and Smalltalk, and many patterns exist to work around the absence of a feature. In a language with first-class functions, Strategy is often just a function argument; in one with duck typing, Adapter is often unnecessary. Adding a pattern where the language already provides the mechanism adds indirection and nothing else.

Singleton deserves particular caution. It is a global object that cannot be substituted in a test, and it creates hidden dependencies that the type system does not show. Dependency injection solves the same problem — one instance, controlled lifetime — without those costs, which is why it is the modern default.

The machine leaves q0 at the first 1 and never returns.
Any string with no 1 stays in q0 and is rejected. The first 1 moves to q1, and every later symbol stays there. So the accepted strings are those with at least one 1.
Every string that contains at least one 1.

blocks: Development Length and Anchorage of Reinforcement is a core model in Design of Reinforced Concrete Structures: A bar must be embedded long enough for the bond between steel and concrete to develop the force in it, and that length scales with bar diameter and stress. The model is used within these stated limits: Uniform bond stress along the embedment, adequate cover and confinement, and no hooks or mechanical anchors. Deformed bars, epoxy coating, congestion and top-cast bars all change the value, which is why codes adjust the base figure with factors.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: stress in the bar at the section, commonly 0.87 f_y
design bond stress, increased for deformed bars

Uniform bond stress along the embedment, adequate cover and confinement, and no hooks or mechanical anchors. Deformed bars, epoxy coating, congestion and top-cast bars all change the value, which is why codes adjust the base figure with factors.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Force travels from the bar into the concrete through bond along the embedded surface, so the force a bar can develop is its surface area - circumference times length - multiplied by the bond stress. Setting that equal to the force in the bar at yield, which is its area times stress, cancels the area and leaves the length proportional to diameter divided by the bond stress. Because the force scales with area and the bond capacity with surface, a larger bar needs proportionally more embedment, which is why a heavily loaded member may be reinforced with more small bars rather than fewer large ones. The relation is also the reason hooks and mechanical anchors exist: they provide the anchorage when the available length is not there.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A 16 mm Fe415 bar is anchored in M20 concrete with a design bond stress of 1.4 MPa. Find the development length.
Take the stress as 0.87 times the yield, then apply the relation.
About 1031 mm, or roughly 64 bar diameters; deformed-bar factors and confinement may allow less, and congestion may force a different bar arrangement.
The same stress is carried by a 12 mm bar. What development length results?
Length is proportional to diameter at constant stress and bond stress.
774 mm, three quarters of the 16 mm bar's requirement: more, smaller bars reduce the anchorage demand in proportion to the reduction in diameter.

blocks: DFT and FFT Compute Cost is a core model in Digital Signal Processing: The DFT's direct evaluation costs N^2 operations while the FFT reuses symmetry to cost N log N - a difference that decides what real-time signal processing is possible. The model is used within these stated limits: Radix-2 FFT on N = 2^k; other algorithms cover composite and prime lengths at similar asymptotic cost.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: transform length, a power of two for radix-2 FFT
direct sum: N outputs x N terms each
Radix-2 FFT on N = 2^k; other algorithms cover composite and prime lengths at similar asymptotic cost.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Each DFT output sums the signal against one complex exponential, and doing that for all N outputs repeats almost identical work. The FFT splits the sum into even- and odd-indexed half-transforms; the twiddle factors connecting them obey W^(k+N/2) = -W^k, so one butterfly computes two outputs from two inputs with a single complex multiply. Recursing the split log2 N levels deep turns N^2 into (N/2) log2 N butterflies - and the same reuse is why spectral analysis went from minutes to microseconds, enabling audio codecs, OFDM radios and vibration monitoring.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: Compare operation counts for N = 1024: direct DFT versus radix-2 FFT.
DFT: 1024^2 = 1,048,576 complex multiplies. FFT: (1024/2) x log2(1024) = 512 x 10 = 5,120 butterflies (~ 5 complex multiplies each, still ~25,600).
About a 100-400 fold saving - the FFT is why a 1024-point spectrum runs in microseconds on a microcontroller.

The instrument is leveled, so the line of sight is horizontal. Staffs are vertical.

blocks: The line of sight is one horizontal plane for a given setup. The reduced level of that plane is the reduced level of the benchmark plus how far the staff at the benchmark rises to meet the plane. At the next point the staff rises a different distance to the same plane, so you subtract that reading. Moving the instrument starts a new plane, which is why a change point needs both a foresight and a new backsight.

blocks: Diffie-Hellman Key Exchange and Forward Secrecy is a core model in Cryptography & Network Security: Two parties can agree on a secret over a public channel because exponentiation is easy while discrete logarithms are not - and ephemeral keys turn that agreement into forward secrecy. The model is used within these stated limits: Security rests on the discrete-logarithm problem in the chosen group and on authenticating the exchange - plain DH is man-in-the-middleable, which TLS solves with signatures or certificates.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Security rests on the discrete-logarithm problem in the chosen group and on authenticating the exchange - plain DH is man-in-the-middleable, which TLS solves with signatures or certificates.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Each side raises g to its own private exponent and publishes the result. Multiplying exponentiation combines: whoever published g^a can raise the received g^b to a and reach g^(ab), exactly what the other side reaches by raising g^a to b. An eavesdropper holds g, g^a and g^b and must recover a or b - a discrete logarithm, believed hard for well-chosen groups. Forward secrecy comes from making a and b ephemeral: if private keys are deleted after the session, stealing a long-term key later cannot reconstruct past session keys.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: Toy DH with p = 23, g = 5. Alice picks a = 6, Bob picks b = 15. Run the exchange.
Compute public values, then each side's shared secret.
Alice sends A = 5^6 mod 23 = 8. Bob sends B = 5^15 mod 23 = 19. Alice computes 19^6 mod 23 = 2; Bob computes 8^15 mod 23 = 2.
Shared secret K = 2 (in the toy group; real deployments use 2048-bit+ groups or elliptic curves).

blocks: Diffusion in Solids: Fick's Second Law and Carburizing is a core model in Materials Science & Engineering: Atoms migrate through solids by thermally activated jumps, so diffusion depth grows with the square root of time - the law that sizes every heat-treatment soak. The model is used within these stated limits: Constant D (dilute, isothermal); exact carburizing profiles use the error-function solution of the second law, C(x,t) = C_s - (C_s - C_0) erf(x / 2 sqrt(Dt)).
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Diffusion length and Fick's second law
diffusion coefficient, Arrhenius in temperature: D = D_0 exp(-Q/RT)
Constant D (dilute, isothermal); exact carburizing profiles use the error-function solution of the second law, C(x,t) = C_s - (C_s - C_0) erf(x / 2 sqrt(Dt)).
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Fick's first law says flux runs down the concentration gradient; where the gradient varies with position, more atoms enter a slice than leave (or vice versa), and the local concentration's rate of change becomes the second derivative term - the diffusion equation. Its solutions spread as sqrt(Dt) because the random-walk statistics of thermally activated jumps put mean-square displacement linear in time. Temperature enters through D exponentially (Q ~ 140 kJ/mol for carbon in iron), so carburizing at 925 C instead of 850 C is not a modest speed-up - it is the difference between a shift and a week.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: Carbon diffuses in austenite with D = 1e-11 m^2/s at 925 C. Estimate the carburizing case depth for a 4-hour soak.
About 0.4 mm of case in 4 hours - and doubling the depth needs four times the soak, the sqrt(t) law that schedules heat-treat furnaces.

blocks: Distance-Vector Routing and Count-to-Infinity is a core model in Computer Networks: Routers believing only their neighbours' rumours can trap a stale path in a two-node loop that climbs one hop-cost at a time toward infinity. The model is used within these stated limits: Each router knows its own links and its neighbours' advertisements, nothing else; convergence is eventual, not immediate - the gap is where loops live.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Each router knows its own links and its neighbours' advertisements, nothing else; convergence is eventual, not immediate - the gap is where loops live.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Each router periodically tells neighbours its current cost vector, and each recomputes minima. When a link fails, the truth needs several exchanges to propagate. Meanwhile a router whose path ran through the failure may hear a stale low cost from the very neighbour that learned the path from it - each adopts the other's inflated number and increments it every round: cost 3 becomes 4, then 5, climbing until the protocol's infinity (16 in RIP) declares the destination unreachable. Split horizon (don't advertise a route back toward its source) and poison reverse (advertvertise it back as infinite) cut the two-node loop at the cost of larger updates.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A-B cost 1, B-C cost 1, A-C via B cost 2. Link B-C fails but A still advertises 'C at 2' (stale, via B). What happens?
Track the advertisements round by round.

B adopts A's stale route: cost to C = 1 (to A) + 2 = 3, and packets loop B-A-B. Next round A hears 3 and advertises 4; B computes 5... each exchange adds 2 (or 1 per direction) until RIP's 16 marks C unreachable.
Count-to-infinity: a loop persisting several exchange rounds, bounded only by the infinity metric - the reason for split horizon and triggered updates.

blocks: Distillation: McCabe-Thiele Stages and Reflux Ratio is a core model in Mass Transfer Operations: A distillation column is a staircase between an equilibrium curve and two operating lines, and the reflux ratio sets both the staircase's shape and the column's energy bill. The model is used within these stated limits: Constant molal overflow (equal molar heats of vaporization), binary system, total condenser; stages are stepped between the operating line and the equilibrium curve from x_D down to x_B.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: reflux ratio L/D, liquid returned over distillate taken
the diagonal the staircase reflects across
Constant molal overflow (equal molar heats of vaporization), binary system, total condenser; stages are stepped between the operating line and the equilibrium curve from x_D down to x_B.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Material balances around the column top give the rectifying line: slope R/(R+1), intercept x_D/(R+1) - a straight line from the distillate point on the diagonal down toward the feed condition. The equilibrium curve gives what one theoretical stage achieves. McCabe-Thiele walks the staircase between them: horizontal to the curve (equilibrium), vertical to the line (balance), each step one stage, switching lines at the feed. Reflux ratio is the dial: high R flattens the line toward the diagonal, few stages, huge energy; R at minimum pinches the staircase against the curve, infinite stages, least energy - design lives at 1.2-1.5 times R_min.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A column makes x_D = 0.95 distillate at reflux ratio 2. Write its rectifying operating line and evaluate it at x = 0.5.
Substitute R and x_D into the line equation.
y = 0.65 above x = 0.5 - that pair is one theoretical stage's reach on the rectifying section; stepping such pairs to x_B gives the stage count.

blocks: Divergence, Curl, and the Integral Theorems is a core model in Engineering Mathematics III: Divergence measures outward flux density and curl measures local rotation, and the integral theorems let you swap a hard surface or line integral for an easier volume or area one. The model is used within these stated limits: F must be continuously differentiable on a region containing V, and S must be closed and outward-oriented; Stokes' theorem carries the analogous conditions for curl.

blocks: Cut the volume into tiny boxes. On each box the net outward flux is approximately (divergence) x (box volume), because opposite faces nearly cancel except for how the field changes across them. Summing over boxes, interior faces cancel pairwise and only the outer surface remains - the volume integral of the divergence equals the total surface flux.

blocks: Drag Force and Terminal Velocity is a core model in Fluid Mechanics: A body moving through fluid pays a force proportional to velocity squared, and free fall ends when that force balances weight - the terminal velocity. The model is used within these stated limits: Newtonian (turbent, high-Reynolds) drag regime; at very low Reynolds numbers viscous Stokes drag (linear in v) takes over instead.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Newtonian (turbent, high-Reynolds) drag regime; at very low Reynolds numbers viscous Stokes drag (linear in v) takes over instead.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: The moving body continually imparts momentum to the fluid it displaces and drags along; dimensional analysis packages that momentum rate as dynamic pressure (rho v^2/2) times area times a shape coefficient measured in wind tunnels. For a falling body, weight is constant while drag grows as v^2, so the net force - and acceleration - shrinks toward zero: the asymptotic speed where they balance is terminal velocity. It falls with the square root of weight-to-drag-area ratio, which is why parachutes (huge C_D A) land softly and why dense compact objects do not.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: An 80 kg parachutist deploys a canopy of 30 m^2 with C_D = 1.5 in air of density 1.2 kg/m^3. Find the descent speed.
Set drag equal to weight and solve for v.
About 5.4 m/s - a survivable landing speed; free-fall without the canopy (A ~ 0.7 m^2) would exceed 40 m/s.

blocks: Every point on the drill's periphery should travel at the recommended cutting speed for the tool-workpiece pair. Peripheral speed is pi D N per minute with D in metres; converting D from millimetres introduces the factor 1000. blocks: Dynamic Power, Voltage Scaling and Energy per Operation is a core model in VLSI Design: A digital block's power is activity times capacitance times voltage squared times frequency, which is why voltage scaling is the strongest energy lever available and why it slows the circuit down. The model is used within these stated limits: Dynamic (switching) power only, with a constant activity factor and capacitance; leakage and short-circuit power are excluded, and voltage scaling assumes the delay increase is absorbed by a lower frequency.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: P=\alpha C V^2 f,\qquad E_{cycle}=\alpha C V^2
P=α C V^2 f, E_cycle=α C V^2
switching activity: transitions per clock cycle

Dynamic (switching) power only, with a constant activity factor and capacitance; leakage and short-circuit power are excluded, and voltage scaling assumes the delay increase is absorbed by a lower frequency.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Every transition of a node charges or discharges its capacitance through the supply, delivering an amount of energy proportional to voltage squared; switching activity converts that per-transition energy into an average power by multiplying by the transition rate and the clock frequency. Voltage therefore appears squared, which makes it the most powerful knob: ten percent less voltage is nineteen percent less power for the same activity and frequency. The counterweight is delay, which falls roughly linearly with voltage above threshold while leakage rises, so a design that reduces voltage must also reduce frequency, and the product is the energy actually saved per operation. That is the arithmetic behind voltage and frequency pairs, and behind the diminishing returns of pushing voltage down towards the threshold region.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A block has an activity factor of 0.1, 10 nF of switched capacitance and runs at 1.0 V and 1 GHz. Compute its dynamic power and energy per cycle.
Square the voltage for energy, then multiply by the switching rate for power.
1 watt of dynamic power and 1 nanojoule per clock cycle.
The same block runs at 0.9 V and 0.8 GHz. What happens to power and to energy per operation?
Square the new voltage for energy and multiply by the new frequency for power.
E_cycle becomes 0.1 x 10^-8 x 0.81 = 0.81 nJ. P becomes 0.81 nJ x 0.8 x 10^9 = 0.648 W.
Power falls from 1.0 W to 0.65 W and energy per operation from 1.0 nJ to 0.81 nJ, at the cost of twenty percent of the clock rate.

blocks: Every transition of a node charges or discharges its capacitance through the supply, delivering an amount of energy proportional to voltage squared; switching activity converts that per-transition energy into an average power by multiplying by the transition rate and the clock frequency. Voltage therefore appears squared, which makes it the most powerful knob: ten percent less voltage is nineteen percent less power for the same activity and frequency. The counterweight is delay, which falls roughly linearly with voltage above threshold while leakage rises, so a design that reduces voltage must also reduce frequency, and the product is the energy actually saved per operation. That is the arithmetic behind voltage and frequency pairs, and behind the diminishing returns of pushing voltage down towards the threshold region.
standard.title: Derivation

blocks: A block has an activity factor of 0.1, 10 nF of switched capacitance and runs at 1.0 V and 1 GHz. Compute its dynamic power and energy per cycle.
Square the voltage for energy, then multiply by the switching rate for power.
1 watt of dynamic power and 1 nanojoule per clock cycle.
The same block runs at 0.9 V and 0.8 GHz. What happens to power and to energy per operation?
Square the new voltage for energy and multiply by the new frequency for power.
E_cycle becomes 0.1 x 10^-8 x 0.81 = 0.81 nJ. P becomes 0.81 nJ x 0.8 x 10^9 = 0.648 W.
Power falls from 1.0 W to 0.65 W and energy per operation from 1.0 nJ to 0.81 nJ, at the cost of twenty percent of the clock rate.

blocks: DP appears in production wherever an optimal sequence of decisions must be found and the subproblems repeat.

Sequence alignment is the clearest example: the diff algorithm in Git and in every code review tool is a variant of longest common subsequence. blocks: Earthwork Volumes: Trapezoidal and Prismoidal Rules is a core model in Estimating & Costing: Longitudinal earthwork volumes come from cross-section areas at intervals, and the rule chosen to interpolate between them shifts the answer - and the payment - by several percent. The model is used within these stated limits: Even number of intervals for the prismoidal rule; the trapezoidal rule assumes linear area change and typically overestimates volumes where the ground profile is convex (areas shrinking), the prismoidal corrects toward the true parabolic interpolation.
advanced.title: Formal definition

advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Earthwork is irregular, so surveyors sample it: cross-section areas perpendicular to the centreline at fixed spacing. The trapezoidal rule joins consecutive areas with straight interpolation - simple, and biased upward when the area series is convex. Simpson-style prismoidal weighting (1-4-2-...-4-1) fits parabolas between sections instead, capturing curvature in the ground and typically landing nearer the true volume. The difference matters because earthwork is paid by volume: contracts name which rule governs, and quantity-survey disputes over mass-haul diagrams often reduce to this choice.

blocks: ECG Signal Chain: Bandwidth and Common-Mode Rejection is a core model in Biomedical Instrumentation & Devices: An ECG front end must pass a 1 mV, 0.05-150 Hz differential signal sitting on volts of 50 Hz interference picked up by the body - a job for bandwidth discipline and common-mode rejection. The model is used within these stated limits: Electrode impedance imbalance converts common-mode into differential signal, so CMRR is only as good as the electrode matching; right-leg drive actively cancels the common mode in practice.

diagnostic bandwidth; monitoring narrows to 0.5-40 Hz
Electrode impedance imbalance converts common-mode into differential signal, so CMRR is only as good as the electrode matching; right-leg drive actively cancels the common mode in practice.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: The body acts as an antenna: mains fields put nearly equal voltages on both electrodes - common-mode - while the heart's dipole puts a millivolt difference between them. An instrumentation amplifier with high CMRR suppresses the common part by its dB ratio, and the band-pass keeps the diagnostically important content: the ST segment demands near-DC response (hence 0.05 Hz), while QRS detail needs the 100-150 Hz range. Electrode imbalance is the practical enemy - a 1 k ohm mismatch with 100 dB CMRR degrades effective rejection dramatically - which is why skin prep, matched electrodes and driven-right-leg circuits are part of the specification, not accessories.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: An ECG amplifier has A_d = 1000 and CMRR = 100 dB. The body picks up 2 V of 50 Hz common-mode. Find the interference reaching the output and compare with a 1 mV ECG.
100 dB = 10^5 rejection. Interference out = 1000 x 2/10^5 = 0.02 V... precisely: differential-equivalent of 2 V cm is 2/10^5 = 20 uV, amplified to 20 mV - versus the ECG's 1 mV x 1000 = 1 V output.
20 mV of mains artifact against a 1 V ECG trace - a 2% error; worse electrode imbalance or a 60 dB monitor-grade CMRR would make the trace unreadable.

blocks: The body acts as an antenna: mains fields put nearly equal voltages on both electrodes - common-mode - while the heart's dipole puts a millivolt difference between them. An instrumentation amplifier with high CMRR suppresses the common part by its dB ratio, and the band-pass keeps the diagnostically important content: the ST segment demands near-DC response (hence 0.05 Hz), while QRS detail needs the 100-150 Hz range. Electrode imbalance is the practical enemy - a 1 k ohm mismatch with 100 dB CMRR degrades effective rejection dramatically - which is why skin prep, matched electrodes and driven-right-leg circuits are part of the specification, not accessories.

blocks: An ECG amplifier has A_d = 1000 and CMRR = 100 dB. The body picks up 2 V of 50 Hz common-mode. Find the interference reaching the output and compare with a 1 mV ECG.
100 dB = 10^5 rejection. Interference out = 1000 x 2/10^5 = 0.02 V... precisely: differential-equivalent of 2 V cm is 2/10^5 = 20 uV, amplified to 20 mV - versus the ECG's 1 mV x 1000 = 1 V output.
20 mV of mains artifact against a 1 V ECG trace - a 2% error; worse electrode imbalance or a 60 dB monitor-grade CMRR would make the trace unreadable.

blocks: Minimizing total cost subject to the load constraint is a Lagrange problem: the gradient of total cost must align with the gradient of the constraint, which says every free unit's marginal cost equals the multiplier lambda. Intuition matches the math: if unit A's next megawatt is cheaper than unit B's, shifting load from B to A saves money until their slopes meet. With quadratic cost curves the marginal costs are straight lines in P, so solving the linear system plus the load balance gives the dispatch - and lambda emerges as the price the whole system pays for its marginal megawatt.

blocks: Effective Access Time and the Fault-Rate Budget is a core model in Operating Systems: The cost of virtual memory is decided by one product: page-fault rate times fault service time, which sets the maximum fault rate a system can tolerate for a given slowdown. The model is used within these stated limits: Faults are independent and the fault service time is constant; a demand-paging system with a swap device on a slow bus. The model ignores TLB shootdowns and multi-page faults.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Effective access time and its fault-rate budget
page-fault rate: faults per memory access
time to service a hit in the TLB and cache
time to service a fault, including the slow-device read and handling
the effective access time the design budget allows
Faults are independent and the fault service time is constant; a demand-paging system with a swap device on a slow bus. The model ignores TLB shootdowns and multi-page faults.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: EAT is a weighted average of the two service times, weighted by how often each occurs, so a rare event with a very large cost dominates as soon as it is no longer rare. Solving the same equation for p gives the budget: how many faults per access the design can absorb before performance leaves its target. The numbers are unforgiving because t_fault is roughly five orders of magnitude larger than t_hit. A five-percent fault rate is not a five-percent slowdown; it is a machine that spends most of its time waiting for a device.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: t_hit is 100 ns and a fault costs 10 ms. What fault rate keeps the effective access time within a 2x slowdown, that is at most 200 ns?
Convert the fault cost to the same unit, then rearrange EAT for p.
One fault per hundred thousand accesses. A 1 % fault rate would give EAT = 0.99 x 100 + 0.01 x 10,000,000 = 100,099 ns, a thousandfold slowdown.
Four processes have working sets of 60, 80, 70 and 90 pages. The machine has 256 frames. Is the set schedulable, and what is the smallest fix?
Sum the working sets and compare with the frame count.
60 + 80 + 70 + 90 = 300 pages against 256 frames, so 44 pages are missing and every process competes for frames it needs.
Not schedulable. Suspending the 90-page process brings the sum to 210 pages, which fits with 46 frames of headroom.

Faults are independent and the fault service time is constant; a demand-paging system with a swap device on a slow bus. The model ignores TLB shootdowns and multi-page faults.

blocks: EAT is a weighted average of the two service times, weighted by how often each occurs, so a rare event with a very large cost dominates as soon as it is no longer rare. Solving the same equation for p gives the budget: how many faults per access the design can absorb before performance leaves its target. The numbers are unforgiving because t_fault is roughly five orders of magnitude larger than t_hit. A five-percent fault rate is not a five-percent slowdown; it is a machine that spends most of its time waiting for a device.

blocks: t_hit is 100 ns and a fault costs 10 ms. What fault rate keeps the effective access time within a 2x slowdown, that is at most 200 ns?
Convert the fault cost to the same unit, then rearrange EAT for p.
One fault per hundred thousand accesses. A 1 % fault rate would give EAT = 0.99 x 100 + 0.01 x 10,000,000 = 100,099 ns, a thousandfold slowdown.
Four processes have working sets of 60, 80, 70 and 90 pages. The machine has 256 frames. Is the set schedulable, and what is the smallest fix?
Sum the working sets and compare with the frame count.
60 + 80 + 70 + 90 = 300 pages against 256 frames, so 44 pages are missing and every process competes for frames it needs.
Not schedulable. Suspending the 90-page process brings the sum to 210 pages, which fits with 46 frames of headroom.

blocks: Effective stress is the foundation of geotechnical design, and water control is where most failures actually originate.
Bearing capacity is computed from effective stress and the shear strength parameters

. The Terzaghi equation gives the ultimate capacity, which is then divided by a factor of safety — commonly 3 for foundations. Using total stress here overestimates capacity substantially, because it counts pore pressure as though the soil skeleton carried it.

Consolidation is the slow consequence of the same principle. Loading saturated clay raises the pore pressure immediately, and the load transfers to the soil skeleton only as the water drains. Settlement therefore continues for years, which is why buildings on clay are monitored after completion and why the leaning of some structures is a drainage problem rather than a structural one.

Excavation failures are usually water failures. Seepage into a dig raises the pore pressure and reduces effective stress; past the critical gradient the soil loses strength entirely and the base heaves. Sheet piles, wellpoints and grout curtains are all ways of controlling this, and the design is checked on the gradient rather than on the wall's strength.

Liquefaction is the extreme case. Cyclic loading from an earthquake raises pore pressure faster than it can drain, effective stress approaches zero, and the ground behaves as a liquid. This is why seismic design includes a liquefaction assessment based on soil type, density and water-table depth — it is the mechanism behind a large proportion of earthquake damage to otherwise sound structures.

blocks: Effort Estimation: Function Points and COCOMO is a core model in Software Engineering: Estimation models trade a size measurement for an effort number, and both classic models agree on one thing: effort grows superlinearly with size. The model is used within these stated limits: Basic-mode constants assume an organic (business-style) project; exponent above 1 encodes growing communication overhead, and mode multipliers shift with embedded/semidetached settings.

blocks: Lines of code are cheap to predict from comparable past projects but language-dependent; function points count user-visible capability (inputs, outputs, inquiries, files) weighted by complexity, staying language-neutral at the cost of classification judgement. COCOMO then maps size to effort through a power law: the exponent 1.05 says doubling the code costs slightly more than double the effort, because coordination - not typing - is what scales badly. Duration and staffing follow from effort with their own exponents, which is why crashing a late schedule with bodies famously backfires.

blocks: Object-oriented design in production is mostly about where the seams are, and the language features are secondary.
The most valuable habit is programming to an interface rather than an implementation. A function that takes a

interface can be tested with a fake, and a new provider can be added without touching the caller. This is polymorphism used for testability rather than for cleverness, and it is the single change that most improves a codebase's evolvability.

Deep inheritance hierarchies are the classic failure. A base class accumulates behaviour that some subclasses do not want, so it grows flags and hooks until changing it risks breaking everything below. The usual repair is composition: extract the behaviour into a collaborator and inject it. The rule of thumb — prefer composition over inheritance — exists because this failure is so common.

Encapsulation pays off most at module boundaries. A well-chosen public interface lets the internals change without affecting callers, which is what makes refactoring possible at all. Exposing internal types in a public API is the mistake that locks a design in place.

The performance question is mostly settled: virtual dispatch is cheap, but it blocks inlining, and in hot loops over millions of small calls that matters. JITs devirtualise when only one implementation is ever seen, so idiomatic code usually gets the direct call for free. Profile before restructuring for it.
