blocks: Engine Performance Maps: BSFC and the Torque-Power Curve is a core model in Internal Combustion Engines: Power is torque times speed, but efficiency is brake-specific fuel consumption - and the BSFC map shows the small island where an engine actually earns its fuel. The model is used within these stated limits: Brake values are measured at the shaft (dynamometer), after all engine losses; BSFC maps are measured per operating point, not derived from a single rating.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Brake values are measured at the shaft (dynamometer), after all engine losses; BSFC maps are measured per operating point, not derived from a single rating.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Torque reflects the mean effective pressure doing work per cycle, and multiplying by rotational rate converts work-per-cycle into power - hence the 2 pi N/60 factor. Power therefore peaks at high rpm even as torque falls, because the speed term wins until breathing limits bite. BSFC divides fuel flow by delivered power and exposes what the power curve cannot: a narrow low-island (200-250 g/kWh for good diesels) where combustion, breathing and friction losses balance best. Gearing and hybrid control strategies exist to pin operation inside that island while the power curve merely advertises the extremes.

blocks: A body is in static equilibrium when the vector sum of forces and the sum of moments about any point are both zero. A free body diagram isolates the body and shows all external forces and reactions acting on it.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Planar problems give three independent equations, which solves up to three unknowns. More unknowns than equations means the structure is statically indeterminate and needs deformation compatibility to solve.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: The equilibrium equations come from Newton's laws applied to a body at rest, and their number determines what is solvable.
At rest both accelerations are zero, so
A two-dimensional problem gives three independent scalar equations:

Three equations solve up to three unknowns. A simply supported beam has a pin (two reactions) and a roller (one) — exactly three, so it is statically determinate and solvable by equilibrium alone. Add a third support and there are four unknowns against three equations: statically indeterminate, and the solution requires deformation compatibility, which is where material stiffness enters.

Taking moments about a point where unknown forces act eliminates them from that equation, which is the standard technique for reducing simultaneous equations. Any point may be used — the result is the same — but a well-chosen one does the algebra for you.
Why the free-body diagram is not optional.
The equations above apply to the forces

the body. A force the body exerts on something else must not appear, and a contact that is forgotten leaves the balance unsolvable. Drawing the isolation first is what makes it possible to check that every contact is accounted for and no extra force has been invented.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A 10 kg beam 4 m long is simply supported and carries a 200 N point load at its centre. Find the reactions.
Draw the FBD, take moments about one support to eliminate the other reaction.
Weight = 98.1 N at 2 m, load 200 N at 2 m. Moments about A: R_B x 4 = (98.1 + 200) x 2, so R_B = 149.05 N. By vertical equilibrium R_A = 298.1 - 149.05 = 149.05 N.
Both reactions are 149.05 N, as symmetry requires.

blocks: Free-body diagrams are not an academic exercise; they are the starting point of every structural calculation, and software does not remove the need.

Finite element analysis produces equilibrium-satisfying results whether or not the model is right, so the diagram remains the check. A reaction that does not equal the applied load, or a moment at a pinned support, means the boundary conditions are wrong — and the software will happily report a detailed stress field regardless. Hand-checking the global equilibrium of an FEA result is standard practice for exactly this reason.

Statically indeterminate structures are the norm rather than the exception. Continuous beams, portal frames and moment-resisting connections all have more unknowns than equilibrium equations, so their internal forces depend on relative stiffness. That has a real consequence: a stiffer member attracts more load, so changing a section size changes the force distribution, which is why iteration is normal in structural design.

The assumption of rigidity is where models most often go wrong. Real connections are semi-rigid, foundations settle, and temperature changes induce forces in redundant structures. A pinned connection that is actually partly fixed develops moments the design did not allow for — a classic cause of unexpected cracking.

The discipline that prevents most errors is unchanged: isolate the body, include every contact and the self-weight, and check that the number of unknowns matches the number of available equations before solving.

blocks: Equivalent Standard Axles and Pavement Load Accumulation is a core model in Transportation Engineering: Pavement damage grows roughly with the fourth power of axle load, so one heavy vehicle can be worth thousands of cars and the design traffic is counted in equivalent standard axles. The model is used within these stated limits: The fourth-power law is an empirical damage equivalence derived from road tests on a particular set of pavements and axle configurations; tyre pressure, suspension and climate all shift the real damage, and single, tandem and tridem axles use different reference loads.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Equivalent standard axles and cumulative traffic
axle load in the same units as the standard
the standard single axle load used in the fourth-power law
average number of standard axles per commercial vehicle

The fourth-power law is an empirical damage equivalence derived from road tests on a particular set of pavements and axle configurations; tyre pressure, suspension and climate all shift the real damage, and single, tandem and tridem axles use different reference loads.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Pavement damage accumulates from fatigue and permanent deformation, and road tests showed that the number of load applications a pavement can take falls roughly with the fourth power of axle load. That empirical exponent is what makes the arithmetic dramatic: doubling an axle's load multiplies its damage by sixteen, so a small number of overloaded trucks can consume the design life of a road built for legal traffic. The design traffic is then the sum of daily equivalent axles over the life of the pavement, each year grown by the expected traffic factor, and the resulting total selects a pavement thickness from a design chart. The same expression explains why enforcement matters more than most maintenance budgets: removing the overloaded few protects the pavement for everyone.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A single axle carries 10 tonnes. What is its damage equivalence, and what is the cumulative design traffic for an initial 1000 equivalent axles per day growing at 5 % per year over ten years?
Apply the fourth-power relation, then sum the geometric growth series.
Each 10 tonne axle equals about 2.3 standard axles and the design traffic is about 4.6 million equivalent standard axles.
What does a 20 tonne axle contribute compared with the 10 tonne axle?
The fourth power doubles four times over for a doubling of load.
ESAL = (20,000/8160)^4 = 2.451^4 = 36.1, against 2.26 for the 10 tonne axle.
36.1 against 2.26 - sixteen times the damage for twice the load, exactly as the fourth power implies.

blocks: Pavement damage accumulates from fatigue and permanent deformation, and road tests showed that the number of load applications a pavement can take falls roughly with the fourth power of axle load. blocks: Error-Budget Burn Rate and Two-Window Alerting is a core model in Site Reliability Engineering: A burn rate expresses how fast an error budget is being spent, which turns an SLO into an alerting rule: a short window catches fast burns, a longer window catches slow ones. The model is used within these stated limits: Errors are countable at the service boundary, traffic is roughly stationary across the window, and the SLO is expressed as a fraction of requests. Burn rates assume the budget is measured over the whole window rather than reset by deploys.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Burn rate against an error budget
b=(e)/(1-SLO), budget spent in a window=(b w)/(W)
observed error fraction in the window
burn rate: multiples of the sustainable error rate
length of the SLO budget window

Errors are countable at the service boundary, traffic is roughly stationary across the window, and the SLO is expressed as a fraction of requests. Burn rates assume the budget is measured over the whole window rather than reset by deploys.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: The error budget is the fraction of requests the SLO allows to fail: one minus the objective. Observed error fraction divided by that budget gives how many times faster than sustainable the service is failing. A burn rate of one spends the budget exactly over the full window, and a burn rate of fourteen spends two percent of it in an hour when the window is thirty days. Alerting on the budget rather than on raw error rates is what makes the same rule work for a high-traffic and a low-traffic service: the threshold is expressed in fractions of the budget, so the number of errors required to page scales with traffic. Two windows are used because one window cannot be both fast and quiet: a short window with a high burn rate catches a total outage in minutes, a longer window with a lower rate catches a slow bleed that a short window averages away.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: The SLO is 99.9 % over 30 days. One hour shows a 2 % error rate. What is the burn rate and how much budget did that hour consume?
The budget is 0.001. Express the hour as a fraction of the 30-day window and compare what was spent with what was allowed.

The hour is 1/720 of the window, so the budget allowed in that hour is 0.001/720 = 1.39 x 10^-6 of requests. Observed errors are 0.02 of requests, so the burn rate is 0.02/0.001 = 20 relative to flat consumption, or 20 x 720 = 14,400 in the conventional window-relative form.

Fourteen thousand times the sustainable rate. At that rate the month's entire budget would be gone in about three minutes of sustained failure, which is why a one-hour lookback at burn rate 14.4 is a page.
A service with a 99.9 % SLO records 1 error in 100,000 requests in one hour. What burn rate is that?
Divide the observed error fraction by the budget fraction, both measured over the same window.
Error fraction 1 x 10^-5 against a budget of 0.001 over 30 days scaled to the hour: 1.39 x 10^-6. Burn rate = 1 x 10^-5 / 1.39 x 10^-6 = 7.2.
A burn rate of about 7, which sits near a six-hour ticket threshold: modest, still worth a look, not worth waking anyone.

blocks: Error Propagation in a Derived Measurement is a core model in Measurements & Instrumentation: A computed quantity inherits the errors of its inputs, and the size of the inherited error depends on how the inputs are combined - which tells you which instrument to buy next. The model is used within these stated limits: Independent random errors combined in quadrature; for correlated or systematic errors the contributions add linearly instead, and a worst-case bound uses the linear sum.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Relative error in a product and in a sum
\left(\frac{\Delta z}{z}\right)^2=\left(\frac{\Delta x}{x}\right)^2+\left(\frac{\Delta y}{y}\right)^2,\qquad \Delta z=\sqrt{(\Delta x)^2+(\Delta y)^2}
derived quantity, a product of powers of the inputs
Independent random errors combined in quadrature; for correlated or systematic errors the contributions add linearly instead, and a worst-case bound uses the linear sum.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: When a result is computed from several measurements, each input's relative error contributes to the result according to the exponent it carries in the formula: for a product or ratio the relative errors add in quadrature, and for a parameter raised to a power the contribution is multiplied by that power. Uncertainties of sums and differences, by contrast, combine as absolute quantities, which is why subtracting two large nearly equal numbers amplifies relative error catastrophically. This arithmetic decides instrument selection: if one input dominates the error budget, improving any other instrument changes nothing, and the dominant contribution identifies what to buy. It also warns against deriving a quantity as a small difference of large measurements when a direct measurement is available.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: Power is computed from 100 +/- 1 V and 2.0 +/- 0.02 A. What is the power and its uncertainty?
Compute the relative error of each input, combine in quadrature, then apply the result to the product.
Relative errors are 1 % and 1 %, so the combined relative error is sqrt(0.01^2 + 0.01^2) = 1.41 %. Power = 200 W, so the uncertainty is 2.83 W.
200 W +/- 2.8 W. Both instruments contribute equally, so improving either one alone helps little.
A current of 2.0 A is sensed across a 0.1 ohm shunt accurate to 0.5 % with an amplifier accurate to 1 %. What current uncertainty results at 2 mA of resolution from an 0.8 mV converter step?
Sum the systematic contributions linearly, then convert the converter's voltage step into a current step.
Systematic bound = 1.5 % of 2.0 A = 30 mA. Converter resolution = 0.8 mV/0.1 ohm = 8 mA.
About 30 mA of systematic uncertainty and 8 mA of resolution, so the amplifier and shunt dominate and a better converter would not help.

blocks: Relative error in a product and in a sum
\left(\frac{\Delta z}{z}\right)^2=\left(\frac{\Delta x}{x}\right)^2+\left(\frac{\Delta y}{y}\right)^2,\qquad \Delta z=\sqrt{(\Delta x)^2+(\Delta y)^2}
derived quantity, a product of powers of the inputs

blocks: When a result is computed from several measurements, each input's relative error contributes to the result according to the exponent it carries in the formula: for a product or ratio the relative errors add in quadrature, and for a parameter raised to a power the contribution is multiplied by that power. Uncertainties of sums and differences, by contrast, combine as absolute quantities, which is why subtracting two large nearly equal numbers amplifies relative error catastrophically. This arithmetic decides instrument selection: if one input dominates the error budget, improving any other instrument changes nothing, and the dominant contribution identifies what to buy. It also warns against deriving a quantity as a small difference of large measurements when a direct measurement is available.

blocks: Eutectic Reactions and Reading Phase Diagrams is a core model in Materials Science & Engineering: A phase diagram is a map of stable phases versus temperature and composition, and the eutectic point is its most important landmark: the lowest-melting composition, where one liquid freezes into two solids at once. The model is used within these stated limits: Binary systems with limited solid solubility; at the eutectic, three phases coexist so the reaction runs at constant temperature until one phase is consumed - the halt on a cooling curve.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: L cooling α+β at fixed T_E, C_E
eutectic temperature and composition (e.g. 183 C, 61.9% Sn for Pb-Sn)
the two solid phases formed simultaneously
Binary systems with limited solid solubility; at the eutectic, three phases coexist so the reaction runs at constant temperature until one phase is consumed - the halt on a cooling curve.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Cooling a liquid of exactly eutectic composition reaches a point where no single solid can hold all of both elements: the remaining liquid simultaneously precipitates alternating plates of alpha and beta - the lamellar eutectic microstructure, whose fine spacing is why eutectic alloys cast well and solder flows at one sharp temperature. Off-eutectic (hypoeutectic) alloys freeze primary alpha first as temperature falls along the liquidus, then the leftover liquid hits the eutectic temperature and transforms - giving primary grains embedded in eutectic. Reading the diagram is therefore a timeline: which phase, how much (lever rule), and what texture at the end.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: Pb-Sn has a eutectic at 61.9% Sn and 183 C. Describe solidification of a 40% Sn alloy.
Trace the composition line down the diagram.

Above the liquidus: all liquid. Crossing the liquidus, primary alpha (Sn in Pb, max solubility ~19%) begins to form; the liquid enriches toward 61.9% Sn. At 183 C the remaining liquid transforms to the alpha+beta eutectic. Below, alpha also precipitates from the eutectic beta as solubility shrinks.
Final structure: primary alpha grains in an alpha+beta eutectic matrix - a hypoeutectic solder alloy whose melting range, unlike pure eutectic solder, spans from ~183 C up to its liquidus.

blocks: Evaporator Steam Economy and Multiple Effects is a core model in Heat Transfer Operations: Evaporating water costs steam, and multiple-effect evaporation recycles each kilogram's latent heat across stages - the steam economy counts how many times it gets used. The model is used within these stated limits: Each effect boils at a lower pressure than the last so the previous vapour can heat it; economies below ~0.8n reflect sensible-heat losses, boiling-point elevation and entrainment.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: economy=(kg water vaporized)/(kg steam consumed)≈ 0.8 n for n effects
kg evaporated per kg of live steam
temperature ladder shared among the effects
Each effect boils at a lower pressure than the last so the previous vapour can heat it; economies below ~0.8n reflect sensible-heat losses, boiling-point elevation and entrainment.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: A single effect condenses roughly one kilogram of steam to evaporate roughly one kilogram of water - latent heat in, latent heat out, economy near 1 minus losses. The insight of multiple effects: the vapour from effect 1 is still steam; lower effect 2's pressure until that vapour condenses at a useful temperature difference and it evaporates another kilogram. Chaining n stages multiplies the economy toward 0.8n at the price of capital, vacuum systems and shrinking per-effect temperature difference - the total Delta T from steam to condenser is a fixed budget divided n ways, so very high effect counts starve each stage.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A plant must evaporate 3,000 kg/h of water. Compare steam consumption for a single effect (economy 0.9) and a triple effect (economy 2.5).
Divide the evaporation duty by each economy.
Single effect: 3,000/0.9 = 3,333 kg/h of steam. Triple: 3,000/2.5 = 1,200 kg/h.
Steam use drops 64% - the classic trade: roughly triple the exchanger surface and a vacuum system to buy two-thirds off the largest operating cost.

blocks: Picture the channel between screw flight and barrel as a shallow duct: the barrel surface, moving at pi D N relative to the screw, drags the melt along the helix - the drag-flow term, linear in screw speed and channel depth. Opposing it, the die's resistance builds pressure that pushes melt backwards through the same channel - a Poiseuille term scaling with the cube of depth and the pressure gradient over viscosity. Net output is their difference, which explains the extruder's personality: shallow metering sections give stiff, pressure-insensitive output (good for stable tubing), deep sections give high, soft output (good for compounding), and screw speed remains the primary production dial.

blocks: Fabric Cover: Yarn Spacing, Diameter and Permeability is a core model in Textile Fibre & Fabric Engineering: How much of a fabric's area is yarn rather than hole governs its look, hand, air and water behaviour - and cover is computed from yarn diameter against spacing, system by system. The model is used within these stated limits: Circular-yarn approximation and independent-overlap estimate for the combined cover; woven geometry (crimp, flattening at intersections) shifts real values, and jam limits bound feasible spacing.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Cover factor per system and combined area cover
centre-to-centre spacing of that system (warp or weft)
cover factor of one yarn system, 0 to 1
fraction of fabric area opaque to perpendicular view
Circular-yarn approximation and independent-overlap estimate for the combined cover; woven geometry (crimp, flattening at intersections) shifts real values, and jam limits bound feasible spacing.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Each yarn system covers a fraction of the fabric plane equal to its diameter over its pitch - the cover factor. Where warp and weft overlap, area is covered twice, so the combined cover subtracts the joint probability of both systems missing a point: 1 - (1-CF_w)(1-CF_f). The number predicts function directly: high cover means opacity, wind resistance and stiffness; low cover means breathability, drape and light transmission. It also exposes the designer's levers - finer yarns at tighter spacing, or coarser yarns at open spacing - and the jam limit: spacings below roughly the yarn diameter cannot be woven because the threads physically interfere at every crossing.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A fabric uses 0.20 mm yarns at 0.25 mm spacing in both systems. Find each cover factor and the combined area cover.
Apply the per-system ratio, then the combination rule.
96% area cover - a tightly set, nearly opaque cloth; opening the spacing to 0.35 mm would drop cover to 1 - (0.43)^2 = 0.82, a breathable shirting-type structure.

blocks: Fatigue: Endurance Limit and the Goodman Line is a core model in Machine Design: Cyclic loads fail parts far below yield; the endurance limit bounds infinite life for fully reversed stress, and the Goodman line extends that bound to mean-stress reality. blocks: Crack growth under cycling makes failure a function of stress amplitude, not just peak: laboratory S-N curves flatten for steels below an endurance limit, roughly half the ultimate. Real cycles carry a mean stress too, and means steal amplitude capacity - a tensile mean stress opens cracks wider each cycle. The Goodman line is the straight-line interaction between the two limits: amplitude allowed shrinks linearly as mean stress climbs toward ultimate. Designers plot the operating point (sigma_m, sigma_a) and demand it sit inside the line, with the fatigue stress-concentration factor applied to the amplitude first.

Solve the Goodman relation for sigma_a.
sigma_a / 300 + 150/600 = 1, so sigma_a / 300 = 0.75 and sigma_a = 225 MPa.
225 MPa alternating capacity - the mean stress consumed a quarter of it before any derating factors are applied.

blocks: File system choice is driven by the workload and by what you can afford to lose, and the differences are large.

Journaling is the default for general-purpose systems — ext4, XFS, NTFS. A journal records intent before the change, so a crash leaves either the old state or the new one, never a mixture. The cost is writing some data twice, which is why databases often disable the file system journal and rely on their own write-ahead log instead.

Copy-on-write systems — ZFS, Btrfs — never overwrite in place, which gives snapshots and checksums essentially for free, and detects silent corruption that a traditional file system cannot see. The trade is fragmentation on random writes, which is why databases on ZFS need careful tuning.

Directory performance still degrades with millions of entries on some file systems. And the space reported free can differ from the space available, because of reserved blocks and delayed allocation — which is why "disk full" errors sometimes arrive when
For networked and cloud storage the inode and metadata costs dominate. A workload of a million tiny files is often far slower and more expensive than a thousand large ones holding the same bytes.

blocks: File system choice is driven by the workload and by what you can afford to lose, and the differences are large.

Journaling is the default for general-purpose systems — ext4, XFS, NTFS. A journal records intent before the change, so a crash leaves either the old state or the new one, never a mixture. The cost is writing some data twice, which is why databases often disable the file system journal and rely on their own write-ahead log instead.

Copy-on-write systems — ZFS, Btrfs — never overwrite in place, which gives snapshots and checksums essentially for free, and detects silent corruption that a traditional file system cannot see. The trade is fragmentation on random writes, which is why databases on ZFS need careful tuning.

For networked and cloud storage the inode and metadata costs dominate. A workload of a million tiny files is often far slower and more expensive than a thousand large ones holding the same bytes.

blocks: FIR Filter Length from the Transition Width is a core model in Digital Signal Processing: A linear-phase FIR filter's cost is decided by its transition width: halving the width doubles the number of taps, and the tap count is the arithmetic load you must budget for. The model is used within these stated limits: A Kaiser-window design with the usual beta chosen for the stated attenuation; the estimate excludes the constant offset of a few taps, and multiply-accumulate cost assumes no symmetry exploitation.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Tap estimate from transition width and stopband attenuation
A Kaiser-window design with the usual beta chosen for the stated attenuation; the estimate excludes the constant offset of a few taps, and multiply-accumulate cost assumes no symmetry exploitation.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: A finite impulse response filter's frequency response is the transform of its coefficients, and the sharpness of the transition between passband and stopband is set by how long the coefficient sequence is: windowing the ideal infinite response produces a transition whose width is inversely proportional to the window length. Attenuation and transition width separate cleanly - the window shape sets the sidelobe level, the length sets the transition - which is why a design procedure can estimate the length from the attenuation target and the transition width alone. The estimate is then rounded up and the filter synthesised. Because cost grows linearly with taps, transition width is the parameter that decides whether a filter fits the available real-time budget.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: Design an FIR filter with 60 dB attenuation and a transition width of 5 % of the sampling rate. Estimate the tap count.
Convert the relative transition width to radians per sample, then apply the Kaiser length estimate.
About 73 taps. Every output sample then costs 73 multiply-accumulate operations.
What is the arithmetic load of that 73-tap filter at a 48 kHz sampling rate?
Multiply taps by sample rate to get the multiply-accumulate rate.
73 taps x 48,000 samples/s = 3.5 x 10^6 multiply-accumulate operations per second per channel.
About 3.5 million multiply-accumulates per second: routine for a modern core, decisive on a small microcontroller, and halved if coefficient symmetry is exploited.

blocks: FIR versus IIR Filters: Stability and Phase Trade-Offs is a core model in Digital Signal Processing: FIR filters buy guaranteed stability and exact linear phase with taps; IIR filters buy sharp cutoffs with poles - and the choice is which property the application cannot lose. The model is used within these stated limits: Symmetric-tap FIRs have exactly linear phase; IIR stability requires all poles inside the unit circle, and IIR phase is inherently nonlinear near cutoff.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: H_{\mathrm{FIR}}(z)=\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}b_k z^{-k};\qquad H_{\mathrm{IIR}}(z)=\frac{\sum b_k z^{-k}}{1+\sum a_k z^{-k}};\qquad \tau_{\mathrm{FIR}}=\frac{N-1}{2}
constant group delay of a linear-phase FIR
Symmetric-tap FIRs have exactly linear phase; IIR stability requires all poles inside the unit circle, and IIR phase is inherently nonlinear near cutoff.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: An FIR's output is a weighted window of recent inputs: no feedback, so no poles beyond the origin, so stability is structural and the impulse response is literally finite. Symmetric coefficients make phase exactly linear - every frequency delayed by the same (N-1)/2 samples - which preserves waveform shape at the cost of delay and taps. An IIR feeds its output back, placing poles that let a few coefficients produce very sharp transitions (analog-like selectivity), but poles demand stability checks, finite precision moves them, and phase warps near the edges. The selection rule follows the application: shape matters (audio, comms) go FIR; stopband sharpness per multiply matters (biomedical, control) go IIR.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A 21-tap linear-phase FIR runs at 48 kHz. What is its group delay, and what does an elliptic IIR of order 5 save in multiplies per sample?
Apply the delay formula and compare cost orders.

tau = (21-1)/2 = 10 samples = 10/48000 = 208 microseconds, identical for all frequencies. The order-5 IIR needs roughly 11 multiplies per sample versus the FIR's 21 - and can hit a far sharper cutoff than a 21-tap FIR ever could.
208 us constant delay for the FIR; the IIR halves arithmetic and sharpens the cutoff, but pays with nonlinear phase and a pole-stability obligation.

blocks: The first law states that energy is conserved. For a closed system, Q - W = dU. For an open (control volume) system in steady state, the rate of energy entering equals the rate leaving, with enthalpy carrying the flow work.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Steady state, one inlet and one outlet, uniform properties at each section.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: The first law is a statement that energy is a state function, and the derivation makes clear why heat and work are not.
Why U is a state function.

Joule's experiments showed that the same change of state can be produced by different combinations of heat and work — stirring adiabatically raises the temperature exactly as much as adding the equivalent heat. Since the end state depends only on where the system started and ended, not on the path, there must be a property whose change equals the net energy added:

blocks: Flow Measurement: Orifice Meters and Discharge Coefficients is a core model in Fluid Flow Operations: An orifice converts flow into a pressure difference through Bernoulli's constriction trick, and the discharge coefficient carries all the real-fluid corrections the ideal analysis misses. The model is used within these stated limits: Incompressible flow, sharp-edged concentric orifice, corner or flange taps; the full ISO form multiplies by the approach factor 1/sqrt(1 - beta^4) with beta = d_o/d_pipe, and C_d drifts with Reynolds number and wear.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Q=C_d A_o√((2 Δ P)/(ρ)) (approach-velocity factor omitted)
discharge coefficient, ~0.61 for sharp-edged orifices at high Re

Incompressible flow, sharp-edged concentric orifice, corner or flange taps; the full ISO form multiplies by the approach factor 1/sqrt(1 - beta^4) with beta = d_o/d_pipe, and C_d drifts with Reynolds number and wear.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Bernoulli along a streamline says the constriction trades pressure for velocity: the vena contracta jet runs faster than the pipe, leaving a measurable pressure deficit. Ideal analysis overpredicts flow because the jet contracts below the bore area and friction eats energy; the discharge coefficient - about 0.61 for a sharp-edged orifice at high Reynolds number - folds those realities into one calibrated number. The square-root relation is the operating signature: double the flow, quadruple the differential, which is why DP transmitters report flow through a root extraction, and why orifices lose rangeability at turndown.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A sharp-edged 50 mm orifice in a water line reads 20 kPa differential. With C_d = 0.61, find the flow rate.
Compute the bore area and apply the orifice equation.
About 7.6 L/s - and at half that flow the differential would read only 5 kPa, the square law compressing the low end of the range.

blocks: Fluid statics studies fluids at rest, where shear stress is zero and pressure acts equally in all directions at a point. Pressure varies with depth as dp/dh = rho*g.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: p = p_0 + \rho g h, \qquad F_b = \rho g V_{displaced}
p = p_0 + ρ g h, F_b = ρ g V_displaced
Incompressible fluid, uniform gravity, at rest.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: The hydrostatic equation comes from a force balance on a fluid element, and everything in fluid statics follows from it.
Take a small element of height
. Pressure acts on both faces and weight acts downward, so equilibrium requires
pA - (p + dp)A - \rho g A\, dz = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; \frac{dp}{dz} = -\rho g
pA - (p + dp)A - ρ g A dz = 0 ⇒ (dp)/(dz) = -ρ g
p_2 - p_1 = -\rho g (z_2 - z_1) = \rho g h
is the depth below the reference. Pressure grows linearly with depth because the weight of fluid above grows linearly with depth.
Balancing the unknown pressure against a column of manometer fluid:
P + \rho_1 g h_1 = P_{\text{atm}} + \rho_2 g h_2
P + ρ_1 g h_1 = P_atm + ρ_2 g h_2
P_gauge = ρ_2 g h_2 - ρ_1 g h_1
in height between the two arms appears, which is why adding fluid equally to both arms changes nothing.
A given pressure supports a column of height
A 10-metre water column is impractical; 760 mm of mercury fits on a bench, which is the historical reason for the unit.
A manometer open to the atmosphere reads gauge pressure. Absolute pressure is
and confusing the two is a common and expensive error, particularly in thermodynamic calculations where absolute pressure is required.

industry.title: Real-world applications

blocks: Hydrostatic pressure governs dam design, foundation excavation and anything submerged, and getting the reference right is where mistakes happen.

Dams are the clearest application. Pressure grows linearly with depth, so the resultant force acts at one third of the height from the base, not at the midpoint. That overturning moment is what the dam's weight and shape must resist, which is why gravity dams are triangular in section. Uplift pressure under the base reduces the effective weight and is a leading cause of dam failure, so drainage galleries are designed in deliberately.

In geotechnical work the water table is the dominant variable. Raising it reduces effective stress and therefore bearing capacity, while seepage gradients can liquefy soil entirely. Excavations that fail usually do so through water rather than through the soil's strength being exceeded, which is why dewatering design is central rather than incidental.

The gauge-versus-absolute distinction is a recurring error with real consequences. Thermodynamic relations — the ideal gas law, steam tables, compressible flow — all require absolute pressure. Using a gauge reading there gives an answer that is wrong by about 101 kPa, and at low pressures that is a large relative error.

In instrumentation, differential pressure transmitters are the workhorse for level and flow measurement precisely because only the difference matters. The installation detail that causes trouble is the impulse lines: trapped gas in a liquid line or condensate in a gas line shifts the zero and produces a plausible but wrong reading.

blocks: Flywheels: Energy Fluctuation and Coefficient of Fluctuation is a core model in Theory of Machines: A flywheel is rotational energy storage that smooths a machine's speed: its inertia absorbs the cycle's energy surplus and returns the deficit within a narrow speed band. The model is used within these stated limits: Small fluctuation approximation (omega_max x omega_min ~ omega_mean^2); Delta E is read from the turning-moment diagram as the largest loop area above/below the mean-torque line.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: energy fluctuation of the cycle from the turning-moment diagram
coefficient of speed fluctuation, the smoothness spec
Small fluctuation approximation (omega_max x omega_min ~ omega_mean^2); Delta E is read from the turning-moment diagram as the largest loop area above/below the mean-torque line.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Engine torque pulses: the power stroke delivers more than the mean, other strokes less, and the difference integrates to an energy surplus then deficit each cycle. Without storage, speed swings widely. The flywheel's kinetic energy (1/2)I omega^2 rides the cycle - gaining Delta E at peak speed, returning it at minimum - and the swing between those speeds is exactly Delta E = I(omega_max^2 - omega_min^2)/2, which the small-fluctuation approximation writes as I omega^2 C_s. Designing means reading Delta E off the turning-moment diagram and choosing I so C_s meets the machine's smoothness requirement - crushers tolerate a few percent, engines and generators demand fractions of one.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A machine's turning-moment diagram shows a 400 J energy fluctuation at a mean speed of 100 rad/s, with C_s limited to 0.02. Size the flywheel.
Solve the energy-swing formula for I.
I = 2 kg m^2 holds the speed within +/-1% of mean - and the same flywheel at half speed would need four times the inertia for the same C_s.

blocks: Fouling Resistance and the Controlling Heat Transfer Resistance is a core model in Heat Transfer Operations: An overall coefficient is a sum of resistances in series, and the largest one controls both the duty and where any improvement effort should go. The model is used within these stated limits: Constant coefficients over the exchanger, no conduction resistance in a thin wall, and film coefficients that already account for the surface area ratio on each side. Phase change and flow regime changes an individual coefficient substantially.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Overall coefficient as a series of resistances
individual heat transfer coefficients for the two sides
fouling resistance on both surfaces combined

Constant coefficients over the exchanger, no conduction resistance in a thin wall, and film coefficients that already account for the surface area ratio on each side. Phase change and flow regime changes an individual coefficient substantially.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Heat must cross several resistances in series: the film on one side, the metal and any scale on it, and the film on the other side. Series resistances add as their reciprocals, so the overall coefficient is dominated by the largest single resistance, exactly as a chain is limited by its weakest link. That has two practical consequences: improving a coefficient that is not the controlling one buys almost nothing, and fouling is doubly damaging because it adds a resistance that grows with time and cannot be removed without opening the exchanger. The practical use is the first step of every exchanger troubleshooting procedure: compute the resistances, identify the largest, and act on that one.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: An exchanger has film coefficients of 2000 and 1000 W/m^2 K. Find the overall coefficient, then the value with a fouling resistance of 0.0002 m^2 K/W.
Add the reciprocals of the coefficients and the fouling resistance, then invert.
Without fouling: 1/U = 0.0005 + 0.001 = 0.0015, so U = 667 W/m^2 K. With fouling: 0.0017, so U = 588 W/m^2 K.
667 falling to 588 on fouling: an 11.8 % loss of duty for a fouling resistance that looks small in the formula.
Both film coefficients can be improved by 50 %. Which improvement gains more?
Compare the effect of raising each coefficient with the other held fixed.
Improving the 1000 W/m^2 K side gains 29 %; improving the 2000 side gains only 12 %. Effort belongs on the controlling resistance.

standard.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Heat must cross several resistances in series: the film on one side, the metal and any scale on it, and the film on the other side. Series resistances add as their reciprocals, so the overall coefficient is dominated by the largest single resistance, exactly as a chain is limited by its weakest link. That has two practical consequences: improving a coefficient that is not the controlling one buys almost nothing, and fouling is doubly damaging because it adds a resistance that grows with time and cannot be removed without opening the exchanger. The practical use is the first step of every exchanger troubleshooting procedure: compute the resistances, identify the largest, and act on that one.
standard.title: Derivation

blocks: An exchanger has film coefficients of 2000 and 1000 W/m^2 K. Find the overall coefficient, then the value with a fouling resistance of 0.0002 m^2 K/W.
Add the reciprocals of the coefficients and the fouling resistance, then invert.
Without fouling: 1/U = 0.0005 + 0.001 = 0.0015, so U = 667 W/m^2 K. With fouling: 0.0017, so U = 588 W/m^2 K.
667 falling to 588 on fouling: an 11.8 % loss of duty for a fouling resistance that looks small in the formula.
Both film coefficients can be improved by 50 %. Which improvement gains more?
Compare the effect of raising each coefficient with the other held fixed.
Improving the 1000 W/m^2 K side gains 29 %; improving the 2000 side gains only 12 %. Effort belongs on the controlling resistance.

blocks: Four-Bar Linkages and Grashof's Criterion is a core model in Theory of Machines: Whether a four-bar linkage can rotate a link fully depends on one length inequality - Grashof's condition - and which link is grounded decides the mechanism's personality. The model is used within these stated limits: Planar four-bar with revolute joints; when satisfied, grounding the shortest link gives a double-crank (drag-link), grounding a link adjacent to the shortest gives a crank-rocker; when violated, every inversion is a triple-rocker.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: satisfied => at least one link fully rotates

Planar four-bar with revolute joints; when satisfied, grounding the shortest link gives a double-crank (drag-link), grounding a link adjacent to the shortest gives a crank-rocker; when violated, every inversion is a triple-rocker.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: A link can only rotate fully if it can carry its neighbours past the collinear (toggle) configurations; working those extreme positions geometrically reduces exactly to s + l <= p + q. When it holds, the shortest link sweeps full circles relative to both neighbours, and the mechanism type follows from what is fixed: shortest grounded - both side links crank (drag-link); shortest as an input side link - it cranks while the opposite rocker oscillates (crank-rocker, the workhorse); shortest as coupler - both grounded links oscillate but the coupler spins. Violate the inequality and no link ever completes a revolution.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: Classify a four-bar with links 2, 4, 6, 8 cm when the 2 cm link is grounded, and when the 8 cm link is grounded.
Test Grashof, then apply the inversion rules.
s + l = 2 + 8 = 10 and p + q = 4 + 6 = 10: satisfied (equal case - change-point mechanism). Grounding the shortest (2 cm) gives a drag-link: both other grounded-neighbours rotate fully.
Grashof-satisfied; shortest grounded -> double-crank behaviour. With 2,4,6,9 instead (s+l=11 > 10), every inversion would be a triple-rocker.

blocks: Fourier's law says the heat flux is minus k times the temperature gradient. The minus sign puts the flow in the direction of decreasing temperature.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Steady state, constant k, heat flow only along x, no generation inside the slab.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: The flux definition is q'' = -k dT/dx. Multiply by the area to get the rate. For steady state with constant k and no generation, dT/dx is constant, so the derivative is (T_cold - T_hot) / L if x increases toward the cold face. The two minus signs — the law, and the falling temperature — give a positive heat flow from hot to cold equal to k A (T_hot - T_cold) / L.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A 0.10 m brick wall, k = 0.70 W/(m·K), area 12 m^2, has faces at 30 °C and 10 °C. Find the steady heat flow.
The temperature difference is 20 K. Thickness is 0.10 m.
1680 W from the hot face to the cold face.

A homogeneous slab with a defined freezing point and constant properties, ignoring the sensible heat above and below the freezing range and the effect of the growing ice front's changing conductivity. Real freezing times are somewhat longer, and the relation is used for comparison and design rather than for specification.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: As a product freezes, an ice front advances inward and latent heat must be conducted from that front out to the cold surface. Writing the heat balance at the interface gives a relation in which the time is proportional to the latent heat and inversely proportional to the temperature difference that drives the removal, with two terms: one describing the surface resistance to heat transfer and one describing conduction through the already frozen layer. For a slab the conduction term carries the thickness squared, which is the crucial scaling: doubling thickness quadruples the conduction path length. The practical content is that freezing thick products is disproportionately slow and that surface heat transfer matters only while the frozen layer is thin - which is why blast freezing works well for thin products and poorly for thick blocks.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A 5 cm thick slab with density 1000 kg/m^3, latent heat 300 kJ/kg, surface coefficient 100 W/m^2 K, conductivity 1.5 W/m K, frozen at a 20 K temperature difference, has what freezing time?
Evaluate both terms of the bracket, multiply by the latent heat factor, and take the time.
About 6875 seconds, or 1.9 hours, for a 5 cm slab in that freezer.
The product is reduced to 2.5 cm thick. What is the new freezing time?
Both terms scale with thickness, one linearly and the other with thickness squared.
About 2657 seconds, or 0.74 hours: halving the thickness cut the freezing time by 2.6 times while halving the throughput volume per unit.

blocks: Frequency Response and Bode Plot Asymptotes is a core model in Signals & Systems: A Bode plot sketches gain and phase against frequency with straight-line rules: every pole bends the gain down 20 dB per decade at its corner frequency. The model is used within these stated limits: Asymptotes are sketches: true gain at the corner is 3 dB below the intersection, and each zero adds +20 dB/decade instead.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: f_{c}=\frac{1}{2\pi RC},\qquad |H|\ \text{falls}\ -20\ \mathrm{dB/decade\ per\ pole\ above}\ f_c
f_c=(1)/(2π RC), |H| falls -20 dB/decade per pole above f_c
resistance and capacitance setting the corner
Asymptotes are sketches: true gain at the corner is 3 dB below the intersection, and each zero adds +20 dB/decade instead.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: At low frequency the capacitor's impedance 1/(j omega C) dwarms R and the output follows the input; at high frequency the capacitor shorts and the output collapses. The crossover is where the two impedances are equal - omega RC = 1 - giving the corner frequency and the exact -3 dB point. Away from the corner the ratio changes by a factor of ten per decade of frequency, which is 20 dB per decade on a log-gain plot; stacking poles and zeros adds their slopes, so a whole transfer function becomes a piecewise-linear sketch before any computation.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: An RC low-pass has R = 1 k ohm and C = 1 uF. Find the corner frequency and the asymptotic gain 10 times above it.
Apply the corner formula, then the slope rule.
f_c = 1 / (2 pi x 1000 x 1e-6) = 1 / (6.283e-3) = 159 Hz. One decade above (1.59 kHz) the single-pole asymptote gives -20 dB, i.e. gain 0.1.
159 Hz corner; about 0.1 V out per 1 V in at 1.59 kHz (true value slightly below the asymptote).

blocks: Freshness Lifetimes and Origin Load is a core model in Web Technologies: Caching reduces origin load as a function of freshness lifetime, and the same arithmetic predicts the stampede that a deployment can cause when every cached object expires at once. The model is used within these stated limits: Each object expires once per lifetime, the cache is shared and effective, and traffic is steady. Objects that are never requested again contribute no load, so the estimate is an upper bound.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Origin requests per second from expiring cache entries
number of cacheable objects in active use
origin requests per second caused by revalidation
lifetime with a jitter band applied
Each object expires once per lifetime, the cache is shared and effective, and traffic is steady. Objects that are never requested again contribute no load, so the estimate is an upper bound.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: A cached response is authoritative for T seconds, after which the next request revalidates or refills it. That makes the origin's revalidation rate one per object per lifetime, independent of how popular each object is: a popular object is served many times between expirations while an unpopular one is served once. The consequence is that origin load is inversely proportional to the lifetime, so doubling a lifetime halves revalidation traffic. It also means the object count matters more than the request rate, which is why a fleet of 100,000 objects with a sixty-second lifetime generates about 1,600 revalidations per second no matter how much traffic arrives. A deployment that invalidates everything at once converts that steady rate into a single burst, so lifetimes carry jitter and the cache serves stale content briefly while one request refills.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: Three thousand objects are actively requested and the freshness lifetime is 60 seconds. What revalidation rate does the origin see?
Divide the object count by the lifetime.
R = 3,000/60 = 50 requests per second. With a 600-second lifetime: 3,000/600 = 5 requests per second.
Fifty requests per second, falling to five if the lifetime is raised tenfold. The load is set by object count and lifetime, not by popularity.
A deployment flushes 100,000 objects from a cache. What burst hits the origin, and how do you flatten it?
Count the objects and describe the lifetime mechanism that removes the synchronised flush.
One request per object arrives together: 100,000 requests in the flush window.
Apply a jitter band of plus or minus 10 % to lifetimes and a stale-while-revalidate window so each object is refilled by a single request while the cache serves stale content.

blocks: A cached response is authoritative for T seconds, after which the next request revalidates or refills it. That makes the origin's revalidation rate one per object per lifetime, independent of how popular each object is: a popular object is served many times between expirations while an unpopular one is served once. The consequence is that origin load is inversely proportional to the lifetime, so doubling a lifetime halves revalidation traffic. It also means the object count matters more than the request rate, which is why a fleet of 100,000 objects with a sixty-second lifetime generates about 1,600 revalidations per second no matter how much traffic arrives. A deployment that invalidates everything at once converts that steady rate into a single burst, so lifetimes carry jitter and the cache serves stale content briefly while one request refills.

blocks: Friction: Static Limit, Kinetic Slide and the Friction Angle is a core model in Engineering Mechanics: Static friction matches the applied push up to a ceiling of mu_s N; past that ceiling the body slides with a smaller, roughly constant kinetic friction. The model is used within these stated limits: Dry (Coulomb) friction between rigid bodies; coefficients are experiment-dependent ranges, and the model ignores speed and contact-area effects to first order.

advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Surface asperities interlock and bond at micro-contacts. Breaking those bonds takes more force than keeping a sliding body moving, which is why mu_s exceeds mu_k. On an incline, the weight component down the slope grows as sin(theta) while the normal force shrinks as cos(theta); sliding begins when tan(theta) reaches mu_s - the friction angle is therefore a measurable property, obtained by tilting until motion starts.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A 20 kg crate rests on a floor with mu_s = 0.40. What horizontal push starts it moving? (g = 9.81 m/s^2)
Compute the normal force, then the static ceiling.
N = mg = 20 x 9.81 = 196.2 N. F_max = 0.40 x 196.2 = 78.5 N. Any push beyond 78.5 N breaks static grip; after that only mu_k N resists.

blocks: Functions, Scope, and the Call Stack is a core model in Programming Fundamentals: Every call pushes an activation record holding arguments, locals and the return address; scope rules decide which names a line of code can see, and the stack decides what exists right now. The model is used within these stated limits: Assumes fixed-size frames; recursion depth grows d at runtime, which is why unbounded recursion exhausts a finite stack.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Stack cost of a call chain (an accounting identity, not a physical law)
stack memory held by the chain
Assumes fixed-size frames; recursion depth grows d at runtime, which is why unbounded recursion exhausts a finite stack.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: A call must remember where to return and keep the callee's locals separate from the caller's, so the runtime pushes one frame per active call and pops it on return - last in, first out, matching the nesting of calls exactly. Name resolution walks from the innermost visible scope outward, which is why a local shadows a global of the same name and why two functions can each own a variable called total.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A recursive function uses a 48-byte frame and recurses 1,000 deep. How much stack does the chain hold, and what happens at depth 100,000 on an 8 MB stack?
Multiply depth by frame size and compare with the limit.
1,000 x 48 B = 48,000 B ~ 47 KB - harmless. At 100,000: 100,000 x 48 B = 4.8 MB, which fits an 8 MB stack but leaves little margin; a slightly larger frame would overflow it.
47 KB at depth 1,000; 4.8 MB at depth 100,000 - deep recursion is a memory budget, not a free abstraction.

blocks: Gaussian Plume Dispersion and Stack Height is a core model in Environmental Engineering: The ground-level concentration from a stack falls rapidly as the effective stack height rises, which is why stack height and buoyancy are the strongest controls on local air quality. The model is used within these stated limits: A continuous point source in steady, homogeneous turbulence with a Gaussian distribution in both cross-sections, no deposition or chemical reaction, and dispersion coefficients taken from the atmospheric stability class.
advanced.title: Formal definition

horizontal and vertical dispersion coefficients at the receptor distance
effective stack height including plume rise
ground-level concentration on the plume centreline

A continuous point source in steady, homogeneous turbulence with a Gaussian distribution in both cross-sections, no deposition or chemical reaction, and dispersion coefficients taken from the atmospheric stability class.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: A plume released from a stack spreads by turbulent diffusion as it travels downwind, and the concentrations across the resulting cone are approximately Gaussian, so the centreline concentration is the emission rate divided by the dilution the wind has produced - the product of wind speed and the two dispersion widths. The exponential factor accounts for the distance of the plume centre above the ground: a plume that is high relative to its own vertical spread delivers much less to ground level. Because the exponent is negative and quadratic in the height ratio, the reduction is dramatic: doubling the effective stack height raises the exponent fourfold, which can cut the ground-level concentration by more than an order of magnitude. The same expression with a different H explains the effect of plume rise from hot gases.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A stack emits 10 g/s in a 3 m/s wind. At the receptor, dispersion coefficients are 25 m horizontally and 20 m vertically with an effective stack height of 30 m. Find the ground-level concentration.
Evaluate the pre-exponential dilution term, then apply the exponential factor for height.
About 344 micrograms per cubic metre on the centreline, which is the sort of number compared against a short-term air quality limit.
The stack is rebuilt so the effective height becomes 60 m. What is the concentration now?
Only the exponential term changes, with the height ratio squared.
About 11.8 micrograms per cubic metre, a 29-fold reduction from doubling the effective stack height at this distance.

blocks: Gauss's Law Applied: Fields from Symmetric Charge is a core model in Electromagnetic Fields: When charge distribution has enough symmetry, Gauss's law turns a hard integral into an algebra problem: flux out equals charge enclosed, and symmetry says the field is constant on the Gaussian surface you choose. The model is used within these stated limits: Usable directly only with spherical, cylindrical or planar symmetry; without symmetry the law still holds but cannot be solved for E by inspection.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Gauss's law and the point-charge result

field magnitude on a surface where symmetry makes it constant
Usable directly only with spherical, cylindrical or planar symmetry; without symmetry the law still holds but cannot be solved for E by inspection.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: The flux integral counts field lines leaving a closed surface, and the divergence theorem ties that to the charge inside. The engineering move is choosing the surface to match the symmetry: a sphere around a point charge, a cylinder around a line charge, a pillbox across a charged sheet. On each, the field is perpendicular and constant over the faces that matter, so the integral collapses to E times a known area - set equal to Q_enclosed over epsilon_0 and the field pops out with no vector calculus left.

industry.title: Real-world applications

blocks: Graph algorithms are load-bearing infrastructure, and the representation choice usually matters more than the algorithm.

Routing protocols are the canonical use. OSPF runs Dijkstra over a graph of routers, and BGP reasons about paths across autonomous systems. Build systems resolve dependency graphs and detect cycles with DFS — a circular import is literally a cycle in that graph. Package managers, task schedulers and spreadsheet recalculation all do topological sort.
Social and recommendation systems run BFS-like traversals for friend suggestions and reachability, usually bounded to two or three hops because the graph is enormous.

Sparse graphs dominate in practice, so adjacency lists win over matrices. A matrix for a million-node graph needs a terabyte; a list needs memory proportional to the edge count. The exception is dense graphs and GPU work, where the regular memory layout of a matrix allows parallelism that a list cannot.

blocks: Grid Emission Factors: Average, Marginal and What a Saving Really Avoids is a core model in Environmental Studies: Every kilowatt hour saved avoids a different amount of carbon depending on which generator would have supplied it, and the difference between average and marginal factors is where most carbon claims go wrong. The model is used within these stated limits: A grid whose emission factor is reported for a defined year and boundary; the marginal factor depends on which plant responds to the change in demand, which varies by hour and season. Life-cycle factors include construction and fuel, while operational factors count combustion only.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Emissions from electricity and the avoided-emission question
emission factor of the supply being considered

A grid whose emission factor is reported for a defined year and boundary; the marginal factor depends on which plant responds to the change in demand, which varies by hour and season. Life-cycle factors include construction and fuel, while operational factors count combustion only.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Electricity is supplied by a mix of generators, and the average emission factor is simply the total emissions divided by total generation. Introducing a change in demand, however, is answered by the marginal generator, which is the plant that ramps to follow the load - often the most expensive and most carbon-intensive plant on the system, or a gas peaker rather than the coal base load. The two factors therefore answer different questions: the average is appropriate for reporting the carbon content of consumed electricity, while the marginal is the right figure for claiming a saving from avoided consumption or for valuing a storage or efficiency project. Confusing them overstates or understates savings, and the error is largest in systems with a wide spread between base-load and peaking emissions.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A household consumes 1,000 kWh in a month with an average grid factor of 0.71 kg CO2 per kWh. What are its emissions, and what would it report using a marginal factor of 0.9?
Multiply the energy by each factor and compare.
Average: 1000 x 0.71 = 710 kg CO2. Marginal: 1000 x 0.9 = 900 kg CO2.
710 kg on the average factor and 900 kg on the marginal factor: the same consumption, reported 27 % higher or lower depending on the chosen convention.
Replacing ten 60 W lamps with 9 W lamps used 5 hours a day saves what energy and emissions per year?
Compute daily energy saved, extrapolate to a year, then apply the factor.
Power saved = 10 x (60 - 9) = 510 W, so daily saving = 0.51 x 5 = 2.55 kWh and annual saving = 2.55 x 365 = 931 kWh. At 0.71 kg/kWh that is 661 kg of CO2.
About 931 kWh and 661 kg of CO2 a year for one swapped bank of lamps, with the marginal-factor figure 27 % higher.

blocks: Emissions from electricity and the avoided-emission question
emission factor of the supply being considered

A grid whose emission factor is reported for a defined year and boundary; the marginal factor depends on which plant responds to the change in demand, which varies by hour and season. Life-cycle factors include construction and fuel, while operational factors count combustion only.
standard.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Electricity is supplied by a mix of generators, and the average emission factor is simply the total emissions divided by total generation. Introducing a change in demand, however, is answered by the marginal generator, which is the plant that ramps to follow the load - often the most expensive and most carbon-intensive plant on the system, or a gas peaker rather than the coal base load. The two factors therefore answer different questions: the average is appropriate for reporting the carbon content of consumed electricity, while the marginal is the right figure for claiming a saving from avoided consumption or for valuing a storage or efficiency project. Confusing them overstates or understates savings, and the error is largest in systems with a wide spread between base-load and peaking emissions.
standard.title: Derivation

blocks: A household consumes 1,000 kWh in a month with an average grid factor of 0.71 kg CO2 per kWh. What are its emissions, and what would it report using a marginal factor of 0.9?
Multiply the energy by each factor and compare.
Average: 1000 x 0.71 = 710 kg CO2. Marginal: 1000 x 0.9 = 900 kg CO2.
710 kg on the average factor and 900 kg on the marginal factor: the same consumption, reported 27 % higher or lower depending on the chosen convention.
Replacing ten 60 W lamps with 9 W lamps used 5 hours a day saves what energy and emissions per year?
Compute daily energy saved, extrapolate to a year, then apply the factor.
Power saved = 10 x (60 - 9) = 510 W, so daily saving = 0.51 x 5 = 2.55 kWh and annual saving = 2.55 x 365 = 931 kWh. At 0.71 kg/kWh that is 661 kg of CO2.
About 931 kWh and 661 kg of CO2 a year for one swapped bank of lamps, with the marginal-factor figure 27 % higher.

blocks: Hash Functions, Integrity and the Length-Extension Pitfall is a core model in Cryptography & Network Security: A cryptographic hash compresses any message to a fixed fingerprint that is collision-resistant and one-way - but Merkle-Damgard designs leak a forgery channel if you improvise a MAC from them. The model is used within these stated limits: Applies to Merkle-Damgard hashes (MD5, SHA-1, SHA-256); HMAC and SHA-3 are structurally immune, and integrity checking assumes the hash itself reaches you untampered.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: H(m) fixes a fingerprint; MAC=H(k m) is forgeable
Applies to Merkle-Damgard hashes (MD5, SHA-1, SHA-256); HMAC and SHA-3 are structurally immune, and integrity checking assumes the hash itself reaches you untampered.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Iterated hash functions process a message block by block, carrying an internal state. The state after hashing k || m is exactly what the function would hold at the start of hashing m's continuation - and the padding is computable from the length alone. So an attacker holding H(k || m), m and the length can append blocks and compute the new digest without ever knowing k: a forged 'signed' message. HMAC avoids this by hashing twice with two derived keys, breaking the attacker's ability to resume the internal state.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: An API 'signs' requests as H(secret || query) with SHA-256, and query = 'amount=10'. An attacker sees one valid signature. Can they forge 'amount=10&fee=999'?

Yes. The attacker knows the message and its length, so they can reconstruct SHA-256's padding, resume the compression from the observed digest, absorb '&fee=999' (with glue padding), and output a valid signature for the extended message - no secret knowledge required.
Forgery succeeds against H(k || m); the fix is HMAC-SHA256, whose nested construction cannot be resumed.

blocks: Hash tables are the most-used data structure in production software, and most of the engineering effort goes into the hash function and the collision policy rather than the table.
Hash joins are how databases join two large tables: hash the smaller side into memory, then stream the larger side through it. This turns an
and is one of the single biggest query-performance levers.

Cryptographic hashing for integrity and deduplication uses the same structure with a very different hash function. Content-addressable storage — Git objects, Docker layers, backup deduplication — names each blob by its hash, so identical content is stored once. That is a hash table used as a filesystem index.
The adversarial case matters for anything exposed to the network. If an attacker can choose keys that all collide, they can force

lookups and turn a fast service into a denial of service. This has been exploited against web frameworks through crafted form parameters, which is why production hash functions are randomised per process.

blocks: Haulage Cycles: Truck Productivity and Fleet Matching is a core model in Mine Planning & Operations: A haul fleet's output is trucks times trips times payload, and matching the loader's capacity to the trucks' cycle time is what turns equipment rates into tonnes per shift. The model is used within these stated limits: Steady cycle times over the shift; grades and rolling resistance live inside t_cycle's haul leg, and the MF definition varies slightly by convention but always compares the two queues.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: load + haul + dump + return + spot time
match factor: 1.0 = balanced, <1 = trucks queue-starved, >1 = loader waits
Steady cycle times over the shift; grades and rolling resistance live inside t_cycle's haul leg, and the MF definition varies slightly by convention but always compares the two queues.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: One truck's productivity is trips per hour times payload - and the cycle time, dominated by the loaded haul against the grade, sets the trips. A fleet's productivity is not simply that times truck count: if the match factor is below one, trucks arrive at the loader faster than it can fill them and queue; above one, the loader idles waiting for empties. Both queues are money - idle capital at 2 million rupees an hour for a large truck - so fleet sizing solves MF = 1 first, then rounds to whole trucks and checks the shift's tonnage target. Cycle-time simulation refines this against grade profiles and dispatch systems that reassign trucks dynamically.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A 60-tonne truck's cycle is 30 min and the shovel loads one truck in 6 min. Find per-truck productivity and the truck count that balances the shovel.
P_truck = (60/30) x 60 = 2 x 60 = 120 t/h per truck. Balanced fleet: N = t_cycle/t_load = 30/6 = 5 trucks, giving the shovel 600 t/h.
Five trucks per shovel at 600 t/h - a sixth truck (MF = 1.2) would leave the shovel waiting 20% of the time, adding tonnes only if truck downtime is frequent.

blocks: Priority queues are how schedulers decide what runs next, and the heap is usually the right implementation.

Operating system schedulers use multi-level feedback queues rather than a single heap, because they need several priority classes with different time quanta, but within each level the selection is a priority queue. Event-driven simulators — network simulators, discrete-event models of a factory — keep scheduled events in a heap and pop the earliest, which is the whole of the simulation loop.
Dijkstra's algorithm and A* both depend on a priority queue, so their performance is the priority queue's performance. Using a binary heap gives
; a Fibonacci heap improves the asymptotics but the constant factors mean the binary heap usually wins in practice.

blocks: Priority queues are how schedulers decide what runs next, and the heap is usually the right implementation.

Operating system schedulers use multi-level feedback queues rather than a single heap, because they need several priority classes with different time quanta, but within each level the selection is a priority queue. Event-driven simulators — network simulators, discrete-event models of a factory — keep scheduled events in a heap and pop the earliest, which is the whole of the simulation loop.
Dijkstra's algorithm and A* both depend on a priority queue, so their performance is the priority queue's performance. Using a binary heap gives
; a Fibonacci heap improves the asymptotics but the constant factors mean the binary heap usually wins in practice.

blocks: Hydraulic Jump and Specific Energy is a core model in Hydraulics & Hydraulic Machinery: A supercritical flow can return to subcritical only through a hydraulic jump - an abrupt, energy-destroying transition whose conjugate depths follow from momentum, not energy. The model is used within these stated limits: Horizontal rectangular channel, hydrostatic pressure at the control sections; momentum conserves across the jump while energy does not - the loss is the point.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Conjugate depth relation and jump energy loss
sequents (conjugate) depths before and after the jump
specific energy destroyed in the jump
Horizontal rectangular channel, hydrostatic pressure at the control sections; momentum conserves across the jump while energy does not - the loss is the point.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Specific energy E = y + v^2/2g has two depths for every value above the minimum: the shallow supercritical branch and the deep subcritical one. Energy alone cannot connect them - that would require passing over the critical hump - but momentum can: applying the momentum principle across the abrupt transition yields the conjugate-depth relation in terms of the upstream Froude number. The energy difference between the two depths is destroyed as turbulence, which is exactly why stilling basins below spillways deliberately provoke a jump: it converts destructive kinetic energy into heat within a protected concrete apron.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A spillway apron receives flow at Froude number 3 and depth 0.5 m. Find the conjugate depth and the energy dissipated.
Apply the conjugate-depth relation, then the loss formula.
The jump deepens 0.5 m to 1.89 m and destroys 0.71 m of head - about 35% of the incoming specific energy, dissipated as turbulence inside the basin.

alone, because the leftmost prefix is what the tree is sorted by.

blocks: Induced Drag, Aspect Ratio and the Lift-to-Drag Trade is a core model in Aerodynamics & Flight Mechanics: Wings make lift by deflecting air downward, and that same mechanism produces drag that falls as the wing gets longer and thinner - which is why gliders have long wings and fighters do not. The model is used within these stated limits: Subsonic attached flow with an elliptical or near-elliptical spanwise loading, and a drag polar that is parabolic in lift coefficient. Compressibility, separation and interference all raise the drag above this estimate.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Induced drag coefficient and its share of total drag
span efficiency factor, about 0.7 to 0.9 for a clean wing
aspect ratio: span squared divided by area

Subsonic attached flow with an elliptical or near-elliptical spanwise loading, and a drag polar that is parabolic in lift coefficient. Compressibility, separation and interference all raise the drag above this estimate.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Lift is produced by deflecting air, and the trailing vorticity that goes with it induces a downwash that tilts the lift vector backwards, creating a drag component proportional to the square of the lift coefficient. The same physical picture explains the aspect-ratio dependence: a long wing distributes its vorticity over a greater span, so the downwash and the induced drag fall. Total drag is the sum of the parasite term, which is roughly constant, and the induced term, which grows with the square of lift coefficient, so the lift-to-drag ratio has a best value at one particular speed - and that speed is precisely where the two drag components are equal. This is the arithmetic behind best-glide and best-range speeds, and behind the classic design tension between aerodynamic efficiency and structural weight.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A wing with an aspect ratio of 8, a span efficiency of 0.8 and a zero-lift drag coefficient of 0.02 flies at a lift coefficient of 0.5. Find the induced drag coefficient and the lift-to-drag ratio.
Square the lift coefficient and divide by the induced-drag factor, then add the parasite term and form the ratio.
Induced drag 0.0124, total 0.0324 and a lift-to-drag ratio of 15.4 - with induced drag 38 % of the total.
Span is increased so the aspect ratio becomes 12 at the same lift coefficient. What happens to induced drag and to the lift-to-drag ratio?
Induced drag is inversely proportional to aspect ratio.
Induced drag falls by a third and lift-to-drag improves from 15.4 to 17.7, a 15 % gain for a 50 % longer span - which the structure must pay for in weight.

blocks: Industrial Networks: Determinism and Scan Cycles is a core model in Industrial Automation & PLC Systems: Control networks are judged not by average speed but by worst-case delivery - a 10 ms guaranteed cycle beats a 1 ms average with jitter, because control loops live on the guarantee. The model is used within these stated limits: Closed-loop regulation quality degrades as sampling approaches the process dynamics; hard-motion control tightens the ratio further, while slow thermal loops relax it.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Closed-loop regulation quality degrades as sampling approaches the process dynamics; hard-motion control tightens the ratio further, while slow thermal loops relax it.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: A controller acts on data whose age is bounded by the scan cycle, and control theory says sampling must be fast relative to the dynamics being controlled - the rule of thumb is ten times faster than the dominant time constant, tighter for precision motion. Determinism is what makes 'fast' meaningful: an Ethernet frame that usually arrives in 1 ms but occasionally queues 50 ms breaks the bound in the tail, where control failures live. Industrial protocols therefore replace best-effort arbitration with schedules, token passing or time slots - PROFINET IRT, EtherCAT and CIP Motion all trade raw throughput for a provable cycle - and the scan budget must cover every node's slot plus the controller's own logic execution.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A temperature loop's process time constant is 20 s; a servo axis needs 1 ms position updates. Set the scan/update cycles and explain why they differ by four orders.
Apply the sampling guideline to each loop.
Temperature: T_scan <= 20,000/10 = 2,000 ms - a 1 s PLC scan is ample. Servo: 1 ms deterministic cycle, hence a dedicated motion network segment or drive-level interpolation.
One plant, two time scales: slow loops on standard scans, motion on isochronous networks - the process time constant, not the cable speed, sets each requirement.
