blocks: Initialisation Variance and Signal Preservation is a core model in Deep Learning: A network trains because variance is preserved across layers; the standard initialisers are exactly the weight variance that keeps the forward pass from collapsing or exploding. The model is used within these stated limits: Inputs and weights are independent and zero-mean, activations are symmetric, and the layer behaves linearly in variance terms. Residual and attention blocks need their own scaling.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Inputs and weights are independent and zero-mean, activations are symmetric, and the layer behaves linearly in variance terms. Residual and attention blocks need their own scaling.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: For a layer output that sums n_in products of independent zero-mean terms, the variance of the sum is n_in times the product of the variances. Requiring the output variance to equal the input variance therefore fixes the weight variance at one over the fan-in. A rectified linear unit discards the negative half of a symmetric input, halving its variance, so the factor two restores what the activation removed. For a symmetric activation such as hyperbolic tangent, averaging the forward-pass fan-in with the backward-pass fan-out gives the balanced factor. Get this wrong in the other direction and the effect compounds: without the factor two, each ReLU layer halves the variance, and ten layers leave roughly a thousandth of the original signal.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A layer has 512 inputs and uses ReLU activations. What is the He initialisation variance and the corresponding standard deviation?
Apply the variance rule and take the square root.
Variance 3.9 x 10^-3 and standard deviation 0.0625, which is the familiar 1/sqrt(512) times sqrt(2).
A ten-layer ReLU stack uses Var(w) = 1/n_in without the factor two. What happens to the activation scale by layer ten?
Each ReLU halves the variance, so the factor compounds multiplicatively across layers.
Variance scales by 0.5^10 = 1/1024. Standard deviation scales by sqrt(1/1024) = 1/32.
Variance falls about a thousandfold and amplitude about 32-fold, so late layers see a signal too small to produce useful gradients.

standard.title: Formula and variables

blocks: For a layer output that sums n_in products of independent zero-mean terms, the variance of the sum is n_in times the product of the variances. Requiring the output variance to equal the input variance therefore fixes the weight variance at one over the fan-in. A rectified linear unit discards the negative half of a symmetric input, halving its variance, so the factor two restores what the activation removed. For a symmetric activation such as hyperbolic tangent, averaging the forward-pass fan-in with the backward-pass fan-out gives the balanced factor. Get this wrong in the other direction and the effect compounds: without the factor two, each ReLU layer halves the variance, and ten layers leave roughly a thousandth of the original signal.

blocks: A layer has 512 inputs and uses ReLU activations. What is the He initialisation variance and the corresponding standard deviation?
Apply the variance rule and take the square root.
Variance 3.9 x 10^-3 and standard deviation 0.0625, which is the familiar 1/sqrt(512) times sqrt(2).
A ten-layer ReLU stack uses Var(w) = 1/n_in without the factor two. What happens to the activation scale by layer ten?
Each ReLU halves the variance, so the factor compounds multiplicatively across layers.
Variance scales by 0.5^10 = 1/1024. Standard deviation scales by sqrt(1/1024) = 1/32.
Variance falls about a thousandfold and amplitude about 32-fold, so late layers see a signal too small to produce useful gradients.

blocks: Melt pressure inside the cavity acts on every surface, but only the component normal to the parting direction tries to open the mould - which integrates to pressure times the projected area, exactly like a piston. If clamp force falls short, the mould flashes: plastic escapes into the parting-line gap, parts weld to tooling, and dimensions drift. blocks: Interconnect Delay: Elmore Delay and RC Trees is a core model in VLSI Design: Once wires stopped being ideal, gate delay stopped being the whole story: the Elmore delay of an RC tree estimates signal arrival with one first-moment sum. The model is used within these stated limits: RC-tree topology (no resistive loops), driving step input; it estimates the first moment of the impulse response - accurate to within ~15% for typical trees, optimistic in general.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: total resistance shared between the source and node k
RC-tree topology (no resistive loops), driving step input; it estimates the first moment of the impulse response - accurate to within ~15% for typical trees, optimistic in general.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Each capacitor must charge through the resistances between it and the driver, and charging one node's capacitor also flows through the shared upstream resistance of others. The Elmore sum captures exactly that coupling: weight every capacitance by the total resistance its charging current shares with the source. The result is the dominant time constant of the tree - not the whole waveform, but a reliable 50%-delay estimate that scales correctly with wire length: doubling a uniform wire's length quadruples its RC delay, the quadratic law that made repeaters and low-k dielectrics necessary.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A two-segment interconnect: R1 = 1 k ohm feeding C1 = 1 pF, then R2 = 1 k ohm feeding C2 = 1 pF at the far end. Estimate the delay at C2.
tau_D = R1(C1 + C2) + R2 C2 = 1000 x 2e-12 + 1000 x 1e-12 = 2 ns + 1 ns = 3 ns. The 50% arrival is roughly 0.69 x tau_D = 2.1 ns.
About 2-3 ns - and note R1 carries both capacitors' current, the shared-path effect the formula encodes.

standard.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Each capacitor must charge through the resistances between it and the driver, and charging one node's capacitor also flows through the shared upstream resistance of others. The Elmore sum captures exactly that coupling: weight every capacitance by the total resistance its charging current shares with the source. The result is the dominant time constant of the tree - not the whole waveform, but a reliable 50%-delay estimate that scales correctly with wire length: doubling a uniform wire's length quadruples its RC delay, the quadratic law that made repeaters and low-k dielectrics necessary.
standard.title: Derivation

blocks: A two-segment interconnect: R1 = 1 k ohm feeding C1 = 1 pF, then R2 = 1 k ohm feeding C2 = 1 pF at the far end. Estimate the delay at C2.
tau_D = R1(C1 + C2) + R2 C2 = 1000 x 2e-12 + 1000 x 1e-12 = 2 ns + 1 ns = 3 ns. The 50% arrival is roughly 0.69 x tau_D = 2.1 ns.
About 2-3 ns - and note R1 carries both capacitors' current, the shared-path effect the formula encodes.

blocks: Interrupts: Latency, Priorities and ISR Design is a core model in Microprocessors & Microcontrollers: An interrupt is the processor's doorbell for asynchronous events: it bounds reaction time to roughly one instruction, and priority logic decides which doorbell wins when several ring. The model is used within these stated limits: Assumes interrupts are enabled and not masked by priority; nested interrupts require hardware priority schemes and disciplined ISR re-entrancy.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: polling loop period, whose average miss is half of it
Assumes interrupts are enabled and not masked by priority; nested interrupts require hardware priority schemes and disciplined ISR re-entrancy.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Polling forces a trade: poll often and waste cycles, poll rarely and react late - on average half the poll period late. An interrupt inverts the flow: the event signals, the processor finishes the current instruction, saves enough context to resume, and jumps through a vector table to the handler - so worst-case latency is one instruction plus dispatch, independent of how rare events are. Priority logic (fixed levels or a controller like the 8259) resolves simultaneous requests and decides whether a running ISR may itself be interrupted. The ISR contract follows from the mechanism: do the urgent minimum, defer the slow work, and touch shared state carefully because you run at an arbitrary point in the main program.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A 1 ms polling loop watches a sensor that can change at any time; interrupts on the same chip respond within a 0.5 us worst-case instruction plus 0.5 us dispatch. Compare reaction times.
Polling averages T/2 = 0.5 ms delay and costs CPU on every pass. Interrupt delay is bounded by about 1 us worst case.
About 500x faster worst-case response, with zero idle cost - and the ISR keeps the urgent path to a few microseconds by deferring processing.

blocks: Inverse Kinematics and Workspace Limits for a Planar Arm is a core model in Robotics Kinematics & Control: Forward kinematics maps angles to a tip position; inverse kinematics runs it backwards - solving for the angles that reach a target, and refusing targets outside the workspace annulus. The model is used within these stated limits: Reachable targets satisfy (L1-L2)^2 <= x^2+y^2 <= (L1+L2)^2; beyond the workspace cos(theta2) leaves [-1,1] and no real solution exists.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Reachable targets satisfy (L1-L2)^2 <= x^2+y^2 <= (L1+L2)^2; beyond the workspace cos(theta2) leaves [-1,1] and no real solution exists.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: The distance from base to target fixes theta2 through the law of cosines applied to the link triangle - one equation, two mirror solutions (elbow up/down) that a robot must choose between by convention or obstacle context. Theta1 then points the first link at the target minus the wrist offset the bent elbow introduces. The solvability condition is geometric: the target must lie within the outer circle the fully stretched arm sweeps and outside the inner circle the folded arm cannot cross - the annular workspace. Near the boundaries the two solutions merge and the arm loses a degree of freedom: the shoulder singularity that motion planners avoid.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A two-link arm has L1 = L2 = 1 m. Solve for joint angles reaching the target (1, 1).
Apply the IK formulas, elbow-up branch.
r^2 = 2. cos(theta2) = (2 - 1 - 1)/(2 x 1 x 1) = 0, so theta2 = 90 degrees. theta1 = atan2(1,1) - atan2(sin 90, 1 + cos 90) = 45 - atan2(1, 1) = 45 - 45 = 0 degrees.
theta1 = 0 degrees, theta2 = 90 degrees: link one along x, link two straight up - the tip lands exactly at (1, 1).

Why a wrong mask breaks local traffic first.

Two hosts decide whether to communicate directly by masking the destination with their own prefix. If the masks disagree they can disagree about whether the destination is on-link, and one will send to the gateway while the other expects a direct reply — which is why a misconfigured mask produces one-way failures rather than an obvious error.

industry.title: Real-world applications

blocks: Address planning is done once and lived with for years, so the decisions are made on growth rather than current need.

The standard practice is to allocate on boundaries that make future splits easy. A /24 per site allows splitting into two /25s or four /26s later without renumbering. Allocating exactly what is needed today — a /28 for twelve hosts — guarantees a painful renumber when the site grows.

NAT changed the economics. Private ranges (10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16) mean internal addressing no longer consumes public space, so most organisations use 10/8 internally and plan freely. Public addresses are now mostly reached through NAT or a load balancer, which also means the address a server sees is not the client's — a constant source of bugs in logging, rate limiting and geolocation.

IPv6 adoption is partial but real, and the planning rule inverts: with 128 bits there is no reason to conserve, so the guidance is to allocate generously — typically a /64 per link regardless of host count, because that is what stateless autoconfiguration requires. Subnetting for address conservation is an IPv4 habit that has no place in IPv6.

The operational detail that bites people is that a /31 is valid for point-to-point links under RFC 3021 but not under the usual formula, and that DHCP relay must be configured per subnet or clients on remote segments get nothing.

blocks: Irrigation Scheduling: Soil Moisture Depletion and Refill Amount is a core model in Agricultural Machinery & Irrigation Systems: The soil is a reservoir between field capacity and wilting point, and scheduling means irrigating when depletion reaches the managed allowable - then refilling exactly the deficit. The model is used within these stated limits: Root-zone-averaged contents and a uniform soil; rainfall and rising water tables reduce the irrigation amount, and stress begins before wilting point as MAD is approached.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: AW=(θ_FC-θ_WP)× Z, irrigate at depletion=MAD× AW
volumetric water content at field capacity and wilting point
plant-available water in the root zone
Root-zone-averaged contents and a uniform soil; rainfall and rising water tables reduce the irrigation amount, and stress begins before wilting point as MAD is approached.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: After saturation drains, the soil holds field capacity - the full reservoir. Roots extract water down toward the wilting point, but yield loss starts before that floor, so managers set a trigger at MAD, a chosen fraction of the available band. The depth to irrigate is the depletion since the last event - refill to field capacity, not beyond (the excess percolates past roots, carrying nitrates with it). Turning contents into millimetres is what makes the soil a measurable tank: each millimetre of root zone times the content difference is a millimetre of water the crop can actually use.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A loam holds theta_FC = 0.30 and theta_WP = 0.15 with a 500 mm root zone. Find AW, the 50% MAD trigger, and the irrigation amount at trigger.
Convert contents to millimetres of water, then apply MAD.
AW = (0.30 - 0.15) x 500 = 75 mm. Trigger depletion = 0.5 x 75 = 37.5 mm. Irrigate 37.5 mm (plus any leaching requirement) to return the profile to field capacity.
Refill 37.5 mm at the trigger - scheduling reduces to tracking depletion against a 75 mm tank with a 37.5 mm alarm line.

KCL is conservation of charge and holds at every node. KVL is conservation of energy and holds around every closed loop, provided the changing magnetic flux through the loop is negligible - otherwise Faraday's law adds an EMF term.

SPICE — and every simulator descended from it — formulates modified nodal analysis, which writes KCL at every node and adds branch equations for voltage sources. The result is a sparse linear system solved at each time step. So the law taught by hand is literally the code that runs inside every analogue design tool.

The practical skill is knowing when the lumped model stops applying. KVL assumes no changing flux through the loop, which fails at high frequency or near magnetics. A PCB trace longer than about a tenth of the signal wavelength is a transmission line, not a wire, and KVL applied across it gives a wrong answer. This is the boundary where circuit theory hands over to signal-integrity engineering.

Ground is where KCL meets reality. A "ground" node is not an ideal zero-ohm reference: it has impedance, so current flowing through it produces a voltage that appears as noise elsewhere. That is why analogue and digital grounds are separated and joined at one point, and why measuring with a long ground lead on an oscilloscope picks up noise that is not in the circuit.

The most common practical error is sign convention. Assigning current directions arbitrarily is fine — a wrong guess gives a negative answer — but changing convention partway through a calculation gives a wrong one that looks plausible.

blocks: An isolation barrier is never perfect: capacitance across it passes a displacement current proportional to frequency, capacitance and voltage. At mains frequency the current is small for picofarad-scale capacitance, but the limits for applied parts are also small - tens of microamps - so the arithmetic is not academic. The frequency dependence explains why the same barrier that is safe at 50 Hz passes twenty times the current at 1 kHz, and why high-frequency surgical and diathermy equipment is assessed under different rules. Design decisions that follow from this are straightforward: keep the barrier capacitance low, avoid high-frequency currents crossing the patient path, and verify the measured leakage rather than trusting a calculation.

blocks: Limit State Design: Partial Safety Factors is a core model in Design of Reinforced Concrete Structures: Limit-state design separates what might happen (factored loads) from what material actually delivers (divided strengths), so a single inequality guarantees a target reliability. The model is used within these stated limits: IS 456 / Eurocode-style partial factors quoted; characteristic values are 5%-fractile strengths, and other load combinations (wind, seismic) carry their own gamma_f sets.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: γ_f S_d≤ Rl(f_ck/γ_m, f_y/γ_msr), γ_f=1.5 (ULS DL+LL), γ_mc=1.5, γ_ms=1.15
load factor on the effect (moment, shear)
material factors for concrete and steel
characteristic concrete cube strength and steel yield strength
design load effect and design resistance
IS 456 / Eurocode-style partial factors quoted; characteristic values are 5%-fractile strengths, and other load combinations (wind, seismic) carry their own gamma_f sets.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Loads and strengths are both random; characteristic values pick conservative points on each distribution (rare load, weak-tail strength), and the partial factors close the remaining gap to a target failure probability. Loads are multiplied up because overloads are common and correlated; concrete is divided by 1.5 for casting variability and in-situ workmanship; steel only by 1.15 because mill production is far more consistent. The inequality reads as one statement: the factored demand must not exceed the resistance computed from the discounted materials - and every code design formula is this inequality with the factors already baked in.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A beam sees dead load moment 40 kN m and live load moment 25 kN m, using M25 concrete and Fe415 steel. Find the factored moment and the design material strengths.
Apply the ULS load combination and the material factors.
M_u = 1.5 x (40 + 25) = 97.5 kN m. Design strengths: f_ck/gamma = 25/1.5 = 16.7 MPa for concrete; f_y/gamma = 415/1.15 = 361 MPa for steel.
Design against 97.5 kN m using 16.7 MPa and 361 MPa - the partial factors have already priced in the uncertainty on both sides.

The second is numerical differentiation. The derivative is defined as a limit, but a computer cannot take one, so it uses a finite step:

The third is convergence of iterative methods. Newton-Raphson and every fixed-point iteration depend on the sequence having a limit, and they diverge or oscillate when the conditions fail. blocks: Line Balancing: Takt Time and Workstation Count is a core model in Production Planning & Control: A paced line must finish each unit within the takt - the heartbeat demand sets - and the theoretical station count is the total task time divided by that heartbeat. The model is used within these stated limits: Task times fixed and precedence-respecting; rounding up to whole stations plus precedence constraints leave idle time - the balance loss eta measures.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: T_takt=(available time)/(demand), N_min=(∑ t_i)/(T_takt), η=(∑ t_i)/(N T_takt)
Task times fixed and precedence-respecting; rounding up to whole stations plus precedence constraints leave idle time - the balance loss eta measures.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Demand sets the pace: if 480 units must ship in a 480-minute day, one unit every 60 seconds is the takt. Summing the work content and dividing gives the minimum stations any assignment could achieve - a bound, not a plan, because tasks cannot be split arbitrarily and precedence orders them. Real assignment packs tasks into stations up to the takt (largest-candidate or ranked-positional-weight heuristics), and the leftover idle time per station is the balance loss the efficiency ratio exposes. The managerial consequences follow directly: demand rises mean takt falls, and either content shrinks (method improvements) or stations multiply.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A day offers 480 productive minutes for 480 units of demand; total work content is 270 s per unit. Find takt, minimum stations, and balance efficiency at 5 stations.

blocks: Linear Programming: Graphical Method and Corner-Point Optimality is a core model in Operations Research & Optimization: A linear objective over linear constraints reaches its optimum at a corner of the feasible polygon - so solving a two-variable LP is drawing the region and pricing its vertices. The model is used within these stated limits: Feasible region bounded and non-empty; optimality at corners holds for linear problems, with unbounded or infeasible cases diagnosed separately.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: LP standard form and corner optimality
\max Z=c^{T}x\ \ \text{s.t.}\ Ax\le b,\ x\ge0;\qquad Z^{*}\ \text{occurs at a vertex}
max Z=c^Tx s.t. Ax≤ b, x≥0; Z^* occurs at a vertex
Feasible region bounded and non-empty; optimality at corners holds for linear problems, with unbounded or infeasible cases diagnosed separately.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Each constraint carves a half-plane; their intersection is a convex polygon. The objective's level sets are parallel lines, and improving Z slides the line outward - the last point it touches before leaving the polygon is always a vertex, because a flat line meeting a convex polygon tangentially meets it at a corner (or along an edge between two equal-value corners). The graphical method makes this visible in two variables: enumerate vertices, price each, read the winner. The simplex method is the same insight in high dimensions, walking vertex to vertex along improving edges, and its shadow prices (constraint duals) tell management what one more unit of a binding resource is worth.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: Maximize Z = 3x + 5y subject to x <= 4, 2y <= 12, 3x + 2y <= 18 (x, y >= 0). Solve by corner pricing.
List the feasible polygon's vertices and evaluate Z.
Optimum at (2, 6) with Z = 36 - both 2y<=12 and 3x+2y<=18 binding, x<=4 slack; the simplex method's duals would price those two resources directly.

blocks: Link Budgets and Free-Space Path Loss is a core model in Communication Systems: A radio link closes when the received power exceeds the receiver's sensitivity; free-space path loss plus a link budget is the arithmetic that answers whether it does. The model is used within these stated limits: Free-space propagation with no obstruction, ground reflection or rain. Antenna gains are in the direction of the path, and cable and connector losses must be subtracted separately.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Free-space path loss and received power
Free-space propagation with no obstruction, ground reflection or rain. Antenna gains are in the direction of the path, and cable and connector losses must be subtracted separately.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Path loss comes from the spreading of a fixed amount of power over a sphere whose area grows with the square of distance, which is the twenty-decibel-per-decade term in distance, and from the effective aperture of the receive antenna, which shrinks with the square of frequency and contributes the twenty-decibel-per-decade term in frequency. Both terms add in decibels, so a link budget is a sum: transmitted power plus both antenna gains minus path loss minus any cable loss must exceed the receiver's sensitivity by the margin the design chooses. The margin is the design decision: a link with zero margin works on a bench and fails in rain, so budgets are written with an explicit fade margin.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A 2.4 GHz link runs 1 km with 20 dBm transmit power and 6 dBi antennas. The receiver needs -90 dBm. Does the link close?
Compute the path loss, then add the gains and subtract the loss from the transmit power.
Received power about -68 dBm against a -90 dBm sensitivity, a 22 dB margin, so the link closes with room for fading.
The same link moves to 2 km. How much margin remains?
Distance enters the loss logarithmically, so doubling it adds about 6 dB.
Margin falls to about 16 dB, still adequate for a line-of-sight path but noticeably tighter in rain.

blocks: Path loss comes from the spreading of a fixed amount of power over a sphere whose area grows with the square of distance, which is the twenty-decibel-per-decade term in distance, and from the effective aperture of the receive antenna, which shrinks with the square of frequency and contributes the twenty-decibel-per-decade term in frequency. The margin is the design decision: a link with zero margin works on a bench and fails in rain, so budgets are written with an explicit fade margin.

industry.title: Real-world applications

blocks: Linked lists survive in production mainly where insertion and deletion dominate and lookup is rare. The classic case is the operating system kernel: free lists of available memory blocks, run queues of runnable threads, and inode caches are all linked structures, because blocks are constantly being allocated and released and are never searched by index.

The most common application-level use is the LRU cache, where a doubly linked list holds entries in access order and a hash table maps key to node. Removal from the middle is O(1) given the node pointer, which an array cannot offer. Redis, the Linux page cache and most database buffer pools use some form of this.

Outside those cases a linked list is usually the wrong choice on modern hardware. The pointer chasing defeats the prefetcher, and each node carries an extra word of pointer plus allocator overhead — for 8-byte payloads that is a 100% tax. Benchmarks that show arrays beating linked lists by 10x on traversal are measuring cache behaviour, not algorithmic efficiency.

blocks: Little's Law: WIP, Throughput and Lead Time is a core model in Production Planning & Control: In any steady flow system, work in process equals throughput times lead time - no assumptions about routing, variability or process detail, which is why the law is a management lever. The model is used within these stated limits: Steady state over the averaging window; remarkably assumption-free otherwise - it holds for queues, factories, hospitals and code-review pipelines alike.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: average throughput (arrival = departure rate at steady state)
average time a job spends in the system
Steady state over the averaging window; remarkably assumption-free otherwise - it holds for queues, factories, hospitals and code-review pipelines alike.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Over a long window, every job that entered also left, so counting job-time-units inside the system two ways - average count times window, versus sum of individual sojourn times - gives identical totals; dividing by the window squared yields L = lambda W. The practical reading is causal-sounding but disciplined: with throughput pinned by the bottleneck, extra WIP buys only longer lead time (and hiding places for defects). Halve WIP at constant throughput and lead time halves - the quantitative backbone of kanban pull systems, which cap WIP explicitly to make flow visible and fast.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A job shop completes 20 jobs per hour with an average lead time of 3 hours. Find WIP. What happens to lead time if WIP is capped at 30 jobs at the same throughput?
Apply L = lambda W both directions.
WIP = 20 jobs/h x 3 h = 60 jobs. Capping at 30: W = L/lambda = 30/20 = 1.5 h.
Halving WIP halves lead time to 1.5 hours at unchanged throughput - the kanban argument in one line of arithmetic.

blocks: LL(1) Parsing: FIRST and FOLLOW Sets is a core model in Compiler Design: A predictive parser chooses each production from one lookahead token, which works exactly when the alternatives' prediction sets do not overlap. The model is used within these stated limits: Requires the grammar to be left-factored and free of left recursion; k-token lookahead generalizes this to LL(k).
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: terminals that can begin strings derived from x
terminals that can appear just after variable A
the single next token driving the choice
Requires the grammar to be left-factored and free of left recursion; k-token lookahead generalizes this to LL(k).
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: A top-down parser must commit to a production before seeing the whole sentence, so each alternative must announce itself by its first possible token. FIRST collects those announcing terminals; when an alternative can vanish (derive epsilon), what follows the variable - FOLLOW - announces in its place. Two alternatives sharing an announcing token make the choice undecidable with one token of lookahead: the grammar is not LL(1), and the repair is left factoring - pull the shared prefix out and decide the suffix after consuming it.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: Is S -> aB | abD LL(1)? If not, repair it.
Compute the predict sets, then left-factor.
FIRST(aB) = {a} and FIRST(abD) = {a} - they collide on 'a'. Left-factor: S -> aX, X -> B | bD. Now after consuming 'a' the next token (b or whatever FIRST(B) holds) chooses inside X.
Not LL(1) as written; after left factoring the choice is decidable with one lookahead token.

blocks: Log-Mean Temperature Difference and Exchanger Duty is a core model in Heat & Mass Transfer: A heat exchanger's duty is its overall conductance times area times a mean temperature difference, and the logarithmic mean is the number that correctly averages the two ends of the exchanger. The model is used within these stated limits: Counter-current flow, steady state, constant overall coefficient and constant specific heats, with no phase change. Multi-pass and cross-flow arrangements need a correction factor multiplying the log-mean value.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: \Delta T_{lm}=\frac{\Delta T_1-\Delta T_2}{\ln(\Delta T_1/\Delta T_2)},\qquad Q=U\,A\,\Delta T_{lm}
Δ T_lm=(Δ T_1-Δ T_2)/(ln(Δ T_1/Δ T_2)), Q=U A Δ T_lm
terminal temperature differences at the two ends

Counter-current flow, steady state, constant overall coefficient and constant specific heats, with no phase change. Multi-pass and cross-flow arrangements need a correction factor multiplying the log-mean value.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: The driving temperature difference falls steadily from one end of an exchanger to the other, so an arithmetic mean of the two ends would overstate the duty because the heat transfer rate is proportional to the difference at every point along the area. Integrating the local rate over the whole area produces the logarithmic mean, which is always smaller than the arithmetic average and becomes equal to it only when the two terminal differences are equal. The duty then follows as conductance times area times that mean difference. The relation also exposes the limits of the machine: as the two fluids approach each other, the log-mean difference and the duty both fall, so extra area buys less and less, which is the practical limit on heat recovery.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A counter-flow exchanger has terminal differences of 80 K and 40 K, an overall coefficient of 1000 W/m^2 K and 10 m^2 of area. Find the duty.
Compute the log-mean difference from the two terminals, then multiply by U and A.
577 kW, compared with 600 kW if the arithmetic mean of 60 K had been used - the log-mean value is lower, as it must be.
The same exchanger is upgraded so that U rises to 1500 W/m^2 K. What happens to the duty, and why not more?
The duty is proportional to the coefficient at fixed area and temperature difference.

866 kW for a 50 % higher coefficient, because the terminal differences were held fixed. In practice raising the coefficient changes the outlet temperatures, which reduces the log-mean difference and cuts the gain.

blocks: Logic Families: Noise Margin and Fan-Out is a core model in Digital Electronics: Two voltage windows and two current budgets decide whether one gate's output can be another gate's reliable input - noise margin for voltage, fan-out for current. The model is used within these stated limits: DC specifications at rated supply and temperature; both margins must be positive, and mixing families requires checking every one of the four voltage numbers, not just the supply.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: output current the gate can source/sink while holding levels
DC specifications at rated supply and temperature; both margins must be positive, and mixing families requires checking every one of the four voltage numbers, not just the supply.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: A driver promises its output will stay above V_OH(min) and below V_OL(max) while sourcing/sinking its rated current; a receiver promises to read anything above V_IH(min) as 1 and anything below V_IL(max) as 0. The gap between promise and expectation is the noise budget - noise picked up between the gates must fit inside it or bits flip. Fan-out is the current version of the same contract: each input leaks a little current, and the output can feed only as many inputs as its rated source/sink current covers before its guaranteed levels sag.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A family specifies V_OH = 2.4 V, V_OL = 0.4 V, V_IH = 2.0 V, V_IL = 0.8 V, I_OH = 400 uA, I_OL = 8 mA, I_IH = 40 uA, I_IL = 0.4 mA. Find both noise margins and the fan-out.
NM_H = 2.4 - 2.0 = 0.4 V. NM_L = 0.8 - 0.4 = 0.4 V. High-side fan-out = 400 uA / 40 uA = 10; low-side = 8 mA / 0.4 mA = 20.
Noise margins 0.4 V each; fan-out = min(10, 20) = 10 - the sourcing side is the binding constraint, as in classic TTL.

blocks: Loom Production Rate and Weaving Efficiency is a core model in Textile Fibre & Fabric Engineering: How much fabric a loom produces follows from its speed and the picks per unit length, with an efficiency factor for stops - a calculation that decides machine numbers and delivery dates. The model is used within these stated limits: One weft insertion per loom revolution, a single width and a constant weft density. Wider looms and multiple beams need the same relation applied per unit width, and efficiency falls as the weft density and stoppage rate rise.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: weaving efficiency: running time over available time

One weft insertion per loom revolution, a single width and a constant weft density. Wider looms and multiple beams need the same relation applied per unit width, and efficiency falls as the weft density and stoppage rate rise.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Each loom revolution inserts one pick, so the picks per minute divided by picks per centimetre gives centimetres per minute, and multiplying by sixty gives metres per hour at ideal running. Real looms stop for weft breaks, warp breaks and beam changes, and the efficiency factor - running time divided by available time - converts the ideal figure into the delivered one. The equation is worth internalising because it carries both of weaving's levers: raising speed or reducing picks per centimetre raises production linearly, while improvements in stoppage rates raise it through efficiency, and it also caps delivery promises, since a fabric with twice the weft density takes twice as long to weave at the same speed.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A loom runs at 700 picks per minute weaving a fabric with 20 picks per centimetre at 85 % efficiency. Find the production rate.
Convert picks per minute to fabric length through the weft density, then apply the efficiency.
About 17.9 metres per hour per loom, which sets the loom count for a given order.
The same loom weaves a denser fabric at 30 picks per centimetre. What is the production rate?
Reapply the relation at the new weft density with the same speed and efficiency.
Ideal rate = 42,000/(30 x 100) = 14 m/h, and actual = 14 x 0.85 = 11.9 m/h.
About 11.9 metres per hour, so a fabric with 50 % more picks takes 50 % longer per metre and needs proportionally more loom hours.

blocks: Margin of Error, Sample Size and Multiple Comparisons is a core model in Data Science Foundations: A confidence interval's width is decided before the study by three numbers - variability, confidence level and sample size - and testing many hypotheses at once inflates false positives unless the threshold is adjusted. The model is used within these stated limits: Observations are independent and identically distributed, sigma is known or well estimated, and the sample is large enough for the normal approximation. Small samples with estimated sigma need the t quantile instead.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Margin of error and the sample size it implies
half-width of the confidence interval (margin of error)
standard normal quantile for the chosen confidence level, 1.96 at 95 %

Observations are independent and identically distributed, sigma is known or well estimated, and the sample is large enough for the normal approximation. Small samples with estimated sigma need the t quantile instead.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: The sample mean of n independent observations has standard error sigma over root n, and the central limit theorem makes its standardised form approximately normal for large n. Multiplying the standard error by the quantile that covers the middle 1 - alpha of that distribution gives the interval half-width, so the interval is a statement about the estimator's spread rather than about any single observation. Rearranging for n turns the question 'how many samples do I need?' into a calculation: the required size grows with the square of the ratio of sigma to the target margin. The same arithmetic explains multiple comparisons: a test at alpha 0.05 called twenty times independently is expected to produce one significant result by chance alone.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A measurement has standard deviation 10 units. How many samples are needed for a 95 % confidence interval with a margin of error of 2 units?
Substitute z = 1.96 into the sample size formula and round up.
97 samples. Note the quadratic sensitivity: halving the margin of error to 1 unit would need about 384 samples.
A study tests 20 hypotheses, each at alpha = 0.05, and all nulls are true. How many significant results are expected, and what does Bonferroni use as the threshold?
Expected false positives are the per-test rate times the number of tests; Bonferroni divides alpha by the number of tests.
Expected false positives = 20 x 0.05 = 1. Bonferroni threshold = 0.05/20 = 0.0025.
One false positive is expected with a conventional threshold, and Bonferroni requires p below 0.0025 for any of the twenty to count.

blocks: Material Balance and Drive Mechanisms is a core model in Reservoir Engineering: The reservoir is a closed accounting system: what leaves the pore space must equal what expands into it - and which term balances the books identifies the drive mechanism. The model is used within these stated limits: Tank-wide averages (P, B_o, R_s per pressure step); plotting F against the drive terms as a straight line both solves N and reveals which mechanism dominates.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Havlena-Odeh material balance (undersaturated, no gas cap)
F=N\,E_{o}+N\,E_{g}\ +\ \text{water terms},\qquad F=N_{p}B_{o}\ (\text{no gas cap, early life})
F=N E_o+N E_g + water terms, F=N_pB_o (no gas cap, early life)
underground withdrawal: produced oil expanded to reservoir volume
oil-and-rock expansion drive term per unit of N
original oil in place, the fitted unknown
Tank-wide averages (P, B_o, R_s per pressure step); plotting F against the drive terms as a straight line both solves N and reveals which mechanism dominates.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: As reservoir pressure falls, everything compressible expands: the oil itself, dissolved gas coming out of solution, any free gas cap, the connate water and the rock pores. The material balance states that cumulative underground withdrawal equals the sum of these expansion contributions plus any water influx. Havlena and Odeh's insight is to treat it as a straight line: F plotted against the candidate E-terms should pass through the origin with slope N - a wrong drive assumption curves the line, so the plot diagnoses the mechanism (vigorous aquifer shows as F rising slower than E_o alone can explain) while solving for the inventory.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: After a pressure step, cumulative production gives F = 0.5 MM reservoir-m^3, and the oil-expansion term is E_o = 0.05 per stock-tank m^3 with no gas cap or water influx. Estimate N and the produced stock-tank volume.
F = N E_o gives N = 0.5/0.05 = 10 MM sm^3. With B_o = 1.25, N_p = F/B_o = 0.4 MM stock-tank m^3 = 2.5 MMbbl.
N = 10 MM m^3 in place, 0.4 MM m^3 produced so far - and repeating the plot each pressure step shows whether N stays constant, the sign of a correctly identified drive.

blocks: Material and energy balances are how a process is designed, and how a plant's performance is audited once it is running.

In design, the balance closes around every unit operation and determines stream flows, which then size pumps, heat exchangers, columns and vessels. The recycle stream is the part that makes it iterative: the output of a separator feeds back to the reactor, so the flows cannot be solved in one pass and the calculation converges by iteration. Getting the tear stream right is the practical skill.

In operation, the balance becomes a diagnostic. If the measured inputs and outputs do not close, something is unaccounted for — a leak, an unmeasured stream, or an instrument drifting. A closing balance is the basis of the efficiency figures that decide whether a plant is performing, so the measurement quality matters as much as the arithmetic.

The convention that causes the most trouble is the enthalpy reference state. Enthalpy is only defined relative to a reference, and every stream must use the same one. Mixing a steam-table basis with a heat-of-formation basis produces a balance that is off by a large constant and shows no obvious symptom — the numbers look reasonable and the duty calculation is wrong.

The energy side increasingly drives decisions rather than following them. Heat integration — pinching the hot and cold streams so one's waste heats the other — can cut utility consumption substantially, and it is found by plotting the composite curves rather than by optimising exchangers individually. That analysis starts from the same balances.

blocks: Maximum Power Transfer and Its 50% Efficiency is a core model in Circuit Theory: A source delivers peak power to a load exactly when the load resistance mirrors the source's internal resistance - and that condition wastes half the power by construction. The model is used within these stated limits: Fixed source, adjustable resistive load; AC generalizes to conjugate matching Z_L = Z_src*; maximizing transferred power and maximizing efficiency are different goals.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Fixed source, adjustable resistive load; AC generalizes to conjugate matching Z_L = Z_src*; maximizing transferred power and maximizing efficiency are different goals.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Load power is V_th^2 R_L / (R_th + R_L)^2. Differentiating with respect to R_L and setting to zero gives R_L = R_th; the second derivative confirms a maximum, and substituting yields V_th^2/(4R_th). At that point the load and the internal resistance drop equal voltages and dissipate equal power - hence exactly 50% efficiency. The theorem is therefore a signal-world result (extract the most from a weak source) and a warning in the power world (never run a supply at matched load: half the energy heats the wiring).
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A sensor's Thevenin model is 5 V with 1 k ohm internal resistance. Find the matched load and its power.
Match and apply the power formula.
R_L = 1 k ohm. P_max = 25 / (4 x 1000) = 6.25 mW. The source internally dissipates the same 6.25 mW.
6.25 mW delivered at 50% efficiency - fine for a signal port, unacceptable for a power supply feeding it.

blocks: Maxwell's equations are the design basis for essentially all of electrical and communications engineering, and different subsets do different jobs.

Circuit design uses the quasi-static approximation, where the fields are assumed to settle instantly. This is valid while the physical size of the circuit is small compared with the wavelength — roughly below a tenth of it. At 1 GHz the wavelength is 30 cm, so above about 3 cm a PCB trace stops being a wire and becomes a transmission line, and the full field treatment is required. That transition is what signal-integrity engineering is about.

Antenna design is Faraday and Ampere-Maxwell working together: an accelerating charge produces a changing field that sustains itself and propagates. The radiation pattern, gain and impedance all follow from solving the equations for a given geometry, which is what simulation tools do.
Waveguides, optical fibres and photonic devices are solved from the same equations with boundary conditions. The cutoff frequency of a waveguide falls straight out of them.

The practical engineering consequence is the speed of light as a hard limit. In a distributed system, a 1000 km round trip takes about 6.7 ms in fibre no matter how the software is written. Consensus protocols, synchronous replication and high-frequency trading all run into this, and it is why geographic redundancy and low latency are in direct conflict.

blocks: Measurement-Derived Thevenin Equivalents and Maximum Power Transfer is a core model in Circuit Theory: Any linear two-terminal network looks like one voltage source and one resistance; two measurements find both, and the resulting pair decides what load extracts the most power. The model is used within these stated limits: The network is linear and time-invariant with no independent sources inside the measured port that switch during the measurement; the matched-load result assumes a resistive source and load, so a reactive source needs a conjugate match.

blocks: Thevenin parameters from measurement and the matched-load power
power delivered to a matched load

The network is linear and time-invariant with no independent sources inside the measured port that switch during the measurement; the matched-load result assumes a resistive source and load, so a reactive source needs a conjugate match.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Linear networks can be reduced to a single source and series resistance as seen from any pair of terminals, and the reduction is unique. Measuring the open-circuit voltage gives the equivalent source directly, because no current flows and therefore no drop appears across the equivalent resistance. Shorting the terminals gives the current the source can drive into zero ohms, and the ratio of the two measured quantities is the equivalent resistance - no internal component needs to be identified. Once the pair is known, the load that receives the most power is the one equal to the equivalent resistance, and its power is fixed by the source and that resistance, which is why the maximum power transfer condition is a statement about the source rather than about the load.

blocks: Linear networks can be reduced to a single source and series resistance as seen from any pair of terminals, and the reduction is unique. Measuring the open-circuit voltage gives the equivalent source directly, because no current flows and therefore no drop appears across the equivalent resistance. Shorting the terminals gives the current the source can drive into zero ohms, and the ratio of the two measured quantities is the equivalent resistance - no internal component needs to be identified. Once the pair is known, the load that receives the most power is the one equal to the equivalent resistance, and its power is fixed by the source and that resistance, which is why the maximum power transfer condition is a statement about the source rather than about the load.

industry.title: Real-world applications

blocks: Everything about modern memory management follows from the cost of a TLB miss, which is why huge pages exist.

A 4 KB page means a process using 16 GB needs four million entries. No TLB holds that, so the hit rate collapses and every access pays a page walk. Huge pages — 2 MB or 1 GB — cut the entry count by three orders of magnitude and are standard for databases, JVMs with large heaps and anything touching large buffers. The trade-off is internal fragmentation: a 2 MB page wastes up to 2 MB per mapping.

The out-of-memory killer is the other production reality. Linux overcommits memory, promising more virtual address space than exists, on the assumption that not all of it will be used. When that assumption fails the OOM killer scores processes and kills one. This is why containers need memory limits set deliberately, and why a JVM heap sized to the container limit behaves very differently from one sized to the host.
Copy-on-write is what makes fork cheap and what lets a dozen processes share one copy of a library until one of them writes. Without it, every process spawn would copy the whole address space.

blocks: Merkle Trees and Efficient Transaction Proofs is a core model in Distributed Ledger & Smart Contract Engineering: A block commits to thousands of transactions with a single root hash, and a Merkle tree lets anyone verify one transaction's inclusion with only a logarithmic handful of hashes. The model is used within these stated limits: Hash collisions computationally infeasible; unbalanced trees duplicate nodes, and light clients must also verify the root sits in a validly-mined/attested header.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Proof size in a Merkle tree
proof size=_2N hashes for N transactions
single hash in the block header committing to all N
sibling hashes along the leaf-to-root path
Hash collisions computationally infeasible; unbalanced trees duplicate nodes, and light clients must also verify the root sits in a validly-mined/attested header.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Hash the transactions into leaves, pair them up and hash each pair, repeat level by level, and one root hash remains - a commitment to the entire set where changing any leaf changes the root. To prove one transaction is included, a verifier needs only the sibling hash at each level along that leaf's path - log2(N) values - and recomputes upward to check the root. The asymmetry is the engineering prize: committing is cheap for the chain (one root in the header), while inclusion checks cost a light client kilobytes instead of the whole block, which is what makes phone wallets and cross-chain bridges feasible.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A block contains 1,024 transactions. How large is an inclusion proof, and what would naive verification require?
Proof = log2(1024) = 10 sibling hashes (~320 bytes for 32-byte hashes). Naive: download and hash all 1,024 transactions (~300 KB+).
10 hashes versus a thousand transactions - a ~1000x verification saving that grows logarithmically with block fullness.

blocks: A symmetric simply-supported truss carries 10 kN downward at midspan. A support reaction is 5 kN upward, and at that support one horizontal bottom chord and one 30-degree inclined member meet. Find the inclined member's force.
Solve vertical equilibrium at the support joint.
Vertical: F_inclined x sin(30) + 5 = 0 gives F = -10 kN (the member pushes toward the joint). Horizontal: the bottom chord takes F cos(30) = 8.66 kN in tension.
Inclined member: 10 kN compression; bottom chord: 8.66 kN tension.

blocks: Minor Losses and Equivalent Length is a core model in Fluid Mechanics: Fittings, valves and bends cost head that is usually written as a multiple of the velocity head, and converting it into an equivalent length of straight pipe shows whether it can be ignored. The model is used within these stated limits: Fully developed turbulent flow with K values taken from standard tables for the fitting in question, referred to the pipe velocity rather than a port velocity. K depends on geometry and Reynolds number, so table values carry real uncertainty.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Minor loss and its equivalent pipe length
Darcy friction factor of the pipe

Fully developed turbulent flow with K values taken from standard tables for the fitting in question, referred to the pipe velocity rather than a port velocity. K depends on geometry and Reynolds number, so table values carry real uncertainty.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Each fitting disturbs the flow and dissipates energy in eddies, and the loss is proportional to the velocity head, so a single coefficient describes it. Converting the coefficient into an equivalent length uses the friction loss relation in reverse: the length of pipe whose friction loss equals the fitting's loss is K times diameter divided by the friction factor. That conversion is what makes a decision possible, because the resulting length can be compared directly with the pipe run. A valve with K = 2.5 in a hundred-metre main is negligible; the same valve in a three-metre branch dominates the system curve, and the pump then has to supply head that no amount of pipe sizing can remove.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A valve has K = 2.5 in a 100 mm pipe carrying water at 3 m/s with a friction factor of 0.02. Find the head loss and the equivalent length.
Compute the velocity head, multiply by K, then convert to an equivalent length.
Velocity head = 9/(2 x 9.81) = 0.459 m. Head loss = 2.5 x 0.459 = 1.15 m. Equivalent length = 2.5 x 0.1/0.02 = 12.5 m.
A 1.15 m loss equal to 12.5 m of straight pipe. Compare that with the friction loss of the run before deciding whether to neglect it.
For the same pipe, find the friction head loss over 50 m and the share contributed by the valve.
Use the Darcy relation with the friction factor, length and diameter, then compare with the minor loss.
Friction head = 0.02 x (50/0.1) x 0.459 = 4.59 m. The valve contributes 1.15 m.
The valve is about 25 % of the friction loss over 50 m. In a 200 m run it would be 6 %, and ignoring it there is defensible.

blocks: Miss Rates and Average Memory Access Time Across Cache Levels is a core model in Computer Organization & Architecture: Memory performance is a sum of expected penalties: each level's miss rate multiplies the cost of the level beneath it, so a small improvement where misses are frequent beats a large one where they are rare. The model is used within these stated limits: In-order access with no overlap between levels, constant latencies, and miss rates measured on the reference workload. Out-of-order execution and prefetching can hide part of the penalty.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Average memory access time with two cache levels
local L2 miss rate: L2 misses divided by L1 misses
In-order access with no overlap between levels, constant latencies, and miss rates measured on the reference workload. Out-of-order execution and prefetching can hide part of the penalty.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: The processor first pays the L1 hit time on every access. On the fraction m_L1 of accesses that miss, it pays the L2 hit time, and on the fraction m_L2 of those it continues to memory. Explanding the recursion one level happens by multiplying the conditional probabilities, which is why the two levels enter as a product rather than a sum of miss rates. The practical consequence is that a level-two miss rate is conditioned on level-one misses: 2 % L1 misses with a 25 % local L2 miss rate means only 0.5 % of all accesses reach memory. Effective design work therefore attacks the level where the product of frequency and cost is largest.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A core has t_L1 = 1 ns, t_L2 = 5 ns, t_mem = 60 ns, m_L1 = 4 % and L2 local miss rate 25 %. Compute AMAT.
Evaluate the inner parentheses first: the expected L2 penalty per L1 miss.
1.8 ns per access, so missing L1 adds 80 % to the 1 ns hit time even though only 4 % of accesses miss.
The same core halves its L1 miss rate to 2 %. What is AMAT, and what is the speed-up on memory-bound code?
Recompute AMAT with the same inner term, then compare the two values.
AMAT = 1 + 0.02 x 20 = 1.4 ns. Against 1.8 ns, the ratio is 1.8/1.4 = 1.29.
1.4 ns, a 29 % improvement in average access time. On code that is purely memory-bound the overall speed-up approaches that ratio.

blocks: The processor first pays the L1 hit time on every access. On the fraction m_L1 of accesses that miss, it pays the L2 hit time, and on the fraction m_L2 of those it continues to memory. The practical consequence is that a level-two miss rate is conditioned on level-one misses: 2 % L1 misses with a 25 % local L2 miss rate means only 0.5 % of all accesses reach memory. Effective design work therefore attacks the level where the product of frequency and cost is largest.

blocks: Modulus of Elasticity and the Stiffness of Concrete is a core model in Concrete Technology: Concrete's modulus can be estimated from its strength grade, which links a mix design decision to the deflection of the finished member. The model is used within these stated limits: Normal-weight concrete with conventional aggregates and standard curing; lightweight or high-strength mixes need their own relation, and the value is a secant modulus measured at a defined stress rather than an initial tangent.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Modulus of elasticity from cylinder or cube strength

Normal-weight concrete with conventional aggregates and standard curing; lightweight or high-strength mixes need their own relation, and the value is a secant modulus measured at a defined stress rather than an initial tangent.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Concrete is a composite of aggregate and cement paste, and its stiffness is governed by the aggregate, which is far less compressible than the paste. Because the stress-strain curve rises and then flattens, an increase in strength does not translate proportionally into stiffness: the modulus follows the square root of the compressive strength, which is why doubling the grade raises stiffness by only about forty percent. The consequence for design is direct, because deflection falls in proportion to the modulus, so a stiffness problem is not solved as easily by increasing the grade as intuition suggests. That is why designers change section depth rather than strength when a member is too flexible, and why the strength choice is usually driven by load capacity instead.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: Estimate the modulus of elasticity of M30 concrete and find the deflection of a beam whose computed deflection at a lower grade was 20 mm.
Apply the relation, then scale deflection inversely with the modulus.
25.7 GPa. Compared with M25 at 23.5 GPa, the deflection falls by the modulus ratio 23.5/25.7 = 0.914, so 20 mm becomes about 18.3 mm.
A member is upgraded from M25 to M40. What change in modulus and in deflection results?
Evaluate the relation at both grades and compare.
Stiffness rises 26 % and deflection falls about 21 % - a useful but not proportional gain for a 60 % increase in strength.

blocks: Moment Distribution: Distribution Factors and Carry-Over is a core model in Structural Analysis: Hardy Cross's method finds indeterminate moments by releasing one joint at a time, and its two numbers - the distribution factor and the carry-over half - make the iteration mechanical. The model is used within these stated limits: Prismatic members with fixed far ends and no joint translation, which gives the factor of one half for carry-over. Sidesway frames need the method applied to a sway-corrected structure or a computer analysis.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Distribution factor at a joint, and carry-over
rotational stiffness of member i, proportional to I/L
share of the unbalanced moment the member takes

Prismatic members with fixed far ends and no joint translation, which gives the factor of one half for carry-over. Sidesway frames need the method applied to a sway-corrected structure or a computer analysis.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: At a joint, the members resist rotation in proportion to their rotational stiffness, which for a prismatic member is proportional to its second moment of area divided by its length. Summing the stiffnesses and taking each member's share gives the distribution factor, and the factors at a joint always sum to one because the moment has to go somewhere. When a member's far end is fixed, half of the moment applied at the near end is induced there, which is the carry-over. Releasing one joint, distributing its unbalanced moment and carrying over half to the far ends sets up a smaller imbalance at the neighbouring joints; repeating the process converges quickly because each cycle reduces the residual. The final member moments are the sum of everything distributed into them.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A joint connects a 6 m member and a 4 m member of equal section. Find the distribution factors, and distribute an unbalanced moment of 30 kN m.
Stiffness is proportional to one over length, so the factors come from the reciprocals of the lengths.
k1 = 1/6 = 0.1667 and k2 = 1/4 = 0.25, so the sum is 0.4167 and DF1 = 0.4, DF2 = 0.6. Distribute 30 kN m as 12 kN m and 18 kN m.
The 6 m member takes 12 kN m and the 4 m member 18 kN m, with 6 kN m and 9 kN m carried over to their far ends.
A residual moment of 3 kN m remains at the neighbouring joint. How much is distributed there, and what remains after one more cycle?
Apply the same distribution factors, then carry over half.
With the same factors, distributing 3 kN m gives 1.2 kN m and 1.8 kN m, carrying over 0.6 and 0.9 kN m - residuals that are now small fractions of the original.
The residual falls rapidly: from 30 to 3 to well under 1 kN m in two cycles, which is why two or three cycles are usually sufficient for a hand check.

rotational stiffness of member i, proportional to I/L
share of the unbalanced moment the member takes

Prismatic members with fixed far ends and no joint translation, which gives the factor of one half for carry-over. Sidesway frames need the method applied to a sway-corrected structure or a computer analysis.
standard.title: Formula and variables

blocks: At a joint, the members resist rotation in proportion to their rotational stiffness, which for a prismatic member is proportional to its second moment of area divided by its length. Summing the stiffnesses and taking each member's share gives the distribution factor, and the factors at a joint always sum to one because the moment has to go somewhere. When a member's far end is fixed, half of the moment applied at the near end is induced there, which is the carry-over. Releasing one joint, distributing its unbalanced moment and carrying over half to the far ends sets up a smaller imbalance at the neighbouring joints; repeating the process converges quickly because each cycle reduces the residual. The final member moments are the sum of everything distributed into them.
standard.title: Derivation

blocks: A joint connects a 6 m member and a 4 m member of equal section. Find the distribution factors, and distribute an unbalanced moment of 30 kN m.
Stiffness is proportional to one over length, so the factors come from the reciprocals of the lengths.
k1 = 1/6 = 0.1667 and k2 = 1/4 = 0.25, so the sum is 0.4167 and DF1 = 0.4, DF2 = 0.6. Distribute 30 kN m as 12 kN m and 18 kN m.
The 6 m member takes 12 kN m and the 4 m member 18 kN m, with 6 kN m and 9 kN m carried over to their far ends.
A residual moment of 3 kN m remains at the neighbouring joint. How much is distributed there, and what remains after one more cycle?
Apply the same distribution factors, then carry over half.
With the same factors, distributing 3 kN m gives 1.2 kN m and 1.8 kN m, carrying over 0.6 and 0.9 kN m - residuals that are now small fractions of the original.
The residual falls rapidly: from 30 to 3 to well under 1 kN m in two cycles, which is why two or three cycles are usually sufficient for a hand check.

blocks: Monitoring everything guarantees missing what matters; the discipline is choosing signals that map to user experience. Latency must separate success from error latency (a fast 500 is still a failure); errors count explicit failures and degraded responses; saturation predicts the near-future failure of the tightest resource. Alerts then fire on symptom thresholds calibrated to the SLO's burn rate: a page means the budget is draining fast enough to need a human now, while slower burns open tickets. Cause-level signals (CPU of one node) stay on dashboards for diagnosis, out of the page path - which is how teams escape alert fatigue.

Fast burns - outage-scale events - exhaust 43.2 minutes within hours and page immediately. Slow burns, like a single region at 99.5% for a day, consume comparable budget over weeks and become tickets with the same measured numbers.
Two-tier alerting on one budget: pages for hours-scale exhaustion, tickets for days-scale - every notification traces to SLO arithmetic, not intuition.

blocks: MOSFET Operating Regions: Cut-Off, Triode and Saturation is a core model in Electronic Devices & Circuits: One gate-voltage inequality chain decides whether a MOSFET is an open switch, a voltage-controlled resistor, or a current source - and analog and digital design live in different regions on purpose. The model is used within these stated limits: Long-channel square-law model; short-channel devices velocity-saturate and the quadratic flattens, but the region inequalities still classify behaviour.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: V_GS<V_th: off; V_DS<V_GS-V_th: I_D=kl[(V_GS-V_th)V_DS-(V_DS^2)/(2)r]; V_DS≥ V_GS-V_th: I_D=(k)/(2)(V_GS-V_th)^2
Long-channel square-law model; short-channel devices velocity-saturate and the quadratic flattens, but the region inequalities still classify behaviour.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Below threshold the channel has no mobile carriers and only leakage flows. Above threshold an inversion layer forms and behaves like a resistor whose value the gate controls - the triode region, where current grows with V_DS but bends over as the drain end of the channel weakens. When V_DS reaches the overdrive V_GS - V_th, the channel pinches off at the drain; further V_DS increases mostly drop across the pinched-off region, so current levels off at the square-law value - saturation, the amplifier's home, because I_D then depends on the gate, not the drain.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A MOSFET has V_th = 1 V and k = 1 mA/V^2, and its saturation current follows I_D = (k/2)(V_GS - V_th)^2. With V_GS = 3 V, find the saturation current and the minimum V_DS to stay saturated.
Compute overdrive, apply the square law, check the region condition.
Overdrive = 3 - 1 = 2 V. I_D = 0.5 x (2)^2 = 2 mA. Saturation needs V_DS >= 2 V.
I_D = 2 mA for any V_DS >= 2 V - a gate-set current source, which is exactly what an amplifier stage wants.

blocks: MTBF, MTTR and Steady-State Availability is a core model in Site Reliability Engineering: Availability is the fraction of time a system is up, and it decomposes into how often it fails (MTBF) and how fast you recover (MTTR) - both are engineering targets, not fate. The model is used within these stated limits: Steady state with repair-as-good-as-old assumptions; planned maintenance windows count against availability unless contractually excluded, and nines translate logarithmically (99.9% = 8.8 h/year down).
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Availability from failure and repair times
fraction of calendar time in service

Steady state with repair-as-good-as-old assumptions; planned maintenance windows count against availability unless contractually excluded, and nines translate logarithmically (99.9% = 8.8 h/year down).
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Over a long horizon a repairable system alternates up-periods (averaging MTBF) and down-periods (averaging MTTR); the fraction of time spent up is the ratio of the up mean to the full cycle. The decomposition drives strategy: doubling MTBF (hardening, redundancy) and halving MTTR (runbooks, fast failover, good alerting) each buy availability, and for software systems MTTR usually wins - deploys are cheap, physics is not. Redundancy changes the failure side entirely: independent parallel units push system MTBF up multiplicatively while MTTR covers the single-unit repair.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A service fails every 500 hours on average and recovers in 2 hours. Find availability. What MTTR would reach 99.9% at the same MTBF?
Apply the availability formula, then invert it.
99.6% today; 30-minute mean recovery would deliver 99.9% - an availability nines climb bought mostly by faster recovery, not fewer failures.

blocks: Multiplexers and Decoders as Combinational Building Blocks is a core model in Digital Logic Design: A 2^n-to-1 multiplexer routes one of 2^n data inputs to the output by an n-bit select, which makes it a lookup table in hardware - and any Boolean function can be wired into its data inputs. The model is used within these stated limits: Combinational only - no memory; an n-variable function maps onto a 2^n-to-1 mux directly, or onto a 2^(n-1)-to-1 mux by Shannon expansion on one variable.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Y=\sum_{i=0}^{2^{n}-1} m_i\, I_i,\qquad f(x)=\text{mux with } I_i=f(\text{row } i)
Y=∑_i=0^2^n-1 m_i I_i, f(x)=mux with I_i=f(row i)
minterm asserted by the select value i
data input chosen when select = i
Combinational only - no memory; an n-variable function maps onto a 2^n-to-1 mux directly, or onto a 2^(n-1)-to-1 mux by Shannon expansion on one variable.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: The select lines decode to exactly one active minterm, so the output is the data input indexed by the select value - a hardware array subscript. That makes the mux a stored truth table: tie each data input to 0, 1, or another variable and the device computes whatever function that column of the table describes. Decoders run the mapping backwards, asserting one of 2^n output lines from n inputs, and with OR gates attached they synthesize any sum of minterms - which is why both parts are called universal building blocks.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: Implement f(A,B) = A AND B using only a 2-to-1 multiplexer.
Use A as select and wire the data inputs from B.
Select = A: when A = 0 output must be 0, when A = 1 output must be B. Tie I0 = 0, I1 = B. Output = A'B*0... precisely: Y = A'.0 + A.B = AB.
One 2:1 mux with I0 = 0, I1 = B, select = A computes AND - the truth table wired in hardware.

blocks: Two prefixes are equivalent when no suffix can tell them apart: whatever continuation is appended, both or neither land in L. The relation is right-invariant, so its classes respect the transition function and form a well-defined automaton whose states are the classes - the canonical or minimal DFA. No other DFA can use fewer states, because states reachable by distinguishable prefixes cannot be merged: any DFA that merged them would accept a string it must reject. Equivalence classes therefore give a two-sided result: the construction proves a language is regular, and the count proves the smallest machine that recognises it.

blocks: Negative Feedback: Gain Desensitization and Its Price is a core model in Analog Circuits: Feeding a fraction of the output back in opposition trades raw gain for precision: the closed-loop gain stops depending on the amplifier and starts depending on the feedback network. The model is used within these stated limits: Negative (subtractive) feedback with large loop gain; the same factor widens bandwidth and cuts distortion, at the cost of gain and a stability margin that must be checked.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: feedback fraction set by passive parts
loop gain margin - the desensitization factor
Negative (subtractive) feedback with large loop gain; the same factor widens bandwidth and cuts distortion, at the cost of gain and a stability margin that must be checked.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: The closed-loop gain A/(1 + A beta) is algebra, but the engineering content is in the limit: when loop gain A beta is huge, A_f approaches 1/beta - a ratio of stable resistors, immune to transistor spreads, temperature and ageing. Differentiating shows any open-loop variation reaches the output divided by (1 + A beta): a 10% change in A with loop gain 1000 moves A_f by 0.01%. The same factor linearizes distortion and extends bandwidth; the price is raw gain, and the risk is that phase shift turns subtraction into addition at some frequency - the stability problem compensation solves.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: An amplifier has A = 100,000 with beta = 0.01. Find A_f, and how much A_f moves if A drops 10%.
Apply the closed-loop and desensitization formulas.
A beta = 1000, so A_f = 100000/1001 = 99.9, essentially 1/beta = 100. A 10% open-loop drop changes A_f by 10%/1001 = 0.01%.
Gain 99.9 with thousand-fold insensitivity to the amplifier itself - precision bought with passive parts.

blocks: Newton-Raphson: Quadratic Convergence and Its Failure Modes is a core model in Engineering Mathematics III: One iteration of Newton's method replaces the function by its tangent, and the number of correct digits doubles each step - until the derivative vanishes or the starting point is badly chosen. The model is used within these stated limits: The function is continuously differentiable near the root, the derivative does not vanish there, and the initial guess is close enough to be inside the region of convergence. Repeated roots and inflection points where the derivative changes sign need modified schemes.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Newton-Raphson iteration and its local error relation

The function is continuously differentiable near the root, the derivative does not vanish there, and the initial guess is close enough to be inside the region of convergence. Repeated roots and inflection points where the derivative changes sign need modified schemes.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Newton's method replaces the function by its tangent line at the current point and takes the tangent's root as the next iterate. Expanding the function in a Taylor series about the root shows why the error behaves as it does: the next error is proportional to the square of the current one, multiplied by the curvature-to-slope ratio at the root. Squaring a small number makes it very small, so the correct digits roughly double with each step, which is why three or four iterations typically reach machine precision. The failure modes follow from the same expression: if the derivative is small in magnitude, the correction is large and the method overshoots, and if the function has an inflection the iterates can cycle or diverge.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: Estimate the square root of 2 by Newton's method from the guess 1, tracking the correct digits.
Apply the iteration and compare each iterate with the true value 1.41421356.
1.5, then 1.416667, then 1.414216: one correct digit, then three, then five - the doubling of accuracy in action.
Check that the error ratio matches the predicted curvature-to-slope constant.
Form the ratios of consecutive squared errors and compare them with the theoretical constant.
Errors are 0.0858, 0.00245 and 2.1 x 10^-6. The ratios are 0.00245/0.0858^2 = 0.333 and 2.1 x 10^-6/0.00245^2 = 0.35. The theoretical constant f''/(2f') at the root is 2/(2 x 2.828) = 0.354.
The observed ratios 0.333 and 0.35 match the predicted 0.354, confirming quadratic behaviour with that constant.

The function is continuously differentiable near the root, the derivative does not vanish there, and the initial guess is close enough to be inside the region of convergence. Repeated roots and inflection points where the derivative changes sign need modified schemes.
standard.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Newton's method replaces the function by its tangent line at the current point and takes the tangent's root as the next iterate. Expanding the function in a Taylor series about the root shows why the error behaves as it does: the next error is proportional to the square of the current one, multiplied by the curvature-to-slope ratio at the root. Squaring a small number makes it very small, so the correct digits roughly double with each step, which is why three or four iterations typically reach machine precision. The failure modes follow from the same expression: if the derivative is small in magnitude, the correction is large and the method overshoots, and if the function has an inflection the iterates can cycle or diverge.

Check that the error ratio matches the predicted curvature-to-slope constant.

Errors are 0.0858, 0.00245 and 2.1 x 10^-6. The ratios are 0.00245/0.0858^2 = 0.333 and 2.1 x 10^-6/0.00245^2 = 0.35. The theoretical constant f''/(2f') at the root is 2/(2 x 2.828) = 0.354.

blocks: Normalization is the default for transactional systems and deliberately abandoned for analytics, and knowing which side you are on is the real skill.

OLTP databases are normalized to 3NF because they are write-heavy and correctness-critical: one place per fact means one write and no inconsistency. OLAP warehouses are denormalized into star schemas — a central fact table surrounded by dimension tables — because reads dominate and joins are the expensive part. A star schema trades duplicate dimension data for far fewer joins per query.

The middle ground is where most real systems live. A normalized core with carefully chosen denormalized read models — a materialized view, a cache, a search index — gives correctness where it matters and speed where it is needed. The cost is that the read model can lag, so anything user-visible must tolerate eventual consistency.

The mistake to avoid is denormalizing to fix a slow query without first checking the plan. A missing index or stale statistics cause far more slowness than normalization does, and denormalizing introduces a consistency problem that does not go away.
