blocks: Nozzle Flow: Enthalpy Drop to Exit Velocity is a core model in Engineering Thermodynamics: A nozzle converts enthalpy into kinetic energy, so the exit velocity follows from the enthalpy drop alone - and the speed of sound tells you whether the flow is choked. The model is used within these stated limits: Steady, adiabatic flow with no work or heat transfer and a negligible inlet velocity. Real nozzles lose a few percent to friction, expressed as a velocity coefficient.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Exit velocity from an enthalpy drop, and the local sonic speed

advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: The steady-flow energy equation with no heat, no work and a small inlet velocity leaves the exit kinetic energy equal to the enthalpy drop, so exit velocity is the square root of twice the drop. Because enthalpy is a state function, the velocity depends only on the two states and not on the shape of the passage, which is what makes nozzle calculations so robust. The second relation decides the character of the flow: if the local sonic speed at the throat is lower than the velocity the enthalpy drop demands, the nozzle cannot pass more mass and becomes choked, and further expansion requires a diverging section. Together the two relations explain why supersonic nozzles are convergent-divergent rather than merely narrow.

The same nozzle expands from 600 K to 450 K. What is the new exit velocity?
Velocity depends on the square root of the temperature drop.
549 m/s for a 150 K drop against 448 m/s for a 100 K drop, confirming the square-root relationship.

blocks: Exit velocity from an enthalpy drop, and the local sonic speed

standard.title: Formula and variables

blocks: The steady-flow energy equation with no heat, no work and a small inlet velocity leaves the exit kinetic energy equal to the enthalpy drop, so exit velocity is the square root of twice the drop. Because enthalpy is a state function, the velocity depends only on the two states and not on the shape of the passage, which is what makes nozzle calculations so robust. The second relation decides the character of the flow: if the local sonic speed at the throat is lower than the velocity the enthalpy drop demands, the nozzle cannot pass more mass and becomes choked, and further expansion requires a diverging section. Together the two relations explain why supersonic nozzles are convergent-divergent rather than merely narrow.
standard.title: Derivation

blocks: Air enters a nozzle at 500 K and leaves at 400 K. Find the exit velocity and compare it with the local sonic speed at the exit.
Apply the enthalpy-drop relation with air properties, then the sonic-speed relation at the exit temperature.
Exit velocity 448 m/s against a sonic speed of 401 m/s, so the exit Mach number is about 1.12 and the passage must diverge after the throat.
The same nozzle expands from 600 K to 450 K. What is the new exit velocity?
Velocity depends on the square root of the temperature drop.
549 m/s for a 150 K drop against 448 m/s for a 100 K drop, confirming the square-root relationship.

blocks: Op-Amp Gain-Bandwidth Product is a core model in Analog Circuits: An op-amp's open-loop gain rolls off at 20 dB per decade, so gain times bandwidth stays fixed - choose closed-loop gain and the amplifier hands you the matching bandwidth. The model is used within these stated limits: Holds for voltage-feedback op-amps under a single dominant pole; current-feedback parts do not obey the constant product, and slew rate caps large signals independently.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: unity-gain frequency quoted on the datasheet
Holds for voltage-feedback op-amps under a single dominant pole; current-feedback parts do not obey the constant product, and slew rate caps large signals independently.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Internal compensation forces one dominant pole so the open-loop gain falls as 20 dB/decade: A(f) = f_T / f. Closing the loop with feedback factor beta sets the closed-loop gain near 1/beta, and the loop gain A beta drops to 1 exactly where the closed-loop response bends over - at f = beta f_T = f_T / A_CL. The product is therefore invariant: ten times the gain costs ten times the bandwidth. Signal amplitude adds a second ceiling - the slew rate - beyond which the output simply cannot move fast enough regardless of small-signal bandwidth.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: An op-amp has f_T = 1 MHz. What bandwidth remains at closed-loop gains of 20 and 100?
Divide the GBP by each gain.
At gain 20: BW = 1e6 / 20 = 50 kHz. At gain 100: BW = 10 kHz.
50 kHz and 10 kHz - the gain-bandwidth trade is a budget, and audio designs split gain across stages to spend it well.

blocks: Open-Channel Flow: Manning's Equation is a core model in Hydraulics & Hydraulic Machinery: Gravity drives open-channel flow, and Manning's equation ties depth, slope and surface roughness to velocity through the hydraulic radius - the workhorse of drain, canal and sewer design. The model is used within these stated limits: Uniform, steady, turbulent flow; n comes from surface tables (0.013 concrete, 0.030 natural channels), and the relation is empirical, not derived from first principles.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: hydraulic radius, flow area over wetted perimeter
energy slope ~ bed slope for uniform flow
Uniform, steady, turbulent flow; n comes from surface tables (0.013 concrete, 0.030 natural channels), and the relation is empirical, not derived from first principles.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: In uniform flow the gravity component down the slope exactly balances bed friction. Manning packaged that balance empirically: velocity grows with the two-thirds power of the hydraulic radius - a shape efficiency measure rewarding deep narrow sections over wide shallow ones - and the square root of slope, with roughness dividing the result. Designers invert it constantly: given a required discharge Q = A v, choose slope and lining, then solve for the depth that delivers it; freeboard and Froude-number checks follow.

blocks: The OSI model describes seven layers - physical, data link, network, transport, session, presentation, application - each providing services to the layer above. The TCP/IP model collapses these into four: link, internet, transport and application.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Header overhead as a fraction of the frame
With a 1500-byte MTU the overhead is about 58 bytes, giving roughly 96% efficiency. Small payloads are much worse, which is why Nagle's algorithm and TCP segmentation offload exist.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Encapsulation overhead is fixed per packet, so it hurts small payloads disproportionately.
A TCP segment carries a 20-byte TCP header and is wrapped in a 20-byte IP header and an 18-byte Ethernet header plus trailer:
. For a 40-byte payload — a typical acknowledgement —
, so most of the packet is headers.

A protocol that sends many small messages pays the overhead repeatedly. This is the justification for Nagle's algorithm, which coalesces small writes, and for batching in application protocols. It also explains MTU discovery: a larger MTU amortises the same 58 bytes over more data.

Each layer adds its header without knowing the payload's meaning, so a change in one layer does not require changes in another. That is why IPv6 could replace IPv4 at layer 3 without touching TCP at layer 4 — the separation is what makes the protocol stack evolvable.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: You type https://example.com and press Enter. Trace what happens, layer by layer.
Walk DNS, TCP handshake, TLS handshake, HTTP request, then the return path.

DNS resolves the name to an IP (UDP port 53). 2) TCP three-way handshake to port 443. 3) TLS handshake negotiates keys. 4) HTTP GET is encrypted and segmented. 5) IP adds addressing, Ethernet adds MAC framing. 6) The response reverses the process.
Six round trips in the worst case; HTTP/2 and TLS 1.3 cut this substantially.

blocks: The layered model is how the internet stays evolvable, and the layer where a problem lives determines who can fix it.
The most common production confusion is diagnosing at the wrong layer. A firewall dropping ICMP makes a host look unreachable at layer 3 when it is serving traffic fine at layer 7.
failing tells you about ICMP policy, not about the service. The discipline is to test each layer: link with
, transport with a TCP connect, application with an actual request.

Load balancers make the layer distinction concrete. A layer-4 balancer forwards TCP connections without reading the payload, so it is fast and protocol-agnostic but cannot route on URL. A layer-7 balancer terminates TLS, reads HTTP and can route on path or header — far more capable, and far more expensive per connection. Knowing which one you have explains what is and is not possible.

Encapsulation overhead is a real design constraint at scale. Protocols that send many small messages pay 58 bytes of headers per message, which is why batching and binary formats like Protocol Buffers are used for internal traffic, and why gRPC multiplexes many calls over one TCP connection.
The model also explains why IPv6 took so long: replacing layer 3 requires every device on the path to support both, because a packet must traverse routers that may not understand it.

blocks: Otto Cycle: Compression Ratio and Efficiency is a core model in Engineering Thermodynamics: The spark-ignition engine's ideal efficiency is fixed by one geometric number - the compression ratio - raised to a power set by the gas. The model is used within these stated limits: Air-standard assumptions (closed cycle, ideal gas, constant heats, isentropic compression/expansion); knock limits how far real petrol engines can push r.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Air-standard assumptions (closed cycle, ideal gas, constant heats, isentropic compression/expansion); knock limits how far real petrol engines can push r.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Compressing isentropically from bottom to top dead centre raises temperature by r^(gamma-1); heat addition at constant volume then burns on top of that elevated temperature, and expansion gives the same ratio back. Working the four-process energy balance, every temperature ratio collapses into powers of r, and the efficiency reduces to 1 - r^(1-gamma). The lesson is geometric: higher compression means a bigger expansion ratio, which extracts more work from the same combustion - until knock (autoignition of the end gas) intervenes, which is why high-octane fuel and direct injection exist.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: An air-standard Otto cycle has compression ratio 8 with gamma = 1.4. Compute ideal efficiency, and the gain at r = 10.
56.5% at r = 8, rising to 60.2% at r = 10 - about 1.9 efficiency points per compression-ratio point at this level.

blocks: Heat crosses each layer in turn, so temperature differences add while the flux stays constant - thermal resistances in series, exactly like electrical ones. The sum is dominated by its largest term, which is the smallest h: a gas-side coefficient of 50 W/m^2K swamps a water-side 2,000, which is why air-cooled exchangers wear fins (multiplying the weak side's area). Fouling resistance is the tax time levies - scale, coke, biofilm - and design practice sizes surface for the fouled U while checking the clean one: the gap between them is the exchanger's maintenance clock.

blocks: An air-water exchanger has h_water = 2000 and h_air = 50 W/m^2K with a thin metal wall. Find the clean U, then U with a 0.001 m^2K/W fouling layer on the water side.
Clean: 1/U = 1/2000 + 1/50 = 0.0005 + 0.02 = 0.0205, so U = 48.8 W/m^2K - essentially the air film alone. Fouled: 1/U = 0.0215, U = 46.5.
U ~ 47-49 W/m^2K either way: the air side rules the total, so fouling the water side barely matters - fouling the air side (dust on fins) would hurt far more.

blocks: Oxygen Transfer: kLa and the Fermenter Oxygen Balance is a core model in Bioprocess Engineering: Aerobic fermentation is usually oxygen-limited, and the transfer rate from bubble to broth - kLa times the driving force - must meet the culture's uptake or the cells downshift. The model is used within these stated limits: Steady state sets OTR = OUR; C* follows Henry's law from the oxygen partial pressure - raised by air enrichment or headspace pressure - and kLa grows with agitation and aeration power.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: saturation dissolved-oxygen concentration at the bubble interface
dissolved oxygen actually in the broth
culture's oxygen uptake rate that OTR must match
Steady state sets OTR = OUR; C* follows Henry's law from the oxygen partial pressure - raised by air enrichment or headspace pressure - and kLa grows with agitation and aeration power.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Oxygen is barely soluble and cells are hungry, so the whole aeration system exists to keep C_L above the critical level where uptake becomes oxygen-limited. The driving force is the gap between saturation (set by gas composition and pressure) and the actual dissolved level; kLa packages everything else - bubble size, interfacial area, turbulence, broth rheology - into one measurable coefficient. At steady state the culture consumes exactly what transfers: OUR = OTR. When demand exceeds kLa(C* - C_L) capacity, C_L crashes toward zero and metabolism shifts - the classic scale-up failure, because kLa falls as vessels grow if agitation power per volume is not held up.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A fermenter has kLa = 500 /h, C* = 7 mg/L (air, 30 C) and holds C_L = 2 mg/L. Find the maximum supportable OUR. What if the culture needs 4 g/L/h?
Compute OTR and compare with demand.

OTR = 500 x (7 - 2) = 2,500 mg/(L h) = 2.5 g/L/h. Demand 4 g/L/h exceeds it: C_L would fall, so raise C* (oxygen enrichment or 2 bar headspace doubles it toward 5 g/L/h capacity) or raise kLa with agitation.
Capacity 2.5 g/L/h versus 4 g/L/h demand - oxygen-limited; enrichment, pressure or power input must close a 60% gap before the culture can run at full rate.

blocks: Packed-Bed Pressure Drop: The Ergun Equation is a core model in Fluid Flow Operations: Flow through a bed of particles loses head to viscous drag at low speed and to form drag at high speed, and the Ergun equation is the sum of both regimes with the bed's geometry folded in. The model is used within these stated limits: Packed beds of roughly uniform particles; the laminar term dominates at low Reynolds numbers, the quadratic term at high - most real beds sit where both matter.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: superficial velocity (as if the bed were empty)
Packed beds of roughly uniform particles; the laminar term dominates at low Reynolds numbers, the quadratic term at high - most real beds sit where both matter.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: A packed bed is a bundle of tortuous channels whose size is set by the particles and voidage. At creeping speeds, viscous shear on the particle surfaces governs and the loss is linear in velocity - a Carman-Kozeny-type term with (1-epsilon)^2/epsilon^3 packaging the geometry. At higher speeds, flow separates behind particles and the loss goes quadratic - a Burke-Plummer term. Ergun simply summed the two asymptotes with empirically fitted constants 150 and 1.75, giving one equation that tracks data across the whole range - the reason it sizes everything from catalytic reactors to water filters.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: Water (mu = 1e-3 Pa s, rho = 1000 kg/m^3) flows at 0.01 m/s superficial velocity through a bed of 5 mm particles, voidage 0.4. Find the pressure gradient.
Total about 666 Pa/m - with both terms nearly equal, this bed sits exactly at the regime crossover where Ergun's two-part structure earns its keep.

standard.title: Formula and variables

blocks: A packed bed is a bundle of tortuous channels whose size is set by the particles and voidage. At creeping speeds, viscous shear on the particle surfaces governs and the loss is linear in velocity - a Carman-Kozeny-type term with (1-epsilon)^2/epsilon^3 packaging the geometry. At higher speeds, flow separates behind particles and the loss goes quadratic - a Burke-Plummer term. Ergun simply summed the two asymptotes with empirically fitted constants 150 and 1.75, giving one equation that tracks data across the whole range - the reason it sizes everything from catalytic reactors to water filters.

blocks: Water (mu = 1e-3 Pa s, rho = 1000 kg/m^3) flows at 0.01 m/s superficial velocity through a bed of 5 mm particles, voidage 0.4. Find the pressure gradient.
Total about 666 Pa/m - with both terms nearly equal, this bed sits exactly at the regime crossover where Ergun's two-part structure earns its keep.

advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: A fault occurs whenever the referenced page is not resident, and the policy only decides which resident page dies next. FIFO kills the oldest arrival regardless of use; LRU kills the page untouched longest, betting on temporal locality. Belady discovered that FIFO can fault more with four frames than with three: extra frames shift which pages are 'oldest' at the wrong moments, evicting pages the bigger memory would have kept. Monotonic policies like LRU and optimal never exhibit this - more frames cannot hurt them.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: Reference string 1,2,3,4,1,2,5,1,2,3,4,5 with FIFO. Count faults for 3 frames, then 4.
Simulate the queue; the oldest entry is the victim.

3 frames: faults on 1,2,3,4,1,2,5,3,4 = 9 (hits at the second 1, second 2, third 1, third 2, final 5... trace: 9 faults). 4 frames: 1,2,3,4 fault; 1,2 hit; 5 evicts 1; next 1 evicts 2; 2 evicts 3; 3 evicts 4; 4 evicts 5; 5 evicts 1 = 10 faults.
9 faults with 3 frames but 10 with 4 - Belady's anomaly: more memory, worse FIFO.

blocks: Password Storage: Salts and Slow Password Hashing is a core model in Cryptography & Network Security: A server stores a salted, deliberately expensive password verifier rather than plaintext or a fast general-purpose hash. The model is used within these stated limits: Use a maintained password-hashing KDF such as Argon2id, scrypt, or PBKDF2 with parameters chosen for the deployment; never invent a KDF.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Use a maintained password-hashing KDF such as Argon2id, scrypt, or PBKDF2 with parameters chosen for the deployment; never invent a KDF.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: A unique salt makes identical passwords produce different stored verifiers and prevents reusable precomputed tables. A memory- or CPU-expensive KDF raises the cost of each offline guess; the salt is stored alongside the verifier and is not secret.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: Two accounts choose the same password. Why should their stored verifiers still differ?
Each account receives an independently generated random salt before the password KDF.
Different salts make the KDF inputs different, so the resulting verifiers differ even when the password is the same.
Use a unique random salt for each account and a slow password KDF.

blocks: Rounding each sample to one of 2^n levels injects an error uniformly spread over +/- half a step. blocks: Pearson Correlation: Computation and Its Limits is a core model in Data Science Foundations: The correlation coefficient standardizes covariance to [-1, 1] so linear association becomes comparable across datasets - and 'linear' is the word that gets forgotten. The model is used within these stated limits: Measures linear association only; r near 0 does not mean independence, and outliers can manufacture or destroy r single-handedly.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: correlation, sign gives direction, magnitude gives linear strength
Measures linear association only; r near 0 does not mean independence, and outliers can manufacture or destroy r single-handedly.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Covariance averages the product of paired deviations: positive when both variables sit on the same side of their means, negative when they split. Its scale depends on both units, so dividing by the two standard deviations normalizes it into a pure number between -1 (perfect negative line) and +1 (perfect positive line). The geometry explains the limits: r is a cosine between centered variables, and a cosine only reads linear alignment - a perfect parabola can have r = 0 while y is fully determined by x.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: Temperature and ice-cream sales give r = 0.95. A U-shaped dataset y = x^2 sampled symmetrically around zero gives r near 0. Explain both.
Read r as a linear-alignment measure.

The 0.95 says sales track temperature along a line - strong linear association (causation still unproven; a third variable may drive both). For y = x^2 with x symmetric about 0, positive and negative x contribute cancelling products, so r ~ 0 despite a deterministic relation.
High r: strong linear link. r ~ 0 with y = x^2: association exists but is not linear - always plot before trusting r.

industry.title: Real-world applications

blocks: Fault studies are a regulatory requirement, not an academic exercise, and their output sets the specification of real equipment.

Protection settings come directly from the fault current. A circuit breaker must interrupt the maximum prospective fault current at its location, and a relay must operate fast enough to protect the cable downstream. Both ratings are chosen from the study, so an error propagates into hardware that cannot be changed cheaply later.

The calculations use subtransient reactance for the first few cycles — the highest current, which decides breaker interrupting capacity — and transient or synchronous reactance for later times, when the current has decayed. Using the wrong one gives a rating that is either unsafe or unnecessarily expensive.

The base conversion is where studies go wrong most often. Equipment nameplates give impedance on the equipment's own rating, and every contribution must be converted to one common base before they can be added. Missing this produces a fault current wrong by the ratio of the ratings, and it is not obvious in the output.

Asymmetrical faults are more common than symmetrical ones, and need all three sequence networks. A single line-to-ground fault is usually the most frequent, while a three-phase fault is usually the largest. Both are calculated, and they govern different equipment ratings.

Arc flash assessment has become a separate requirement. It converts the same fault current into incident energy at a working distance, which determines the personal protective equipment category and the warning labels on the panel — a safety obligation with legal force in many jurisdictions.

Asymmetrical faults are more common than symmetrical ones, and need all three sequence networks. A single line-to-ground fault is usually the most frequent, while a three-phase fault is usually the largest. Both are calculated, and they govern different equipment ratings.

Arc flash assessment has become a separate requirement. It converts the same fault current into incident energy at a working distance, which determines the personal protective equipment category and the warning labels on the panel — a safety obligation with legal force in many jurisdictions.

blocks: Photoelectric Effect and Work Function is a core model in Engineering Physics: Electrons are ejected only when each photon individually carries more energy than the metal's work function; brighter light adds electrons but never energy per electron. The model is used within these stated limits: One photon ejects at most one electron; below the threshold frequency f0 = phi/h nothing is emitted at any intensity.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: One photon ejects at most one electron; below the threshold frequency f0 = phi/h nothing is emitted at any intensity.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Energy arrives in quanta hf. An electron pays the work function phi to escape the surface, and whatever is left appears as kinetic energy; the fastest electrons come from the surface with no extra losses. Measuring the stopping potential that just halts them gives eV_s = hf - phi, a straight line in f whose intercept on the frequency axis is the threshold and whose slope is Planck's constant over e.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A metal has work function 2.0 eV. Light of 400 nm strikes it. Find the stopping potential (use hc = 1240 eV nm).
Compute photon energy, subtract the work function, convert to stopping potential.
Photon energy = 1240 / 400 = 3.1 eV. K_max = 3.1 - 2.0 = 1.1 eV. Since K_max = e V_s, the stopping potential is numerically 1.1 V.

blocks: Pipelining: Hazards, Stalls and Real Speedup is a core model in Computer Organization & Architecture: A k-stage pipeline promises k-fold throughput, but data, control and structural hazards tax the promise; the honest speedup divides by the stall cycles actually paid. The model is used within these stated limits: Assumes equal stage delays and ignores pipeline fill/drain, which cost k-1 cycles per program boundary rather than per instruction.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: average stall cycles charged per instruction
Assumes equal stage delays and ignores pipeline fill/drain, which cost k-1 cycles per program boundary rather than per instruction.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Splitting instruction execution into k stages lets k instructions occupy the machine at once, so ideal throughput is one instruction per cycle - not k times faster per instruction, but k times more instructions finished per unit time. Hazards break the overlap: a data hazard stalls until an operand is written (or forwarding shortcuts the wait), a control hazard stalls until a branch resolves, a structural hazard means two stages need one resource. Each stall inserts a bubble, and the average bubble cost per instruction is what moves CPI above 1.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A 5-stage pipeline runs at 1 GHz. 20% of instructions take one extra stall cycle. Find effective CPI and instruction throughput.
Charge the stalls and invert for throughput.
CPI = 1 + 0.20 = 1.2. Throughput = 1 GHz / 1.2 = 833 million instructions/s versus the ideal 1,000 million.
CPI 1.2, about 833 MIPS - hazards cost 17% of the ideal pipeline.

blocks: Poles, Zeros and Stability in the s-Plane is a core model in Signals & Systems: A transfer function's pole locations are the system's natural behaviours: real parts set decay or growth, imaginary parts set oscillation, and the left half-plane is the border of stability. The model is used within these stated limits: Linear time-invariant systems with rational transfer functions; poles on the imaginary axis give sustained oscillation (marginal), right-half-plane poles grow without bound.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: decay rate, the pole's distance left of the imaginary axis
oscillation frequency from the imaginary part
every pole satisfies sigma > 0 (strictly left half-plane)
Linear time-invariant systems with rational transfer functions; poles on the imaginary axis give sustained oscillation (marginal), right-half-plane poles grow without bound.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Partial-fraction expansion writes any response as a sum of terms 1/(s - s_p), each inverting to an exponential e^(s_p t). Splitting s_p into -sigma + j omega turns that into a decaying sinusoid: the real part is the envelope's exponent, the imaginary part the oscillation rate, and a real pole is the zero-frequency special case. Stability is then geometry - every mode dies exactly when every pole sits left of the imaginary axis - which is why root-locus plots and the Routh criterion (a pole-location test without computing poles) are stability's two native languages.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A system has H(s) = 1/(s^2 + 2s + 5). Locate the poles and describe the step response's shape.
Solve the quadratic, then read decay and frequency off the pole.
s = (-2 +/- sqrt(4 - 20))/2 = -1 +/- 2j. Envelope e^(-t) (sigma = 1, time constant 1 s), oscillation at 2 rad/s, decaying sinusoid toward the final value.
Underdamped: rings at 2 rad/s inside a 1-second decay envelope - stable because both poles sit in the left half-plane.

blocks: Position Tolerance at Maximum Material Condition is a core model in Engineering Drawing & CAD: A hole made at its maximum size can be offset further and still assemble, and that bonus tolerance is what makes the maximum-material modifier useful on production drawings. The model is used within these stated limits: A circular tolerance zone perpendicular to the datum plane, a clearance hole with a fastener, and the stated tolerance applied at the maximum material condition. Fixed-fastener and floating-fastener cases give different expressions, and datum shift adds further available tolerance.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Bonus tolerance and the fixed-fastener position tolerance
position tolerance stated at maximum material condition
maximum material condition size of the feature
hole at its smallest permitted size
fastener at its largest permitted size

A circular tolerance zone perpendicular to the datum plane, a clearance hole with a fastener, and the stated tolerance applied at the maximum material condition. Fixed-fastener and floating-fastener cases give different expressions, and datum shift adds further available tolerance.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Geometric tolerancing separates the size of a feature from its location tolerance, and the maximum material condition modifier links them. A hole produced at its smallest permitted size has no spare clearance, so it carries only the stated tolerance; the same hole produced larger has more room for the fastener and can therefore be positioned further off while still assembling. The difference between actual and maximum material size becomes an addition to the allowed position tolerance, and the drawing expresses this with a single symbol rather than a table. The reason it matters commercially is that the modifier is a gift to the manufacturing process: the tolerance is available exactly when the process is drifting to the easy side, so fewer parts are rejected without any loss of function.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A hole is specified at 10.0 mm minimum with a 0.2 mm position tolerance at maximum material condition. What position tolerance applies if the hole is produced at 10.15 mm?
The bonus is the difference between the actual size and the maximum material size.
Bonus = 10.15 - 10.00 = 0.15 mm, so the total available position tolerance is 0.2 + 0.15 = 0.35 mm.
0.35 mm, a 75 % increase over the stated tolerance, purely from producing the hole to the easy side of its size range.
A clearance hole has a maximum material condition of 10.0 mm and the fastener a maximum of 9.8 mm. What position tolerance makes assembly possible in the worst case?
For a floating fastener the available position tolerance is the difference of the two maximum material sizes.
0.2 mm of position tolerance at maximum material condition, which leaves no clearance to spare when both parts are at their worst sizes.

blocks: Power-Angle Equation and Transmission Limits is a core model in Power Systems: Real power across a transmission link is a sine of the angle between the two end voltages, and that curve sets both the steady transfer limit and the stability story. The model is used within these stated limits: Lossless line (R << X), constant voltage magnitudes; practical steady-state operation stays well below 90 degrees - typically 30-45 - for stability margin.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: power angle between the voltage phasors
Lossless line (R << X), constant voltage magnitudes; practical steady-state operation stays well below 90 degrees - typically 30-45 - for stability margin.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: With negligible resistance, the current through the series reactance is set by the phasor difference of the two end voltages, and real power turns out to be (V_s V_r / X) sin delta. The sine caps transfer at delta = 90 degrees - the static limit - but the deeper issue is slope: below 90 degrees, a disturbance that pushes delta up reduces the transmitted power imbalance and swings the rotor back; beyond 90, more angle means less power, and the machine accelerates away - loss of synchronism. Operating points therefore sit at modest angles, and transient stability is the question of whether a fault's angle swing stays inside the decelerating area of this curve.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A line has V_s = V_r = 1.0 pu and X = 0.4 pu. Find the transfer limit and the power at delta = 30 degrees.
P_max = 1.0 x 1.0 / 0.4 = 2.5 pu at delta = 90. At 30 degrees: P = 2.5 x sin 30 = 2.5 x 0.5 = 1.25 pu.
2.5 pu limit; 1.25 pu transferred at a comfortable 30-degree angle - halving the reactance (series compensation) would double both numbers.

blocks: Every threshold choice trades false positives against false negatives: lower the bar and recall rises while precision falls. Precision answers 'when it alarms, is it real?' and recall answers 'when it is real, does it alarm?'. Accuracy averages over both error types weighted by class frequency, which is why a 99%-negative dataset flatters a do-nothing classifier. F1 combines P and R harmonically, so 0.9 precision with 0.2 recall scores 0.33, not 0.55 - the weak side drags the mean down.

blocks: A process is a program in execution with its own address space, file descriptors and process control block. A thread is the smallest unit of CPU scheduling within a process; threads of one process share code, data and open files but keep separate stacks and registers.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: A process switch also flushes the address-space state and usually the TLB, so it costs more than a thread switch. Shrinking the time quantum raises throughput only until switch overhead dominates.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: The cost difference between a process and a thread switch comes from what has to be replaced.
Same address space, so only registers and the stack pointer change:
The page-table base register changes, which invalidates the TLB because virtual addresses now mean something different:

Refilling the TLB is not a one-time cost: the new process's working set must be re-walked, so the first accesses after the switch miss. The measured cost is typically several microseconds plus a warm-up period.
Why the shared heap is a liability.
Two threads writing the same location without synchronisation can interleave at instruction level. A non-atomic
compiles to load, add, store; if both threads load before either stores, one increment is lost:
expected lost updates > 0 for unsynchronised shared writes

That is the race condition, and it is why shared memory requires locks while separate processes do not — a process cannot address another's memory, so the interleaving is impossible by construction rather than by discipline.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: The process-versus-thread choice is now usually made on isolation and failure containment rather than raw performance.

The clearest example is the browser. Chrome runs each tab and each extension in its own process, so a crash or a memory leak in one cannot take down the others, and the operating system enforces the boundary. The cost is memory — every process has its own copy of the runtime — which is why browsers are memory hungry and why they pool processes for same-site tabs.

Servers went the other way and then partly back. One-thread-per-connection is simple but does not scale past a few thousand connections, so event loops with coroutines took over: Node, nginx, asyncio. They handle tens of thousands of concurrent connections in one process, but a single blocking call stalls everything, which is why the discipline around not blocking is strict.

Containers changed the calculus again. A container is a process with isolated namespaces and resource limits, so it gives much of the isolation of a VM at the cost of a process. The modern default is one process per container, with isolation handled outside the application — which is why the old many-threads-in-one-process design is less common than it was.
The one thing that has not changed: shared mutable state is the source of races, and the cheapest fix is usually to stop sharing rather than to add a lock.

Same address space, so only registers and the stack pointer change:
The page-table base register changes, which invalidates the TLB because virtual addresses now mean something different:

Refilling the TLB is not a one-time cost: the new process's working set must be re-walked, so the first accesses after the switch miss. The measured cost is typically several microseconds plus a warm-up period.

Two threads writing the same location without synchronisation can interleave at instruction level. A non-atomic

That is the race condition, and it is why shared memory requires locks while separate processes do not — a process cannot address another's memory, so the interleaving is impossible by construction rather than by discipline.

blocks: Propeller Slip, Pitch and Theoretical Speed is a core model in Marine Propulsion & Power Systems: A propeller is a screw in a fluid that gives way: its theoretical speed comes from pitch times RPM, and the shortfall against actual speed - slip - measures the thrust being made. The model is used within these stated limits: Slip is not loss in itself - zero slip means zero thrust; real propellers run 5-25% apparent slip, and negative slip appears only with current push or towing.

Slip is not loss in itself - zero slip means zero thrust; real propellers run 5-25% apparent slip, and negative slip appears only with current push or towing.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Each revolution geometrically advances the screw one pitch through a solid nut; through water it advances less because the blade pushes water backwards to make thrust - momentum exchange demands relative motion. The speed the screw would make in a solid is pitch times RPM; the difference from the actual advance, as a fraction, is the slip. Slip therefore rises with load: a clean ship at sea trial shows modest slip, a fouled hull or heavy weather raises resistance, the propeller works against more load and slip climbs - which makes slip trend a free, continuous hull-fouling monitor computed from shaft log and GPS speed alone.

blocks: Psychrometrics: Humidity Ratio and Comfort Cooling is a core model in Refrigeration & Air Conditioning: Moist air behaves as a mixture whose water content is tracked by the humidity ratio, and comfort cooling is as much a dehumidification problem as a temperature one. The model is used within these stated limits: Ideal-gas mixture behaviour, valid for atmospheric comfort ranges; p_sat comes from steam tables or the Antoine relation.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: humidity ratio, kg water per kg dry air
saturation vapour pressure at the dry-bulb temperature
molar mass ratio of water to dry air
Ideal-gas mixture behaviour, valid for atmospheric comfort ranges; p_sat comes from steam tables or the Antoine relation.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Water vapour in air obeys its own partial pressure, capped at saturation by temperature; relative humidity is the fraction of that cap currently used. The humidity ratio converts the vapour pressure into a mass-per-mass figure that survives heating and cooling unchanged - until water condenses out, which is exactly what a cooling coil below the dew point does. Comfort design follows the physics: cooling air below its dew point condenses moisture (dehumidification), reheating adjusts temperature at constant W, and the psychrometric chart plots every such process as a line, making coil selection a geometry exercise.
advanced.title: Derivation

Get the vapour pressure, then apply the ratio formula.
About 9.9 g of water per kg of dry air - the middle of the comfort band; a coil at 10 C would condense part of it, since saturation at 10 C holds only ~7.6 g/kg.

blocks: Pump Affinity Laws and Speed Control is a core model in Hydraulics & Hydraulic Machinery: Changing a pump's speed moves its whole characteristic: flow in proportion, head with the square and power with the cube - which is why speed control saves energy that throttling wastes. The model is used within these stated limits: Geometrically similar operation with the same impeller and no change in viscosity, so the efficiency curve keeps its shape. Trimming an impeller changes the geometry and uses a slightly different exponent.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Affinity laws for a constant-impeller pump

Geometrically similar operation with the same impeller and no change in viscosity, so the efficiency curve keeps its shape. Trimming an impeller changes the geometry and uses a slightly different exponent.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: The affinity laws follow from the velocity triangles inside the impeller: velocities scale with speed, head depends on the velocity head and therefore on its square, and power is the product of head and flow, which gives the cube. The practical consequence is the shape of the energy saving: a twenty percent speed reduction cuts flow to eighty percent but power to fifty-one percent, so the saving is disproportionate and grows with the reduction. This is why variable-speed drives are the standard solution for systems whose demand varies, while throttling a fixed-speed pump simply moves the operating point along the pump curve and dissipates the excess head in the valve. Both approaches reduce flow, but only one reduces power in proportion.
advanced.title: Derivation

Apply the three affinity relations to the full-speed point.

blocks: The affinity laws follow from the velocity triangles inside the impeller: velocities scale with speed, head depends on the velocity head and therefore on its square, and power is the product of head and flow, which gives the cube. The practical consequence is the shape of the energy saving: a twenty percent speed reduction cuts flow to eighty percent but power to fifty-one percent, so the saving is disproportionate and grows with the reduction. This is why variable-speed drives are the standard solution for systems whose demand varies, while throttling a fixed-speed pump simply moves the operating point along the pump curve and dissipates the excess head in the valve. Both approaches reduce flow, but only one reduces power in proportion.

Steady flow with a single liquid phase and no dissolved gas; the available NPSH calculation uses the absolute pressure at the suction vessel and the vapour pressure at the actual pumping temperature. Entrained air and viscosity need additional allowances.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: The hydraulic power a pump delivers is the product of density, gravity, flow and head, and dividing by the efficiency gives the shaft power that must be supplied, which is why a pump's efficiency matters financially but not hydraulically. The suction side has a separate and stricter requirement: the absolute pressure at the impeller eye must exceed the liquid's vapour pressure by an amount that keeps bubbles from forming. Available NPSH is the absolute pressure head at the suction vessel, converted to metres, minus the vapour pressure head, minus the static lift and the suction line's friction loss. If the available value is below the pump's required value, cavitation occurs, and it damages the impeller even when the pump appears to be working, so the margin is specified and checked at the highest liquid temperature the process will see.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A pump handles 0.02 m^3/s of water at 30 m head with 70 % efficiency. Find the shaft power.
Apply the hydraulic power relation and divide by efficiency.
About 8.4 kW of shaft power, against 5.9 kW of hydraulic power - the difference being the losses the efficiency represents.
The pump lifts water at 40 degrees C, where the vapour pressure is 7.4 kPa, from an open tank 3 m below with 1.2 m of suction friction loss. Find the available NPSH.
Convert the pressure difference to metres of water, then subtract the lift and friction.
5.37 m available. If the pump requires 4 m, the margin is 1.37 m, which is adequate; at 70 degrees C the vapour pressure rises and the margin shrinks sharply.

Available NPSH is the absolute pressure head at the suction vessel, converted to metres, minus the vapour pressure head, minus the static lift and the suction line's friction loss. If the available value is below the pump's required value, cavitation occurs, and it damages the impeller even when the pump appears to be working, so the margin is specified and checked at the highest liquid temperature the process will see.
standard.title: Derivation

blocks: A pump handles 0.02 m^3/s of water at 30 m head with 70 % efficiency. Find the shaft power.
Apply the hydraulic power relation and divide by efficiency.
About 8.4 kW of shaft power, against 5.9 kW of hydraulic power - the difference being the losses the efficiency represents.
The pump lifts water at 40 degrees C, where the vapour pressure is 7.4 kPa, from an open tank 3 m below with 1.2 m of suction friction loss. Find the available NPSH.
Convert the pressure difference to metres of water, then subtract the lift and friction.
5.37 m available. If the pump requires 4 m, the margin is 1.37 m, which is adequate; at 70 degrees C the vapour pressure rises and the margin shrinks sharply.

blocks: PV Array Sizing: Peak Sun Hours and System Derates is a core model in Renewable Energy Systems & Storage: A PV array's daily energy is its rating times the site's peak sun hours times a stack of loss factors - an arithmetic that sizes arrays, batteries and economics from one irradiation number. The model is used within these stated limits: Grid-tied or off-grid steady calculation; PSH comes from measured or modelled irradiation for the tilt and orientation, and monthly (not annual-average) PSH sizes off-grid systems.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: array rating at standard test conditions (1 kW/m^2, 25 C)
peak sun hours - daily irradiation expressed as equivalent hours of 1 kW/m^2
combined derate: temperature, dirt, wiring, inverter, mismatch (~0.70-0.80)
Grid-tied or off-grid steady calculation; PSH comes from measured or modelled irradiation for the tilt and orientation, and monthly (not annual-average) PSH sizes off-grid systems.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Peak sun hours compress a day's variable irradiation into equivalent full-sun hours - 5 PSH means the day delivered 5 kWh per square metre however it was distributed. Multiplying the array's STC rating by PSH gives the ideal yield; the derate stack then charges reality: cells lose roughly 0.4%/C above 25 C, dust and shading take a few percent, wiring and inverter conversion more, and module mismatch and degradation the rest - a 0.75 system factor is a honest planning number in hot dusty climates. Off-grid design repeats the calculation for the worst month, not the annual average, because the battery and generator must survive December's irradiation, not July's.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A 5 kWp rooftop array sits at a site with 5.5 peak sun hours and a 0.75 system derate. Estimate daily and annual energy.
E_day = 5 x 5.5 x 0.75 = 20.6 kWh/day. Annual ~ 20.6 x 365 = 7,530 kWh, assuming year-round average irradiation.
About 20.6 kWh per day, 7.5 MWh per year - a capacity factor of 7530/(5 x 8760) = 17.2%, typical for fixed-tilt PV, and the baseline for the payback arithmetic.

blocks: PWM Inverters: Modulation Index and Fundamental Control is a core model in Power Electronics: A PWM inverter chops a DC rail at high frequency, and the ratio of modulating to carrier amplitude - the modulation index - linearly sets the fundamental output voltage. The model is used within these stated limits: Sinusoidal modulation under a triangular carrier in the linear region; overmodulation (m_a > 1) gains up to ~15% more voltage but distorts, and the switching harmonics sit around the carrier frequency where filters remove them.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: fundamental component of the switched output

Sinusoidal modulation under a triangular carrier in the linear region; overmodulation (m_a > 1) gains up to ~15% more voltage but distorts, and the switching harmonics sit around the carrier frequency where filters remove them.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Comparing a sine reference with a fast triangle makes the output pulse-width vary sinusoidally: wide pulses near the sine's peak, narrow near zero. Averaged over each carrier period the output equals the reference scaled by the DC rail - so the fundamental is m_a V_dc/2 and every harmonic bunches around the carrier frequency and its multiples, far above the fundamental where small LC filters kill them cheaply. This is the trick that makes modern drives both efficient (switches are fully on or off) and clean (harmonics pushed out of band), and frequency comes from the reference sine's rate, independent of amplitude.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A 400 V DC-link inverter modulates at m_a = 0.8 and 50 Hz reference. Find the fundamental output peak and where its dominant harmonics sit for a 10 kHz carrier.
Apply the SPWM amplitude relation and the harmonic-bunching rule.
V_1 peak = 0.8 x 400/2 = 160 V (about 113 V rms per phase). Dominant harmonics cluster around 10 kHz and 20 kHz - ratios 200 and 400 times the fundamental.
160 V peak fundamental at 50 Hz, with switching harmonics parked at 10 kHz+ where a small filter removes them.

blocks: Newtonian cooling of a section and its time constant
T(t)=T_\infty+(T_0-T_\infty)e^{-t/\tau},\qquad \tau=\frac{\rho c_p V}{h A}=\frac{\rho c_p D}{4h}\ \text{(long cylinder)}
T(t)=T_∞+(T_0-T_∞)e^-t/τ, τ=(ρ c_p V)/(h A)=(ρ c_p D)/(4h) (long cylinder)

Lumped-capacitance cooling, valid when the Biot number is small, with a constant heat transfer coefficient. Real quenching passes through film boiling and nucleate boiling, so the early cooling is faster than a single exponential and the centre lags the surface.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: A quenched section loses heat from its surface, so the rate at which its temperature falls is set by the ratio of surface area to volume - the bigger the section, the longer the time constant, and for a cylinder the time constant is proportional to diameter at constant surface coefficient. Temperature then decays exponentially towards the quenchant's temperature. Against that decay sits the steel's own transformation behaviour: it must be cooled past the pearlite and bainite regions faster than those transformations can start, which is what the continuous-cooling diagram records. The engineering decision is therefore always the same pair of numbers - how fast this section actually cools, and how fast it must - and the ways to close a gap are a more severe quenchant, a smaller section, or an alloy that shifts the transformation curves to slower times.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A 50 mm steel cylinder at 850 degrees C is quenched into oil at 50 degrees C with h = 1000 W/m^2 K. Find the time constant and the centre temperature after 10 s.
Compute the time constant from density, specific heat, diameter and surface coefficient, then apply the exponential decay.
Time constant 48.8 s and about 702 degrees C after ten seconds, which is still above the pearlite nose, so the surface would transform before the core.
What is the centre temperature after 60 s, and what does it mean for the core?
Continue the same exponential decay to the longer time.
The core reaches about 284 degrees C by sixty seconds, below a typical martensite start range of 300 to 350 degrees C, so the core has entered the martensitic transformation.

blocks: Query Cost: Selectivity and the Index Break-Even Point is a core model in Database Management Systems: A planner chooses an index over a table scan when the rows it would fetch are a small enough fraction of the table; that break-even point is a computation you can reproduce. The model is used within these stated limits: Costs are in page reads; statistics are assumed current, the index is on the filtered column, and the table is larger than memory so every fetch is a disk access.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Cost of an indexed lookup versus a full scan
C_index≈ h+ s N r, C_scan≈ N r_seq
index height: pages read to reach the first matching entry
selectivity: fraction of rows the predicate matches
cost of a random row fetch, in units of a sequential page read
cost of reading a row during a sequential scan
Costs are in page reads; statistics are assumed current, the index is on the filtered column, and the table is larger than memory so every fetch is a disk access.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: A full scan reads every page of the table once, in order, so its cost is proportional to N with a small per-row constant. An index lookup pays a fixed B-tree descent of h pages and then pays for the rows it returns; because those rows arrive in index order they are usually scattered across the heap, so each one costs a random page fetch with r roughly an order of magnitude larger than a sequential one. Adding an index becomes a bad idea exactly when s N r exceeds N r_seq, that is when s exceeds r_seq/r. That threshold is why a predicate matching half the table should not use an index while one matching two percent should.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A table has 1,000,000 rows, an index of height 3, and a random row fetch costs 4 sequential page reads. Evaluate a predicate with selectivity 2 %.
Compute the two estimated costs in page reads and compare them, then state the plan you expect.

The index costs about 80,000 pages against 1,000,000 for the scan, roughly 12 times cheaper, so the indexed plan wins. Raising selectivity to 30 % would give 1,200,003 against 1,000,000 and the scan wins.
A query filters tenant_id = ? and a timestamp range. Which composite index supports a seek, and what does the other order do?
A B-tree seeks on a leftmost prefix; equality columns must come before range columns.

Index (tenant_id, created_at) seeks to the tenant's slice and reads a contiguous range. Index (created_at, tenant_id) can only seek on created_at if it is an equality; a range on created_at is scanned across tenants.
(tenant_id, created_at) is the correct order. The reversed index degenerates to a range scan of all tenants, and the planner may fall back to a full scan.

That threshold is why a predicate matching half the table should not use an index while one matching two percent should.

The index costs about 80,000 pages against 1,000,000 for the scan, roughly 12 times cheaper, so the indexed plan wins. Raising selectivity to 30 % would give 1,200,003 against 1,000,000 and the scan wins.
A query filters tenant_id = ? and a timestamp range. Which composite index supports a seek, and what does the other order do?
A B-tree seeks on a leftmost prefix; equality columns must come before range columns.

Index (tenant_id, created_at) seeks to the tenant's slice and reads a contiguous range. Index (created_at, tenant_id) can only seek on created_at if it is an equality; a range on created_at is scanned across tenants.
(tenant_id, created_at) is the correct order. The reversed index degenerates to a range scan of all tenants, and the planner may fall back to a full scan.

blocks: Queueing Headroom and Replica Sizing is a core model in Cloud Computing: Capacity is not max throughput divided by per-replica throughput: because waiting time grows without bound as utilisation approaches one, replicas are sized to a utilisation ceiling, not to the peak. The model is used within these stated limits: Arrivals are approximately Poisson and service times approximately exponential, one request occupies one replica, and replicas are independent. Sustained utilisation must stay strictly below one.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Utilisation, replica count and Little's law
ρ=(λ)/(c μ), c≥(λ)/(μ ρ_max), L=λ W
Arrivals are approximately Poisson and service times approximately exponential, one request occupies one replica, and replicas are independent. Sustained utilisation must stay strictly below one.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Each replica clears mu requests per second when fully occupied, so a fleet of c replicas has a ceiling of c mu and a utilisation of lambda over c mu. The reason to plan below the ceiling is queueing rather than throughput: for a single-server queue the mean waiting time is proportional to rho over one minus rho, so at 80 % utilisation the wait is four times the service time and at 95 % it is nineteen times. The ceiling therefore becomes a design parameter, chosen so that a traffic surge or the loss of one replica still leaves every remaining replica below it. Little's law ties the same system together from the other side: the number of requests in flight equals the arrival rate times the time each spends inside, which is the number that sizes connection pools and worker queues.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: Arrivals are 180 requests per second, one replica serves 100 requests per second, and the utilisation ceiling is 0.6. How many replicas are required?
Divide the arrival rate by the product of per-replica service rate and the ceiling, then round up.
Three replicas. Two replicas would run at 90 % utilisation and queue badly; three give 60 % and absorb the loss of one replica at 90 %.
Two hundred requests per second each occupy a connection for 0.25 s. What concurrency is needed, and what happens with a pool of 40?
Apply Little's law: concurrency equals arrival rate times time in system.
Fifty connections are in flight on average, so a pool of 40 forces requests to wait for a connection before they are served, adding latency that grows with load.

blocks: Radial Flow into a Well and the Log-Term Insensitivity is a core model in Reservoir Engineering: Steady radial flow into a well depends only logarithmically on the drainage radius, which is why infill wells add far less production than a linear estimate suggests. The model is used within these stated limits: Steady-state, single-phase, radial flow with a constant permeability and no skin damage; the drainage radius is an equivalent radius representing the no-flow boundary. Transient behaviour before the boundary is felt follows a different solution.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Steady-state radial inflow into a well
q=(2π k h Δ p)/(μ ln(r_e/r_w))
drawdown: reservoir pressure minus flowing bottom-hole pressure

Steady-state, single-phase, radial flow with a constant permeability and no skin damage; the drainage radius is an equivalent radius representing the no-flow boundary. Transient behaviour before the boundary is felt follows a different solution.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Fluid flows radially toward the wellbore, so its velocity rises as the flow area shrinks; the pressure gradient follows Darcy's law, and integrating from the drainage radius to the wellbore gives the rate equation. The logarithm is the whole story: because it is the ratio of the radii inside it, the production rate responds only weakly to the drainage radius and strongly to permeability, thickness and drawdown. Doubling drainage radius changes the logarithm by a small fraction, so halving well spacing does not double production, while near-wellbore conditions sit inside the logarithm too - which is precisely why stimulation and skin removal deliver outsized gains for their cost. Reading the equation's structure tells an engineer where the leverage lies before any numbers are entered.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A well with 1 x 10^-13 m^2 permeability, 20 m of pay, 2 MPa drawdown, 1 mPa s viscosity and a drainage to wellbore radius ratio of 3000 produces at what rate?
Evaluate the numerator, then divide by the viscosity times the logarithm of the radius ratio.
About 3.1 litres per second, or 271 cubic metres per day.
The drainage radius is halved by adding an infill well. What percentage gain does the original well's inflow calculation suggest?
The change enters through the logarithm of the radius ratio.
About 9.5 %, not the doubling that halving the drainage area implies - the arithmetic behind cautious infill drilling economics.

blocks: Rankine Earth Pressure and the Effect of Water Behind a Wall is a core model in Soil Mechanics / Geotechnical Engineering: A retaining wall is designed against the lateral thrust of the soil behind it, and if that soil is saturated the water pressure can exceed the soil's own contribution. The model is used within these stated limits: A smooth vertical wall with a horizontal cohesionless backfill, no surcharge and no wall friction; the retained soil is assumed to move slightly to mobilise active conditions. Cohesive backfill and sloping fills use different expressions.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Rankine active pressure coefficient and resultant thrust
bulk unit weight of the retained soil
resultant thrust per metre of wall

A smooth vertical wall with a horizontal cohesionless backfill, no surcharge and no wall friction; the retained soil is assumed to move slightly to mobilise active conditions. Cohesive backfill and sloping fills use different expressions.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: The soil behind a wall pushes outward because the wall moves away from it, reducing the horizontal stress until the soil is on the verge of failure; the ratio of horizontal to vertical stress at that condition is the active pressure coefficient, which falls as the friction angle rises. Because the vertical stress grows linearly with depth, the lateral pressure does too, and the resultant is the triangle's area - half the coefficient times unit weight times the square of the height. The squared term is the important one: doubling wall height quadruples the thrust. Water is worse than soil in this respect, because its pressure is also triangular but with the full unit weight of water and no friction to reduce it, so an undrained backfill adds a water pressure that can exceed the soil thrust and also loads the wall at a different point.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A wall 4 m high retains sand with a friction angle of 30 degrees and a unit weight of 18 kN/m^3. Find the active thrust per metre and the overturning moment about the base.
Compute the coefficient, then the thrust, then apply it at one third of the height.
48 kN per metre of wall acting at 1.33 m above the base, giving an overturning moment of 64 kN m per metre.
The backfill becomes saturated, adding a water pressure of half the water unit weight times height squared. Compare the water thrust with the soil thrust.
Compute the triangular water pressure resultant at the same height.
Water thrust = 0.5 x 9.81 x 16 = 78.5 kN/m, against the soil's 48 kN/m.
The water adds 78.5 kN/m, more than the soil itself, and acts at one third height as well. Total thrust rises to about 126 kN/m, a factor of 2.6.

blocks: Rate Analysis: Building Up a Unit Rate with Overheads and Profit is a core model in Estimating & Costing: A tender rate is built from measured quantities, current prices and explicit factors for overheads, profit and waste - and every one of those factors is visible in the arithmetic. The model is used within these stated limits: Rates at current market prices for a defined item of work, with the productivity assumed in the labour figure and the wastage allowance applied only to materials that actually waste. Taxes and escalation are separate line items, not hidden in the factors.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Unit rate from direct cost, overhead and profit
overhead as a fraction of direct cost
profit as a fraction after overhead

Rates at current market prices for a defined item of work, with the productivity assumed in the labour figure and the wastage allowance applied only to materials that actually waste. Taxes and escalation are separate line items, not hidden in the factors.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: The direct cost of an item of work is what it costs to put it in place: the materials consumed including waste, the labour at the productivity the site can actually achieve, and the plant needed to do the operation. Overheads cover everything the project needs but no single item does - supervision, temporary works, insurance, site facilities - and are usually applied as a percentage of direct cost. Profit is applied after overheads because it is a return on the whole cost, not on a fraction of it. Dividing by the quantity converts the whole build-up into a rate per unit, which is the number the bill of quantities multiplies by measured quantity. The value of writing it this way is that every assumption can be challenged separately: a low rate may be thin wastage, optimistic productivity or a deliberate commercial decision.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: An item of 10 m^3 costs 48,000 in materials, 6,000 in labour and 3,000 in plant. With 10 % overhead and 8 % profit, find the rate per cubic metre.
Sum the direct costs, apply overhead, apply profit, then divide by the quantity.
Direct = 57,000. With overhead: 62,700. With profit: 67,716. Rate = 67,716/10 = 6771.6.
About 6,772 per cubic metre, which is the rate that goes into the bill of quantities.
The same item is reassessed with 3 % wastage on materials. What is the new unit rate?
Wastage raises the material cost only, and then flows through the same overhead and profit factors.
Materials = 48,000 x 1.03 = 49,440, so direct = 58,440. With overhead: 64,284. With profit: 69,427. Rate = 6,943.
About 6,943 per cubic metre, 2.5 % above the original rate: a small assumption moving the price by a visible amount.

blocks: Unit rate from direct cost, overhead and profit
overhead as a fraction of direct cost

Rates at current market prices for a defined item of work, with the productivity assumed in the labour figure and the wastage allowance applied only to materials that actually waste. Taxes and escalation are separate line items, not hidden in the factors.
standard.title: Formula and variables

blocks: The direct cost of an item of work is what it costs to put it in place: the materials consumed including waste, the labour at the productivity the site can actually achieve, and the plant needed to do the operation. Overheads cover everything the project needs but no single item does - supervision, temporary works, insurance, site facilities - and are usually applied as a percentage of direct cost. Profit is applied after overheads because it is a return on the whole cost, not on a fraction of it. Dividing by the quantity converts the whole build-up into a rate per unit, which is the number the bill of quantities multiplies by measured quantity. The value of writing it this way is that every assumption can be challenged separately: a low rate may be thin wastage, optimistic productivity or a deliberate commercial decision.

blocks: Reading Charts Honestly: Axes, Scales and Visual Distortion is a core model in Communication Skills: A chart's visual message is the ratio its ink shows; when the axis is truncated or the scale is uneven, that ratio silently exaggerates the data ratio. The model is used within these stated limits: Applies to bar charts, whose length encodes value from the baseline; line charts of rates or indices may legitimately use a non-zero baseline if labelled.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: how many times taller the change looks than it is
Applies to bar charts, whose length encodes value from the baseline; line charts of rates or indices may legitimately use a non-zero baseline if labelled.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: A bar's length is read as value-from-baseline. Start the baseline at 95 instead of 0 and a rise from 98 to 100 draws five times the ink it deserves, because the visible change is measured against the truncated span, not the true value. The distortion factor follows by dividing the drawn change ratio by the real change ratio; the cure is a zero baseline, or switching to a chart type that does not encode value by length.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: Sales move from 98 to 100 units. A bar chart starts its axis at 95. How exaggerated is the visual growth?
Compare the ink ratio with the true ratio.

True relative growth = 2/98 = 2.0%. Drawn growth = (100-95)/(98-95) = 5/3 = 167% of the first bar's height above baseline. The visual overstates the change by roughly 5/3 divided by 2/98... in ink terms the second bar looks 67% taller than the first, versus a 2% real rise.
The chart makes a 2% rise look like a two-thirds jump - read the axis before the bars.

blocks: Reciprocal Levelling and the Curvature Correction is a core model in Surveying: Two instrument setups across a river separate the true level difference from the instrument's own collimation error, and the curvature and refraction correction quantifies what the Earth's surface does to a level line. The model is used within these stated limits: Reciprocal levelling assumes the collimation error is the same at both setups and that the targets are stable between them. The correction applies to a single sight length, with refraction taken as about one seventh of the curvature effect.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Reciprocal levelling and the combined curvature-refraction correction
backsight and foresight from the first setup
backsight and foresight from the second setup, instrument moved across
true difference in level between the two points
combined correction for curvature and refraction

Reciprocal levelling assumes the collimation error is the same at both setups and that the targets are stable between them. The correction applies to a single sight length, with refraction taken as about one seventh of the curvature effect.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: A level instrument whose line of sight is not perfectly horizontal produces a systematic error proportional to distance, and one with a mis-set striding level can be badly out. Setting the instrument up on one bank and then on the other changes the sign of the error relative to the true difference while leaving its magnitude the same, so averaging the two differences cancels it. The second relation deals with a different systematic effect: a horizontal line of sight diverges from the curved equipotential surface and is bent by atmospheric refraction, which together raise or lower the apparent position of a distant staff by an amount proportional to the square of the distance. Both corrections are small per setup and significant in aggregate, which is why long lines of levels are adjusted rather than trusted.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A level is set up on one bank and then on the other. From setup A the backsight is 1.500 and the foresight 2.000; from setup B the backsight is 1.200 and the foresight 1.680. Find the true difference in level.
Form the two differences, then average them to cancel the collimation error.
The far point is 0.490 m below the near one, and the 0.020 m spread between the two setups is the collimation error effect.
What is the combined curvature and refraction correction for a 2 km sight?
Apply the correction relation with the distance in kilometres.
269 mm of correction, far too large to ignore in a 2 km sight, and the reason long sights are avoided.

standard.title: Formula and variables

blocks: A level instrument whose line of sight is not perfectly horizontal produces a systematic error proportional to distance, and one with a mis-set striding level can be badly out. Setting the instrument up on one bank and then on the other changes the sign of the error relative to the true difference while leaving its magnitude the same, so averaging the two differences cancels it. The second relation deals with a different systematic effect: a horizontal line of sight diverges from the curved equipotential surface and is bent by atmospheric refraction, which together raise or lower the apparent position of a distant staff by an amount proportional to the square of the distance. Both corrections are small per setup and significant in aggregate, which is why long lines of levels are adjusted rather than trusted.
standard.title: Derivation

blocks: A level is set up on one bank and then on the other. From setup A the backsight is 1.500 and the foresight 2.000; from setup B the backsight is 1.200 and the foresight 1.680. Find the true difference in level.
Form the two differences, then average them to cancel the collimation error.
The far point is 0.490 m below the near one, and the 0.020 m spread between the two setups is the collimation error effect.
What is the combined curvature and refraction correction for a 2 km sight?
Apply the correction relation with the distance in kilometres.
269 mm of correction, far too large to ignore in a 2 km sight, and the reason long sights are avoided.

blocks: Averaging |V_m sin(omega t)| over a full period gives 2V_m/pi: the absolute value makes both half-cycles contribute positively. Half-wave rectification averages only V_m/pi and leaves gaps at line frequency; the bridge conducts two diodes at a time but delivers pulses at twice the input frequency, which is also why smoothing it needs only half the capacitance.

blocks: A bridge rectifier is fed by a 10 V peak transformer secondary with a resistive load. What is the average output with ideal diodes, and roughly with silicon diodes?
Apply the averaging factor, then subtract two diode drops.

About 6.37 V ideal, about 5.5 V with real silicon diodes.

blocks: Recurrences, Characteristic Roots and Closed Forms is a core model in Discrete Mathematics: A linear recurrence describes cost, count or state growth; its characteristic roots turn the recursion into a closed form whose dominant root is the growth rate. The model is used within these stated limits: The recurrence is homogeneous with constant coefficients and the roots are distinct. Repeated roots need a factor n on the second term, and inhomogeneous recurrences need a particular solution added.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Solution of a second-order linear recurrence
a_n=A r_1^ n+B r_2^ n, r^2=c_1r+c_2
constants fixed by the initial conditions
The recurrence is homogeneous with constant coefficients and the roots are distinct. Repeated roots need a factor n on the second term, and inhomogeneous recurrences need a particular solution added.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Substitute the trial solution a geometric sequence into the recurrence and divide through by the smallest power, which is legal for a non-zero root. The result is the characteristic equation, a quadratic whose roots are the possible growth factors. Because the recurrence is linear, any sum of solutions is a solution, so the general form is a combination of the two roots, and the two initial conditions pin the constants. The dominant root controls the growth: if its magnitude exceeds one the sequence grows geometrically, if it is inside the unit circle the sequence decays, and if the roots are complex conjugates the sequence oscillates. This is the same characteristic-root method that decides stability of a sampled control loop and gives the closed form for Fibonacci-like counting recurrences.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: Fibonacci numbers satisfy F_n = F_{n-1} + F_{n-2} with F_0 = 0 and F_1 = 1. What does the closed form give for F_10?
Solve the characteristic equation, then apply the initial conditions to get the coefficients.
r^2 = r + 1 gives roots phi = 1.6180 and psi = -0.6180. With the initial conditions, A = 1/root 5 and B = -1/root 5. Then phi^10 = 122.9919, psi^10 = 0.0081, and (122.9919 - 0.0081)/2.2361 = 55.0.
F_10 = 55, matching the recurrence, and the growth rate is the golden ratio.
Solve a_n = 5a_{n-1} - 6a_{n-2} with a_0 = 1 and a_1 = 4. What is a_2?
Find the roots, fit the constants to the initial conditions, then check the answer against the recurrence.
r^2 - 5r + 6 = 0 gives roots 2 and 3. A + B = 1 and 2A + 3B = 4 give A = -1, B = 2. So a_n = -2^n + 2 x 3^n and a_2 = -4 + 18 = 14.
a_2 = 14, which the recurrence also gives as 5 x 4 - 6 x 1 = 14.

blocks: Recursion is the natural way to write tree and grammar algorithms, and backtracking is how constraint problems get solved when no better method is known.

Compilers and interpreters are recursive-descent parsers: one function per grammar rule, each calling the others. That is readable and fast enough, but it is vulnerable to stack exhaustion on deeply nested input, so production parsers bound nesting depth explicitly — a real CVE class.

Backtracking powers regex engines, SAT solvers, configuration finders and route planners. The engineering work is almost entirely in the pruning. A naive backtracking search over a schedule is intractable; the same search with a good bound and variable-ordering heuristic finishes in seconds. Constraint solvers are essentially backtracking with sophisticated propagation.

The practical warning is stack depth. A recursion whose depth is proportional to input size will overflow on input an attacker controls. Converting to an explicit stack is the standard fix, and it also removes the per-call frame overhead.

blocks: Recycle, Bypass and Purge Balances is a core model in Process Calculations: Recycle loops make balances iterative on purpose: what leaves unreacted comes back to the reactor, and the steady-state balance closes only when accumulation around the loop is zero. The model is used within these stated limits: Steady state; choose the system boundary first - the overall balance ignores internal recycle entirely, which is what makes the algebra solvable.

blocks: A recycle loop seems circular - the reactor feed depends on its own output - but steady state breaks the circle: the overall balance over the whole flowsheet contains no recycle term, so solving it first fixes the net flows, and only then do mixing-point balances resolve R. Per-pass conversion is deliberately low while overall conversion is high; the separator sends unreacted material back. Purge streams bleed inerts that would otherwise accumulate without limit, and their size is itself a balance: purge fraction times loop inventory must equal inert inflow at steady state.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A reactor converts 20% per pass. Fresh feed is 1,000 kg/h and overall conversion must be 100% of the fresh feed's reactant, with unreacted material recycled. Find the recycle rate.

Overall: all 1,000 kg/h converts to product, so the separator returns every unreacted kilogram. Reactor inlet = 1,000 + R and 20% of it must equal 1,000: 0.2(1,000 + R) = 1,000, giving 1,000 + R = 5,000.
R = 4,000 kg/h recycled - the reactor processes 5 tonnes per hour to net one, the standard price of low per-pass conversion with full recycle.
