blocks: Recycle, Overall Conversion and the Law of Diminishing Returns is a core model in Process Calculations: A recycle loop raises overall conversion beyond what one pass achieves, but the improvement saturates: each further increment of recycle buys less and costs more circulation. The model is used within these stated limits: A single reaction with unreacted feed separated and returned, no purge or by-product withdrawal, and steady state. A purge to control inerts means the relation must be written with the purge fraction included.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Overall conversion with recycle of unreacted feed
conversion per pass through the reactor
fraction of unreacted material recycled to the reactor

A single reaction with unreacted feed separated and returned, no purge or by-product withdrawal, and steady state. A purge to control inerts means the relation must be written with the purge fraction included.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Each pass through the reactor converts a fixed fraction of what enters, and the unreacted portion returns. The material leaving the loop is the fresh feed minus what has been converted in total, so the overall conversion can be written in terms of the per-pass conversion and the fraction recycled. The algebra shows saturation clearly: as the recycle fraction approaches one the denominator approaches the per-pass conversion, so the overall conversion approaches one only very slowly, and the circulating flow grows without bound while the product flow barely changes. In practice a purge is always present to remove inerts, which caps the achievable recycle fraction and therefore the overall conversion, and the reactor's size and the separation train's capacity both scale with the circulation rate rather than with the fresh feed.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A reactor converts 50 % per pass with 80 % of the unreacted material recycled. Find the overall conversion.
Overall conversion 83.3 % from a 50 % per-pass conversion, with an average of about two passes per molecule.
Recycle is raised to 95 %. What is the overall conversion now?
Reapply the relation with the higher recycle fraction.
95.2 % against 83.3 %, but the recycled flow rises from 0.8 to 0.95 of the unreacted stream per pass - a large increase in circulation for an eleven point gain.

The model is used within these stated limits: The motor is at standstill so the rotor appears as a short circuit, and the per-phase equivalent circuit is linear. Star-delta applies a factor of one third to current and torque; an autotransformer at tap fraction x applies x squared.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Starting current and torque under reduced voltage

The motor is at standstill so the rotor appears as a short circuit, and the per-phase equivalent circuit is linear. Star-delta applies a factor of one third to current and torque; an autotransformer at tap fraction x applies x squared.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: At standstill the rotor's slip is one, the slip frequency is the supply frequency, and the rotor circuit presents its lowest impedance, so the motor behaves almost like a short circuited transformer and draws a large current. Because the developed torque depends on the square of the applied voltage, any method that reduces the voltage reduces starting current and starting torque by the same factor. That is the whole design conversation: enough voltage reduction to stay within the supply's current limit, but not so much that the torque can no longer accelerate the load, since the load may need more torque than a heavily reduced start can provide. Star-delta is popular because the factor is exact and the components are just three contactors, and the transition between star and delta must be made fast to avoid a large current transient.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A motor draws six times full-load current, 40 A, when started direct on line. What are the starting current and torque with a star-delta starter?
Star-delta applies a one-third factor to both current and torque.
Direct-on-line starting current = 6 x 40 = 240 A. In star the winding voltage falls by root 3, so the current falls by one third: 240/3 = 80 A, and torque also falls to one third.
80 A and one third of the direct-on-line torque, which is often enough to accelerate a fan or pump load.
An autotransformer starter uses a 65 % tap. What fraction of direct-on-line current and torque results?
Both scale with the square of the tap fraction.
0.65^2 = 0.4225, so 240 x 0.4225 = 101.4 A and 42 % of direct-on-line torque.
About 101 A and 42 % torque: less reduction than star-delta for current, but more torque, which is the reason the tap is selectable.

blocks: Reflection, Standing Waves and Impedance Matching is a core model in Electromagnetic Fields: Whenever a guided wave meets an impedance change, part of it reflects back; the reflection coefficient and the standing-wave ratio quantify the mismatch and tell you what matching will buy. The model is used within these stated limits: A single transverse-electromagnetic mode on a uniform line, a purely resistive load for the scalar form, and a lossless line so that all reflected power returns to the load. Reactive loads need the complex reflection coefficient.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Reflection coefficient, VSWR and return loss

A single transverse-electromagnetic mode on a uniform line, a purely resistive load for the scalar form, and a lossless line so that all reflected power returns to the load. Reactive loads need the complex reflection coefficient.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: A wave travelling toward a load carries power in the ratio of voltage to current set by the line's characteristic impedance. A load with a different ratio cannot absorb all of it, so the unmatched part reflects and travels back, interfering with the incident wave to produce a standing-wave pattern whose maxima and minima are separated by a quarter wavelength. The reflection coefficient is the ratio of the reflected to incident voltage at the load, the standing-wave ratio converts its magnitude into the peak-to-trough ratio an instrument measures, and the return loss expresses the same information in decibels as power lost to the reflection. Matching improves all three and, just as importantly, protects the source from reflected power.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A 75 ohm load terminates a 50 ohm line. Find the reflection coefficient, the VSWR and the return loss.
Apply the ratio of the impedance difference to the sum, then convert.
Reflection coefficient 0.2, VSWR 1.5, return loss about 14 dB, or 4 % of incident power reflected.
What impedance transforms a 50 ohm line to a 75 ohm load at a single frequency?
A quarter-wave section with a geometric-mean impedance matches two real impedances.
A quarter-wavelength section of about 61 ohm line, which is why 75 ohm coaxial cable appears in 50 ohm systems and vice versa; the match holds over a narrow band.

blocks: Refrigeration COP and the Condenser Temperature Penalty is a core model in Refrigeration & Air Conditioning: A vapour-compression cycle's efficiency is bounded by the Carnot limit between its two temperatures, and the condenser temperature costs more than the evaporator temperature is worth. The model is used within these stated limits: Absolute temperatures in kelvin, a cycle with no pressure drop in the lines and no subcooling or superheat effects on the limit. Real compressors, fans and pumps all reduce the practical figure below the second-law fraction.

cooling delivered per unit of compressor work

blocks: The Carnot bound takes the temperature difference across the cycle in kelvin as the denominator, so a larger difference for the same cold temperature costs efficiency directly. Both temperatures are absolute, so a condenser running ten degrees hotter costs proportionally more than intuition suggests, and the second-law efficiency converts the theoretical bound into the fraction a real compressor achieves. The arithmetic is the reason why condenser maintenance pays: dirty coils and blocked airflow raise the condensing temperature, the temperature difference widens, and the compressor runs longer, so the penalty compounds into electricity consumption without any change in the cooling delivered.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A chiller runs at an evaporating temperature of 5 degrees C and a condensing temperature of 40 degrees C with a second-law efficiency of 0.6. Find the actual COP and the compressor power for 10 kW of cooling.
Convert to kelvin, apply the Carnot relation, multiply by the efficiency, then divide the cooling duty by the COP.
T_L = 278 K, T_H = 313 K, so the difference is 35 K and COP_Carnot = 278/35 = 7.94. Actual COP = 0.6 x 7.94 = 4.77. Power = 10/4.77 = 2.10 kW.
COP 4.77 and about 2.1 kW of compressor power for 10 kW of cooling.
The condenser temperature rises to 50 degrees C through fouling. What happens to the compressor power for the same 10 kW of cooling?
Recompute the Carnot COP with the new condenser temperature and keep the same second-law efficiency.
T_H = 323 K, difference 45 K, COP_Carnot = 278/45 = 6.18, actual COP = 0.6 x 6.18 = 3.71, so power = 10/3.71 = 2.70 kW.
Power rises from 2.10 kW to 2.70 kW - a 28 % increase for a ten-degree change that a cleaning would remove.

blocks: Weight decay adds a quadratic penalty whose gradient pulls every weight toward zero each step, which keeps the function's curvature gentle and limits how hard the model can contort to memorize noise. Dropout zeroes each unit with probability 1-p per training step, so no unit can rely on a specific partner being present - co-adaptation breaks, and the network learns redundantly useful features. Because each step trains a different subset, dropout approximates training an exponential ensemble and averaging it at test time, which is the variance-reduction reading of the same trick.

An astronomically large implicit ensemble, collapsed to one deterministic network at test time by scaling.

blocks: selection: keep rows satisfying predicate p
join: pair rows with equal keys
Operators consume and produce relations (sets of tuples), so results compose freely; set semantics mean duplicates are removed unless bag semantics are stated.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Selection cuts rows, projection cuts columns, join multiplies matching rows - and because each operator's output is again a relation, any query is a tree of these cuts. The algebra's value is equivalence: pushing sigma below the bowtie (filter before join) produces the same answer on far fewer pairs, and pushing pi early shrinks tuples. Optimizers search exactly these rewrites, which is why 'write the predicate on the joined table' and 'write it in WHERE' usually compile to the same plan.

blocks: Orders has 1,000 rows, 100 of them for city = Pune. Customers has 5,000 rows. Compare join-then-filter with filter-then-join.
Count the row pairs each order of operations handles.
Join first: 1,000 orders matched against customer keys, then filter 100 surviving rows. Filter first: sigma leaves 100 orders, and only those 100 probe the customer index.
Same 100-row answer, but filter-first does the join work on 10% of the rows - the optimizer's standard rewrite.

blocks: Selection cuts rows, projection cuts columns, join multiplies matching rows - and because each operator's output is again a relation, any query is a tree of these cuts. blocks: Relative Volatility and Minimum Stages in Distillation is a core model in Chemical Engineering Thermodynamics: The ease of a distillation separation is captured by relative volatility, and the minimum number of theoretical stages needed follows from it by a single logarithm. The model is used within these stated limits: Constant relative volatility across the column, total reflux with no product withdrawal, and a binary or a key-component pair in a multicomponent mixture. Real columns need more stages than this minimum and have a reflux ratio above the minimum.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Fenske equation for minimum stages at total reflux
distillate mole fraction of the light component
bottoms mole fraction of the light component
average relative volatility of the pair
minimum number of theoretical stages at total reflux

Constant relative volatility across the column, total reflux with no product withdrawal, and a binary or a key-component pair in a multicomponent mixture. Real columns need more stages than this minimum and have a reflux ratio above the minimum.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Relative volatility is the ratio of the two components' tendencies to enter the vapour, so a value close to one means the pair barely prefers the vapour phase and the separation is hard. Each theoretical stage performs one equilibrium contacting, and at total reflux the composition change per stage is a fixed ratio when the volatility is constant. Cascading that ratio from the bottoms composition to the distillate composition gives a geometric progression, and solving it for the number of stages produces the logarithm of the composition ratio divided by the logarithm of the relative volatility. The equation is used for two things in practice: a fast estimate of column height for a proposed separation, and the demonstration of how sharply stage count grows as volatility approaches one.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A separation requires 98 % light component overhead and 2 % in the bottoms with a relative volatility of 2.4. Find the minimum number of stages.
Form the composition ratio, then divide its logarithm by the logarithm of the volatility.
About 9 theoretical stages at total reflux, so a real column with a finite reflux ratio needs more, and the packing height or tray count follows from the stage efficiency.
The relative volatility falls to 1.2 for a different pair with the same purity targets. How many stages are needed?
Reapply the relation with the new volatility, keeping the same composition ratio.
About 43 stages against 9 - nearly five times the column height for the same separation, which is why close boilers are expensive to separate.

blocks: Ridge Regularisation and Numerical Conditioning is a core model in Machine Learning: Adding a squared penalty turns an ill-posed least-squares problem into a well-conditioned one, at the cost of a deliberate, quantifiable shrinkage of the coefficients. The model is used within these stated limits: The penalty applies to the coefficients only, the features are already scaled comparably, and the intercept is either centred out or not penalised.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: design matrix of n rows and d features
The penalty applies to the coefficients only, the features are already scaled comparably, and the intercept is either centred out or not penalised.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Start from the least-squares loss and add a penalty on the squared coefficient norm. Differentiating with respect to w gives a gradient of minus two X transposed times the residual plus two lambda w; setting it to zero yields the normal equations with lambda on the diagonal. The effect is geometric: every eigenvalue of X transposed X increases by lambda, so the smallest eigenvalue is no longer near zero and the inverse is stable. Shrinkage is the price: coefficients fall below the unregularised solution, with the bias increasing and the variance falling, and the condition number improving from the ratio of squared singular values to the same ratio with lambda added to both terms.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A one-feature problem has sum of x squared equal to 4 and sum of x times y equal to 8. Compare the unregularised coefficient with lambda = 4.
The scalar case of the ridge solution divides the cross-product by the sum of squares plus lambda.
The coefficient halves, from 2 to 1. Shrinkage grows with lambda; at lambda = 4 the penalty is as strong as the data term for this single feature.
Eigenvalues of X transposed X are 100 and 0.01. Compute the condition number before and after ridge with lambda = 1.
Condition number is the ratio of the largest to the smallest eigenvalue.
The condition number improves from 10,000 to 100, a hundredfold improvement in sensitivity to perturbation.

standard.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Start from the least-squares loss and add a penalty on the squared coefficient norm. Differentiating with respect to w gives a gradient of minus two X transposed times the residual plus two lambda w; setting it to zero yields the normal equations with lambda on the diagonal. The effect is geometric: every eigenvalue of X transposed X increases by lambda, so the smallest eigenvalue is no longer near zero and the inverse is stable. Shrinkage is the price: coefficients fall below the unregularised solution, with the bias increasing and the variance falling, and the condition number improving from the ratio of squared singular values to the same ratio with lambda added to both terms.
standard.title: Derivation

blocks: A one-feature problem has sum of x squared equal to 4 and sum of x times y equal to 8. Compare the unregularised coefficient with lambda = 4.
The scalar case of the ridge solution divides the cross-product by the sum of squares plus lambda.
The coefficient halves, from 2 to 1. Shrinkage grows with lambda; at lambda = 4 the penalty is as strong as the data term for this single feature.
Eigenvalues of X transposed X are 100 and 0.01. Compute the condition number before and after ridge with lambda = 1.
Condition number is the ratio of the largest to the smallest eigenvalue.
The condition number improves from 10,000 to 100, a hundredfold improvement in sensitivity to perturbation.

blocks: Routh-Hurwitz Stability Criterion is a core model in Control Systems Engineering: The Routh array counts right-half-plane poles from the characteristic polynomial's coefficients alone - no root solving, and it answers 'for which gains is the system stable?' directly. The model is used within these stated limits: Necessary first check: every coefficient present and of one sign; the array then counts RHP poles, with special epsilon/auxiliary-polynomial handling for zero rows.

advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Build the array: two rows from alternating coefficients, then each further row by the cross-determinant recursion. The theorem says the number of sign changes down the first column equals the number of poles with positive real part - a consequence of how the recursion tracks root locations as a parameter sweeps. When the polynomial's coefficients depend on a gain K, the first-column entries are expressions in K; demanding they all stay positive produces inequalities whose intersection is the stabilizing gain range. The boundary case - a zero in the first column - marks the exact gain where roots cross onto the imaginary axis, giving the oscillation frequency from the auxiliary polynomial.

Stable for -1 < K < 8; at K = 8 the s^1 row vanishes and the auxiliary 3s^2 + 9 = 0 puts poles at +/- j1.73 rad/s - sustained oscillation at the boundary.

blocks: SQL injection occurs when untrusted strings are merged into a SQL program. NoSQL injection occurs when callers can shape query operators or objects instead of supplying a validated scalar. blocks: Draw many samples of size n and plot their means: that histogram is the sampling distribution, and its spread is not the data's spread but the data's spread divided by sqrt(n). The CLT is why the shape converges to normal regardless of the population's own shape - averaging drowns out skew in both tails symmetrically. Every confidence interval and z/t test stands on this: the sqrt(n) law is what makes 'four times the data halves the error bar' the fundamental price of precision.

advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Sampling a signal at a rate below twice its highest frequency folds energy from above half the sampling rate down into the band of interest. Placing a filter before the converter must therefore attenuate everything above half the rate - and because the first band that folds down begins at the sampling rate minus the passband edge, the filter's transition band runs from the highest signal frequency to that edge. The order needed grows with the ratio of those two frequencies in decades: a narrow gap demands a high order. Raising the sampling rate widens the gap without touching the analogue filter, which is why oversampling converters and digital decimation filters are cheaper than steep analogue filters.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A 1 kHz band must be preserved with 80 dB rejection. Compare the filter order needed at 2.5 kHz and at 10 kHz sampling.
The alias edge is the sampling rate minus the passband edge; the order follows from the attenuation divided by 20 dB per decade of the frequency ratio.
At 2.5 kHz: edge = 1.5 kHz, ratio = 1.5, so n = 80/(20 x 0.176) = 22.7, about 23 sections. At 10 kHz: edge = 9 kHz, ratio = 9, so n = 80/(20 x 0.954) = 4.2, about 5 sections.
Twenty-three sections against five: quadrupling the sampling rate turns an impractical analogue filter into a routine one.
A 1.3 kHz tone is sampled at 2 kHz without filtering. Where does it appear in the digitised spectrum?
Frequencies above half the sampling rate fold back, mirrored about that rate.
Half the sampling rate is 1 kHz, so the tone above it folds to 2 - 1.3 = 0.7 kHz.
It appears at 700 Hz, indistinguishable from a genuine 700 Hz signal; no amount of digital processing afterwards can remove it.

blocks: Sampling Rate, Loop Delay and the Torque Budget is a core model in Mechatronic System Design: A closed-loop mechatronic design is bounded by two calculations: the sampling rate that keeps the digital loop behaving like the analogue one it replaces, and the torque the actuator must supply. The model is used within these stated limits: A rigidly coupled load with the inertia reflected through the transmission, a bandwidth set by the required settling time, and a sampling rate at least an order of magnitude above it. Compliance in the transmission and structural resonances limit the achievable bandwidth below this estimate.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Sampling guidance and the actuator torque budget
required actuator torque before safety factor

A rigidly coupled load with the inertia reflected through the transmission, a bandwidth set by the required settling time, and a sampling rate at least an order of magnitude above it. Compliance in the transmission and structural resonances limit the achievable bandwidth below this estimate.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: A digital controller acts on a delayed and quantised version of the measurement, so its loop behaves like a continuous controller with an extra delay of about one sample. That delay costs phase margin, and the phase it costs is proportional to frequency, so the sampling rate must be high enough that the phase loss at the crossover frequency is negligible - which is where the ten-to-twenty times bandwidth guidance comes from. The torque budget is separate: accelerating the reflected inertia is unavoidable, friction has to be overcome, and any external load adds on top. Adding a safety factor covers the estimates that the model does not capture, and checking the result against the motor's peak torque and its continuous rating separates a design that works from one that overheats.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A rotary axis has 0.01 kg m^2 of reflected inertia and must accelerate at 100 rad/s^2 with 0.2 N m of friction and 0.5 N m of load. Find the required torque before the safety factor.
Multiply inertia by acceleration, then add friction and load.
1.7 N m, so a motor rated near 3.4 N m peak to give a two-times margin, and a continuous rating checked against the rms torque of the duty cycle.
The loop bandwidth is 20 Hz. What sampling rate is appropriate, and what phase does a one-millisecond delay cost at 10 Hz?
Apply the sampling guidance, then use the linear phase relation of a pure delay.
Sampling should be 200 to 400 Hz or higher, so 1 kHz is a comfortable choice. A 1 ms delay costs 360 x 10 x 0.001 = 3.6 degrees at 10 Hz, and 36 degrees at 100 Hz.
1 kHz is appropriate. The same delay is negligible at 10 Hz but significant at 100 Hz, which is why bandwidth and sampling rate are chosen together.

standard.title: Formula and variables

blocks: A digital controller acts on a delayed and quantised version of the measurement, so its loop behaves like a continuous controller with an extra delay of about one sample. That delay costs phase margin, and the phase it costs is proportional to frequency, so the sampling rate must be high enough that the phase loss at the crossover frequency is negligible - which is where the ten-to-twenty times bandwidth guidance comes from. The torque budget is separate: accelerating the reflected inertia is unavoidable, friction has to be overcome, and any external load adds on top. Adding a safety factor covers the estimates that the model does not capture, and checking the result against the motor's peak torque and its continuous rating separates a design that works from one that overheats.
standard.title: Derivation

blocks: A rotary axis has 0.01 kg m^2 of reflected inertia and must accelerate at 100 rad/s^2 with 0.2 N m of friction and 0.5 N m of load. Find the required torque before the safety factor.
Multiply inertia by acceleration, then add friction and load.
1.7 N m, so a motor rated near 3.4 N m peak to give a two-times margin, and a continuous rating checked against the rms torque of the duty cycle.
The loop bandwidth is 20 Hz. What sampling rate is appropriate, and what phase does a one-millisecond delay cost at 10 Hz?
Apply the sampling guidance, then use the linear phase relation of a pure delay.
Sampling should be 200 to 400 Hz or higher, so 1 kHz is a comfortable choice. A 1 ms delay costs 360 x 10 x 0.001 = 3.6 degrees at 10 Hz, and 36 degrees at 100 Hz.
1 kHz is appropriate. The same delay is negligible at 10 Hz but significant at 100 Hz, which is why bandwidth and sampling rate are chosen together.

blocks: Scan Time and Worst-Case Input-to-Output Latency is a core model in Industrial Automation & PLC Systems: A PLC's response to an input is not instant: the worst case is two scan cycles plus input filter and output delays, and safety functions are verified against that number. The model is used within these stated limits: Synchronous scan execution in which inputs are read at the start and outputs written at the end of each scan. Interrupt-driven logic, distributed I/O over a fieldbus and safety processors each add their own timing terms.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Synchronous scan execution in which inputs are read at the start and outputs written at the end of each scan. Interrupt-driven logic, distributed I/O over a fieldbus and safety processors each add their own timing terms.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: A PLC reads every input, executes the program and writes every output once per scan. An input that changes immediately after the read is not seen until the next read, and the resulting output cannot appear until the scan after that, so the worst-case latency is two scans before the module delays. Input filtering adds a deliberate debounce delay that protects against noise but is paid on every transition, and output modules and contactors add a final delay. The arithmetic matters because safety and process functions are specified in milliseconds: a guard door that must stop a drive within fifty milliseconds gives a budget that either fits in two scans or requires a safety-rated processor with a shorter cycle, faster inputs or hardwired logic.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A PLC scans in 10 ms with a 3 ms input filter and a 1 ms output delay. Find the worst-case response time.
Apply two scan times plus the filter and output delays.
24 milliseconds worst case, which fits a 50 ms requirement with 26 ms of margin.
Additional logic raises the scan to 18 ms. Is the 50 ms requirement still met, and what are the options?
Recompute the worst-case latency and compare with the requirement.
t_resp = 2 x 18 + 3 + 1 = 40 ms, so the requirement is met with only 10 ms of margin.
It still passes, but the margin is thin. Options are moving the interlock to a safety PLC with a 5 ms scan, which gives 14 ms, or reducing input filtering and output delay.

blocks: Second-Order Linear ODEs: Characteristic Roots and Damping is a core model in Engineering Mathematics II: A constant-coefficient second-order ODE is solved by one quadratic: the roots decide whether the response decays smoothly, oscillates, or sits exactly on the boundary. The model is used within these stated limits: Coefficients must be constant and the equation linear and homogeneous; the same discriminant logic later reappears as the damping ratio in control systems.

advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Substitute the trial solution y = e^(mx). Each derivative multiplies by m, so the ODE becomes the algebraic equation (am^2 + bm + c)e^(mx) = 0, and since the exponential is never zero the quadratic alone decides everything: two real roots give a sum of decays or growths, complex roots give an exponential envelope times sine and cosine, and a repeated root needs the extra t-weighted term to keep two independent solutions.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: Form the characteristic quadratic and inspect the discriminant.
m^2 + 4m + 4 = 0 gives discriminant 16 - 16 = 0, so a repeated root m = -2. The repeated root supplies only e^(-2t), so the second independent solution is t*e^(-2t).

blocks: The characteristic equation s^2 + 2 zeta omega_n s + omega_n^2 fixes poles at -zeta omega_n +/- j omega_n sqrt(1 - zeta^2). The real part is the decay rate - settling time is roughly four time constants, 4/(zeta omega_n). The pole angle from the negative real axis has cosine zeta, and the step response's first peak comes from one half-cycle of the damped sinusoid, giving the exponential overshoot formula. The trade is geometric: smaller zeta moves poles toward the imaginary axis - faster rise, bigger overshoot, longer ringing - and zeta around 0.7 is the classic compromise (about 5% overshoot).

industry.title: Real-world applications

blocks: The pn junction is the building block of nearly every active device, and its limits set the limits of the systems built from it.

The exponential current-voltage relation is why a diode has a "turn-on" voltage rather than a gradual onset, and why that voltage is temperature dependent — roughly 2 mV per kelvin for silicon. That drift is a nuisance in precision circuits and a feature in temperature sensors, which are often just a transistor junction measured carefully.

Temperature is the governing constraint everywhere. Reverse leakage roughly doubles every 10 K, and the maximum junction temperature is typically 150 °C for silicon. Exceeding it does not fail the device immediately; it degrades it over time, which is why thermal design is a reliability question rather than a performance one. This is the real reason power electronics are built around heat sinks and thermal interface materials.

Breakdown is used deliberately in Zener diodes for voltage reference and clamping, and destructively avoided elsewhere. The distinction is doping: a heavily doped junction breaks down by tunnelling at a well-defined low voltage and recovers; a lightly doped one avalanches at a high voltage and may be damaged by the energy dissipated.

Photovoltaics and LEDs are the same junction run in reverse. A solar cell uses light-generated carriers separated by the built-in field; an LED injects carriers that recombine and emit. Both are limited by the same physics that governs the diode, which is why cell efficiency and LED wall-plug efficiency are both far below the thermodynamic limits — the gap is recombination and resistive loss.

blocks: Sensor Fusion: Complementary Filtering Basics is a core model in Mechatronic System Design: A gyro knows fast changes but drifts; an accelerometer knows the horizon but vibrates - a complementary filter sums their strengths with one tunable constant. The model is used within these stated limits: Small-angle tilt sensing with a low-vibration environment; the same structure generalizes to full attitude estimation, where the Kalman filter makes alpha state-dependent and optimal.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: θ arrow α (θ+ω Δ t)+(1-α) θ_acc, τ=(α Δ t)/(1-α)
Small-angle tilt sensing with a low-vibration environment; the same structure generalizes to full attitude estimation, where the Kalman filter makes alpha state-dependent and optimal.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Integrating the gyro gives a smooth short-term angle whose error grows without bound (bias integrates to drift); the accelerometer's tilt angle is drift-free long-term but jittery under acceleration. The complementary filter passes the gyro through a high-pass role and the accelerometer through a low-pass role - the two weights summing to one is what makes them 'complementary': every frequency is covered exactly once. The single constant alpha sets the crossover: near 1, the gyro rules and drift accumulates over the time constant tau; lower, tilt corrections bite faster and vibration leaks in. It is a two-line algorithm that stabilizes drones and wearables where a full Kalman filter is overkill.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A tilt sensor runs at 50 Hz (dt = 0.02 s) with alpha = 0.98. Find the correction time constant, and what a 1 deg/s gyro bias does to the fused angle over 10 s.
Compute tau, then weigh bias drift against correction.

tau = 0.98 x 0.02 / 0.02 = 0.98 s. The integrator alone would accumulate 10 deg of drift in 10 s; the accelerometer term pulls the estimate back toward truth with a ~1 s time constant, holding the steady error near bias x tau = about 1 deg.
tau ~ 1 s bounds gyro drift to roughly the bias times tau - the single constant trading smoothness against drift, exactly as the filter's structure promises.

The formula is a proxy for difficulty built from two measurable quantities, not a measure of writing quality; it ignores jargon, structure and whether the content is correct. It applies to English prose produced for a general technical audience.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Readability formulas exist because two features of prose predict how hard it is to read more reliably than anything else: how many words sit between full stops, and how long those words are. The formula simply weights the two, and the useful part is the ratio, because it makes an editorial instruction concrete: shorten sentences and prefer shorter words, and the score moves. The reason this matters in engineering is not literary preference but the reader's behaviour, since a technical document is usually skimmed for a decision before it is read in full. Structure carries the same weight: a heading hierarchy, a first-line conclusion and a labelled table let a skimming reader extract the answer, and a readable score with no structure still fails.

A score of 19, which is dense reading even for a technical audience; splitting sentences at conjunctions and cutting nominalisations would move it substantially.

blocks: Separation of Variables for the Heat Equation is a core model in Engineering Mathematics III: Assuming a PDE solution factors into a time part times a space part converts one hard equation into two ordinary ones joined by a single separation constant. The model is used within these stated limits: Needs a linear PDE with homogeneous boundary conditions; general solutions are sums of modes, and the method fails outright for nonlinear equations.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: separation constant set by boundary conditions
Needs a linear PDE with homogeneous boundary conditions; general solutions are sums of modes, and the method fails outright for nonlinear equations.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Substitute u = X(x)T(t) into u_t = alpha u_xx and divide by alpha X T. One side depends only on t, the other only on x, and a function of t cannot equal a function of x unless both are the same constant. Call it -lambda^2: the time equation gives exponential decay e^(-alpha lambda^2 t) and the space equation gives sines and cosines, with the boundaries selecting which lambda values survive.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A rod of length L has ends held at zero. What happens to the mode sin(pi x / L) over time?
Identify lambda from the spatial mode and apply the decay law.
The mode matches the boundary condition with lambda = pi/L, so its time factor is exp(-alpha (pi/L)^2 t). Higher modes have larger lambda and decay faster.
It decays exponentially as e^(-alpha pi^2 t / L^2), and any rougher initial profile smooths toward this slowest mode.

blocks: Series RLC Resonance, Bandwidth and Q is a core model in Basic Electrical Engineering: At one frequency the inductive and capacitive reactances cancel, the series circuit looks purely resistive, and the sharpness of that peak is set by Q. The model is used within these stated limits: Series RLC driven by a sinusoid; Q = omega0 L / R and the half-power points sit where |Z| = sqrt(2) R.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Series RLC driven by a sinusoid; Q = omega0 L / R and the half-power points sit where |Z| = sqrt(2) R.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Impedance is Z = R + j(omega L - 1/omega C). The imaginary part passes through zero at omega0 = 1/sqrt(LC): below it the capacitor dominates, above it the inductor does. At resonance current peaks at V/R and the inductor and capacitor voltages individually reach Q times the supply voltage - which is why a low-voltage radio stage can swing hundreds of volts inside a tuned circuit.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A series RLC has L = 100 mH and C = 10 microfarad. Find f0, and Q if R = 10 ohm.

blocks: A function f: A -> B is a subset of A x B such that for every a in A there is exactly one b in B with (a, b) in f. A is the domain and B is the codomain.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Function as a set of pairs
f \subseteq A \times B,\quad \forall a \in A\ \exists!\ b \in B:\ (a,b) \in f
f ⊆ A × B, ∀ a ∈ A ∃! b ∈ B: (a,b) ∈ f
The unique-existence quantifier is the whole definition. Dropping it leaves a relation.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: A x B is every ordered pair with the first element from A and the second from B. A relation is any subset of that product. blocks: Setup and Hold Slack in a Synchronous Path is a core model in Digital Electronics: Timing closure is arithmetic on one path: the clock period must exceed the total delay around the launch-flop-to-capture-flop path, and the hold check must pass no matter how fast the logic is. The model is used within these stated limits: Single clock domain, no multi-cycle or false paths, and static timing analysis with worst-case corner delays. On-chip variation and jitter need extra margin beyond the numbers used here.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: clock arrival difference between launch and capture
Single clock domain, no multi-cycle or false paths, and static timing analysis with worst-case corner delays. On-chip variation and jitter need extra margin beyond the numbers used here.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: At each active clock edge the launching flip-flop presents new data after its clock-to-output delay, the combinational logic propagates it, and the capturing flip-flop needs the data stable for its setup time before the next edge. Adding those terms gives the minimum period the path supports; subtracting the requirement from the available period gives the slack. Positive slack means the path closes, negative slack means the design fails at that frequency. Clock skew enters with a sign that differs between the setup and hold checks: skew that helps setup hurts hold, which is why the two checks are always performed together.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A path has t_cq = 1.5 ns, combinational delay 6 ns, setup time 0.5 ns and skew 0.3 ns against a 10 ns period. What is the setup slack?
Sum the delays and the skew, then subtract from the period.
1.7 ns of positive slack, which is a comfortable margin at 100 MHz.
The same path is asked to run at 125 MHz. What happens, and what is the smallest fix?
Recompute the slack with a period of 8 ns.
The path fails setup by 0.3 ns. Shortening the combinational logic by 0.3 ns - or moving slack from an adjacent path - closes the frequency.

blocks: Shaft Critical Speed and Lateral Vibration is a core model in Machine Design: A rotating shaft has a natural frequency of lateral vibration; running near it magnifies deflection without limit, so the operating speed is kept well away from the critical. The model is used within these stated limits: A single lumped mass on a massless simply supported shaft, small damping, and a deflection measured statically under the same weight. Multi-mass rotors need a Rayleigh or a finite-element solution, and the bearing stiffness enters the answer.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Critical speed of a simply supported shaft with a central mass
static deflection under the rotor weight

A single lumped mass on a massless simply supported shaft, small damping, and a deflection measured statically under the same weight. Multi-mass rotors need a Rayleigh or a finite-element solution, and the bearing stiffness enters the answer.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: A shaft deflected by a rotating mass carries a centrifugal force proportional to the deflection, so the shaft behaves like a spring-mass system whose natural frequency is the square root of the stiffness-to-mass ratio. Written in terms of the static deflection under the rotor's own weight, that natural frequency becomes the square root of g over the deflection - a relation that is easy to use because stiffness and mass disappear. The significance of the critical speed is that at it the excitation from residual unbalance is in resonance, and deflection grows until either damping or the nonlinearity limits it, at which point the machine destroys itself. Practical design therefore places the operating range either well below the first critical - a stiff shaft - or above it for machines designed to pass through quickly, such as some turbines.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A shaft deflects 0.5 mm under its rotor's weight. Find its critical speed.
Convert the deflection to metres, apply the relation, then convert to revolutions per minute.
About 1338 rpm, so a 1000 rpm machine is adequately below it while a 1300 rpm machine would be in trouble.
The rotor must run at 1200 rpm. What deflection is required to keep the critical speed at least 20 % above the operating speed?
Set the target critical speed, convert to angular frequency, then invert the relation for deflection.
Target N_c = 1200 x 1.2 = 1440 rpm, so omega_c = 1440 x 2 pi/60 = 150.8 rad/s. Then delta = g/omega_c^2 = 9.81/22,740 = 0.000431 m.
A static deflection no greater than 0.43 mm, which is a stiffness target for the shaft and its supports.

blocks: Shear and Bending Moment Diagrams for Beams is a core model in Structural Analysis: Load, shear and moment are derivatives of one another, so each diagram is the integral of the last - and the peak moment lives where shear crosses zero. The model is used within these stated limits: Prismatic beam, small deflections, consistent sign convention; point loads make V jump, point moments make M jump.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Prismatic beam, small deflections, consistent sign convention; point loads make V jump, point moments make M jump.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Equilibrium of a beam slice says the shear changes by minus the load over that slice, and the moment changes by the shear - the calculus chain from w to V to M. Graphically: a uniform load draws a sloping shear line and a parabolic moment; a point load steps the shear and kinks the moment. The maximum moment sits where shear passes through zero, because that is where the moment's derivative changes sign. Drawing the diagrams is bookkeeping with this chain: reactions first, then walk the beam left to right, accumulating areas - the moment at any point equals the area under the shear diagram up to it.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A simply supported 6 m beam carries 10 kN/m uniformly. Draw the key values: reactions, shear extremes and maximum moment.
Use symmetry, then the area relations.

Reactions = 10 x 6 / 2 = 30 kN each. Shear runs linearly from +30 at the left support to -30 at the right, crossing zero at midspan. M_max = area under shear to midspan = triangle = 0.5 x 3 x 30 = 45 kN m - matching wL^2/8 = 10 x 36/8 = 45.
V_max = 30 kN at the supports, M_max = 45 kN m at midspan, where shear crosses zero.

blocks: Equilibrium of a beam slice says the shear changes by minus the load over that slice, and the moment changes by the shear - the calculus chain from w to V to M. Graphically: a uniform load draws a sloping shear line and a parabolic moment; a point load steps the shear and kinks the moment. The maximum moment sits where shear passes through zero, because that is where the moment's derivative changes sign. Drawing the diagrams is bookkeeping with this chain: reactions first, then walk the beam left to right, accumulating areas - the moment at any point equals the area under the shear diagram up to it.

blocks: Shear Design of RC Beams and Stirrup Spacing is a core model in Design of Reinforced Concrete Structures: Concrete carries part of the shear; stirrups carry the rest - and their spacing follows directly from how much shear force the steel must intercept on each potential crack. The model is used within these stated limits: Vertical stirrups, ductile steel yielding across the crack; codes cap spacing (typically 0.75d or 300 mm) and cap V_s to protect against web crushing.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Stirrup spacing from required shear steel
area of stirrup legs crossing a crack
Vertical stirrups, ductile steel yielding across the crack; codes cap spacing (typically 0.75d or 300 mm) and cap V_s to protect against web crushing.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: A shear crack runs diagonally from the compression zone toward the support; stirrups crossing it resist by yielding, and a 45-degree crack over depth d crosses stirrups spaced s apart d/s times. Force equilibrium gives V_s = A_sv f_y d / s, which rearranges to the spacing formula. Concrete's own contribution V_c (aggregate interlock, dowel action, compression-zone shear) is subtracted first, so the steel only covers the excess - but minimum shear steel is required regardless, because a crack that forms must find something crossing it.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A beam must resist V_u = 150 kN with V_c = 70 kN. Using 2-legged 8 mm stirrups (A_sv = 100 mm^2), f_y = 415 MPa, d = 450 mm, find the spacing.
Compute the steel's share, then the spacing.
230 mm spacing - and near midspan where V_u drops below V_c, only minimum stirrups at the code-maximum spacing are needed.

blocks: Sheet-Metal Bend Allowance and Flat Development is a core model in Workshop Practice: Bent sheet parts are cut flat, so the flat pattern must add back the arc length the neutral axis travels through each bend - the bend allowance. The model is used within these stated limits: Constant-thickness sheet, uniform radius; K shifts with the R/t ratio and material, and springback makes the achieved angle slightly less than the tool angle.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Constant-thickness sheet, uniform radius; K shifts with the R/t ratio and material, and springback makes the achieved angle slightly less than the tool angle.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Outside fibres stretch and inside fibres compress, but one layer in between keeps its length - the neutral axis, sitting at a fraction K of the thickness from the inner surface. Through the bend that layer traces a circular arc of radius (R + Kt) spanning theta degrees, and arc length is angle-in-radians times radius, which is the formula. The flat pattern length is the sum of straight flange legs plus one bend allowance per bend.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: Develop the bend allowance for a 90-degree bend, R = 2 mm, t = 1.5 mm, K = 0.33.
BA = 3.92 mm, added once for each such bend in the flat pattern.

blocks: Ship Resistance Components and Effective Power is a core model in Marine Propulsion & Power Systems: A hull's total resistance is the sum of friction, waves and appendages, and the effective power to overcome it at speed - divided by the propulsive coefficient - becomes the shaft power the engine room must supply. The model is used within these stated limits: Calm water at design draught; sea margin, shallow-water and fouling allowances are added on top for engine selection, and R_F scales with wetted surface while R_R grows steeply near hull speed.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: propulsive coefficient, hull efficiency x propeller efficiency x relative rotative efficiency, ~0.5-0.7
Calm water at design draught; sea margin, shallow-water and fouling allowances are added on top for engine selection, and R_F scales with wetted surface while R_R grows steeply near hull speed.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Frictional resistance is the boundary layer's toll on wetted surface - dominant at low speed and for full-form ships. Residuary resistance is the wave system the hull must generate, rising sharply as speed approaches the hull-speed regime set by waterline length. Appendages (shafts, rudders, bilge keels) and air resistance add the remainder. Multiplying total resistance by speed gives the useful tow-rope power; the propulsive coefficient then charges for everything between the waterjet the propeller makes and the hull's benefit - wake, thrust deduction, rotative effects. Engine selection adds sea margin on top: the MCR rating must cover a fouled hull in weather, not the clean trial condition.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A vessel needs 400 kN total resistance at 15 knots (7.72 m/s) with propulsive coefficient 0.6. Find effective power and the shaft power required.
P_E = 400,000 x 7.72 = 3.09 MW. P_D = 3.09/0.6 = 5.15 MW at the shaft (before sea margin; with 15% margin the engine MCR sits near 5.9 MW).
About 3.1 MW effective, 5.2 MW delivered - the propulsive coefficient alone costs 2 MW, which is why hull-propulsor interaction is a design discipline of its own.

blocks: Frictional resistance is the boundary layer's toll on wetted surface - dominant at low speed and for full-form ships. Residuary resistance is the wave system the hull must generate, rising sharply as speed approaches the hull-speed regime set by waterline length. Appendages (shafts, rudders, bilge keels) and air resistance add the remainder. Multiplying total resistance by speed gives the useful tow-rope power; the propulsive coefficient then charges for everything between the waterjet the propeller makes and the hull's benefit - wake, thrust deduction, rotative effects. Engine selection adds sea margin on top: the MCR rating must cover a fouled hull in weather, not the clean trial condition.

blocks: Shortest Paths: Dijkstra and Edge Relaxation is a core model in Data Structures & Algorithms: Dijkstra's algorithm locks in the cheapest known distance to one vertex at a time, and every lock-in is justified by relaxing edges out of the just-settled vertex. The model is used within these stated limits: Weights must be non-negative; with negative edges the greedy lock-in is unsound and Bellman-Ford is the correct tool.

blocks: weight of edge u to v
Weights must be non-negative; with negative edges the greedy lock-in is unsound and Bellman-Ford is the correct tool.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Maintain a tentative distance per vertex, initially infinity except zero at the source. Repeatedly settle the unsettled vertex with the smallest tentative value: with non-negative weights, no later path can undercut it, because any detour through other unsettled vertices only adds non-negative cost. Settling u then relaxes every edge (u,v), improving d[v] whenever going through u is cheaper - each vertex is settled once and each edge relaxed once from its tail.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: Edges: A-B = 2, B-C = 3, A-C = 7. Find the shortest A-to-C distance by relaxation.
Settle vertices in order of tentative distance.
Settle A (d=0): relax to d[B]=2, d[C]=7. Settle B (smallest, 2): relax d[C] = min(7, 2+3) = 5. Settle C at 5.
d[C] = 5 via A-B-C, not the direct 7.

blocks: Skin Depth and High-Frequency Conduction is a core model in Electromagnetic Fields: AC current crowds toward a conductor's surface, and the skin depth formula says how deep it penetrates - the reason high-frequency resistance rises with sqrt(frequency). The model is used within these stated limits: Good-conductor approximation (sigma >> omega epsilon); depth shrinks with frequency, permeability and conductivity, and the current profile is exponential.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: depth where the field falls to 1/e of its surface value
Good-conductor approximation (sigma >> omega epsilon); depth shrinks with frequency, permeability and conductivity, and the current profile is exponential.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: A time-varying magnetic field inside the conductor induces eddy fields that oppose current in the interior and reinforce it near the surface - Lenz's law applied locally. Solving the diffusion equation for the field inside a good conductor gives an exponential decay with distance, whose 1/e length is the skin depth. Beyond a few delta, the core carries essentially nothing: effective cross-section shrinks, AC resistance climbs as the square root of frequency, and magnetic materials (large mu) crowd current even harder.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: Copper has sigma = 5.8e7 S/m and mu ~ mu_0 = 4 pi e-7 H/m. Find the skin depth at 1 MHz.
omega = 2 pi x 1e6 = 6.283e6 rad/s. omega mu sigma = 6.283e6 x 1.2566e-6 x 5.8e7 = 4.58e8. delta = sqrt(2 / 4.58e8) = sqrt(4.37e-9) = 6.6e-5 m.
About 66 micrometres - why RF inductors use litz wire, silver plating, or hollow tubing.

The model is used within these stated limits: The device is biased in the forward-active region, signals are small compared with V_T times a few, and the collector resistance and early effect are ignored. Large signals need the exponential characteristic instead.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: thermal voltage, about 25 mV at room temperature
voltage gain, negative because the stage inverts

The device is biased in the forward-active region, signals are small compared with V_T times a few, and the collector resistance and early effect are ignored. Large signals need the exponential characteristic instead.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: The bipolar junction transistor's collector current depends exponentially on the base-emitter voltage, so its slope - the change in collector current per change in base-emitter voltage - is the current divided by the thermal voltage. That slope is the transconductance, and it is remarkably predictable from bias current alone. Because the collector current flows through R_C, the same relation gives the stage's voltage gain as transconductance times collector resistance, with a minus sign for the inversion. The intrinsic emitter resistance is the reciprocal of the transconductance, which makes the gain expression easy to remember as the ratio of the collector load to the emitter resistance. The practical reading is that a transistor is a transconductance device, and voltage gain is something the circuit does with that transconductance.

blocks: A stage is biased at 2 mA with a 2.2 kilohm collector resistor. Compute the transconductance and the voltage gain.
Divide the bias current by the 25 mV thermal voltage, then multiply by the collector resistance.

The same stage adds a 100 ohm emitter degeneration resistor. What is the gain, and why would anyone do that?
Degenerated gain is the collector resistance divided by the sum of intrinsic emitter resistance and the external resistor.
Gain falls from 176 to about 20, but the gain becomes almost independent of bias current and temperature because the external resistor dominates r_e.

industry.title: Real-world applications

blocks: The practices that actually reduce defects are measurable, and they are not the ones most often debated.

Code review catches a large share of defects before test, and its value is at least as much in knowledge sharing as in bug finding. The evidence is consistent across studies: reviewed code has fewer escaped defects, and the effect is strongest on design-level problems that no test would find.

Continuous integration shortens the feedback loop to minutes, which is the whole point. A build broken for a day is expensive to untangle; broken for five minutes it is trivial. The discipline that makes it work is small, frequent commits and a fast test suite — which is why test speed is a feature.

Trunk-based development with feature flags removes the long-lived branch and the painful merge, and it decouples deploying from releasing, so a change can reach production dark and be enabled gradually. That is also the safest rollback mechanism available: turning a flag off is faster and lower-risk than reverting a deployment.

The testing pyramid still holds: many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests, a small number of end-to-end tests. Inverting it produces a suite that is slow and flaky, and a slow flaky suite gets ignored, which is worse than none.
The metric worth tracking is escaped defects and time to restore, not lines of code or commit counts. The second in particular is what tells you whether the rest of the process is working.

blocks: Soil Compaction: Optimum Moisture Content and Field Density is a core model in Soil Mechanics / Geotechnical Engineering: Every soil has a moisture content at which a given compactive effort packs it densest; field acceptance is measured as a percentage of that laboratory maximum. The model is used within these stated limits: Standard or modified Proctor energy defines the lab maximum - quote which one; dry density, not wet, is the comparison because water mass would flatter a wet sample.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: moisture content, mass water over mass solids
relative (percent) compaction versus the Proctor maximum
Standard or modified Proctor energy defines the lab maximum - quote which one; dry density, not wet, is the comparison because water mass would flatter a wet sample.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Water lubricates soil particles so effort rearranges them tighter - but beyond the optimum, water occupies space that solids should fill and dry density falls, tracing the classic bell-shaped compaction curve. The laboratory Proctor test finds that peak for a defined hammer energy; the field converts every density test to dry density (dividing out the water) and expresses it as a percentage of the lab peak. blocks: Solving Initial-Value Problems with Laplace Transforms is a core model in Engineering Mathematics II: The Laplace transform turns differentiation into multiplication by s, so an ODE with initial conditions becomes an algebra problem you solve and then invert. The model is used within these stated limits: Requires a function of exponential order on t >= 0; initial conditions enter the transform itself, which is why the method suits IVPs rather than boundary-value problems.

blocks: Apply the transform to every term of the ODE. Each derivative contributes a factor of s minus its initial-condition term, so the whole equation becomes linear in Y(s). Solve algebraically for Y(s), split it into pieces by partial fractions, and invert each piece from the standard table - exponentials become 1/(s+a), sines become omega/(s^2+omega^2).

blocks: (sY - 3) + 2Y = 0, so Y(s)(s + 2) = 3 and Y(s) = 3/(s + 2). The table entry 1/(s+a) -> e^(-at) inverts it directly.

but the I/O pattern matters more than the comparisons.
Quicksort is the usual in-memory default, but production implementations are introsort: quicksort that switches to heapsort when the recursion gets too deep, guaranteeing
worst case and removing the quadratic blowup on adversarial input. Choosing the pivot well — median-of-three, or a random pivot — is what keeps the average case real.

The model is used within these stated limits: Uniform pressure and nozzle wear matched across the boom; the 600 collects the unit conversions (1 ha = 10,000 m^2, 1 h = 60 min).
advanced.title: Formal definition

output per nozzle at operating pressure
Uniform pressure and nozzle wear matched across the boom; the 600 collects the unit conversions (1 ha = 10,000 m^2, 1 h = 60 min).
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Each nozzle wets a strip as wide as its spacing; in one minute that strip covers v x 1000/60 metres of length times s metres of width - an area in hectares - while the nozzle pours q litres onto it. Dividing flow by area and collecting the constants yields the 600 formula. Every term is a calibration lever: pressure changes q (roughly with the square root of pressure for flat-fan nozzles), gear choice changes v, and nozzle selection changes both q and s. Field calibration - catching each nozzle's output over a measured course - is mandatory because a 10% rate error means a 10% dose error, which is an efficacy or a residue problem depending on the direction.

The most common failure is a join on columns with different types or collations. The planner cannot use an index across an implicit cast, so what should be an index lookup becomes a scan. This is invisible in the SQL and only appears in the plan.

Aggregation at scale is usually pushed down rather than done at the end: aggregate within each partition first, then combine. Average is too, if you carry sum and count separately — averaging averages is wrong, and it is a recurring bug in reporting code.
is a performance decision as well as a correctness one. Filtering before grouping reduces the rows that must be grouped; filtering after groups everything and then discards. Pushing a predicate into
when it applies to individual rows is usually a large win.
The general discipline is the same as for indexes: read the plan, check that estimated row counts match actual, and fix the statistics before reaching for a rewrite.

blocks: Both are everywhere, and in production the queue matters far more than the stack, because a queue is how one component hands work to another without blocking on it.

Message brokers — RabbitMQ, Kafka, SQS — are queues at system scale. They exist because the producer and consumer run at different speeds and must not be coupled. The hard part in practice is not the data structure but the guarantees around it: at-least-once versus exactly-once delivery, dead-letter queues for messages that repeatedly fail, and back-pressure so a slow consumer does not cause unbounded memory growth.

The stack is mostly implicit. Every function call uses the hardware stack, and the two failure modes engineers actually meet are stack overflow from unbounded recursion on user-supplied input, and stack exhaustion in threaded servers where each thread reserves a megabyte or more. That is a large part of why async and coroutine-based servers replaced one-thread-per-connection designs.

blocks: Stall Speed and Load Factor in Turns is a core model in Aerodynamics & Flight Mechanics: Stall is an angle-of-attack event, but the airspeed at which it arrives grows with the square root of load factor - which is why steep turns and turbulence pull stalls out of comfortable flight. The model is used within these stated limits: Level coordinated turns and rigid-wing behaviour; stall itself occurs at the critical angle of attack regardless of speed, attitude or weight - the speed formulas are its shadows at given n.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: stall speed at load factor n
Level coordinated turns and rigid-wing behaviour; stall itself occurs at the critical angle of attack regardless of speed, attitude or weight - the speed formulas are its shadows at given n.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: In a bank, lift must both hold the aircraft up and turn it: the vertical component still equals weight, so total lift - and the load factor - rises as 1/cos(bank). Lift is proportional to C_L V^2, so holding that higher lift at the stall angle of attack demands the square-root-of-n speed penalty. The numbers are unforgiving: 60 degrees of bank doubles the load, raising a 50-knot stall to 71; at 45 degrees the wing already carries 1.41 g. Gusts add load factor through the same mechanism, and maneuvering speed V_A is defined so that full control deflection stalls the wing before it breaks - the stall-speed relation written into the airspeed indicator's colour arcs.

blocks: Steady-State Error, System Type and the Final Value Theorem is a core model in Control Systems Engineering: How well a closed loop tracks a command is decided by the number of free integrators in its loop: type zero lags a step, type one lags a ramp, and the error is a number you can compute before the loop is built. The model is used within these stated limits: A unity-feedback loop, a stable closed loop, and a final value that exists (no poles on the imaginary axis other than the integrator counted by the system type). The constants describe the loop, not the closed-loop response shape.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: position error constant: lim s-to-0 of G(s)
steady-state error for a unit input of that shape

A unity-feedback loop, a stable closed loop, and a final value that exists (no poles on the imaginary axis other than the integrator counted by the system type). The constants describe the loop, not the closed-loop response shape.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Steady-state error follows from the final value theorem applied to the error transfer function, which is one over one plus the loop transfer function. Evaluating that limit depends on how many poles the loop has at the origin: with none, a constant command leaves a constant error; with one, a constant command is tracked exactly but a ramp leaves a constant lag equal to the reciprocal of the velocity error constant; with two, even a ramp is tracked. The trade-off is that each integrator adds phase lag at the crossover frequency, which is why high-type loops tend to oscillate and why designers add a zero through proportional-derivative action to buy the accuracy back. Steady-state accuracy and stability margin are therefore purchased from the same budget.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A loop has G(s) = 20/(s(s+2)). Compute the steady-state error for a unit step and a unit ramp.
Count the integrators to fix the system type, then evaluate the error constants.
One pole at the origin makes this a type 1 system, so the step error is zero. K_v = lim s-to-0 of s x 20/(s(s+2)) = 20/2 = 10, so the ramp error is 1/10 = 0.1.
Zero steady-state error for a step and 0.1 (10 % of the ramp rate) for a unit ramp.
A type-zero loop has 1/(s+1) with a proportional gain of 9. What is the step error, and what does adding an integrator change?
Compute the position error constant for the type-zero loop, then consider the effect of a pole at the origin.
K_p = 9/1 = 9, so e_ss = 1/(1+9) = 0.1. Adding an integrator makes the loop type 1, so the step error becomes zero, at the cost of 90 degrees of phase lag.
Ten percent error without the integrator and zero with it; the cost appears as reduced phase margin and slower settling.

standard.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Steady-state error follows from the final value theorem applied to the error transfer function, which is one over one plus the loop transfer function. Evaluating that limit depends on how many poles the loop has at the origin: with none, a constant command leaves a constant error; with one, a constant command is tracked exactly but a ramp leaves a constant lag equal to the reciprocal of the velocity error constant; with two, even a ramp is tracked. The trade-off is that each integrator adds phase lag at the crossover frequency, which is why high-type loops tend to oscillate and why designers add a zero through proportional-derivative action to buy the accuracy back. Steady-state accuracy and stability margin are therefore purchased from the same budget.
standard.title: Derivation

blocks: A loop has G(s) = 20/(s(s+2)). Compute the steady-state error for a unit step and a unit ramp.
Count the integrators to fix the system type, then evaluate the error constants.
One pole at the origin makes this a type 1 system, so the step error is zero. K_v = lim s-to-0 of s x 20/(s(s+2)) = 20/2 = 10, so the ramp error is 1/10 = 0.1.
Zero steady-state error for a step and 0.1 (10 % of the ramp rate) for a unit ramp.
A type-zero loop has 1/(s+1) with a proportional gain of 9. What is the step error, and what does adding an integrator change?
Compute the position error constant for the type-zero loop, then consider the effect of a pole at the origin.
K_p = 9/1 = 9, so e_ss = 1/(1+9) = 0.1. Adding an integrator makes the loop type 1, so the step error becomes zero, at the cost of 90 degrees of phase lag.
Ten percent error without the integrator and zero with it; the cost appears as reduced phase margin and slower settling.

The model is used within these stated limits: Open-loop stepping within the pull-out torque curve; torque falls roughly with speed as back-EMF and inductance starve the winding current, so size against the curve at operating RPM.
advanced.title: Formal definition

Open-loop stepping within the pull-out torque curve; torque falls roughly with speed as back-EMF and inductance starve the winding current, so size against the curve at operating RPM.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: The motion profile fixes alpha: a trapezoidal speed ramp from zero to N rpm in t_r seconds gives alpha = omega/t_r. Multiplying by the total inertia reflected to the motor shaft yields the torque that exists only during ramps - often the largest term in fast indexing machines. Add steady load and friction, apply a safety factor for resonance dips and torque-vs-speed decay, and compare against the motor's pull-out curve at the operating speed - not its holding torque, the marketing number that applies only at standstill. Where the budget fails, gearing multiplies torque (and divides inertia quadratically) or microstepping smooths the resonance zones that steal torque mid-range.

Compute alpha, acceleration torque, total, and apply the safety factor.
0.81 N m required from the pull-out curve at 500 rpm - a motor with 1 N m holding torque might only deliver 0.4 N m there, which is why the curve, not the nameplate, sizes the drive.

blocks: Sterilisation: D-Value, Del Factor and the Temperature Trade is a core model in Bioprocess Engineering: Thermal sterilisation is a log-reduction calculation: the hold time follows from the initial bioburden, the target sterility and the D-value at the chosen temperature. The model is used within these stated limits: Well-mixed heating of a liquid medium with first-order thermal death kinetics and a known initial bioburden; heating and cooling contributions are added separately. Dry heat, filtration and chemical sterilisation follow entirely different relations.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Sterilisation hold time and its temperature sensitivity
decimal reduction time: time for a tenfold reduction at the temperature used
temperature change for a tenfold change in D, about 10 for spores

Well-mixed heating of a liquid medium with first-order thermal death kinetics and a known initial bioburden; heating and cooling contributions are added separately. Dry heat, filtration and chemical sterilisation follow entirely different relations.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Thermal death follows first-order kinetics, so each interval of time reduces the population by a constant fraction rather than a constant number, and the decimal reduction time is the interval for one tenfold reduction. The total reduction needed is the logarithm of the initial bioburden divided by the acceptable surviving count, and multiplying that by the D-value gives the hold time. Because D falls tenfold for each z-degree rise in temperature, the same reduction can be achieved in a fraction of the time at a higher temperature - and since the nutrient medium is being damaged by the same heat, high-temperature short-time sterilisation is preferred for both sterility assurance and medium quality. The practical numbers explain the industry's standard: a bioburden of a million spores down to a thousandth of a spore is nine log reductions, which at a one-and-a-half-minute D-value is thirteen and a half minutes at 121 degrees.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A medium carries 10^6 spores per mL and must reach 10^-3 survivors. With D = 1.5 min at 121 degrees C, find the hold time.
Take the logarithm of the ratio, then multiply by the D-value.
13.5 minutes at 121 degrees C, excluding the heating and cooling contributions, which the design must add.
The same reduction is attempted at 115 degrees C. What hold time is needed?
D changes tenfold for each ten-degree change when z is ten.
About 54 minutes at 115 degrees against 13.5 minutes at 121 degrees, a fourfold longer exposure that also degrades the medium more.

The practical numbers explain the industry's standard: a bioburden of a million spores down to a thousandth of a spore is nine log reductions, which at a one-and-a-half-minute D-value is thirteen and a half minutes at 121 degrees.

blocks: A medium carries 10^6 spores per mL and must reach 10^-3 survivors. With D = 1.5 min at 121 degrees C, find the hold time.
Take the logarithm of the ratio, then multiply by the D-value.
13.5 minutes at 121 degrees C, excluding the heating and cooling contributions, which the design must add.
The same reduction is attempted at 115 degrees C. What hold time is needed?
D changes tenfold for each ten-degree change when z is ten.
About 54 minutes at 115 degrees against 13.5 minutes at 121 degrees, a fourfold longer exposure that also degrades the medium more.

blocks: Storage Sizing and Round-Trip Efficiency on a Renewable System is a core model in Renewable Energy Systems & Storage: Matching variable generation to demand is an energy balance, and round-trip efficiency means each stored kilowatt hour costs more than one to put in. The model is used within these stated limits: A single daily cycle with constant efficiencies and a known depth of discharge; ageing, temperature effects and standby losses are additional derates, and long-duration storage needs its own self-discharge term.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Storage energy balance with round-trip efficiency
usable depth of discharge of the battery

A single daily cycle with constant efficiencies and a known depth of discharge; ageing, temperature effects and standby losses are additional derates, and long-duration storage needs its own self-discharge term.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Charging storage loses energy on the way in and again on the way out, so each delivered kilowatt hour costs more than one to store. The round-trip efficiency is the product of the two, and dividing the delivered energy by it gives the charging energy the renewable source must provide. Separately, the battery's chemistry limits how much of its nameplate capacity can be used repeatedly, so the installed capacity is the delivered energy divided by the depth of discharge. Together the two relations decide whether a system closes: whether the daily generation surplus exceeds the charging requirement, and whether the installed capacity is enough to cover the demand during the no-generation period. Both are checked at the design margin the owner accepts, since a system sized exactly to the average will fail on the days that matter.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A solar plant generates 4 MWh a day while the load needs 3 MWh, with 95 % charge and 95 % discharge efficiency. How much of the night load can the surplus cover?
Compute the round-trip efficiency, then convert the surplus into delivered energy.
Round trip = 0.95 x 0.95 = 0.9025. Charging 1 MWh of surplus delivers 0.9025 MWh, so the surplus covers 0.90 MWh of the 3 MWh night load.
0.90 MWh covered, leaving 2.10 MWh short: the daily generation is not enough to run the load off storage alone.
The load needs 3 MWh overnight and the battery has a 90 % depth of discharge. What nameplate capacity is required, and what charging energy does it need?
Divide the delivered energy by the depth of discharge, and divide again by the round-trip efficiency for the charging requirement.
3.33 MWh of nameplate capacity needing 3.32 MWh of charging, which fits inside the 4 MWh daily generation with 0.68 MWh to spare.

blocks: Strain Gauges and Gauge Factor is a core model in Measurements & Instrumentation: A strain gauge converts deformation into resistance change, and the gauge factor is the sensitivity constant that turns ohms into microstrain. The model is used within these stated limits: Linear elastic range and temperature-compensated installation; the factor bundles geometric stretch with the resistivity change (piezoresistive effect).
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: gauge factor, ~2 for metallic foil gauges
Linear elastic range and temperature-compensated installation; the factor bundles geometric stretch with the resistivity change (piezoresistive effect).
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Stretching a conductor lengthens it, thins it (Poisson effect) and slightly changes its resistivity - all three shift resistance. The gauge factor collects these into one constant: fractional resistance change per unit strain. A GF of 2 means 1000 microstrain moves resistance by only 0.2% - 0.24 ohm on a 120 ohm gauge - which is why gauges live in Wheatstone bridges with amplification: the raw signal is millivolts, and temperature compensation (dummy gauges or half/full bridges) separates mechanical strain from thermal expansion.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A 120 ohm gauge with GF = 2 measures a resistance rise of 0.24 ohm. Find the strain.
1000 microstrain - a 0.1% elongation, squarely in the elastic range of structural steel.

blocks: Stretching a conductor lengthens it, thins it (Poisson effect) and slightly changes its resistivity - all three shift resistance. The gauge factor collects these into one constant: fractional resistance change per unit strain. A GF of 2 means 1000 microstrain moves resistance by only 0.2% - 0.24 ohm on a 120 ohm gauge - which is why gauges live in Wheatstone bridges with amplification: the raw signal is millivolts, and temperature compensation (dummy gauges or half/full bridges) separates mechanical strain from thermal expansion.
