blocks: A loop runs 1,000,000 iterations, each computing an array address with one integer multiply. Multiply costs 3 cycles and add costs 1 in the target's pipeline. What does strength reduction save?
Use the difference per iteration times the trip count.
Delta T = 1,000,000 x (3 - 1) = 2,000,000 cycles. On a 3 GHz core that is 2 x 10^6 / 3 x 10^9 s = 0.67 ms.

About 2 million cycles, or 0.67 ms. If the loop's body costs 10 cycles per iteration the saving is 20 %; if it costs 100 cycles it is noise, which is why the transform is measured rather than assumed.

The element stride is constant, so maintain a running pointer instead of computing 4*i.

industry.title: Real-world applications

blocks: Elastic analysis is the first stage of every structural calculation, and the code requirements around it are where the real work is.

Design codes do not use the yield stress directly; they divide by a partial safety factor to get a design strength, and separately factor the loads upward. The result is that a structure is designed to remain elastic under factored loads, with a defined margin before yield. The factors differ by material and by consequence of failure, which is why a hospital and a shed are not designed to the same numbers.

Deflection usually governs before strength. A floor joist may carry the load comfortably but sag enough to crack finishes or alarm occupants, so serviceability limits — span over a few hundred — often decide the member size rather than stress. Checking strength alone is a common and visible mistake.

Fatigue is what the elastic analysis does not cover. A stress well below yield, repeated enough times, will still cause failure, because cracks grow from microscopic defects. This is why aircraft and bridges are designed against an S-N curve and inspected on a schedule rather than calculated once. The stress range, not the peak, is the governing quantity.

Material variability is handled statistically. Steel is tightly controlled, so the partial factor is modest; concrete is produced on site and varies considerably, so its factor is larger and it is tested by cubes or cylinders at 7 and 28 days. Assuming a nominal strength without checking the test results is how real failures happen.

blocks: String Building, Immutability and the Cost of Repeated Concatenation is a core model in Programming Fundamentals: Appending to an immutable string inside a loop copies the whole string each time, turning a linear job quadratic - the classic first lesson in choosing the right primitive. The model is used within these stated limits: Strings are immutable and concatenation allocates a new string and copies both operands; the build path appends into a mutable buffer whose capacity grows geometrically. Fragments of varying size change the constant but not the growth rate.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Characters copied by repeated concatenation versus building in one pass
number of characters or fragments assembled

Strings are immutable and concatenation allocates a new string and copies both operands; the build path appends into a mutable buffer whose capacity grows geometrically. Fragments of varying size change the constant but not the growth rate.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: An immutable string cannot be extended in place, so every concatenation allocates a fresh string and copies all the characters from both sides. In a loop that builds a result of length n, the first concatenation copies one character, the second copies two, and so on, so the total work is the sum of the first n integers - quadratic in n. Building into a mutable buffer changes the same loop into one pass with amortised growth, so total copies stay proportional to n. The arithmetic is worth internalising because the same pattern appears wherever an accumulating operation returns a fresh value: lists, immutable data structures and database rows all have it, and the fix - accumulate mutably and freeze once - is always the same shape.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A loop appends one character at a time until the string is 100,000 characters long. How many characters are copied, and how does that compare with building the whole string in one pass?
The naive total is the sum of the first n integers; the single-pass total is n.
C_naive = 100,000^2/2 = 5 x 10^9 characters copied. C_build = 100,000 characters, plus amortised reallocation.
Five billion copies against a hundred thousand: a factor of fifty thousand for the same result.
A mutable buffer grows by doubling. How many total copies does it perform building the same 100,000 characters?
Geometric growth means the sum of all the copies is proportional to the final size.
Copies at sizes 1, 2, 4, 8, ... up to 100,000 total less than twice the final size, so about 200,000 characters.
About 200,000 characters copied: the amortised cost is O(n), and the ratio to the naive approach is 25,000 to one.

blocks: A loop appends one character at a time until the string is 100,000 characters long. How many characters are copied, and how does that compare with building the whole string in one pass?
The naive total is the sum of the first n integers; the single-pass total is n.
C_naive = 100,000^2/2 = 5 x 10^9 characters copied. C_build = 100,000 characters, plus amortised reallocation.
Five billion copies against a hundred thousand: a factor of fifty thousand for the same result.
A mutable buffer grows by doubling. How many total copies does it perform building the same 100,000 characters?
Geometric growth means the sum of all the copies is proportional to the final size.
Copies at sizes 1, 2, 4, 8, ... up to 100,000 total less than twice the final size, so about 200,000 characters.
About 200,000 characters copied: the amortised cost is O(n), and the ratio to the naive approach is 25,000 to one.

Strings are immutable and concatenation allocates a new string and copies both operands; the build path appends into a mutable buffer whose capacity grows geometrically. Fragments of varying size change the constant but not the growth rate.
standard.title: Formula and variables

blocks: An immutable string cannot be extended in place, so every concatenation allocates a fresh string and copies all the characters from both sides. In a loop that builds a result of length n, the first concatenation copies one character, the second copies two, and so on, so the total work is the sum of the first n integers - quadratic in n. Building into a mutable buffer changes the same loop into one pass with amortised growth, so total copies stay proportional to n. The arithmetic is worth internalising because the same pattern appears wherever an accumulating operation returns a fresh value: lists, immutable data structures and database rows all have it, and the fix - accumulate mutably and freeze once - is always the same shape.

blocks: A vehicle rounding a curve needs centripetal acceleration v^2/R. Banking the road at angle theta makes the normal force contribute g sin(theta) ~ g e toward the centre, and tyre-pavement friction adds up to g f. Dividing the balance by g gives the design relation: the fixed geometric demand v^2/(gR) is shared between superelevation and friction. Design practice caps e for slow traffic and ice, computes the needed friction, and demands it stay under the comfortable limit - or slows the design speed, or widens the radius, or adds a transition spiral so e builds up gradually.

blocks: Surface Roughness from Feed and Tool Nose Radius is a core model in Workshop Practice: The theoretical roughness left by a turning tool is set by the feed and the nose radius, and the squared feed term explains why halving the feed improves the finish fourfold. The model is used within these stated limits: An ideal tool with a circular nose and no built-up edge, vibration or wear, cutting a ductile material at a speed where the chip forms cleanly. Measured roughness is always greater, and the relation is a lower bound that guides parameter choice.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Theoretical arithmetic mean roughness in turning

An ideal tool with a circular nose and no built-up edge, vibration or wear, cutting a ductile material at a speed where the chip forms cleanly. Measured roughness is always greater, and the relation is a lower bound that guides parameter choice.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: As the tool advances one feed per revolution, its circular nose leaves a series of scallops in the surface, exactly as a ball-nose cutter leaves cusps in milling. The geometry of the arc over a chord equal to the feed gives a scallop height proportional to the square of the feed divided by eight times the nose radius, and empirical work relates the arithmetic mean roughness to that geometry with a factor of about four - which is where the 32 in the denominator comes from. Two consequences follow immediately: roughness improves with the square of the feed reduction, so halving the feed quarters the theoretical value, and a larger nose radius improves the finish for the same feed but increases cutting forces and the risk of chatter. Roughness specs are therefore met by choosing the largest nose radius the operation tolerates, then reducing the feed until the arithmetic is satisfied.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A turning operation uses a 0.2 mm per revolution feed with a 0.8 mm nose radius tool. Estimate the theoretical roughness.
Square the feed, then divide by thirty-two times the nose radius.
About 1.56 micrometres, which corresponds to a fine turned finish.
The feed is halved to 0.1 mm per revolution. What happens to roughness and to cycle time?
Roughness scales with the square of the feed, and time scales inversely with it.
R_a = 0.01/25.6 = 0.00039 mm, and the cutting time doubles.
Roughness improves from 1.56 to 0.39 micrometres - a factor of four - at the cost of twice the machining time.

industry.title: Real-world applications

blocks: Almost no application code uses raw semaphores now; the primitives are wrapped, and the bugs moved up a level.

The standard toolkit is the mutex, the condition variable, the read-write lock and the atomic. Semaphores survive where a counted resource is genuinely being modelled — a connection pool limiting concurrent database connections is literally a counting semaphore, and so is a bounded work queue.

The dominant bug class is no longer forgetting to lock; it is lock ordering and holding a lock too long. Inconsistent lock acquisition order deadlocks under concurrency that testing rarely reproduces, which is why the rule is to give locks a global order and always acquire ascending. Holding a lock across a network call or a disk read serialises everything behind it and shows up as latency that no profiler attributes to the lock.

The modern answer is often to avoid shared state entirely. Actor models and message passing give each unit of work its own state and communicate by sending, so there is nothing to lock. Go's guidance — do not communicate by sharing memory, share memory by communicating — is this idea in one line, and it is why so much concurrent code now looks like channels rather than locks.
Where shared state is unavoidable, the discipline is: keep critical sections short, never call out to unknown code while holding a lock, and test with a race detector rather than hoping.

blocks: Almost no application code uses raw semaphores now; the primitives are wrapped, and the bugs moved up a level.

The standard toolkit is the mutex, the condition variable, the read-write lock and the atomic. Semaphores survive where a counted resource is genuinely being modelled — a connection pool limiting concurrent database connections is literally a counting semaphore, and so is a bounded work queue.

The dominant bug class is no longer forgetting to lock; it is lock ordering and holding a lock too long. Inconsistent lock acquisition order deadlocks under concurrency that testing rarely reproduces, which is why the rule is to give locks a global order and always acquire ascending. Holding a lock across a network call or a disk read serialises everything behind it and shows up as latency that no profiler attributes to the lock.

The modern answer is often to avoid shared state entirely. Actor models and message passing give each unit of work its own state and communicate by sending, so there is nothing to lock. Go's guidance — do not communicate by sharing memory, share memory by communicating — is this idea in one line, and it is why so much concurrent code now looks like channels rather than locks.
Where shared state is unavoidable, the discipline is: keep critical sections short, never call out to unknown code while holding a lock, and test with a race detector rather than hoping.

blocks: Synchronous Generator EMF and Voltage Regulation is a core model in Electrical Machines II: A synchronous machine's generated voltage is set by flux, frequency and winding layout through the 4.44 law - and its terminal voltage under load falls by the synchronous-impedance drop. The model is used within these stated limits: Sinusoidal flux distribution; the 4.44 is 2 sqrt(2) pi from integrating a sinusoid, and regulation is computed from E versus terminal V through the synchronous impedance.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Sinusoidal flux distribution; the 4.44 is 2 sqrt(2) pi from integrating a sinusoid, and regulation is computed from E versus terminal V through the synchronous impedance.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Faraday's law applied to a full-phase winding under sinusoidal flux gives the familiar form-factor constant 4.44; the winding factor discounts it for coils spread across slots and short-pitched, both of which trim harmonics. Under load the terminal voltage differs from E by the drop across armature resistance and synchronous reactance - the latter bundling leakage plus armature reaction. Regulation follows: (E - V)/V at rated load, strongly power-factor dependent, with lagging loads drooping and leading loads potentially boosting the terminal voltage above no-load.

blocks: Taylor Linearisation and the Size of the Error is a core model in Engineering Mathematics I: Nearly every engineering formula in a first-year course is a truncated Taylor series, and the remainder term tells you how good the approximation is before you use it. The model is used within these stated limits: The function is twice differentiable on the interval between a and x, and the expansion point is close enough that higher-order behaviour is captured by the bound. The bound is a worst case, so the actual error is usually smaller.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: First-order Taylor approximation with its remainder bound
point about which the function is expanded
point where the value is wanted

The function is twice differentiable on the interval between a and x, and the expansion point is close enough that higher-order behaviour is captured by the bound. The bound is a worst case, so the actual error is usually smaller.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: The Taylor series rewrites a smooth function as its value, slope, curvature and so on at a chosen point. Keeping only the first two terms gives a straight line that agrees with the function in value and slope at the expansion point, which is exactly what engineers mean when they speak of small-signal or linearised behaviour. The remainder term bounds what is thrown away: it is the second derivative evaluated somewhere in the interval, times the square of the distance from the expansion point, divided by two. That is why the approximation improves so quickly - halving the step quarters the error - and why the second derivative matters when choosing an expansion point, since a function with large curvature linearises badly.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: Estimate the square root of 4.1 by linearising the square root function about 4, and compare with the true value.
Evaluate the function and its derivative at the expansion point, then add the linear correction.
f(4) = 2 and f'(x) = 1/(2 sqrt x) gives f'(4) = 0.25. The estimate is 2 + 0.25 x 0.1 = 2.025. The true value is 2.02485.
2.025 against a true 2.02485, an absolute error of about 0.00015, or 0.007 %.
Bound the error of the previous estimate using the second derivative.
Find the maximum magnitude of the second derivative on the interval and apply the bound.
f''(x) = -1/(4 x^{3/2}), which is largest in magnitude at x = 4, giving 1/(4 x 8) = 0.03125. The bound is 0.03125 x 0.1^2/2 = 0.000156.
The bound is 1.56 x 10^-4 against the actual error of 1.54 x 10^-4: correct, and tight enough to be useful.

blocks: TCP tuning is mostly about long-distance and high-bandwidth links, where the defaults were set for a much smaller internet.

The bandwidth-delay product is the number that matters. A 10 Gb/s link with 100 ms RTT has a BDP of about 125 MB, so a connection needs a window that large to fill it. Default socket buffers are far smaller, which is why a transfer between continents is often a fraction of the link speed no matter how fast the link is. Raising the buffer limits — and enabling window scaling, which is on by default now — is the fix.

Bufferbloat is the modern problem. Oversized buffers in consumer routers hold packets for seconds, so latency under load climbs into the hundreds of milliseconds. TCP interprets the resulting loss as congestion and backs off, but by then the delay damage is done. This is why active queue management and BBR-style congestion control, which probe for bandwidth and RTT directly rather than inferring from loss, have largely replaced loss-based algorithms on long-fat paths.

The practical warnings: don't disable Nagle's algorithm globally to fix latency —it exists to prevent tinygram floods; don't assume loss means congestion on a wireless link, because radio errors look identical to TCP; and measure with
before and after any change, since TCP behaviour is hard to reason about from first principles.

blocks: The Betz Limit and Wind-Turbine Power is a core model in Renewable Energy Systems & Storage: Wind power scales with the cube of speed and the swept area, but physics caps the extractable share at 59.3% - the Betz limit - before any machine inefficiency is counted. The model is used within these stated limits: Actuator-disc, incompressible flow; real turbines reach C_p ~ 0.45-0.50 near rated speed, and the cubic V dependence dominates siting economics.

advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: The kinetic-energy flux through the swept disc is half rho A V cubed. A rotor that stopped the air completely would collect all of it but pass zero mass flow; one that ignores the wind collects nothing. Optimizing the trade-off - how much to slow the stream - gives a maximum extractable fraction of 16/27, the Betz limit, reached when downstream speed is one third of upstream. Real rotors then pay aerodynamic, tip-loss and drivetrain tolls, landing at C_p near 0.45-0.5. The cubic speed term is the siting story: a site averaging 8 m/s carries twice the power density of one at 6.35 m/s - a 20% speed gain doubles the energy, which is why hub heights keep climbing.

blocks: The CPU Performance Equation and Amdahl's Law is a core model in Computer Organization & Architecture: Program time is instructions times cycles-per-instruction divided by clock rate, and Amdahl's law caps what speeding up any one part can do for the whole. The model is used within these stated limits: Amdahl assumes the fraction p is measured on the original execution; overall speedup saturates at 1/(1-p) no matter how large s grows.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: fraction of time the improved part originally took
Amdahl assumes the fraction p is measured on the original execution; overall speedup saturates at 1/(1-p) no matter how large s grows.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: The time equation makes the three levers explicit: compilers and ISAs cut IC, microarchitecture cuts CPI, technology raises f - and they multiply, so a 10% gain on each lever is a 33% total gain, not 30%. Amdahl's law is the pessimism check: if a part accounts for fraction p of the time and becomes s times faster, the new total is (1-p) + p/s of the old, so the overall speedup is the reciprocal. As s approaches infinity the speedup approaches 1/(1-p) - the unimproved remainder becomes the whole budget.
advanced.title: Derivation

Apply the time equation, then Amdahl.
0.5 s before, about 95 ms after - and even an infinite speedup of that 90% would only reach 0.5/10 = 50 ms.

blocks: The Drag Polar and Best Glide Speed is a core model in Aerodynamics & Flight Mechanics: An aircraft's drag is a baseline plus the price of lift, and the polar's minimum-drag point hands pilots the best glide speed and engineers the maximum lift-to-drag ratio. The model is used within these stated limits: Subsonic, moderate angles of attack where the parabolic polar fits; the best-glide airspeed follows by setting the required C_L* into the lift equation at the aircraft's weight.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Parabolic drag polar and best L/D
glide ratio: distance forward per altitude lost
Subsonic, moderate angles of attack where the parabolic polar fits; the best-glide airspeed follows by setting the required C_L* into the lift equation at the aircraft's weight.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Parasite drag is the airframe's friction and pressure drag at zero lift; induced drag is the vortex-system toll for producing lift, falling as speed rises because less angle of attack is needed. The sum has a minimum where the two terms are equal - the geometric fact that the parabola's tangent through the origin touches it at C_D0 = k C_L^2. Flying at the corresponding speed yields the flattest glide: L/D is the glide ratio, so an aircraft with L/D of 16 travels 16 km forward per km of altitude. Heavier aircraft glide at the same ratio but a higher best-glide speed - weight moves the speed, not the polar's shape.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: An aircraft has C_D0 = 0.02 and k = 0.05. Find the best-glide lift coefficient and the maximum glide ratio.
Locate the polar minimum, then form L/D.
Glide ratio about 15.8:1 - the number that turns an engine-out altitude into a reachable-airport radius, flown at the speed that makes C_L = 0.632.

blocks: Parasite drag is the airframe's friction and pressure drag at zero lift; induced drag is the vortex-system toll for producing lift, falling as speed rises because less angle of attack is needed. The sum has a minimum where the two terms are equal - the geometric fact that the parabola's tangent through the origin touches it at C_D0 = k C_L^2. Flying at the corresponding speed yields the flattest glide: L/D is the glide ratio, so an aircraft with L/D of 16 travels 16 km forward per km of altitude. Heavier aircraft glide at the same ratio but a higher best-glide speed - weight moves the speed, not the polar's shape.

blocks: The ideal gas law is PV = nRT. P is absolute pressure, V is volume, n is amount of substance, T is absolute temperature, and R is the gas constant.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Ideal-gas behaviour: low pressure relative to the critical pressure, and temperature well above the point where the gas would liquefy.

blocks: Boyle's law says PV is constant at fixed n and T. Charles's law says V/T is constant at fixed n and P. Avogadro's law says V/n is constant at fixed P and T. The single equation that satisfies all three is PV = nRT, with R fixed by measuring one known gas. The kinetic theory arrives at the same relation by equating pressure to the momentum transferred by elastic collisions.

blocks: The Jacobian, Singularities and Joint-Speed Demand is a core model in Robotics Kinematics & Control: The Jacobian maps joint rates to end-effector velocity, and its determinant tells you when the arm loses a degree of freedom - and how much extra joint speed the remaining directions demand. The model is used within these stated limits: A two-link planar arm with revolute joints and no joint limits, evaluated at a configuration away from the wrist centre. Higher-degree-of-freedom arms have a Jacobian whose rank loss defines the same singular conditions.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Jacobian determinant for a two-link planar arm
elbow angle, zero when the arm is straight

A two-link planar arm with revolute joints and no joint limits, evaluated at a configuration away from the wrist centre. Higher-degree-of-freedom arms have a Jacobian whose rank loss defines the same singular conditions.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: End-effector velocity is the sum of each joint's contribution, and the Jacobian collects those contributions as a matrix that multiplies the joint-rate vector. Its determinant measures how much end-effector motion a set of joint motions can produce: when the determinant vanishes, some end-effector direction can no longer be produced at all, and the arm is at a singularity. Near that configuration the inverse mapping is ill-conditioned, so producing a commanded Cartesian velocity requires very large joint rates, which is why a robot moving along a straight line through a fully extended pose demands joint speeds far beyond its nominal ratings. The same determinant also sets force capability in reverse, since joint torques map through the transpose of the Jacobian.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: An arm has 0.5 m and 0.4 m links and an elbow angle of 30 degrees. Evaluate the Jacobian determinant and compare it with a straight-arm pose.
Multiply the link lengths by the sine of the elbow angle, then compare with the straight configuration.
det J = 0.5 x 0.4 x sin(30) = 0.5 x 0.4 x 0.5 = 0.1 m^2. At a straight arm the elbow angle is zero and the determinant is zero.
0.1 square metres at 30 degrees against zero when the arm is straight, which is the classic singular configuration.
At an elbow angle of 5 degrees, by what factor does the required joint speed rise for the same end-effector velocity?
Compare the determinants at the two configurations.
det J at 5 degrees = 0.2 x sin(5) = 0.2 x 0.0872 = 0.0174 m^2, against 0.1 m^2 at 30 degrees, a factor of 5.75.
Joint speeds must be about 5.8 times higher near the straight-arm pose, which is usually beyond the drive's rating.

blocks: Jacobian determinant for a two-link planar arm
elbow angle, zero when the arm is straight

A two-link planar arm with revolute joints and no joint limits, evaluated at a configuration away from the wrist centre. Higher-degree-of-freedom arms have a Jacobian whose rank loss defines the same singular conditions.
standard.title: Formula and variables

blocks: End-effector velocity is the sum of each joint's contribution, and the Jacobian collects those contributions as a matrix that multiplies the joint-rate vector. Its determinant measures how much end-effector motion a set of joint motions can produce: when the determinant vanishes, some end-effector direction can no longer be produced at all, and the arm is at a singularity. Near that configuration the inverse mapping is ill-conditioned, so producing a commanded Cartesian velocity requires very large joint rates, which is why a robot moving along a straight line through a fully extended pose demands joint speeds far beyond its nominal ratings. The same determinant also sets force capability in reverse, since joint torques map through the transpose of the Jacobian.
standard.title: Derivation

blocks: An arm has 0.5 m and 0.4 m links and an elbow angle of 30 degrees. Evaluate the Jacobian determinant and compare it with a straight-arm pose.
Multiply the link lengths by the sine of the elbow angle, then compare with the straight configuration.
det J = 0.5 x 0.4 x sin(30) = 0.5 x 0.4 x 0.5 = 0.1 m^2. At a straight arm the elbow angle is zero and the determinant is zero.
0.1 square metres at 30 degrees against zero when the arm is straight, which is the classic singular configuration.
At an elbow angle of 5 degrees, by what factor does the required joint speed rise for the same end-effector velocity?
Compare the determinants at the two configurations.
det J at 5 degrees = 0.2 x sin(5) = 0.2 x 0.0872 = 0.0174 m^2, against 0.1 m^2 at 30 degrees, a factor of 5.75.
Joint speeds must be about 5.8 times higher near the straight-arm pose, which is usually beyond the drive's rating.

blocks: The Newsvendor Quantity and the Critical Ratio is a core model in Operations Research & Optimization: When a decision must be made before demand is known, the optimal quantity depends only on the ratio of the cost of being short to the total cost of being wrong in either direction. The model is used within these stated limits: A single ordering opportunity for a single period, demand described by a normal distribution, and costs linear in the amount short or left over. Repairable or carry-over inventory needs a multi-period model instead.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Critical ratio and the resulting order quantity
underage cost: margin lost per unit short
overage cost: loss per unit left over
critical ratio, the service level to target
mean and standard deviation of demand
standard normal quantile for the critical ratio

A single ordering opportunity for a single period, demand described by a normal distribution, and costs linear in the amount short or left over. Repairable or carry-over inventory needs a multi-period model instead.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Ordering one more unit pays off when demand exceeds the quantity already ordered, and it loses money when demand falls short of it; the balance point is where the probability of being short has fallen to the ratio of the loss from being short to the total spread between the two losses. That is the critical ratio, and it is a quantile of the demand distribution rather than a mean, which is the whole insight: the optimal quantity is a mean plus a quantile offset scaled by the demand's standard deviation. Perishable goods, seasonal stock, tickets and spare capacity all fit the same structure, and the ratio makes the trade explicit, because a high-margin item with a large markdown cost pushes the quantile up while a cheap alternative pushes it down.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A product sells for 25 and costs 10, with unsold units recoverable at 5. Demand averages 100 with a standard deviation of 20. Find the critical ratio and the order quantity.
Compute the underage and overage costs, form the ratio, find the normal quantile and apply it.
Underage cost = 25 - 10 = 15. Overage cost = 10 - 5 = 5. CR = 15/20 = 0.75, whose normal quantile is 0.674. Q = 100 + 0.674 x 20 = 113.5.
Order about 114 units, which will be short on 25 % of periods by design; stocking to the mean would be short half the time.
Demand variability doubles to a standard deviation of 40. What is the order quantity now?
The critical ratio is unchanged; only the quantile offset scales with the deviation.
About 127 units, 13 more than before: extra uncertainty is absorbed by ordering further into the right tail, not by changing the target service level.

blocks: The Propeller Law and the Cost of Speed is a core model in Marine Propulsion & Power Systems: A ship's power demand rises with the cube of propeller speed, so a modest reduction in service speed saves a disproportionate amount of fuel - the single largest lever in shipping economics. The model is used within these stated limits: A fixed-pitch propeller in open water with the ship's resistance following the same law, and no change in displacement or trim. Sea state, fouling and wind add resistance that raises the power required for the same speed.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Propeller law, shaft power and fuel flow

A fixed-pitch propeller in open water with the ship's resistance following the same law, and no change in displacement or trim. Sea state, fouling and wind add resistance that raises the power required for the same speed.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Propeller thrust comes from accelerating water astern, and the momentum theory of propellers shows that both thrust and the torque needed to produce it scale with the square and the cube of rotational speed respectively for a fixed advance ratio. Because a ship's resistance also rises roughly with the square of speed, the shaft power demand follows the cube, which makes speed the most powerful operating variable available. Multiplying the shaft power by specific fuel consumption converts the mechanical demand into a fuel rate, and the two relations together explain why slow steaming is the first measure any operator applies when fuel prices rise. The same cube is why a fouled hull or a damaged propeller is so expensive: a small extra power demand compounds with speed.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A ship's engine delivers 15,000 kW at full speed with an SFC of 170 g/kWh. What power and fuel flow result at 90 % shaft speed?
Apply the cube law to the power, then multiply by the specific fuel consumption.
About 10.9 MW and 1,860 kg of fuel per hour against 2,550 kg at full speed: a 27 % reduction in fuel for a 10 % reduction in speed.
What power and fuel flow correspond to 80 % shaft speed?
Apply the cube law again to the same full-speed reference.
7.7 MW and about 1,306 kg/h: a 20 % speed reduction nearly halves the fuel rate, which is why slow steaming changed the industry's economics.

blocks: The Pumping Lemma and Non-Regular Languages is a core model in Theory of Computation: Every sufficiently long string accepted by a finite automaton contains a loop, and re-traversing that loop must stay inside the language - one contradiction away from proving non-regularity. The model is used within these stated limits: Holds for every regular language; used contrapositively - if some long string cannot be pumped, the language is not regular. It can never prove a language regular.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: \forall s\in L,\ |s|\ge p:\ s=xyz,\ |xy|\le p,\ |y|\ge1,\ \forall i\ge0:\ xy^{i}z\in L
∀ s∈ L, |s|≥ p: s=xyz, |xy|≤ p, |y|≥1, ∀ i≥0: xy^iz∈ L
pumping length (at least the automaton's state count)
number of times the loop is re-traversed
Holds for every regular language; used contrapositively - if some long string cannot be pumped, the language is not regular. It can never prove a language regular.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: A DFA with p states reading a string of p or more symbols must visit some state twice (pigeonhole): the segment between visits is y. Walking that cycle zero times, once, or i times all end in the same accepting state, so every xy^i z is accepted. To prove L non-regular, assume some p works, choose a long string in L cleverly (the adversary picks after you see p), consider every legal split, and exhibit one i that throws the string out of L - the contradiction shows no automaton of any size can exist.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: Prove L = {a^n b^n : n >= 0} is not regular.
Pick s = a^p b^p and pump the forced a-only segment.
Any split with |xy| <= p puts y entirely inside the a's, |y| = k >= 1. Pump i = 2: xy^2 z has p + k a's but still p b's, so it is not of the form a^n b^n - not in L.
Contradiction for every p: L is not regular, so no finite memory can count unboundedly - a pushdown stack can.

blocks: The Two-Wattmeter Method for Three-Phase Power is a core model in Basic Electrical Engineering: Two wattmeters measure total active power in a balanced three-phase load and, from the difference of their readings, reactive power and power factor as well. The model is used within these stated limits: A balanced three-phase load with the current coil in two lines and the voltage coil between that line and the third; readings are taken with the correct polarity convention, so one may be negative for low power factor.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Two-wattmeter power relations for a balanced load
wattmeter readings, signed in the standard connection

A balanced three-phase load with the current coil in two lines and the voltage coil between that line and the third; readings are taken with the correct polarity convention, so one may be negative for low power factor.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Each wattmeter measures the product of one line current and the voltage from that line to the third, so the two readings are line quantities projected on axes sixty degrees apart. Summing them recovers the total active power because the third line carries the negative sum of the other two. Subtracting them leaves a quantity proportional to the reactive power, since the projections differ in sign for the reactive component. With both relations available, the load's impedance angle follows from the ratio, which is why this single connection replaces a separate reactive-power instrument and why an operator can diagnose a poor power factor from two dial readings.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: Two wattmeters read 5 kW and 3 kW. Find the total active power, the reactive power and the power factor.
Sum and difference give P and Q; the impedance angle comes from the tangent relation.
8 kW active, 3.46 kvar reactive, power factor 0.918 lagging.
For a balanced load the two readings are equal. What is the power factor, and what is it when one reading is zero?
Use the difference term to deduce the impedance angle in both cases.
Equal readings give Q = 0 and therefore phi = 0, so cos(phi) = 1. A zero reading gives Q = root-3 times the remaining reading, so tan(phi) = root-3 and phi = 60 degrees.
Power factor 1 with equal readings; power factor 0.5 when one reading falls to zero, which is the lowest factor this method can resolve without a sign-aware meter.

blocks: Thermal Radiation: Stefan-Boltzmann Exchange is a core model in Heat & Mass Transfer: Every surface radiates with the fourth power of its absolute temperature, and net exchange between surfaces is the difference of those fourth powers, trimmed by emissivity. The model is used within these stated limits: Small grey surface exchanging with large isothermal surroundings (view factor 1); general surface pairs need view factors and radiosity accounting.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Radiative exchange between a surface and large surroundings
Small grey surface exchanging with large isothermal surroundings (view factor 1); general surface pairs need view factors and radiosity accounting.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Thermodynamics of photon emission gives total emissive power proportional to T^4 - the steep law that makes radiation negligible at room temperature differences and dominant in furnaces and fires. A real surface emits epsilon times the blackbody value and absorbs alpha times what arrives; for grey surfaces Kirchhoff ties alpha to epsilon, so net exchange between a body and big surroundings collapses to the difference of fourth powers times epsilon sigma A. The fourth-power sensitivity explains everyday engineering: a 10% rise in absolute temperature boosts emission by 46% (1.1^4 = 1.46), and spacecraft, having no convection at all, live or die by radiator emissivity and area.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A furnace door, emissivity 0.9 and area 1 m^2, sits at 500 K in a 300 K hall. Find the radiative loss.
About 2.8 kW radiated from one square metre - and at 600 K the same door would radiate 7.4 kW, the T^4 law compounding.

blocks: Thermodynamics of photon emission gives total emissive power proportional to T^4 - the steep law that makes radiation negligible at room temperature differences and dominant in furnaces and fires. A real surface emits epsilon times the blackbody value and absorbs alpha times what arrives; for grey surfaces Kirchhoff ties alpha to epsilon, so net exchange between a body and big surroundings collapses to the difference of fourth powers times epsilon sigma A. The fourth-power sensitivity explains everyday engineering: a 10% rise in absolute temperature boosts emission by 46% (1.1^4 = 1.46), and spacecraft, having no convection at all, live or die by radiator emissivity and area.

blocks: Thevenin and Norton Equivalents is a core model in Circuit Theory: Any two-terminal linear network collapses to one voltage source with one series resistance - or one current source with one parallel resistance - and every load question gets simpler. The model is used within these stated limits: Linear networks only; dependent sources stay active while zeroing independents, in which case R_th = V_oc / I_sc is the safe route.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: V_{th}=V_{\mathrm{oc}},\quad R_{th}=R_{\mathrm{seen\ with\ sources\ zeroed}},\quad I_{N}=\frac{V_{th}}{R_{th}}
V_th=V_oc, R_th=R_seen with sources zeroed, I_N=(V_th)/(R_th)
equivalent resistance with independent sources zeroed
Linear networks only; dependent sources stay active while zeroing independents, in which case R_th = V_oc / I_sc is the safe route.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Linearity guarantees the terminal behaviour is a straight line in the I-V plane, and a straight line is fully described by its two intercepts: the open-circuit voltage and the short-circuit current. Their ratio is the slope - the equivalent resistance. Zeroing independent sources (voltage sources shorted, current sources opened) exposes that slope directly for source-free-resistance networks; with dependent sources, measuring or computing both intercepts and dividing is the general method. Once found, the two-source models convert freely: V_th = I_N R_th.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A 10 V source feeds a 2 k ohm series resistor, with a 2 k ohm resistor from the output node to ground. Find the Thevenin equivalent at the output.
Compute V_oc, then zero the source for R_th.
V_oc = 10 x 2/(2+2) = 5 V (divider under open circuit). Zero the source: 2 k in series with the shorted source leaves 2k || 2k = 1 k ohm.
Thevenin: 5 V with 1 k ohm series - equivalently Norton 5 mA with 1 k parallel.

blocks: Thin-Film Interference and Anti-Reflection Coatings is a core model in Engineering Physics: A quarter-wave film makes two reflected waves cancel, which is how a lens is made almost non-reflective at one wavelength - and the arithmetic is a single division. The model is used within these stated limits: Normal incidence, a coating much thinner than the substrate, and coherence over the film thickness. Oblique incidence and multiple layers need the full matrix formulation, which is how broadband coatings are designed.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Quarter-wave coating thickness and residual reflectance
refractive indices of air and substrate

Normal incidence, a coating much thinner than the substrate, and coherence over the film thickness. Oblique incidence and multiple layers need the full matrix formulation, which is how broadband coatings are designed.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Light reflected from the top surface of a thin film and light reflected from the film-substrate boundary travel different path lengths, so they interfere. At normal incidence the round trip through the film adds a phase difference of twice its optical thickness, and a quarter-wave film makes that difference half a wavelength, so the two reflected waves are out of phase and cancel. The reflected amplitude also depends on the index mismatch at each interface, and the residual reflectance relation shows that the match is perfect only when the coating's index is the geometric mean of the media either side. A single-layer coating on glass therefore reduces reflection substantially but not to zero, and broadband performance needs several layers whose thicknesses are chosen by the same quarter-wave idea at different wavelengths.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: Find the thickness of a magnesium fluoride coating (n = 1.38) that minimises reflection at 550 nm.
Divide the wavelength by four times the refractive index.
About 100 nanometres, a quarter of the wavelength measured in the film.
How much light does the coating reflect at the design wavelength, and what would a perfect coating reflect?
Apply the residual reflectance relation and compare with the ideal index.
About 1.3 % reflected, down from roughly 4 % uncoated. A perfect single layer would need n = sqrt(1.52) = 1.23, which is why real broadband coatings use several layers.

advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Machine code and high-level syntax both hide structure: one in bits, the other in nesting. Breaking every operation into 'result = operand op operand' with explicit temporaries exposes the dataflow - which value feeds which - as a flat sequence. That flatness is what optimizers need: constant folding sees t1 = 3 * 4 directly, dead-code elimination sees temporaries nobody reads, and common-subexpression elimination spots identical right-hand sides. Emitting the IR once lets every source language reuse every optimization for every target.

blocks: Two line conductors see the phasor difference of two phase voltages 120 degrees apart. Subtracting two equal phasors at 120 degrees yields a magnitude sqrt(3) times one of them - the same geometry applies to currents in delta, where each line feeds two windings. Power is 3 x V_ph I_ph cos(phi) either way, which rearranges to sqrt(3) V_L I_L cos(phi) in both topologies.

blocks: Tillage Draft, Implement Width and Tractor Power is a core model in Agricultural Machinery & Irrigation Systems: The force needed to pull a tillage implement through soil depends on the soil's resistance, the working width and the depth, and multiplying by speed converts it into the power the tractor must deliver. The model is used within these stated limits: A uniform soil with a constant specific resistance for the given tool and moisture condition, and a steady working depth. Speed raises draft slightly in reality, and the drawbar figure is a fraction of engine power because of transmission, slip and rolling losses.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: specific soil resistance (draft per unit soil area)

A uniform soil with a constant specific resistance for the given tool and moisture condition, and a steady working depth. Speed raises draft slightly in reality, and the drawbar figure is a fraction of engine power because of transmission, slip and rolling losses.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: The implement must fail the soil across its working area, so the draft force is the specific resistance of the soil multiplied by the width and depth being loosened. Because the depth term is linear, going deeper costs proportionally more force, and because the width term is also linear, a wider implement needs proportionally more pull. Multiplying draft by speed gives the power delivered at the drawbar, which is the number the engine must supply after transmission losses and slip, and those losses are large enough that implement selection starts from a drawbar-to-engine-power ratio rather than from the engine's rated output. The same arithmetic explains why a compaction layer at depth is so expensive: it forces either more depth or a heavier implement to reach it.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A cultivator works 2 m wide and 0.2 m deep in soil of specific resistance 60 kN/m^2 at 1.5 m/s. Find the draft and the drawbar power.
Multiply width by depth by specific resistance, then by speed.
24 kN of draft and 36 kW at the drawbar, which with typical tractor losses corresponds to an engine of roughly 50 to 60 kW.
The same implement is worked at 2.5 m/s. What is the drawbar power, and what limits the choice?
Draft stays the same in the simple model; power rises linearly with speed.
P = 24 x 2.5 = 60 kW at the drawbar, so an engine of roughly 85 to 95 kW with losses, plus a ballast and tyre configuration that can transmit 24 kN.
60 kW at the drawbar. Traction, not engine power, usually limits the speed increase, since the soil can only react a force proportional to the weight on the drive wheels.

blocks: Timer Programming and Baud-Rate Generation is a core model in Microprocessors & Microcontrollers: Microcontroller timers turn the system clock into measurable time by counting divided ticks, and serial baud rates are generated by choosing the divisor that makes one bit last exactly the right length. The model is used within these stated limits: Classic 16x-oversampled UARTs; the divisor must be an integer (or the peripheral's fractional mode engaged), and both ends must agree within a few percent per character.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: standard oversampling factor of classic UARTs
Classic 16x-oversampled UARTs; the divisor must be an integer (or the peripheral's fractional mode engaged), and both ends must agree within a few percent per character.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: A UART samples each bit 16 times to locate its centre robustly, so its internal clock must run at 16 x baud; a divisor register divides the system clock down to exactly that. The same counting idea sizes every timer task: a prescaler divides the clock, the counter counts divided ticks, and the compare/match value converts a desired period into a tick count. Non-integer divisors are where baud errors come from - the accumulated sampling drift across ten bits must stay under roughly half a bit, which bounds how far a crystal's frequency can sit from the ideal table values.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A UART clock of 1.8432 MHz must produce 115200 baud. Find the divisor, and the bit period a 12 MHz clock's nearest integer divisor would produce.
Apply the divisor formula, then check the second clock's error.

Divisor = 1.8432e6 / (16 x 115200) = 1.8432e6 / 1.8432e6 = 1 exactly - the classic crystal choice. For 12 MHz: 12e6/(16 x 115200) = 6.51, rounds to 7 (or fractional mode); integer 7 gives 12e6/(16 x 7) = 107,143 baud, a 7% error - too far, so fractional division is required.
Divisor 1 for the classic clock; a 12 MHz part needs its fractional baud mode because the integer-only error (7%) exceeds UART tolerance.

blocks: Timer Reload Values, PWM Resolution and Their Trade is a core model in Microprocessors & Microcontrollers: A hardware timer turns a clock into a controlled period and duty; the reload value, the prescaler and the duty resolution cannot all be chosen freely, and that constraint is arithmetic. The model is used within these stated limits: The timer counts at the divided clock rate, the counter is wide enough to hold N, and the compare register is updated safely with respect to the counter. Register preloading and dead-time insertion are separate concerns.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: reload count: timer ticks per period

The timer counts at the divided clock rate, the counter is wide enough to hold N, and the compare register is updated safely with respect to the counter. Register preloading and dead-time insertion are separate concerns.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: The timer increments at the clock divided by the prescaler, so the number of ticks in one output period is that rate divided by the output frequency. The reload value therefore sets the period, and the compare value sets the duty as a fraction of the same count. Because both share the counter's range, the duty resolution is the base-two logarithm of the tick count: a 16-bit counter can express very fine duty at low frequency, and almost none at high frequency. This single trade decides many embedded designs: a motor drive wants a high switching frequency for quiet operation, an LED dimmer wants fine resolution for smooth fades, and a design needing both must raise the clock or use a dedicated peripheral.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A 16 MHz timer with a prescaler of 8 must generate 1 kHz PWM. Find the reload value and the duty register value for a 25 % duty cycle.
Divide the divided clock by the target frequency, then take the fraction of that count.
Timer rate = 16 MHz / 8 = 2 MHz. N = 2,000,000 / 1000 = 2000 ticks. Duty register = 0.25 x 2000 = 500.
Reload 1999 for a zero-based counter and compare 500, giving a 25 % duty with 2000 steps of resolution, about 11 bits.
The same 16 MHz timer needs 12-bit duty resolution. What is the highest PWM frequency possible?
Resolution is the logarithm of the tick count, so invert it and apply the timer clock.
12 bits means 4096 ticks per period. With a prescaler of 1 the rate is 16 MHz, so f_pwm = 16,000,000/4096 = 3906 Hz.
About 3.9 kHz with no prescaler, and proportionally lower with any prescaler; 12-bit resolution at 20 kHz would need a clock above 80 MHz.

blocks: Toolpath Step-Over, Scallop Height and Machining Time is a core model in CAD / CAM: A CAM toolpath is a set of trades: feed rate buys cycle time, step-over buys surface finish, and the cusp left between passes can be predicted before the part is cut. The model is used within these stated limits: A ball-nose cutter with a shallow depth of cut and a step-over small compared with the tool radius, which is what makes the cusp approximation accurate. The scallop relation is for a flat surface; curved surfaces add tool deflection.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Feed rate, machining time and scallop height for a ball-nose tool

A ball-nose cutter with a shallow depth of cut and a step-over small compared with the tool radius, which is what makes the cusp approximation accurate. The scallop relation is for a flat surface; curved surfaces add tool deflection.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Feed rate is the distance the tool advances per tooth multiplied by the number of teeth and the spindle speed, so it is chosen from the chip load the tool can tolerate. Machining time is simply path length divided by feed rate, which makes the two work together: a faster feed shortens the cycle but raises cutting force and tool wear. Surface finish is set separately by the step-over between adjacent passes, because a ball-nose cutter leaves material between the passes in a scalloped ridge whose height grows with the square of the step-over and falls with the tool radius. The practical consequence is that finish costs time quadratically: halving the cusp height requires halving the step-over, which doubles the number of passes and therefore the machining time.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A four-tooth cutter runs at 8000 rpm with 0.1 mm feed per tooth over a 1.5 m path. Find the feed rate and the machining time.
Multiply feed per tooth by teeth and speed for the feed rate, then divide path length by it.
3200 mm/min and about 28 seconds of cutting time on that pass, before rapid moves and tool changes.
A ball-nose cutter of 6 mm diameter leaves a scallop of what height with a 0.5 mm step-over, and how does it change at 1 mm?
Apply the cusp relation with the tool radius, noting the quadratic dependence on step-over.
About 10 micrometres at half a millimetre and 42 micrometres at one millimetre: doubling the step-over quadruples the cusp.

blocks: Feed rate, machining time and scallop height for a ball-nose tool

A ball-nose cutter with a shallow depth of cut and a step-over small compared with the tool radius, which is what makes the cusp approximation accurate. The scallop relation is for a flat surface; curved surfaces add tool deflection.
standard.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Feed rate is the distance the tool advances per tooth multiplied by the number of teeth and the spindle speed, so it is chosen from the chip load the tool can tolerate. Machining time is simply path length divided by feed rate, which makes the two work together: a faster feed shortens the cycle but raises cutting force and tool wear. Surface finish is set separately by the step-over between adjacent passes, because a ball-nose cutter leaves material between the passes in a scalloped ridge whose height grows with the square of the step-over and falls with the tool radius. The practical consequence is that finish costs time quadratically: halving the cusp height requires halving the step-over, which doubles the number of passes and therefore the machining time.
standard.title: Derivation

blocks: A four-tooth cutter runs at 8000 rpm with 0.1 mm feed per tooth over a 1.5 m path. Find the feed rate and the machining time.
Multiply feed per tooth by teeth and speed for the feed rate, then divide path length by it.

A ball-nose cutter of 6 mm diameter leaves a scallop of what height with a 0.5 mm step-over, and how does it change at 1 mm?
Apply the cusp relation with the tool radius, noting the quadratic dependence on step-over.
About 10 micrometres at half a millimetre and 42 micrometres at one millimetre: doubling the step-over quadruples the cusp.

blocks: Torsion of Circular Shafts is a core model in Strength of Materials: A circular shaft under torque develops shear stress rising linearly to its surface, and the polar second moment packages the geometry that carries the twist. The model is used within these stated limits: Circular cross-section (plane sections stay plane and undistorted), linear-elastic material, uniform torque along L; hollow shafts use J = pi(d_o^4 - d_i^4)/32.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: angle of twist over length L
Circular cross-section (plane sections stay plane and undistorted), linear-elastic material, uniform torque along L; hollow shafts use J = pi(d_o^4 - d_i^4)/32.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Symmetry keeps circular cross-sections plane under twist, so shear strain grows linearly from zero at the centre to maximum at the surface; Hooke's law in shear carries the linearity into stress. Moment equilibrium of those stresses about the axis introduces the polar second moment J, giving tau = Tr/J, and the same geometry plus the shear modulus gives the twist per unit length. Power transmission follows immediately through P = T omega: for a given power, higher speed means lower torque means a lighter shaft - the reason gearboxes step up before long transmission runs.

blocks: Traffic Flow Fundamentals: Speed, Flow and Density is a core model in Transportation Engineering: Flow equals density times speed - one identity whose curve against density explains capacity, congestion and why adding demand past a point destroys throughput. The model is used within these stated limits: Homogeneous flow on a single lane; speed falls with density along an empirical speed-density line, making the q-k curve a parabola-like arc through the origin and the jam density.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: q=k\times u,\qquad q_{\max}\ \text{at the critical density}\ (k_c,\ u_c)
q=k× u, q_max at the critical density (k_c, u_c)
capacity at the flow-density curve's peak
Homogeneous flow on a single lane; speed falls with density along an empirical speed-density line, making the q-k curve a parabola-like arc through the origin and the jam density.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Count the vehicles crossing a line: each of the k vehicles per kilometre passes at u kilometres per hour, so q = k u. As density rises from zero, flow rises; but speed declines with density, and past the critical density the speed loss outweighs the added vehicles - flow falls even as density grows. That descending branch is congestion: the same road carries fewer vehicles per hour while holding more of them. The identity also explains shockwaves (demand exceeding capacity queues backward) and metering (ramp signals hold density below critical so flow stays near maximum).
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A lane carries traffic at density 40 veh/km and mean speed 50 km/h. Find the flow. What happens to flow if density doubles to 80 and speed falls to 20 km/h?
Apply q = k u on both states.
q = 40 x 50 = 2,000 veh/h. At the denser state: q = 80 x 20 = 1,600 veh/h.
Flow fell from 2,000 to 1,600 veh/h while density doubled - the descending congestion branch, where more cars on the road means fewer through it.

blocks: Trajectory Planning: Trapezoidal Velocity Profiles is a core model in Robotics Kinematics & Control: Moving between two points fast without slamming the drives means shaping velocity as a trapezoid: ramp up within acceleration limits, cruise, ramp down. The model is used within these stated limits: Symmetric accel/decel; jerk (rate of acceleration change) is ignored here - S-curve profiles add it to protect gears and payloads from vibration.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: t_total=(d)/(v_max)+(v_max)/(a) (full cruise reached); else triangular with t=2√(d/a)
distance too short to reach v_max
Symmetric accel/decel; jerk (rate of acceleration change) is ignored here - S-curve profiles add it to protect gears and payloads from vibration.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: A point-to-point move bounded by velocity and acceleration has a canonical fastest shape: accelerate at the limit until either cruising speed or the midpoint is reached, then mirror down. If the distance is short, cruise never happens and the profile is triangular, peaking below v_max. The time formula splits accordingly, and the acceleration phase adds v_max/a seconds of pure ramp overhead to the ideal d/v_max - which is why high-throughput pick-and-place machines fight for every m/s^2 of acceleration, not top speed. Trapezoids command torque within motor limits; the residual jerk at the corners is what excites structural resonance, motivating smoother S-curves where precision matters.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A gantry must move 1 m with v_max = 0.5 m/s and a = 1 m/s^2. Find the move time and compare with an unaccelerated estimate.
Check the profile reaches cruise, then sum the phases.
Cruise is reached since d > v_max^2/a = 0.25 m. t = 1/0.5 + 0.5/1 = 2.0 + 0.5 = 2.5 s.

2.5 s versus the naive 2.0 s - acceleration limits add 25% to the move. Halving v_max to 0.25 m/s stays trapezoidal (v^2/a = 0.0625 m < d) at t = 4 + 0.25 = 4.25 s: slower speeds pay mostly the cruise term.

blocks: A point-to-point move bounded by velocity and acceleration has a canonical fastest shape: accelerate at the limit until either cruising speed or the midpoint is reached, then mirror down. If the distance is short, cruise never happens and the profile is triangular, peaking below v_max. The time formula splits accordingly, and the acceleration phase adds v_max/a seconds of pure ramp overhead to the ideal d/v_max - which is why high-throughput pick-and-place machines fight for every m/s^2 of acceleration, not top speed. blocks: Isolation level is a performance dial, and the default is often chosen without anyone deciding.

Most databases default to READ COMMITTED or REPEATABLE READ rather than SERIALIZABLE, because full serialisation costs throughput. That means anomalies are possible by default: a report run twice can give different answers if another transaction commits in between. Whether that matters is a business question, not a technical one, and it is worth asking explicitly.

Hot rows are the usual throughput ceiling. A single counter — a global sequence, a daily total, an inventory count — serialises every transaction that touches it, so throughput is capped regardless of hardware. Sharding the counter across k rows and summing on read restores parallelism, at the cost of an approximate read while writes are in flight.

The write-ahead log is why durability has a floor. Group commit batches several transactions into one fsync, which is why throughput improves with concurrency even though each commit still waits for a flush. Disabling
for performance is the classic way to lose data on a power cut, and it is a decision that should never be made quietly.

For distributed systems the trade is starker: cross-node transactions need two-phase commit, which blocks if the coordinator fails. Most large systems avoid them entirely and design for eventual consistency with idempotent operations instead.

The model is used within these stated limits: Sinusoidal steady state at rated frequency; maximum efficiency occurs where variable copper loss equals fixed core loss, and regulation depends on load power factor.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: core loss, roughly constant with load
secondary terminal voltage at no load and full load
Sinusoidal steady state at rated frequency; maximum efficiency occurs where variable copper loss equals fixed core loss, and regulation depends on load power factor.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Core loss (hysteresis plus eddy currents) depends on flux and frequency - both fixed at rated volts - so it is constant from no-load to overload. Copper loss is I^2 R and grows with the square of load fraction. Efficiency therefore peaks where the two are equal, typically below full load, which is why distribution transformers are sized to sit near that point at average demand. Regulation measures the internal impedance drop: the referred resistance and leakage reactance subtract from the induced voltage under load, with the drop's size and sign set by the load's power factor - capacitive loads can even raise terminal voltage.
advanced.title: Derivation

97.1% efficient with 4.55% regulation - and at half load copper loss falls to 50 W while core loss stays 100 W, shifting the loss balance.

blocks: A transformer is a static device that transfers electrical energy between two or more circuits through electromagnetic induction, changing voltage and current while keeping frequency and (ideally) power constant.

blocks: The turns ratio comes from Faraday's law applied to a shared flux, and the power relation follows from assuming no loss.
links both windings, so by Faraday's law each turn has the same induced EMF
This is why the ratio depends only on turns, not on core material or frequency — though frequency does set the flux density the core must carry.
An ideal transformer stores no energy, so input power equals output power:
Current transforms inversely to voltage. There is no way around this: stepping voltage up necessarily steps current down, and the product is preserved.
so doubling the transmission voltage quarters the loss for the same power delivered. That single relation is the reason national grids run at hundreds of kilovolts and step down only near the user.

and no voltage is induced in the secondary. Switching DC on and off works — that is what a switched-mode power supply does — but a plain DC supply does nothing.

blocks: Transformer engineering in practice is about losses, heat and lifetime, none of which appear in the ideal model.
Losses come in two kinds. Copper loss is

in the windings and varies with load. Iron loss is hysteresis and eddy currents in the core and is roughly constant, since it depends on flux density and frequency, not load. The total efficiency curve therefore peaks at the load where the two are equal, which is usually well below full load — a detail that matters when sizing a transformer for a duty cycle rather than a peak.

Cooling decides rating. The same core and windings carry more power with forced oil circulation than with natural convection, so ratings are quoted per cooling class. Winding temperature, not current, is what ages the insulation, and the rule of thumb is that every 6 K above the design temperature halves the insulation life. This is why load guides are based on hot-spot temperature rather than on nameplate current.

Inrush current is a real operational problem. Energising a transformer at the wrong point on the voltage wave can drive the core into saturation, drawing many times rated current for several cycles. This is why differential protection must distinguish inrush from an internal fault — usually by looking for second harmonic content — or it will trip on every energisation.

Harmonics from non-linear loads cause extra eddy-current loss that rises with the square of the harmonic order, so a transformer supplying rectifiers and variable-speed drives must be derated or specified with a K-factor. This has become the normal case rather than the exception in commercial buildings.

blocks: Traversing: Latitude, Departure and Bowditch Balancing is a core model in Surveying: A closed traverse must return to its start, so the latitudes and departures of all legs must sum to zero - and the residual error is distributed by a defined rule, not hidden. The model is used within these stated limits: Closed loop or link between known points; Bowditch (compass) rule distributes the error in proportion to leg length, suiting angles and distances of similar relative precision.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: Closed loop or link between known points; Bowditch (compass) rule distributes the error in proportion to leg length, suiting angles and distances of similar relative precision.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Each leg's bearing and length decompose into a latitude (north component) and departure (east component). In a closed traverse the walk returns to its origin, so both component sums must vanish; any nonzero sums are the closure error, whose magnitude and direction quantify the survey's accuracy. The Bowditch rule corrects each leg by minus the total error times that leg's share of the perimeter - longer legs, more measurement opportunity, more correction. The relative closure (error over perimeter) is then compared against the specification (1:5000 for typical boundary work) to accept or reject the survey.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A closed traverse of perimeter 500 m has closure errors of -0.05 m in latitude and +0.12 m in departure. Find the linear misclosure and relative accuracy, and the Bowditch correction to a 100 m leg.
Combine the errors, ratio to perimeter, apportion the correction.

Linear misclosure = sqrt(0.05^2 + 0.12^2) = sqrt(0.0025 + 0.0144) = sqrt(0.0169) = 0.13 m. Relative accuracy = 0.13/500 = 1:3846. Correction to the 100 m leg = 0.13 x (100/500) = 0.026 m, applied opposite the error direction.
0.13 m misclosure at relative accuracy 1:3846 - coarser than a 1:5000 specification allows, so this traverse fails that class and needs rework or a lower-accuracy designation.

blocks: True Length and Inclination from Orthographic Projections is a core model in Engineering Graphics: A line appears shortened in every orthographic view unless it is parallel to the plane of projection, and its true length is recovered from one view plus the distance difference in the other. The model is used within these stated limits: First-angle orthographic projection with the two views correctly aligned across the reference line, and a straight line whose end points are both visible. Curved and cylindrical features need their own constructions.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: True length of a line from its projections
length of the line in the front view
difference between the two end points' distances from the reference line in the plan
true inclination of the line to the horizontal plane

First-angle orthographic projection with the two views correctly aligned across the reference line, and a straight line whose end points are both visible. Curved and cylindrical features need their own constructions.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: An orthographic view compresses any dimension perpendicular to the plane of projection to nothing and foreshortens dimensions at an angle to it. The front view therefore shows the true horizontal extent of the line and the true height difference, while the plan shows the true horizontal extent and the true depth difference. Combining the front view's length with the difference in plan distances recovers the depth component that the front view cannot show, and Pythagoras gives the true length. Inclinations follow by dividing the true length into the relevant projected length, which is why one construction yields three answers - true length, angle to the horizontal plane and angle to the vertical plane - and why this is the fundamental construction that every others in the subject build on.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A line's front view is 40 mm long and its ends are 20 mm and 45 mm from the reference line in the plan. Find the true length and its inclination to the horizontal plane.
Take the difference in plan distances, apply Pythagoras with the front view length, then divide for the angle.
Difference = 25 mm. TL = sqrt(40^2 + 25^2) = sqrt(2225) = 47.2 mm. cos(theta) = 40/47.2 = 0.847, so theta = 32.1 degrees.
True length 47.2 mm at 32.1 degrees to the horizontal plane.
The same line's plan view is 30 mm long. What is its inclination to the vertical plane?
Use the plan length and the true length in the same way.
50.5 degrees to the vertical plane. The three answers - 47.2 mm, 32.1 degrees and 50.5 degrees - all come from the single construction.

blocks: TTT Diagrams and Hardenability is a core model in Physical Metallurgy & Heat Treatment: Austenite's fate is a race against the TTT diagram's noses: quench fast enough to dodge pearlite and bainite, and the trapped carbon freezes into martensite - if the section is thick enough to stay fast at its core. The model is used within these stated limits: Plain-carbon and low-alloy steels; TTT strictly applies to isothermal holds - continuous cooling uses the sibling CCT diagram, and alloying shifts the noses to lower the critical rate.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: \text{core cooling rate}>\text{critical rate}\ \Rightarrow\ \text{martensite to the core}
core cooling rate>critical rate ⇒ martensite to the core
slowest quench that misses the pearlite nose
position along the standard bar at 50% martensite hardness
depth capacity of hardening, not hardness itself
Plain-carbon and low-alloy steels; TTT strictly applies to isothermal holds - continuous cooling uses the sibling CCT diagram, and alloying shifts the noses to lower the critical rate.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Above the eutectoid temperature, carbon sits dissolved in FCC austenite. Slow cooling lets it diffuse out into pearlite's soft lamellae; the TTT diagram charts how long each temperature takes to start and finish that transformation. Quenching fast enough skips the noses: below the martensite-start temperature the FCC lattice shears into body-centred tetragonal martensite, carbon trapped, hardness maximized - a diffusionless transformation no time-at-temperature can avoid once reached. Hardenability is the depth question: a section's core cools slower than its surface, so alloying elements (which push the noses right, buying time) decide how deep martensite penetrates - measured by the Jominy end-quench test's hardness-versus-distance curve.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A 40 mm plain-carbon steel bar quenches with a core cooling rate of 20 K/s but needs 150 K/s to miss the pearlite nose. What happens, and what is the metallurgical fix?
Compare rates, then apply hardenability logic.

The core transforms to pearlite/ferrite - soft centre, hard shell (surface quenches faster). The fix is not a fiercer quench (cracking risk) but hardenability: an alloy steel (e.g. 4140) whose right-shifted TTT noses drop the critical rate below 20 K/s, or a smaller section.
A hardenability problem, not a quench-severity problem - Jominy data picks the grade whose 50%-martensite distance covers the bar's radius.

blocks: Twist: Helix Angle and Yarn Strength is a core model in Textile Fibre & Fabric Engineering: Twist binds staple fibres into a coherent yarn, and its geometry - the surface helix angle - explains why strength rises with twist to an optimum and then falls away. The model is used within these stated limits: Ideal helical fibre migration; strength-optimum angles are ~20-35 degrees for cotton-type staples, and fibre length, fineness and friction shift the optimum.
advanced.title: Formal definition

blocks: tanα=π d T, T=turns per unit length
Ideal helical fibre migration; strength-optimum angles are ~20-35 degrees for cotton-type staples, and fibre length, fineness and friction shift the optimum.
advanced.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Without twist, a staple yarn is a bundle that pulls apart fibre by fibre - strength is only friction. Inserting twist makes surface fibres helices: when the yarn is tensioned, each helix wants to straighten, converting axial load into radial compression that grips its neighbours - cohesion by geometry. More twist raises that compression, so strength climbs; but the same helix angle increasingly misaligns fibres with the load axis, wasting their tenacity on oblique pulling, and past the optimum angle the misalignment wins and strength falls. The tan(alpha) = pi d T relation lets a spinner convert any twist-per-metre spec into the angle where that trade-off lives.
advanced.title: Derivation

blocks: A yarn of 0.20 mm diameter carries 800 turns per metre. Find the surface helix angle and assess it against the strength optimum.
tan(alpha) = pi x 2e-4 x 800 = 0.503, so alpha = arctan(0.503) = 26.7 degrees.

About 27 degrees - squarely inside the 20-35 degree strength-optimum band for cotton-type staples; adding twist toward 1200 tpm (alpha ~ 37 degrees) would push past the optimum into declining strength and a harder, harsher hand.

Ideal helical fibre migration; strength-optimum angles are ~20-35 degrees for cotton-type staples, and fibre length, fineness and friction shift the optimum.
standard.title: Formula and variables

blocks: Without twist, a staple yarn is a bundle that pulls apart fibre by fibre - strength is only friction. Inserting twist makes surface fibres helices: when the yarn is tensioned, each helix wants to straighten, converting axial load into radial compression that grips its neighbours - cohesion by geometry. More twist raises that compression, so strength climbs; but the same helix angle increasingly misaligns fibres with the load axis, wasting their tenacity on oblique pulling, and past the optimum angle the misalignment wins and strength falls. The tan(alpha) = pi d T relation lets a spinner convert any twist-per-metre spec into the angle where that trade-off lives.
standard.title: Derivation

blocks: A yarn of 0.20 mm diameter carries 800 turns per metre. Find the surface helix angle and assess it against the strength optimum.
tan(alpha) = pi x 2e-4 x 800 = 0.503, so alpha = arctan(0.503) = 26.7 degrees.

About 27 degrees - squarely inside the 20-35 degree strength-optimum band for cotton-type staples; adding twist toward 1200 tpm (alpha ~ 37 degrees) would push past the optimum into declining strength and a harder, harsher hand.
